How this curriculum works:
**Shona from zero, by ear first.** This curriculum teaches **Standard Shona**, the written standard of Zimbabwe, which rests mainly on the Zezuru dialect around Harare. It is built from two courses:

| Course | What it is | What it is for here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **FSI Shona Basic Course** (Stevick, with Mr and Mrs Mataranyika, 1965) | 35 units, each with a recording. Public domain | The spine: the dialogues, the drills, and above all the **recordings** — the only free native audio for the whole course |
| **Hazel Carter, *Shona Language Course*, Books I–III** (Wisconsin, 1986) | Lessons, notes and exercises, **tone marked**, in Zezuru | The standard forms, and the second word on tone |

**One thing to know about FSI from the start.** Its foreword says it is "based on the speech of two individuals, representing **Manyika** varieties of Shona, but with certain systematic emendations in the direction of the more central dialects." Manyika is an eastern dialect. So FSI's recordings are an eastern voice, and where its words differ from the standard, these lessons say so and give the standard form beside it — from Carter, never from guesswork. Your speaking partner is the third voice, and the deciding one: FSI itself tells the student to note "in every instance what his own tutor says."

**How each lesson works.** It teaches its point in full — the sounds, the forms, what they mean — then directs practice: listening to the FSI recording for the unit, repeating, drilling, and, once there are phrases to use, speaking with your partner.

**Listening is the method, not a supplement.** FSI's own instructions for every new dialogue are: listen first with the book closed; imitate without knowing the meanings; imitate as you learn the meanings; then read aloud; then learn to take both roles. That is the order here too.

**How tone is written in this curriculum.** An acute accent marks a high tone: *á*. No mark (or a grave, *à*) is a low tone. The FSI course adds three more marks, because it writes two tone systems at once — the central one and the eastern one: *ǎ* is **low** where the central (standard) pronunciation is taught, high in the east; *â* is **high** centrally, low in the east; *ā*, a macron, is a low tone raised to high after a high. Say the central reading. A dot under a letter (*mẉarara*) means some speakers leave that sound out.
Stress: the next-to-last syllable:
Before tone, the other kind of prominence. FSI's first note: in a Shona sentence some syllables strike the ear as stronger, and not all of that is pitch.

Compare *Mẉarara here?* and *Ndarara zvangu.* Ignore the pitches and there is still a prominence on **he** in the first and **zva** in the second — even though, as far as pitch goes, *he* is low and *zva* is high. What the two share is not pitch but **extra force and extra length**. FSI calls this **accent**, and it "generally falls on the next to last syllable before a pause."

So:

| Phrase | Accented syllable |
| --- | --- |
| *Mẉarara **he**re?* | he |
| *Ndarara **zva**ngu.* | zva |
| *mangwa**na**ni* | na |

In some styles of speech the accent shows as a quite noticeable lengthening of that vowel. FSI's advice is to notice whether your own tutor does this — so ask your speaking partner to say these three phrases, and listen for the long next-to-last vowel.

**Why it matters now.** Accent and tone are separate things in Shona. A syllable can be accented and low (*he* in *here*) or accented and high (*zva*). Learning to hear them apart is the first job of the ear.

**Practice.** Play the FSI recording for Unit 1. Do not look at the text. For each sentence, tap the table on the accented syllable.
High and low tone:
**Shona is a tone language: pitch can change a word, and it can change grammar.** FSI's examples, with each syllable's pitch shown as a level line, as FSI draws it:

| Word | Pitches | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *nhanga* | high – high | pumpkin |
| *nhanga* | low – high | yard |
| *kuchera* | (one pattern) | to dig |
| *kuchera* | (another) | to draw [water] |

The letters are identical; only the pitch differs. Carter's Lesson I has more pairs, tone-marked:

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *mbíra* | rock-rabbit, dassie | *mbira* | hand-xylophone ("piano") |
| *chérá!* | draw water! | *cherá!* | dig! |
| *gúrú* | big | *gurú* | animal's stomach |
| *kuróvá* | to hit, strike | *kurova* | to disappear |
| *kuedza* | to try | *kuédza* | to dawn |

**Tone does grammar, too** — FSI calls this "even more important": *munda* with two low tones is "field"; with high then low it is "it is a field". And one written word, ***vaenda***, is "they went", "[those] who went", or "they having gone, when they have gone", by its tones alone.

**Only two tones.** However many pitch levels you hear in a sentence, FSI says they all reduce to two, **high** and **low**, which differ "primarily in terms of their relative musical pitches, but they also differ from one another in voice quality, and also in loudness." A syllable is high if it is noticeably higher than a neighbour, or level with a neighbouring high.

**Practice.** Carter's advice is the right one: "you will master tone better by hearing and repeating than by trying to read from the marking." Ask your speaking partner to say each pair above, and repeat. Then have them say one word of a pair at random, and name which meaning you heard.
Reading the tone marks:
**How tone is written in this curriculum.** An acute accent marks a high tone: *á*. No mark (or a grave, *à*) is a low tone. The FSI course adds three more marks, because it writes two tone systems at once — the central one and the eastern one: *ǎ* is **low** where the central (standard) pronunciation is taught, high in the east; *â* is **high** centrally, low in the east; *ā*, a macron, is a low tone raised to high after a high. Say the central reading. A dot under a letter (*mẉarara*) means some speakers leave that sound out.

**Why FSI marks two systems.** Shona dialects agree about the grammar but not always about which syllable takes which tone. FSI tries to show "at least two major systems of tone use", one "characteristic of a relatively central area", the other "more typical of eastern practice". It writes them together with two marks you read by imagining a line down the middle of each symbol:

| Mark | Left half (central, west) | Right half (east) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *ˇ* (as in *ǎ*) | low | high |
| *ˆ* (as in *â*) | high | low |

So FSI's ***várǎrǎ*** "they slept" is ***váràrà*** in the centre and ***várárá*** in the east; ***nêchǐpô*** "and a gift" is ***néchìpó*** or ***nèchípò***. A tone that varies in a way that does not follow east and west is marked with an asterisk.

**This curriculum says the central reading**, because it teaches Standard Shona. When you see *ǎ*, say it low; when you see *â*, say it high. FSI's own caution stands, though: the line between the two areas is not the same for every word, so "the student [should note] in every instance what his own tutor says." Where your partner disagrees with the central reading, your partner wins.

**Carter's marks** are simpler: acute for high, nothing for low, a grave (*à*) for "a high tone that has been lowered", and an underline for "a low one that has been raised".

**Practice.** Copy these four into your notebook with both readings written out in full: *várǎrǎ*, *nêchǐpô*, *mẉarárá*, *yárǎrǎ*.
The w-sounds: ngw, mw, pw:
FSI asks you to listen again to ***mangwanani***, ***mwarara*** and ***vapwere***. The sounds written **ngw**, **mw** and **pw** are like **ng**, **m** and **p** "except that there is an extra element which may be called **velarization**" — a backing and raising of the tongue towards the soft palate, with or without a stop or friction. The letter *w* after a consonant is the sign for it.

What it sounds like depends on the consonant:

| Written | What the extra element sounds like (FSI) |
| --- | --- |
| **ngw** | "pretty much what one might call a 'w sound'" |
| **pw** | it "may sound like a /k/ or a scraping sound (a voiceless velar fricative)" — *vapwere* can sound close to *vapkere* |
| **mw** | it may sound like the last sound in English *song*, or like a w-sound, or it "may even include a slight 'smacking' of the lips" |

**So do not say a plain English *w*** after *p* or *m*. Listen for it.

**Practice.** Play the FSI Unit 1 recording and listen only for *mangwanani*, *mwarara* and *vapwere*. Repeat each ten times. Then ask your speaking partner to say *vapwere* slowly, and listen for the k-like or scraping element after the *p*.
The letter v, and vh and w:
FSI: "When the letter **v** is not adjacent to some other consonant letter, it may stand for any of three sounds, depending on dialect":

| Where | What *v* is |
| --- | --- |
| A major part of the **central** area | a voiced sound made with the **lower lip against the upper teeth**, not a stop, and if a fricative, "very light friction". It contrasts with *w* and with **vh** and **f** |
| Other speakers | much the same, but made with **both lips** instead of lip and teeth |
| **Manyika** | the same sound as **w** |

The central sound is the standard's. So *v* is a **gentle** v, much softer than English *v*, and kept distinct from both *w* and the strong ***vh***.

This matters for FSI's recordings: their speakers are Manyika, so in a word like ***varara*** "they slept" you may hear what sounds like *warara*. FSI's own example: in Manyika, *varara* "is pronounced exactly like *warara* 'he slept'". The standard keeps them apart.

**Practice.** Ask your speaking partner to say *varara* "they slept" and *warara* "he slept". If they are central speakers you will hear the gentle v against the w. Repeat each, keeping your v soft and your lips nearly closed rather than biting down.
The whistled sounds: zv and sv:
**zv** is, by FSI's account, "perhaps the most difficult sound in the basic dialogue for Unit 1, from the point of view of the European student." It contrasts with **z**, with **zh** (the middle sound of English *measure*), and with **zw**.

**How it is made — and the two courses describe it differently:**

| Source | Description |
| --- | --- |
| FSI | "produced by pronouncing simultaneously Shona v … and Shona z": "the lips are brought very near to one another, but without touching one another, during the pronunciation of z." The same friction "at the tongue tip and at the lips" is in every consonant spelled with **s** or **z** followed by **v** |
| Carter | "pronounced with the tip of the tongue curled upward and backward touching the roof of the mouth; then try to say 'z'"; **sv** "with the tongue in the same position, but try to say 's'" |

The descriptions differ, which is honest: these sounds are often called whistled because of what they sound like, and they are made differently by different speakers. **Do not choose from the page — copy the recording and your partner.** Then compare what your mouth is doing with the two descriptions.

Carter also notes **ty**, "pronounced as 'tch-k' in 'latch-key'."

**Words to practise:** *zvangu* "as for me", *zvavo*, *zvakanaka* "well", *zvitambo*.

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 1 and repeat *zvángu* and *zvakánáka* until your partner says they sound right. This one may take weeks; come back to it.
The heavy h, and mh and nh:
FSI asks you to listen to the **h** in ***here?***. English *h* (as in *hair*) is unvoiced. **Shona h is voiced, and it always has low pitch** — "these characteristics may cause it to impress the student as 'heavy'." The letter *h* stands for this sound everywhere except in **sh**, **zh**, **ch** and **vh**.

**mh** (as in ***mhuri*** "family") is **m** followed by that same h — low-pitched too. **nh** (as in ***nhanga***) works the same way.

So the *h* in *here?* is a breathy, voiced, low sound, not an English puff of air.

**Practice.** Play FSI Units 1 and 2. Repeat *here?*, *mhuri* and *nhanga*, letting the voice carry through the h and keeping it low. Ask your partner whether your *here* sounds Shona or English.
The dialect marks in FSI:
FSI writes several dialects at once, and marks where they differ. Three marks to know, from its Unit 1 notes:

| Mark | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a **dot under a letter** | some speakers **leave that sound out** | *mẉarara* "you (pl.) slept" is *mwarara* in some places and *marara* in others |
| a **mark under a vowel** | **two different vowels** are used in different places | *nọmwana* "and a child": *nomwana* in some areas, *nemwana* in others, including Manyika |
| *ǎ*, *â* | two tone systems (see *Reading the tone marks*) | *várǎrǎ* |

**What the standard says.** Carter, teaching Zezuru, writes the greeting as ***marárá heré-e?*** — without the w. So the standard is the second of FSI's two pronunciations, ***marara***. Where FSI dots a letter, check Carter or your partner before deciding which form is yours.

**Practice.** Find every dotted letter in the Unit 1 and Unit 2 dialogues (there are several: *mẉarárá*, *sẹ́nyi*). For each, write down both forms.
Good morning:
The first FSI dialogue: a married man (A) and a married woman (B) exchange morning greetings.

| | FSI (Unit 1) | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | *Mangwánaní máǐ.* | Good morning (madam). |
| B | *Mangwánaní babá.* | Good morning (sir). |
| A | *Mẉarárá heré?* | [How] did you sleep? |
| B | *Ndarára zvángu.* | (I slept) [fine]. |
| B | *Várǎrà sẹ́nyi vapwéré?* | How did the children sleep? |
| A | *Várǎrà zvávó zvakánáka.* | They slept well. |

**The same greeting in the standard** (Carter, Lesson I):

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mangwánaní-i,* | good morning, |
| *marárá heré-e?* | have you slept well? |
| *Áiwá, tarárà zvédú* | yes, we have slept |
| *kana máraráo.* | if you have slept also. |

Notice: FSI's *mẉarárá* is the standard *marárá* (the dot under the w). Carter's answer uses **we** (*tarárà*) where FSI's uses **I** (*ndarára*); both are used. And ***here?*** is not "here" — it is the question word that turns a statement into a yes/no question.

**Words:** *mai* mother, madam · *baba* father, sir · *vapwere* children.

**Practice.** FSI's procedure, in order: play the Unit 1 recording with the book closed; imitate without the meanings; imitate with them; read aloud; then take both roles. Then greet your speaking partner with *Mangwanani* and the question, and answer theirs.
A tone that changes in the sentence:
FSI's Unit 1 ends with a rule worth knowing early, because it is everywhere.

Said alone, ***ndarara*** "I slept" has the same tones as ***mẉarárá***: ***ndarárá*** — two highs at the end. But in ***Ndarára zvángu*** the last high has gone. FSI's rule:

> When a verb form ends with **two or more consecutive high tones**, and is followed **immediately** by a word that **begins with a high tone**, then the **last high tone of the verb is replaced by low tone.**

So ***ndarárá*** + ***zvángu*** is said ***ndarára zvángu***, and FSI writes the change with a small grave after the word: ***ndarárá\` zvángù***. You will see that mark in the drills.

FSI adds that if the sentence is said very slowly, with a pause between the words, *ndarara* may keep its full *ndarárá* tones — the change happens only when the words run together.

The same rule is why FSI's drills tell you to separate "the tonal patterns *rárá* before low tone and *rárà* before high tone":

| Before a low tone | Before a high tone |
| --- | --- |
| *Mẉarárá heré?* | *Mẉarárá\` sẹ́nyi?* |
| *Ndarárá zvakánáka.* | *Ndarárá\` zvángu.* |

**Practice.** Say *ndarárá* alone, then *ndarara zvángu* at normal speed, and listen for the drop. Then drill the pairs above with your partner.
Asking after the children:
The second half of the morning greeting asks about others. From FSI Unit 1:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Várǎrà sẹ́nyi vapwéré?* | How did the children sleep? |
| *Várǎrà zvávó zvakánáka.* | They slept well. |

**The pieces.** ***vá-*** in *várǎrǎ* is "they": *várǎrǎ* is "they slept". ***sẹ́nyi*** is "how" — FSI's form, with a dot under the n because some speakers leave it out. ***zvávó*** is "as for them, in their fashion"; it makes the answer gentler, as *zvángu* does for "I". ***zvakánáka*** is "well".

**One more word: how is your family?** From FSI Unit 2:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mhurì yárǎrǎ zvakánáka heré?* | How did the family sleep? ('Did the family sleep well?') |
| *Várǎrǎ\` zvávó zvakánáka.* | They slept fine. |

Notice the ***yá-*** in *yárǎrǎ*: the family is not "they" (*vá-*) but takes its own prefix, because *mhuri* belongs to a different noun class. That is the principle of **concord**, the subject of a later lesson.

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 1 and Unit 2. Then, with your partner: they ask how your children (or family) slept; you answer; swap.
Forms of address:
Greetings in Shona name the person greeted, and the names depend on who is speaking and who is addressed. From FSI:

| Word | Used for | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *babá* | father; sir — to a man | Unit 1 |
| *mái* | mother; madam — to a woman | Unit 1 |
| *shéwe* | a "courteous form of address used by women" | Unit 2 |
| *chirombówe* | a "courteous form of address used by men" | Unit 2 |
| *muzváré* | an unmarried girl over 12 (FSI's "Miss") | Units 3–4 |
| *mwaná* | child, offspring; *mwanángu* "my child" | Unit 4 |

FSI's Unit 2 dialogue, "a bit more formal than those in the dialogue of Unit 1", between a woman (A) and a man (B):

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | *Mangwánaní shéwe.* | Good morning! |
| B | *Mangwánaní chīrombówe.* | Good morning! |
| A | *Mẉarárá heré?* | [How] did you sleep? |
| B | *Áiwá zvitámbó.* | Oh, very well indeed. |

***áiwá*** is, per FSI, a "courteous expression of diffidence or dissent" — so it opens a polite answer, much like a modest "oh" — and ***zvitámbó*** is "fit, having life". Carter uses *Áiwá* the same way to begin *Áiwá, tarárà zvédú*.

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 2. Then greet your partner four times, as four people: as a woman to a man, a man to a woman, an adult to a child, a child to an adult.
A low raised after a high:
FSI Unit 2's first note. Said alone, ***chirombówe*** begins with a low tone. In *Mangwánaní chīrombówe*, it begins with a high.

> In general, when a word that ordinarily begins with **a series of two or more consecutive low tones** is preceded by a word that **ends in a high tone**, then the first syllable of the second word has high tone.

*mangwánaní* ends high; *chirombówe* starts with two lows; so *chi-* is raised: ***mangwánaní chīrombówe***. FSI marks such a raised syllable with a **macron** (*ī*) — and warns that "this 'raising' of certain low tones will soon become habitual with the student, so that the writing of macrons will be discontinued in the later units." Carter marks the same thing with an underline: her ***úrombó*** in *Ndiné úrombó* "I'm sorry" is a raised low.

**Further in some dialects.** "In some forms of Shona, including Ndau, this raising of low after high extends to all the low tones in a series except for the very last." So FSI's *Ndirí kuendà kumundà* may be heard with more highs than the central reading gives.

**Practice.** Say *chirombówe* alone, then *Mangwánaní chīrombówe*. Then drill FSI's Unit 2 reading list, which gives the words without marks: *mangwanani, zvitambo, zvavo, varara, mwarara, aiwa, baba, mhuri yarara, varara here?, mwarara here shewe?* Read each aloud to your partner, and mark the tones only after they confirm them.
I slept, you slept, they slept:
FSI Unit 2, Note 3. Each verb so far contains a **subject prefix**:

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| *ndarárá* | I slept |
| *mẉarárá* | you (pl. or honorific) slept |
| *várǎrǎ* | they slept |

The verb stem "to sleep" is ***-rárá***. The ***a*** before it in each form is the mark of this past tense. The prefixes in front are ***nd-*** "I", ***mw-*** "you (pl.)", ***v-*** "they".

FSI's full set for this tense:

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1st | *nd-* (low) | *t-* (low) |
| 2nd | *w-* (low) | *mw-* (low) |
| 3rd | no prefix, or *w-* (high) — see below | *v-* (high) |

So *warárá* "you (sg.) slept", *tarárá* "we slept".

**Central and eastern, corrected from FSI Unit 5.** FSI's later, fuller table labels two of these as **eastern**: *w-* for "he, she" (central: no consonant, so *á-*) and *mw-* for "you (pl.)" (central: *m-*, so *ma-*). The standard uses the central forms — *arárá* "he slept", *marárá* "you slept" — as Carter's *marárá heré-e?* already showed. **Tone matters here too**: "the third person subject prefix has a high tone, while the first and second person prefixes have low tone."

**And "it" for a family**: *mhuri* is not a person-class noun, so it has its own prefix, ***y-***, also high: *yárǎrǎ*.

**Practice.** FSI's Group 1 drill, from its Unit 2 — say each, with your partner giving the cue word:

| Cue | Sentence | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| | *Mẉarárá heré?* | Did you (pl.) sleep? |
| *sẹ́nyi* | *Mẉarárá\` sẹ́nyi?* | How did you (pl.) sleep? |
| *zvakánáka* | *Mẉarárá zvakánáka heré?* | Did you (pl.) sleep well? |
| *ndarárá* | *Ndarárá zvakánáka.* | I slept well. |
| *zvángu* | *Ndarárá\` zvángu.* | I slept. |
| *warárá* | *Warárá zvakánáka heré?* | Did you (sg.) sleep well? |
| *sẹ́nyi* | *Warárá\` sẹ́nyi?* | How did you (sg.) sleep? |
| *tarárá* | *Tarárá zvakánáka.* | We slept well. |
Saying it gently: zvangu, zvavo, zvayo:
FSI Unit 2, Note 4. These two both mean "I slept":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndarárá.* | I slept. |
| *Ndarárá\` zvángu.* | I slept. |

***zvángu*** is usually glossed "as for me, in my fashion." Adding it "make[s] what one says more gentle or more respectful." The same is true of ***zvávó*** (for them), ***zváyo*** (for the family, class 9), ***zváké*** (for him or her) and the forms for other persons and classes — the word changes to agree with whoever is being spoken of.

| Speaking of | Form |
| --- | --- |
| I | *zvángu* |
| we | *zvédú* (Carter) |
| he, she | *zváké* |
| they (people) | *zvávó* |
| the family (class 9) | *zváyo* |

**A dialect difference, from FSI:** "In Manyika, the corresponding words used in this way begin with **h**, instead of **zv**." Standard Shona uses the *zv-* forms.

**Practice.** Answer each greeting your partner gives you twice — once plain, once softened with the *zv-* word — and ask which sounds more natural to them.
Concord: the first look:
FSI Unit 2, Note 5 — "a preliminary note on the principle of concord", which is the backbone of Shona grammar.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Vapwéré várǎrǎ\` zvávó.* | The children slept. |
| *Mhurì yárǎrǎ\` zváyo.* | The family slept. |

The second and third words differ between the two sentences — ***várǎrǎ / yárǎrǎ***, ***zvávó / zváyo*** — because they "agree with, or are 'in concord' with" the first word, the subject. *Vapwere* (children) is one kind of noun; *mhuri* (family) is another; each makes the words around it take its own form. FSI: "This kind of agreement plays a very large part in the grammar of Shona."

Every Shona noun belongs to a **class**, and each class has its own prefixes for the words that agree with it. You will learn the classes one or two at a time from here to the end of the curriculum.

**FSI's drill, from its Unit 2 Group 2** — the question, then the answer; watch the agreement:

| Cue | 'Did the … sleep?' | 'The … slept.' |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *vapwéré* | *Vapwéré várǎrǎ heré?* | *Vapwéré várǎrǎ\` zvávó.* |
| *babá* | *Babá várǎrǎ heré?* | *Babá várǎrǎ\` zvávó.* |
| *mái* | *Mái várǎrǎ heré?* | *Mái várǎrǎ\` zvávó.* |
| *babá na mái* | *Babá na mái várǎrǎ heré?* | *Babá na mái várǎrǎ\` zvávó.* |
| *mhuri* | *Mhuri yárǎrǎ heré?* | *Mhuri yárǎrǎ zváyo.* |

(*Babá* and *mái* take *vá-*, the plural — the respect plural, the subject of a later lesson.)

**Practice.** Your partner gives the cue; you give both sentences.
Drilling: substitution, and the notched:
A practice lesson: how to drill alone, from FSI's Unit 2 procedures.

**The substitution drill.** Each sentence is partly like the one before. The partner (or the recording) says the first sentence; you repeat it. Then they give a **cue word**, and you produce the next sentence with that word in place:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Partner | *Mẉarárá heré?* |
| You | *Mẉarárá heré?* |
| Partner | *sẹ́nyi* |
| You | *Mẉarárá\` sẹ́nyi?* |
| Partner | *zvakánáka* |
| You | *Mẉarárá zvakánáka heré?* |

"The drill has been completed when the student can respond in this way, easily and correctly, to all the items."

**Alone: the notched card.** FSI's tool for reviewing without a tutor: cover the page with a card that has a notch cut from one corner, so the cue word shows and the sentence beside it is hidden. Say the sentence; slide the card down one line to see whether you were right — which also shows the next cue. Turn the card the other way and the English becomes the cue.

**The transformation drill** combines two columns into little two-line conversations: the cue, a question, and its answer (as in *Concord: the first look*). Your partner asks; you answer.

**Practice.** Make a notched card and run every drill so far — Unit 2's Group 1 and Group 2 — until you can do each without the card.

The flashcards on this site do the same job for single words and sentences; the card is for drills, where the cue changes a sentence rather than naming a word.
Good afternoon: spending the day:
FSI Unit 3: the midday greeting. Where the morning asks how you **slept**, midday asks how you have **spent the day**.

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | *Masíkatí muzváré.* | Good (mid-)day, (Miss). |
| B | *Masíkatí shéwe.* | Good (mid)day. |
| B | *Mẉaswéra heré shéwe?* | [How] have you spent the day? |
| A | *Ndaswéra zvángu kana wásweráwo.* | Fine, and you? ('I have spent the day if you have spent the day also.') |
| A | *Babá váswéra sẹ́nyi?* | How has your father spent the day? |
| B | *Váswéra zvávó zvirínáne.* | He is better [thank you]. ('He spent the day better.') |

**The standard** (Carter, Lesson I):

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Masíkatí-i,* | good afternoon, |
| *maswérá heré-e?* | have you spent the day well? |
| *Áiwá, taswérà zvédú* | yes, we have spent the day well |
| *kana másweráo.* | if you have spent (it) also. |

***Manherú*** is "good evening" (Carter).

**The verb**: ***-swera*** "spend the day". It behaves differently in tone from *-rara*, which is the subject of the next lesson.

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 3. Then, at midday, greet your partner with *Masikati* and the question, and answer theirs with the *kana* reply.
High verbs and low verbs:
FSI Unit 3, Note 1. Compare:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mẉarárá heré?* | Did you sleep? |
| *Mẉaswéra heré?* | Did you spend the day? |

The two have the same shape — subject prefix, past *a*, stem — but different tones. "About half of the verbs in the language behave tonally in one way, while almost all the rest behave in another way." Verbs like ***-rara*** are **high verbs**; verbs like ***-swera*** are **low verbs**. Every verb you learn belongs to one group or the other, and the group decides its tones in every tense — so learn it with the verb.

Verbs are cited in the **infinitive**, which for both groups begins with ***ku-***: ***kurárá*** "to sleep", ***kuswera*** "to spend the day".

**An eastern difference**: FSI warns that speakers from the extreme east and south-east may say *mẉaswérá heré*, so that "the two phrases cited above will not illustrate the point" — but the isolated words *mẉarárá* and *mẉaswéra* still will.

**A third, small group — the pro-verbs — comes in a later lesson.**

**Practice.** FSI's paired questions and answers from Unit 3, to learn "thoroughly, since they will be heard very frequently in everyday life":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mẉarára sẹ́nyi?* | *Áiwá tarára zvédú zvirínáne.* / *Áiwá ndarára zvángu zvirínáne.* |
| *Mẉaswéra sẹ́nyi?* | *Áiwá taswéra zvédú zvirínáne.* / *Áiwá ndaswéra zvángu zvirínáne.* |
| *Babá várǎra sẹ́nyi?* | *Áiwá várǎra zvávó zvirínáne.* |
| *Babá váswéra sẹ́nyi?* | *Áiwá váswéra zvávó zvirínáne.* |

The question and answer in each pair "imply that the person inquired about has not been completely well recently" — hence *zvirínáne*, "better".
\"If you also\": the polite return:
FSI Unit 3, Note 2. Two sentences from its dialogue and drills:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndaswéra zvángu kana mẉásweráwo.* | I spent the day [well] if you spent it also. |
| *Ndarára zvángu kana mẉárárawó.* | I slept [well] if you slept also. |

Literally, "I slept (or spent the day) if you slept (or spent the day) also" — "This formula is widely used in reply to polite inquiries." It is the Shona way of saying "fine, and you?", but folded into the answer.

**The forms after *kana*** (*mẉásweráwo*, *mẉárárawó*) are "tonally and grammatically different" from the ones used in the questions; FSI explains them in its Units 27 onward. For now, learn them whole. The ***-wo*** on the end is "also".

**Carter's standard version** of the same formula: *Áiwá, tarárà zvédú **kana máraráo***; *Áiwá, taswérà zvédú **kana másweráo***.

**Practice.** Your partner greets you with each of the questions below; reply with the full formula every time:

| Question | Reply |
| --- | --- |
| *Mẉarárá heré?* | *Áiwá, kana mẉárárawó.* |
| *Mẉaswéra heré?* | *Áiwá, kana mẉásweráwo.* |
The plural of respect:
FSI Unit 3, Note 3. In ***Babá váswéra sẹ́nyi?*** "How has your father spent the day?", ***babá*** is singular in form and meaning, yet the verb begins with ***va-***, the **third person plural** prefix. And in ***Mẉaswéra heré shéwe?*** only one person is addressed, yet the verb has ***mw-***, the **second person plural**.

> In both the second and the third person, **the plural may be used as a mark of respect** when speaking to or about one person.

This is grammar, not decoration: the choice of *va-* or *w-*, *mw-* or *w-*, says how you regard the person. Parents and elders take the plural; a child, as in FSI's Unit 4 *Wakádiní mukúnda?*, takes the singular.

FSI's paired drills show both, side by side:

| Respectful (plural form) | Plain (singular form) |
| --- | --- |
| *Babá váswéra sẹ́nyi?* | *Mupwéré wáswéra sẹ́nyi?* |
| *Babá várǎra sẹ́nyi?* | *Mupwéré wárǎra sẹ́nyi?* |

**Ask your speaking partner** whom they would address with the plural and whom with the singular, in their own family. The answer is part of the language.

**Practice.** Ask your partner about three people — a parent, an elder, a child — using the right form for each.
Sons, daughters, girls and boys:
FSI Unit 4: a midday greeting between an adult (A) and a child (B), with family words.

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | *Masíkatí mwanángu.* | Good (mid)day, my child. |
| B | *Masíkatí babá.* | Good (mid)day, sir. |
| B | *Mẉaswéra heré shéwe?* | How are you, (sir)? |
| A | *Áiwá, zvitámbó.* | Oh, fine. |
| B | *Wakádiní mukúnda?* | How is your daughter? |
| A | *Múpenyú zváké.* | She is all right. ('She is a living [thing].') |

**The family words** (FSI Unit 4, with each word's noun classes):

| Singular | Plural | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *mwaná* | *vana* | child, offspring (1, 2) |
| *mukúnda* | *vakúnda* | daughter (1, 2) |
| *mukóróre* | *vakóróre* | son |
| *muzváré* | *vazváré* | unmarried girl over 12 |
| *mhandara* | *mhandara* | honorific for a girl of 14 or more — the plural is the same |
| *mujahá* | *majahá* | boy of 14 or more |

***-penyú*** is "alive" and ***-áké*** "his, her"; *Múpenyú zváké* is "she is all right".

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 4. Then ask your partner after each of the six people in the table, and have them answer as FSI's dialogue does.
Noun classes: the table:
FSI Unit 4, Note 1. Compare three singular–plural pairs:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *mukóróre* | *mujahá* | *mhandara* |
| *vakóróre* | *majahá* | *mhandara* |

In the first, singular and plural differ by ***mu-*** and ***va-***. In the second, the singular is again ***mu-*** but the plural is ***ma-***. In the third, neither has *mu-* and the two are identical.

Every Shona noun belongs to a **class**, numbered by convention, and classes pair up as singular and plural. FSI's table of "the most common forms of the prefixes used with nouns of the various classes" — singular and plural pairs bracketed together:

| Class | Prefix | Before a vowel |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 · 2 | *mu-* · *va-* | *mw-* · *v-* (in some words) |
| 3 · 4 | *mu-* · *mi-* | *mw-* · *mw-* |
| 5 · 6 | no prefix syllable (the stem's first consonant may be voiced) · *ma-* | |
| 7 · 8 | *chi-* · *zvi-* | *ch-* · *zv-* (in some words) |
| 9 · 10 | no prefix syllable — most begin with a nasal, and the stem's first consonant may have changed · identical with 9 | (some speakers: *imbá* "house", 9 · *dzimbá* "houses", 10) |
| 11 | *ru-* | *rw-* |
| 12 · 13 | *ka-* · *tu-* | · *tw-* |
| 14 | *hu-* or *u-* | *hw-* |
| 15 | *ku-* | *kw-* |
| 16, 17, 18 | *pa*, *ku*, *mu* | 17 *kw*, 18 *mw* |

So *mwaná* is class 1, *vana* class 2; *mhuri* class 9 (singular) and 10 (plural, identical); *majahá* class 6. Classes 16–18 are places — they come back with the locatives.

**You do not memorise this table now.** You meet each class through its words and its concords; the table is the map. But copy it, and add each new noun you learn to its row.

**Practice.** FSI's Unit 4 Exercise 5: read each aloud with its tones, then write the tones, then the English — *mukunda, vakunda, mukorore, mujaha, majaha, vakorore, vazvare, muzvare, mhandara, vana, mwana*. Check with your partner, and say each one's class.
Which \"they slept\"?:
FSI Unit 4, Note 2. These all mean "they slept":

| Form | Used with |
| --- | --- |
| *várǎrǎ* | plural nouns beginning with ***va-***, and honorific singulars (*babá*, *mái*) |
| *dzárǎrǎ* | plurals **identical with their singulars** — classes 9/10, like *mhandara* |
| *árǎrǎ* | plural nouns beginning with ***ma-*** |

And these both mean "he or she slept":

| Form | Used with |
| --- | --- |
| *wárǎrǎ* | class 1 singulars: *mukúnda*, *muzváré*, *mujahá* |
| *yárǎrǎ* | class 9 singulars: *mhandara*, *mhuri* |

"Choice between them depends on the identity of the noun that is the grammatical subject of the verb."

**One correction, from FSI Unit 5:** *wárǎrǎ* is FSI's **eastern** form for class 1. The central, standard form is ***árǎrǎ*** — *Mukúnda árǎrǎ*, "the daughter slept" — and Unit 5's table gives both. The drill below keeps FSI's spelling; say *á-*. This is concord again: the verb's subject prefix agrees with the noun's class.

FSI's Unit 4 supplementary drill — each answers "How did your … sleep?":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Muzváré wárǎrǎ\` sẹ́nyi?* | *Vazváré várǎrǎ\` sẹ́nyi?* |
| *Mukúnda wárǎrǎ\` sẹ́nyi?* | *Vakúnda várǎrǎ\` sẹ́nyi?* |
| *Mukóróre wárǎrǎ\` sẹ́nyi?* | *Vakóróre várǎrǎ\` sẹ́nyi?* |
| *Mhandara yárǎrǎ\` sẹ́nyi?* | *Mhandara dzárǎrǎ\` sẹ́nyi?* |
| *Mujahá wárǎrǎ\` sẹ́nyi?* | *Majahá árǎrǎ\` sẹ́nyi?* |

**Practice.** Your partner names a noun from the table; you ask how it slept, in the singular and the plural.
The pro-verbs: how, like that, like this:
FSI Unit 4, Note 3. Most verbs are high or low; three are neither. ***-díni*** "to do or say what or how", ***-dáro*** "to do or say like that" and ***-dái*** "to do or say like this" share their own tone behaviour, and stand to other verbs as pronouns stand to nouns — so FSI calls them **pro-verbs**.

Their tones follow a rule: **the first syllable of the stem has the tone opposite to the syllable before it, and the second syllable has the tone opposite to the first.** Hence:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Vákadíni?* | How are they? — *ka* is low, so the stem's *dí* is high, so *ni* is low |
| *Mẉakádiní?* | How are you (pl.)? — *ká* is high, so *di* is low, so *ní* is high |

**How are you?** — the most common use. FSI's Unit 4 paired questions and answers, with the polite return from *"If you also"*:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mẉakádiní?* | *Áiwá, kana mẉákadíniwó.* |
| *Wakádiní?* | *Áiwá, kana wákadíniwó.* |
| *Mukúnda wákadíni?* | *Áiwá, múpenyú zváké.* |
| *Babá vákadíni?* | *Áiwá, vápenyú zvávó.* |
| *Vakóróre vákadíni?* | *Áiwá, vápenyú zvávó.* |
| *Majahá ákadíni?* | *Áiwá, mápenyú zváo.* |
| *Mhandara yákadíni?* | *Áiwá, ímhenyú zváyo.* |

Notice the answer agreeing with the noun each time: *múpenyú zváké* (class 1), *vápenyú zvávó* (2), *mápenyú zváo* (6), *ímhenyú zváyo* (9).

**FSI's form is Manyika-leaning.** *-díni* is the course's form of "how"; ask your partner what they say for "how are you?" and learn theirs beside it.

**Practice.** Your partner asks after each person in the table; you answer with the agreeing form.
Leaving, thanks, and getting by:
The rest of what you need to greet someone and leave again. From Carter's Lesson I, tone-marked:

**Leaving:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Chísaraí* | goodbye (lit. "stay behind now") — said by the one leaving |
| *Fámbáí zvényú zvakánáka* | have a good journey — said to the one leaving |
| *Ává mangwáná* | see you tomorrow (lit. "it has become tomorrow") |

**Courtesies:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mazvíítá* | thank you |
| *Ndapóta* | please |
| *Ruregerero* | excuse me |
| *Ndiné úrombó* | I'm sorry (lit. "I have poverty"); Carter: *Ndiné* "sounds like *ndinó*" |
| *Hazvínà mhósva* | it doesn't matter |
| *Kwázíwáí-i* | be greeted, greetings |
| *Ehóí-i* | answer to a call or greeting |

**Getting by:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Eé* · *Hóngu* | yes |
| *Kwéte* | no |
| *Hamhénó* | I don't know |
| *Handíná kunzwá* | I didn't understand |
| *Ási iníni?* | do you mean me? |
| *Hándizvó heré?* | isn't that right? |
| *Ndízvozvó* | quite right |

**Practice.** End every conversation with your partner from now on with the right goodbye — *Chísaraí* if you are leaving, *Fámbáí zvényú zvakánáka* if they are — and use *Mazvíítá* for anything they do for you.
Greeting for real: practice conversation:
The end of Stage 1, and FSI's last Unit 4 exercise: real greetings, between real roles. No new words or grammar.

**FSI's practice conversation.** You meet a ten-year-old girl at noon.

| You | She |
| --- | --- |
| *Masíkatí mukúnda.* | |
| | *Masíkatí babá.* |
| | *Mẉaswéra heré babá?* |
| *Ndaswéra zvángu.* | |
| | *Váswéra heré mái?* |
| *Váswéra zvávó.* | |
| | *Wáswéra sẹ́nyi mukóróre?* |
| *Áiwá, wáswéra zvirínáne.* | |

FSI's procedure: cover everything but the English cues and speak your side; your partner speaks the other; repeat "until the student can take the first side of the dialogue without hesitation and without mistakes"; then swap roles.

**FSI's free conversation.** Four people: **A**, a married man · **B**, a married woman · **C**, a boy of sixteen · **D**, a girl of sixteen. Practise the greetings appropriate between **A and B, A and C, B and C, A and D, B and D** — at morning and at midday, with the respect plural where it belongs and the courtesy forms (*shéwe*, *chirombówe*, *muzváré*, *mwanángu*) each speaker would use.

**With your speaking partner.** Do the five pairings with them taking every other role. Then greet them for real, every day this week, morning or midday as it falls, with the full exchange and a proper goodbye. Ask them to correct your tones, not just your words.

**Then.** Stage 2 moves to the first noun classes and the verb "to be". Before it, every card from this stage should be reviewed at least once, and you should be able to run the Unit 1–4 dialogues from either side without the book.
Meeting on the road: who are you?:
FSI Unit 5 opens with two strangers meeting on a path.

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | *Masangá chīrombówe.* | Hello! |
| B | *Masangá chīrombówe.* | Hello! |
| A | *Munhu ndíaní?* | Who are you? ('Who is the person?') |
| B | *Ndíní John.* | I am John. ('It is I John.') |

***masangá*** (class 6) is "meeting; a greeting from one traveller to another" — the hello for people who meet on the way, not at a house. It takes the same *chīrombówe* (raised after a high, as in Stage 1) as the morning greeting.

***Munhu ndíaní?*** asks "who is the person?" — the polite way to ask someone's name, by asking about the person rather than at them. ***munhu*** (classes 1, 2) is "person"; ***aní*** is "who?"; ***ndíaní*** is "who is it?". The answer puts ***ndí-*** "it is" before the name or pronoun: ***Ndíní John*** — "it is I, John". FSI's own practice conversation has *Ndíní Gōmo*.

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 5. Then meet your speaking partner "on the road": greet with *Masanga*, ask who they are, and answer with your own name.

Tone marks as in Stage 1: *á* high, unmarked low; FSI's *ǎ* is low in the central (standard) reading, *â* high, *ā* a raised low; a dot under a letter means some speakers leave it out, a mark under a vowel that two vowels are used by dialect (*ndayáną*, *ndingádą*).
Where do you live?:
The rest of the Unit 5 dialogue.

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | *Munógǎra pápǐ?* (or *Munógǎrepí?*) | Where do you live? |
| B | *Ndinógǎra mwáRusápi.* | I live in Rusape. |
| A | *Murí kūitenyí āpo?* | What are you doing there? |
| B | *Ndinósándá muPost Office.* | I work in the Post Office. |

**The words.** ***-gara*** is "to live, sit, stay"; ***pápǐ*** "where?"; ***-ita*** "to do"; ***apo*** "there"; ***-sándá*** "to work". *Rusápi* is the town of Rusape.

**Two forms of the question.** *Munógǎra pápǐ?* puts the question word after the verb; *Munógǎrepí?* fixes ***-pí*** to the end of the verb itself, with its *-a* changed to *-e*. Both are taught in *"Where" questions*, below.

**One form not to analyse yet.** *Murí kūitenyí āpo?* "what are you doing there?" uses a construction FSI explains much later; learn it whole for now.

**Practice.** Play the dialogue, then ask your partner where they live and what they do there, and answer for yourself.
The -no- tense: now, usually, or later:
FSI Unit 5, Note 1. A new prefix sits between the subject prefix and the verb stem:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Munógǎra pápǐ?* | Where do you live? |
| *Ndinósándá muPost Office.* | I work in the Post Office. |

Verbs with ***-no-*** "have either general present or future meaning" — what someone does, habitually or as a fact, or will do.

**Its subject prefixes are not quite the past tense's.** FSI's table sets them side by side — the ***-no-*** tense on the left, the past of Stage 1 (*ndarárá*, *taswéra*) on the right:

| Person | *-no-* tense | Past tense |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | *ndì-* | *ndà-* |
| you (sg.) | *ù-* | *wà-* |
| he, she (class 1) | *á-* (eastern: *ú-*) | *á-* (eastern: *wá-*) |
| we | *tì-* | *tà-* |
| you (pl.) | *mù-* | *mà-* (eastern: *mwà-*) |
| they (class 2) | *vá-* | *vá-* |

So: *ndinósándá* I work · *unósándá* you work · *ánosándá* he works · *tinósándá* we work · *munósándá* you (pl.) work · *vánosándá* they work.

**The pattern** (FSI): "in general the prefix in the right hand list has the tone and the consonant of the first list plus *a*; *u* and initial *i* in the first list are matched by *w* and *y* respectively in the second list, except that in some dialects *mu-* is matched by *ma-* and not by *mwa-*."

**The central forms are the standard ones.** That last exception is the one that matters: the standard says ***ma-*** (*marara*, as Carter writes it), and FSI's *mwa-* is eastern; the standard's third person singular is ***á-*** and FSI's *wa-* is eastern too.

**Practice.** Say all six forms of *-sanda* "work" and of *-gara* "live", then ask your partner where each person in their family lives.

The same FSI table continues past the persons into every noun class — "this table will be useful for future reference":

| Class | *-no-* tense | Past tense |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | *á-* | *á-* |
| 2 | *vá-* | *vá-* |
| 3 | *ú-* | *wá-* |
| 4 | *í-* | *yá-* |
| 5 | *rí-* | *rá-* |
| 6 | *á-* | *á-* |
| 7 | *chí-* | *chá-* |
| 8 | *zví-* | *zvá-* |
| 9 | *í-* | *yá-* |
| 10 | *dzí-* | *dzá-* |
| 11 | *rú-* | *rwá-* |
| 12 | *ká-* | *ká-* |
| 13 | *tú-* | *twá-* |
| 14 | *hú-* | *hwá-* |
| 15 | *kú-* | *kwá-* |
| 16 | *pá-* | *pá-* |
| 17 | *kú-* | *kwá-* |
| 18 | *mú-* | *má-* (or *mwá-*) |

All third-person prefixes are **high**; the first and second persons are low. The right-hand column follows the rule in the last lesson: the left-hand consonant plus *a*, with *u* becoming *w* and *i* becoming *y*.

**Concord in action**, from FSI's Unit 5 drills:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mujahá ánórima.* | The young man farms. (class 1) |
| *Vapwéré vánórima.* | The children farm. (class 2) |
| *Majahá ánórima.* | The young men farm. (class 6) |

**Practice.** Copy the table into your notebook beside the noun-class table from Stage 1. Then, for each noun you know, say "… farms" with the right prefix.
The tones of the -no- tense:
FSI Unit 5: "The tonal differences between high and low verbs in this tense, and between third person and non-third person forms of the indicative, are of great importance if one's Shona is to be easily intelligible."

**The tone of *-no-* itself.** It is **low between a high subject prefix and the stem of a high verb** (including the pro-verbs), and **high everywhere else**:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Vánosándá.* | they work — *vá-* high, *-sándá* high, so *-no-* low |
| *Tinósándá.* | we work — *ti-* low, so *-nó-* high |
| *Ndinógara mwáRusápi.* | I live in Rusape |
| *Vánógara apo.* | they live there — *-gara* is low, so *-nó-* high |

**The stem.** A **high verb** keeps the tones of its infinitive: *vánosándá*, *ndinósándá*. A **low verb's** stem varies by dialect, in three ways:

| Area | Rule | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Central, westerly | every stem syllable low | *vánórima* · *ndinórima* · *ndinórimisa* |
| Farther east | first stem syllable high in 1st and 2nd person; the rest low | *vánórima* · *ndinórima* (with *rí* high) · *ndinórímisa* |
| Still farther east and south-east | every stem syllable but the last high | *vánórímá…* (FSI does not write this set) |

FSI writes the first two together with *ǐ*: ***ndinórǐma***. Read it central — low — as always.

**Practice.** FSI's Group 17, the tense with high and low verbs in all persons — your partner asks, you answer:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Vánórima heré?* | *Vánórima.* |
| *Unórǐma heré?* | *Ndinórǐma.* |
| *Unóváká heré?* | *Ndinóváká.* |
| *Ánováká heré?* | *Ánováká.* |
| *Ánochaira heré?* | *Ánochaira.* |
| *Munópětesa heré?* | *Tinópětesa.* |

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 6 and learn the dialogue both ways.
The -ka- tense: yesterday or before:
FSI Unit 6, Note 1:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mwakáǔyǎ\` ríni pánó?* | When did you come here? |
| *Ndakásvíka musí weChína chàkápěrǎ.* | I arrived last Thursday. |

**The prefix ***-ka-***.** Its subject prefixes are the **past tense's** — the right-hand column of Unit 5's table (*nda-, wa-, a-, ta-, ma-, va-*, and *ra-, cha-, zva-…* for the classes). Its own tone follows the same rule as *-no-*: low between a high subject prefix and a high verb stem, high otherwise.

**What it means.** "With most verb stems, it is used when the action referred to took place on the preceding day or earlier." *Mwakáǔyǎ ríni?* "When did you come?" assumes "the person … to have come before today." So Shona marks what happened **today** differently from what happened **before today** — the today-tense comes in a later stage.

**With some verbs it is a state, not a time.** ***zvákánaka*** "Fine!" is literally "things (class 8) are in the state of having become good", from ***-naka*** "to become good" — and "may be used regardless of time."

**Its stem tones** vary by dialect for both high and low verbs. For high verbs, central speakers have a low stem after a low subject prefix — *takáuyà* "we came", against *kuúyá* "to come" and *vákaúyá* "they came" — and easterners keep it high, *takáúyá*; FSI writes the pair as ***takáǔyǎ***. Low verbs follow the *-no-* pattern: *ndakaénda* "I went".

**Practice.** FSI's Group 1, *-ka-* with low verbs — your partner asks "Did you … on Thursday?", you answer "I … on Wednesday":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Wakásvíka musí weChína heré?* | *Ndakásvíka musí weChítatú.* |
| *Wakáénda musí weChína heré?* | *Ndakáénda musí weChítatú.* |
| *Wakárima musí weChína heré?* | *Ndakárima musí weChítatú.* |
| *Wakágara apo musí weChína heré?* | *Ndakágara apo musí weChítatú.* |
The days of the week:
FSI Unit 6's days — most are simply "the first day", "the second day" and so on, counting from Monday. Each in the sentence "I arrived on …":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndakásvíka musí weMúsūmbunuko.* | … on Monday |
| *Ndakásvíka musí weChípirí.* | … on Tuesday |
| *Ndakásvíka musí weChítatú.* | … on Wednesday |
| *Ndakásvíka musí weChína.* | … on Thursday |
| *Ndakásvíka musí weChíshánǔ.* | … on Friday |
| *Ndakásvíka musí weMugobéra.* | … on Saturday |
| *Ndakásvíka musí weSóndo* (*weSvóndo*). | … on Sunday |

***musí*** (3, 4) is "day"; ***musí we-…*** is "the day of …". Compare the days with the numbers in the next lesson: *-pirí* two, *-tatú* three, *-na* four, *-shánǔ* five.

FSI Unit 6's numbers, each in "I've been here … weeks" (*masóndo*, class 6):

| Stem | | Sentence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *~mwé* | one | *Ndaáne sóndo rímwé ndáya pánó.* |
| *~yirí* | two | *Ndaáną masóndo mayirí ndáya pánó.* |
| *~tatú* | three | *… masóndo matatú …* |
| *~na* or *~rongomuna* | four | *… masóndo mana …* / *… marongomuna …* |
| *~shánǔ* | five | *… masóndo mashánǔ …* |

The ***~*** before a stem means it takes a **concord prefix** — the numbers 1–9 agree with the noun they count, as the next lesson explains. (The dot under the *y* of *~yirí*: some speakers leave it out.)

FSI Unit 6, Note 5: "The concordial prefixes used with numerals are like those used with nouns." So a number takes the prefix of the noun's class:

| --- | --- |

| *vaná vāyirí* | two children (class 2: *va-*) |
| *makoré māyirí* | two years (class 6: *ma-*) |

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *vaná gúmí* | ten children |
| *makoré gúmí* | ten years |

| *Ndingádą símbi ímwé.* | … one iron (class 9) |
| *Ndingádą símbi mbirí.* | … two irons (class 10) |
| *Ndingádą chigěrǒ chímwé.* | … one pair of scissors (7) |
| *Ndingádą zvigěrǒ zvivirí.* | … two pairs of scissors (8) |
| *Ndingádą zingwa rímwé.* | … one loaf (5) |
| *Ndingádą mazingwa mayirí.* | … two loaves (6) |

Notice classes 9 and 10: *ímwé*, *mbirí* — the class 10 form of "two" is *mbirí*, and of "three" *nhatú* (*símbi nhatú*). And ***~nganí*** "how many?" agrees the same way: *símbi nganí?*, *zvigěrǒ zvinganí?*, *mazingwa manganí?*

| --- | --- | --- |
| *goré* · *makoré* | 5 · 6 | year · years |
| *mwedzí* · *mwedzí* | 3 · 4 | month · months |

\"Ago\": the time that has ended:
FSI Unit 6, Note 4: "The Shona way of quantifying the period of time that has elapsed since a certain action":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *mazúvá mātatú akápěrǎ* | three days ago |
| *musí weChína chakápěrǎ* | last Thursday |

"At the end of each of these phrases is a form of the *-ka-* tense of this verb ***-pérá*** 'to come to an end'." So the literal meanings are "three days which ended" and "Fourth-day which passed away". The subject prefix agrees with the time word — ***a-*** for *mazúvá* (class 6), ***cha-*** for the day named *China*. "The low tone of the subject prefix indicates that this is not an indicative form."

**More from FSI:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Takásvíka makoré māna akápěrǎ.* | We arrived four years ago. |
| *Takásvíka masóndo matatú akápěrǎ.* | We arrived three weeks ago. |

**Practice.** FSI's calendar drill: your partner points at a day on a calendar and asks when they arrived; answer "you arrived … ago" or "you arrived last …".
-ndo- and -zo-: go and do, and do later:
FSI Unit 6, Notes 2 and 3 — two **aspect prefixes**. Unlike the tense prefixes (*-no-*, *-ka-*, …), which exclude one another, an aspect prefix can occur in an infinitive and **together with** a tense prefix. "There are about seven prefixes which are like *-ndo-* in these respects." Their basic tone is low.

**-ndo-** (in some easterly areas ***-o-***):

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *kundodzídzísá* (*koodzídzísá*) | to go and teach |

"In some of its uses *-ndo-* corresponds to English 'to go and do something.' In others, it seems to mean that an action is continued longer than might have been expected."

**-zo-:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Munózōitenyí?* | What will you do? |
| *Ndinózōenda …* | I will go … |

"This prefix is frequently used when the action referred to is one that took place, or is expected to take place 'but not immediately'."

So the end of the Unit 6 dialogue — ***Ndinófúnga ndinózōenda kundodzídzísá*** — is "I think I will (later) go (and go to) teach", with both.

**Practice.** Tell your partner three things you will do "not immediately" — next week, next month — with *-zo-*, and one place you will go and do something with *-ndo-*.

FSI Unit 7's dialogue: talk about a family who are coming.

| A | *Ínodá imbá húrú.* | It needs a large house. |

The -cha- tense: will, and still:
FSI Unit 7, Note 1:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Váchásvika.* | They will arrive. |

"The ***-cha-*** tense uses the subject prefixes of the *-no-* tense … but the tonal patterns of the *-ka-* tense." "Its most usual meaning seems to be 'future', but with some stems it corresponds to English 'still.'"

So there are two ways to talk about the future already: ***-no-*** (present or future: what one does, or will do) and ***-cha-*** (will, by and by).

**Time words that go with it** — FSI's "They will arrive …":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Váchásvika garé garé.* | … by and by |
| *… manherú.* | … this evening |
| *… mangwáná.* | … tomorrow |
| *… sẏóndo ríno.* | … this week |
| *… paMugobéra.* | … on Saturday |
| *… paChípirí.* | … on Tuesday |

| | |
| --- | --- |

| *Ucháǔyǎ heré?* | *Ndicháǔyǎ.* |
| *Ucháríma heré?* | *Ndicháríma.* |
| *Ucháénda heré?* | *Ndicháénda.* |

One-syllable verbs:
FSI Unit 7, Note 2. "By far the largest number of Shona verbs have two or more stem syllables. Those with three or more will usually be found to contain one or more derivational extensions in addition to the root" — so ***-rima*** "plough" is the root *-rim-*, and ***-rimisa*** "work as an agricultural demonstrator" is *-rim-* plus the extension ***-is-***. Extensions are a stage of their own later.

"There are a few verbs that have monosyllabic stems. Most of them are high verbs (e.g. ***-dá*** 'want, like'). One common monosyllabic verb (***-ti***) is a low verb."

They mostly follow the usual tone rules. But "some dialect areas which have high tone on first and second person forms of high verbs in the *-ka-*, *-cha-*, and *-no-* tenses have low tones on the stem syllable of monosyllabic high verbs":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *ndinósándá*, *ndakásándá* | I work, I worked |
| but *ndinódà*, *ndakádà* | I want, I wanted |

**-dá** is the everyday "want, like": ***Ínodá imbá húrú*** "it (the family) needs a large house"; ***Ndinódâ imbá yángu*** "I want my house" (from FSI's next drills).

**Practice.** Say "I want / you want / he wants / we want / they want" a house, with *-dá*, and listen to your partner's tones on the stem.
My, your, his: possessives:
FSI Unit 7, Note 3. Some possessives are already familiar: *mhuri yávó* "their family", *múpenyú zváké* "he's all right", *zvángu* "as for me", *yárǎrǎ zváyò* "it (the family) slept".

| | Singular | | Plural | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | *-ángù* | my | *-édú* | our |
| 2 | *-ákó* | your (sg.) | *-ényú* | your (pl.) |
| 3 | *-áké* | his, her | *-ávó* | their |

"All of these except the first have high tone on both syllables."

| Class | Prefix | | Class | Prefix |

| 1 | *w-* | | 10 | *dz-* |
| 2 | *v-* | | 11 | *rw-* |

| 4 | *y-* | | 13 | *tw-* |
| 5 | *r-* | | 14 | *hw-* |
| 6 | (none) | | 15 | *kw-* |
| 7 | *ch-* | | 16 | *p-* |
| 8 | *zv-* | | 17 | *kw-* |
| 9 | *y-* | | 18 | *mw-* |

| | |

| *Ndinódâ mwaná wángu.* | my child (1) |

| *Ndinódâ chikóro chángu.* | my school (7) |
| *Ndinódâ mhuri yángu.* | my family (9) |

**Practice.** Say "my …" and "our …" with every noun you know.
Its, of it: possessives for every class:
FSI Unit 7, Note 3 continues. When the **owner** is not a person but a thing of some class, the possessive stem changes with that class too:

| Class of owner | Stem | | Class of owner | Stem |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | *~áwò* | | 11 | *~árwò* |
| 4 | *~áyò* | | 12 | *~ákò* |
| 5 | *~árò* | | 13 | *~átwò* |
| 6 | *~áwò* | | 14 | *~áhwò* |
| 7 | *~áchò* | | 15 | *~ákwò* |
| 8 | *~ázvò* | | 16 | *~ápò* |
| 9 | *~áyò* | | 17 | *~ákwò* |
| 10 | *~ádzò* | | 18 | *~ámwò* |

"The tone of the last syllable is low in each of these stems." Each is ***-á-*** (possessive) + **the owner's class concord** + ***-ò***.

**So such a possessive carries two concords**, independent of one another: "The one that begins the word is in agreement with the noun that stands for the thing that is possessed; the one that stands between *-á-* and *-ò* is in agreement with the noun that stands for the possessor":

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *basa ráyò* | her work | *r-* for *basa* (5), the thing owned; *-y-* for *mhandara* (9), the owner |
| *vaná váchò* | its children (the school's) | *v-* for *vaná* (2); *-ch-* for *chikóro* (7) |

FSI's note on the personal stems: they follow the same build, "except that not all of them end with *o*, and that the first and second person plural stems begin with *e*."

**Practice.** For each pair, make "the …'s …": the school's teacher, the family's house, the city's hospital.
At the store: what would you like?:
FSI Unit 8: going to the store.

| B | *Tingáéndą zvédú masíkatí.* | We can go in the afternoon. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *símbi* | 9, 10 | an iron for clothing |
| *chitóro* | 7, 8 | store |
| *ngúvá* | 9, 10 | time |
| *newé* | | with you (*na* + *iwé*) |

**Things to buy** (FSI): *símbi* iron (9, 10) · *chigěrǒ* scissors (7, 8) · *munyú* salt (3) · *shúka* sugar (9) · *zingwa* bread (5, 6) · *parafíni* kerosene (9) · *máchisi* match (9, 10) · *sípo* soap (9, 10) · *mbéú* seed (9, 10). Each in *Ndingádą …* "I'd like …".

The -nga- tense: can, may, would like:
FSI Unit 8, Note 1:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndingádą símbi.* | I'd like an iron. |
| *Ndingáéndąwó newé heré?* | May I go with you? |
| *Tingáéndą masíkatí.* | We can go in the afternoon. |

"The ***-nga-*** tense uses the same subject prefixes as the *-no-* and *-cha-* tenses, and the same tonal patterns as the *-cha-* and *-ka-* tenses."

**What it means.** "Forms with *-nga-* have a 'potential' meaning, which is often translated into English by use of one of the modals 'can', 'may', 'might'. It may also be used in stating a desire, in order to give obliqueness to a request" — which is why *Ndingádą símbi* is "I'd like an iron" rather than "I want". FSI calls it a tense because it takes the same slot as *-no-*, *-cha-* and *-ka-*, but in meaning it is "much more like what linguists call 'modes' or 'moods'".

**The final vowel.** "In some important dialects of Shona, the final vowel of an affirmative form that contains *-nga-* is ***e*** and not ***a***: *ndingádê* etc." FSI marks this with the sign under the vowel: *ndingádą*. Ask your partner which they say.

**Practice.** FSI's free conversation: use *-nga-* to ask and give permission to do various things — to go to each of the places in the next lesson. *Ndingáéndą …?* "May I go …?" — *Hóngu, ungáéndą* / or a reason why not.
I, you, he, we, they:
FSI Unit 8's personal pronouns:

| | Singular | | Plural | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | *iní* | I | *isú* | we |
| 2 | *iwé* | you (sg.) | *imwí* | you (pl. or honorific) |
| 3 | *íye* | he, she | *ívo* | they |

The verb already says who did it, through its subject prefix, so a pronoun is **added for emphasis or contrast**, not needed for sense — *Iní ndingádą símbi* "I'd like an iron" (as for me). FSI's Unit 8 drill pairs each pronoun with its prefix:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Iní ndingáéndą ngúvânyǐ?* | What time may **I** go? |
| *Iwé ungáéndą ngúvânyǐ?* | … **you** … |

The pronoun and the prefix always match: *iní* — *ndi-*; *iwé* — *u-*; *íye* — *a-*; *isú* — *ti-*; *imwí* — *mu-*; *ívo* — *va-*. (The dot under the *w* of *imwí*: some leave it out.)

**newé**, "with you" in the dialogue, is *na* "with" joined to *iwé*. The connective with pronouns is a later lesson in FSI (Unit 18).

**Practice.** Your partner says a pronoun; you ask "What time may … go?" with the matching prefix.

Big, small, narrow, white: strong adject:
FSI Units 7–8. Most words that agree with a noun use their own set of prefixes — a subject prefix, a possessive prefix — which "may not be identical with the form of the prefix for that same class as it appears with the nouns. Thus, the subject prefix for Class 1 is *a-*, the prefix used with possessives is *w-*, but the noun itself in the same class has *mu-*."

"There is one group of words which have class prefixes of exactly the same form as the nouns. These words, which number only about two dozen altogether, are called '**strong adjectives**'." Four of the commonest, from Unit 7:

| Stem | Meaning | Class 5 | Classes 9, 10 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *~kúrú* | large, important | *gúrú* | *húrú* |
| *~díki* (*~dóko*, *~dúku*) | small | *díki* | *díki* (or *ndíki*) |
| *~téte* | narrow | *déte* | *nhéte* |
| *~chená* | white | *jená* | *chená* |

"The forms for Classes 5, 9, and 10 must be learnt separately for each adjective"; in every other class the stem simply takes the noun's prefix — *mu-kúrú*, *chi-kúrú*, *va-díki*.

**FSI's drills** — "We live in a large …" and "He works in a large …":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Tinógǎra muguta gúrú.* | … a large town (5) |
| *Tinógǎra muimbá húrú.* | … a large house (9) |
| *Tinógǎra mumushá mukúrú.* | … a large home (3) |
| *Ánosándá muchitóro chikúrú.* | … a large store (7) |
| *Ánosándá mumunda mukúrú.* | … a large field (3) |
| *Ánosándá pachéchi húrú.* | … a large church (9) |

**Practice.** Describe five things you can see with these four adjectives, each with its noun's prefix; then the reading selection's question, *Imba yenyu ihuru here?* "Is your house large?"
He said \"I will go\": reported speech:
FSI Unit 8. In English one may report speech indirectly — *He said he wanted to go* — or directly — *He said, "I want to go."* "In speaking Shona, one does not have this set of choices. Shona quotation is of the direct type."

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndinódâ kuenda.* | I want to go. (the original sentence) |
| *Wákáti ndinódâ kuenda.* | He said he wanted to go — literally, he said "I want to go". (the same speech, reported a day or more later) |

The verb is ***-ti*** "say", in the *-ka-* tense: *ndakáti* "I said", *wákáti* "he said" (FSI's eastern form), *vákáti* "they said".

**FSI's Group 10** — reporting *Ácháenda kuófisi* "He will go to the office":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndakáti ácháenda kuófisi.* | I said he would go to the office. |
| *Vákáti ácháenda kuófisi.* | They said he would go to the office. |
| *Wákáti ndicháénda kuófisi.* | He said he would go to the office. — he said "I will go" |

Notice the last: because the quotation is direct, the man's own *ndi-* "I" stays.

**Practice.** Your partner says a sentence about themselves; you report it to a third person, keeping their words: *Vákáti …*

Selling bananas:
FSI Unit 9: at a market stall.

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | *Ndirí kuténgésá māhobó.* | I am selling bananas. |
| B | *Ánoita marínyi?* | How much are they? ('They do what money?') |
| A | *Ndinóǐta matatú tíki.* | I sell three for a tickey. |
| B | *Ah! murí kūnyanya kani.* | Oh, you're too high. |
| A | *Zvákánaka mungáítą mana.* | All right, you can have ('do') four. |
| B | *Ndingáǒną madázeni mavirí.* | I'll take ('I may get') two dozen. |
| A | *Aya ári pánó.* | Here they are. |
| B | *Kubvani marí yényú īyi.* | Then here's your money. |
| A | *Mwazvíita, tamúsíyá.* | Thank you. Goodbye. ('We have left you.') |

| Word | Classes | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *-rí* | | am, is, are |
| *-téngésá* | | to sell |
| *hobó* | 5, 6 | banana |
| *marí* | 9 | money |
| *tíki* | 9, 10 | threepenny piece (FSI's 1965 coin) |
| *-nyanya* | | to be excessive |
| *kani* | | a politely emphatic interjection |
| *dázeni* | 5, 6 | dozen |
| *kubvani* | | then, so |
| *-siya* | | to leave |

**Price is a verb.** Goods "do" their price: ***Ánoita marínyi?*** — the bananas (class 6, *a-*) do what money? — and the seller answers with the same verb, *Ndinóǐta matatú tíki*, "I do three for a tickey".

**Two old friends.** *Mwazvíita* is the *mazviita* "thank you" of Stage 1, here with FSI's eastern *mw-*; ***tamúsíyá*** "we have left you" is a goodbye from the one leaving.

**The money is history.** FSI's supplementary list is the coinage of 1965 Rhodesia — *tíki* threepence, *sisi* sixpence, *shereni* shilling, *pǒndo* pound. Learn the sentences, not the coins; ask your partner what money is called now.

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 9. Then FSI's free conversation: with real fruit and vegetables if you have them, your partner sells and you price and buy.

Tone marks as before: *á* high, unmarked low; FSI's *ǎ* is low in the central (standard) reading, *â* high, *ā* a raised low, a grave *ì* a lowered (relative) prefix; a dot under a letter means some speakers leave it out, a mark under a vowel that two vowels are used by dialect.
-ri: am, is, are:
FSI Unit 9, Note 1. The dialogue has ***ndirí*** "I am", ***murí*** "you are" and ***ári*** "they (class 6) are". "The stem ***-rí*** is unusual in two ways: (1) it ends with the vowel *-i* instead of *-a*; (2) it does not combine with the tense prefixes. Because it does not have all the kinds of forms that other verbs have, it is called 'defective'. With respect to its meaning, *-rí* corresponds in many respects to English 'am, is, are'."

It takes the subject prefixes alone, straight onto the stem — FSI's Group 4, "Where are you?" "I'm here.":

| | Question | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *iwé* | *Urípi?* | *Ndirí pánó.* |
| *imwí* | *Murípi?* | *Tirí pánó.* |
| *íye* | *Áripí?* | *Ári pánó.* |
| *ívo* | *Váripí?* | *Vári pánó.* |

**With a place.** "Are the children in the house?" — FSI's Group 5, with the locatives of Stage 2:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Vaná várí mumbá heré?* | … in the house? |
| *Vaná várí muchéchi heré?* | … in the church? |
| *Vaná várí mugádheni heré?* | … in the garden? |
| *Vaná várí pātyo heré?* | … near? |
| *Vaná várí mūmunda heré?* | … in the field? |
| *Vaná várí\` pánó heré?* | … here? |
| *Vaná várí\` kúre heré?* | … far? |

And with a thing: *Gádheni rírípí?* "where is the garden?" — *Rírí chīnhambo.* "It's a short way off."

**Practice.** Ask your partner where each member of their family is right now, and where things in the room are.
I am doing: -ri with the infinitive:
FSI Unit 9, Note 2. "In one of its very common uses, *-rí* precedes the infinitive of other verbs":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndirí kuténgésá māhobó.* | I'm selling bananas. |

"This construction is usually best translated into English with the present progressive ('is \_\_\_ing') tense … But there may be some areas of Rhodesia where the construction *-rí* plus the infinitive of a given verb is interchangeable with the *-no-* tense of the same verb." So: ***-no-*** for what one does, ***-rí ku-*** for what one is doing now.

**The question:** ***Murí kūitenyí?*** "What are you doing?" — met whole in Unit 5, now taken apart: *mu-rí ku-ita-nyí*, "you are to-do-what?".

**FSI's answers** — "I'm …":

| --- | --- | --- |
| *Ndirí kunyórá.* | *-nyórá* | writing |
| *Ndirí kūbika.* | *-bika* | cooking |
| *Ndirí kūverenga.* | *-verenga* | reading, counting |
| *Ndirí kutámbá.* | *-támbá* | playing |
| *Ndirí kūgeza.* | *-geza* | washing |
| *Ndirí kūbereka mwaná.* | *-bereka* | carrying a child on the back |
| *Ndirí kūrera mwaná.* | *-rera* | caring for a child |
| *Ndirí kūdirira mbéú.* | *-dirira* | watering seeds |
| *Ndirí kusímá māruva.* | *-símá*; *ruva* (5, 6) | transplanting flowers |
| *Ndirí kutémá mití.* | *-témá*; *mutí* (3, 4) | cutting trees (*mutí*: tree, medicine, wood) |
| *Ndirí kuvádzá\` húní.* | *-vádzá*; *húní* (9, 10) | splitting firewood |

What? The ending -nyi:
FSI Unit 9, Note 3. Compare:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ánoita marínyi?* | How much ('what money') are they? |
| *Unóǐta basanyí?* | What work do you do? |
| *Murí kūitenyí?* | What are you doing? |

"The final syllable in each of these sentences is pronounced either ***-yi*** (westerly) or ***-nyi*** (easterly). It is not a separate word, but is pronounced together with whatever precedes it." So it moves the stress: in *Ndirí kūita **ba**sa* "I'm working" the stressed syllable is *ba*, but in *Urí kūita ba**sa**nyí?* it is *sa*. FSI writes it *-ṇyi* — the dot under the *n* is the westerly speakers leaving it out. Ask your partner which they say.

**Its tone depends on what is before it:**

| Before it | *-nyi* is | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a low tone | high | *basanyí* |
| a single high | low | *marínyi* |
| two highs | (by dialect) low, or high with the syllable before it lowered | *ngúványi* or *ngúvànyí* |

**On a verb** it takes the *-e* of *-pí* "where": *-ita* → *kūitenyí*; *-téngésá* → *Wakáténgésenyí?* "What did you sell?" — *Ndakáténgésǎ\` símbi.* "I sold an iron."

FSI Unit 9, Note 4:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Aya ári pánó.* | These are here. |
| *Marí yényú īyi.* | This [is] your money. |

*aya* (class 6) and *iyi* (class 9) are **proximal demonstratives**, English "this, these". "Demonstratives may be used in positions where one usually finds nouns, as in the above examples, or they may be used as modifiers of nouns": *aya mahobó* these bananas, *iyi marí* this money, *ichi chikóro* this school. Beside them are the **distal demonstratives**, "that, those over there".

| 2 | *ava* | *avo* |

How much is this one?:
FSI Unit 9's Groups 2–3 put the demonstratives, the subject prefixes and the price together. The demonstrative agrees with the noun, and so does the verb:

| This one | These |
| --- | --- |
| *Iri hobó rínóita marínyi?* | *Aya mahobó ánóita marínyi?* |
| *Iyi sípo ínóita marínyi?* | *Idzi sípo dzínóita marínyi?* |
| *Iyi húní ínóita marínyi?* | *Idzi húní dzínóita marínyi?* |
| *Ichi chigěrǒ chínóita marínyi?* | *Izvi zvigěrǒ zvínóita marínyi?* |
| *Iri zingwa rínóita marínyi?* | *Aya mazingwa ánóita marínyi?* |
| *Iyi imbá ínóita marínyi?* | *Idzi dzimbá dzínóita marínyi?* |

Three things agree in each line: *iri* — *hobó* — *rí-*; *aya* — *mahobó* — *á-*. Classes 9 and 10 (*sípo*, *húní*) look the same in the noun, so the demonstrative and the verb are what tell you one from many.

**With a number:** *Aya mahobó māna ánóita marínyi?* "How much are these four bananas?"; *Izvi zvigěrǒ zvina zvínóita marínyi?*

Looking for someone:
FSI Unit 10: someone comes looking for a man who has gone out.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Masíkatí chīrombówe.* | Good day! |
| *Masíkatí.* | Good day. |
| *Murí kūtsvaka aní?* | Who are you looking for? |
| *Ndirí kudá Babá Mukaráti.* | I need Mr. Mukarati. |
| *Ah! Wáenda kwáMutáre.* | Oh! He went to Mutare. |
| *Mwaídenyí kwáwári?* | What did you want of him? |
| *Ndaídâ kutaura navó.* | I wanted to talk with him. |

| Word | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| *-tsvaka* | to look for, seek |
| *aní* (pl. *vanaaní*) | who? |
| *-taura* | to speak |

***navó*** "with him" is *na* "with" and the respect plural *-vó* — Mr. Mukarati is spoken of as "them". ***Wáenda*** "he went (today)" is the tense two lessons on; the dot under FSI's *w* marks the speakers who leave it out, and the standard does (*áenda*), as with every third-person *w-* in Stage 2.

***aní*** has a plural: ***vanaaní?*** "who (all)?", for when the answer is more than one person.

**FSI's place names** for this unit, each "to/at": *kwáMutáre*, *kuHaráre*, *kuMaróndera*, *kuGatóma* (now Kadoma), *kuKwékwe*, *kuGwerú*, *kuBhurúwayo* (Bulawayo), *kuChipínga* (now Chipinge). Mutare takes *kwá-*, the person-or-river form of Unit 5.

The past of today:
FSI Unit 10, Note 2. "The very first verb forms which occurred in this series of lessons were in the greeting formulae. They were in a tense which did not occur outside of such formulae until this unit":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mwarárá heré?* | Did you sleep (during the past night)? |
| *Váswéra heré?* | [How] did they spend the day? |
| *Wáenda kwáMutáre.* | He went to Mutare. |

**How it is made.** "The subject prefixes are as for the *-ka-* tense" — *nda-, wa-, a-, ta-, ma-, va-* — but with no *-ka-*: the subject prefix goes straight onto the stem. "The tones of the verb stems themselves are as for the *-ka-* tense also":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *mwaúyá* | you came (today) |
| *vaǔyǎ* | they came (today) |
| *vásvíka* | they arrived (today) |
| *ndatáura* | I spoke (today) |

"After high tone, westerly dialects have low tone on the stems of high verbs" — hence *vaǔyǎ*. "With low stems, some dialects have high tone on the first stem syllable only."

**What it means.** "Almost without exception, verbs in this tense are used to refer to events that have taken place during the same day or during the preceding night. It may therefore be called the 'past today' tense, or the '**hodiernal**' tense (from the Latin word for 'today')."

So Shona has two pasts already: ***-ka-*** for yesterday and before, and this one for today — which is why every greeting in Stage 1, about last night or this day, was in it.

**Time words for it** (FSI): *mangwánaní áno* this morning · *chinhambwe* a short time ago · *mambákwedzá* dawn. *Ndasvíka chinhambwe chapérá.* "I arrived a short while ago."
What did you do today?:
FSI Unit 10's drills for the past of today.

| --- | --- |
| *Waíta basa rákó heré?* | *Ndaíta basa rángu.* |
| *Waénda kumaheu heré?* | *Ndaénda kumaheu.* |
| *Watáura navó heré?* | *Ndatáura navó.* |
| *Waríma munda heré?* | *Ndaríma munda.* |
| *Waréra mwaná heré?* | *Ndaréra mwaná.* |
| *Waswéra sényi?* | *Ndaswéra zvirínane.* |

The last is the midday greeting of Stage 1, in the singular.

**High verbs** — "Did you cut trees?" "I cut trees.":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Watémá mití heré?* | *Ndatémá mití.* |
| *Wasímá māruva heré?* | *Ndasímá māruva.* |

***-óná*** is "to see"; *vadzídzísi* "teachers".

**Third person, things running out** — Group 6:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ngúvá yápěrǎ.* | The time is up. |
| *Sípo yápěrǎ.* | The soap is all gone. |
