| *Basa rápěrǎ.* | The work is finished. |

Each subject prefix is the past column of Unit 5's table, agreeing with its noun.

**Practice.** FSI's free conversation: "Ask and answer questions about what you and others have actually done during the current day or the preceding night."
The -i- tense: used to, and would like:
FSI Unit 10, Note 1:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mwaídenyí?* | What did you want? |
| *Ndaída kutaura navó.* | I wanted to talk with him. |

"The subject prefixes are the same as those used in the *-ka-* tense … but the tones are those of the *-no-* tense."

**Its two uses.** "First, and central, its use as **past habitual** ('I used to …')":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndaíěnda kudhíbhi masóndo ọ́sé.* | I used to go to the dip tank every week. |
| *Vaírima ngúvá dzọ́sé.* | They used to farm all the time. |
| *Ndaígǎra muimbá yédú.* | I used to live in our house. |
| *Ndaídzídzísá vapwéré goré rakápěrǎ.* | I used to teach children last year. |
| *Ndaírǎpa mwedzí mītatú yakápěrǎ.* | I used to do medical work three months ago. |
| *Ndaítǎura zvakánáka mazúvá ọ́sé.* | I used to speak well every day. |
| *Ndaíchǎira makoré akápěrǎ.* | I used to drive, years ago. |
| *Ndaíténgésá māhobó musí weMúgobéra.* | I used to sell bananas on Saturday. |

"A second and rather frequent use is illustrated in the basic dialogue, where reference is not really to past habitual action, but to a present situation which one wishes to refer to **obliquely**. In this respect, *-i-* is reminiscent of *-nga-*" — *Mwaídenyí?* is a polite "what do you want?", put in the past. It even combines with *-nga-*:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndaíngadą…* | I would like … |

"This is the only instance of two of the so-called tense prefixes occurring together."

**Practice.** Tell your partner five things you used to do, with when; then ask for three things with *Ndaíngadą…*.
Which path goes to town?:
FSI Unit 11: asking the way.

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | *Nzira ínoenda kúpǐ?* | Where does the path go? |
| B | *Ndíyo ìnósvǐka muguta.* | This is the [one] that goes to ('arrives in') the village. |
| A | *Hapáná ìnógúrírá heré?* | Isn't there a shorter [one]? |
| B | *Iyi ndíyo yàkátónaka.* | This is the right [one]. |
| A | *Ínósvika ngepáWatsómba heré?* | Does it go via Watsomba? |
| B | *Kwázvo, ndíyo iyi.* | Oh yes, this is it. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *nzira* | 9, 10 | path, way |
| *-gúrírá* | | to cut (for) — here, a path that cuts across |

**The grave accents.** *ìnósvǐka*, *ìnógúrírá*, *yàkátónaka* have a **low** subject prefix where you would expect a high one. That low tone is the whole difference between "it goes" and "the one that goes" — the next lesson.

*Hapáná …?* "isn't there …?", *ngepá-* "via" and *yàkátónaka* "the right one" FSI leaves unexplained here; learn them whole.

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 11. Then FSI's practice conversation — ask your partner where their house is, whether it's near, whether it's large, and the way there:

| You | Your partner |
| --- | --- |
| *Imbá yákó írípí?* | *Imbá yángu írí mūguta.* |
| *Írí pātyo heré?* | *Írí chīnhambo.* |
| *Íhǔrǔ heré?* | *Húnde íhǔrǔ kwázvo.* |
| *Ndíyo nzira yángu heré?* | *Inóěnda kúpi?* |
| *Inósvǐka muguta.* | *Ndíyo iyi.* |
Relative verbs: the one that …:
FSI Unit 11, Note 1. "Notice the tones on the subject prefixes in these verbs":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndíyo nzira ìnósvǐka muguta.* | That is the path that goes to town. |
| *Ndíyo ìnósvǐka muguta.* | That is the one that gets to town. |
| *Hapáná nzira ìnógúrírá heré?* | Isn't there a path that is shorter? |
| *Ndíyo yàkánáka.* | That is the one that is good. |

"These verbs are formed just like the third person verbs of the *-no-* and *-ka-* tenses that have been met previously, except that they have **low tone on their subject prefixes**. The corresponding verbs with high tone on the subject prefix were **indicative**; an indicative form is one which serves as the main verb in a declarative sentence. The verbs … with low tone on the subject prefix, are **relative**. A relative verb never stands as the main verb in a declarative sentence. Instead, it occupies positions in the sentence which may also be occupied by adjectives or by nouns. English translations … often consist of relative clauses."

| Indicative | Relative |
| --- | --- |
| *Ánosándá muófisi.* He works in an office. | *Ndíaní ànósándá muófisi?* Who works in an office? |
| *Vákasímá māruva.* They transplanted flowers. | *Ndívo vàkásǐmǎ māruva.* They are the ones who transplanted flowers. |

**First and second person sound the same.** "Tonally, relative forms are identical with first and second person indicative forms. It follows that there is no audible difference between indicative and relative forms in the first and second persons":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndinóběreka mwaná.* | I carry the child. |
| *Ndíní ndinóběreka mwaná.* | It is I (I) who carry the child. |

Standard spelling does not mark tone, so on the page *anosanda* is both "he works" and "who works" — only the voice tells them apart. This is the second place, after high and low verbs, where Shona's tone is grammar.

**Practice.** FSI's Group 3 — your partner says the indicative, you ask who:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ánoténgá munyú.* | *Ndíaní ànóténgá munyú?* |
| *Ánováká dhíbhi.* | *Ndíaní ànóváká dhíbhi?* |
| *Ánonyórá zvakánáka.* | *Ndíaní ànónyórá zvakánáka?* |
| *Ánotémá mutí.* | *Ndíaní ànótémá mutí?* |
Adjectives that are verbs:
FSI Unit 11, Note 2. The true adjectives — FSI's *~* words, the strong adjectives of Stage 2 — "are very few in Shona, numbering about two dozen … Most adjectival expressions in Shona are in fact **relative verbs**":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *nzira yàkánáka* | a good path ('a path that is good') |
| compare *Nzira yákánaka.* | The path is good. |

Same consonants, same vowels; the low *yà-* makes it "a good path", the high *yá-* makes it a sentence.

**FSI's road adjectives** — true adjectives, each in "Where is the … road?":

| | Stem | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Mugwagwa mukúrú úripí?* | *~kúrú* | big |
| *Mugwagwa murefú úripí?* | *~refú* | long, tall |
| *Mugwagwa mupamhí úripí?* | *~pamhí* | wide |
| *Mugwagwa mutète úripí?* | *~tète* | narrow |
| *Mugwagwa mupfúpi úripí?* | *~pfúpi* | short |
| *Mugwagwa mutsvá úripí?* | *~tsvá* | new |

***mugwagwa*** or ***muvhá*** (3, 4) is "road"; the adjectives take its *mu-*, and the verb *ú-rí-pí* its class 3 subject prefix.

**Practice.** Describe the roads and paths near where you live to your partner: which is long, which short, which new; then a house, a field and a town, using *yàkánáka* "that is good" beside the true adjectives.
It is, that is the one: ndi-:
FSI Unit 11, Note 3. "One of the most frequently used of the constructions that employ relative verbs is one that begins with ***ndí-*** plus some concordial element":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndíyo yàkánáka.* | That is the one (class 9) that is good. |

"Translations for *ndíyo* are 'it is that', or 'that is the one'."

**The class forms.** "The concordial element of one of these third person forms, Classes 2–18, is identical with the last part of the distal demonstrative (Unit 9, Note 4), or of the possessive pronoun (Unit 7, Note 3), except for Classes 3 and 6." So *idzo* → *ndídzo*, *icho* → *ndícho*; class 3 and 6 are *ndíwo*.

FSI's Group 9 — "Is that your …?":

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Ndícho chikóro chényu heré?* | 7 | school |
| *Ndíwo mushá wényu heré?* | 3 | home |
| *Ndíyo marí yényu heré?* | 9 | money |
| *Ndídzo húní dzényu heré?* | 10 | firewood |
| *Ndíro dangá rényu heré?* | 5 | kraal |
| *Ndíwo maruva ényu heré?* | 6 | flowers |
| *Ndíye mwaná wényu heré?* | 1 | child |
| *Ndívo vaná vényu heré?* | 2 | children |

**The persons:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *ndíní* it is I | *ndísú* (*tísú*) it is we |
| *ndíwé* it is you | *ndímwí* it is you (pl.) |
| *ndíye* it is he, she | *ndívo* it is they |

These are the *Ndíní John* of Unit 5's greeting. With a relative verb after them — Group 10:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ánováká dzimbá.* | *Ndíye ànóváká dzimbá.* He is the one who builds houses. |
| *Ndinóváká dzimbá.* | *Ndíní ndinóváká dzimbá.* |
| *Tinóváká dzimbá.* | *Tísú tinóváká dzimbá.* |

**Practice.** FSI's free conversation: "Collect a number of objects and ask whether each belongs to various individuals."
Who is doing it?:
FSI Unit 11's last groups put the relative after ***ndíaní?*** "who is it?" and ***ndívanaaní?*** "who (all) are they?".

**With -rí**, the relative goes first and the question word after — Groups 5–6, "She is cooking." "Who is the one who is cooking?":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Árí kūbika.* | *Àrí kūbika ndíaní?* |
| *Árí kūverenga.* | *Àrí kūverenga ndíaní?* |
| *Árí kuúyá.* | *Àrí kuúya ndíaní?* He's coming — who is coming? |
| *Árí kunyórá.* | *Àrí kunyóra ndíaní?* |

**Plural** — Groups 7–8:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Várí kusímá māruva.* | *Vàrí kusímá māruva ndívanaaní?* |
| *Várí kūverenga.* | *Vàrí kūverenga ndívanaaní?* |
| *Várí kūenda kuchéchi.* | *Vàrí kūenda kuchéchi ndívanaaní?* |

**The -ka- tense** — Group 2, "Who (all) did his work?":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Vákáita basa ráké.* | *Ndívanaaní vàkáíta basa ráké?* |
| *Vákásvika kumushá.* | *Ndívanaaní vàkásvíka kumushá?* |
| *Vákárera vaná.* | *Ndívanaaní vàkáréra vaná?* |

Each time the only change from statement to question part is the low tone on the subject prefix — *ári* → *àrí*, *vákáita* → *vàkáíta*.

**Practice.** Your partner tells you what people in their house are doing; you ask who is doing each thing.
I don't speak Shona well:
FSI Unit 12: the conversation every learner has.

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | *Handítaúrí chiShóna zvakánáka.* | I don't speak Shona well. |
| B | *Ah! Unótǎura zvakánáka kwázvo.* | Oh, you speak very well. |
| B | *Unódzídzíra kúpǐ mutauro wédú?* | Where do you study our language? |
| A | *KuNyakatsápá.* | At Nyakatsapa. |
| B | *Unópédza ríni?* | When do you finish? |
| A | *Handízívi zvakánáka.* | I don't know for sure. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *chiShóna* | 7 | Shona style of speaking or acting — the Shona language |
| *mutauro* | 3, 4 | language |
| *-dzídzírá* | | to study |
| *-pédzá* | | to finish |
| *-zívá* | | to know |

***chi-*** (class 7) before the name of a people is their language and their ways: *chiShóna*. FSI's languages:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *chiNdevére* | Ndebele |
| *chiNgézi* | English |
| *chirungu* | (any) European language |
| *chiPutukézi* | Portuguese |

Each in *Ánogona kutaura chiNdevére*, "He can speak Ndebele" — ***kugona*** is "to be able".

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 12, and learn A's lines — you will use them. Then FSI's practice conversation: ask your partner what language they speak at school and at home — *Unótǎura mutauronyí?* — and whether the children speak a European language at school.
Not: the negative of -no-:
FSI Unit 12, Note 1:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Handítaúrí chiShóna zvakánáka.* | I don't speak Shona well. |
| *Handízívi zvakánáka.* | I don't know for sure. |

"The various affirmative tenses of Shona form their negatives in quite diverse ways. The negative verbs in the above examples correspond to the affirmative forms *ndinótǎura* and *ndinózívá*."

**How it is made.** "This set of negative forms begins with the negative prefix ***ha-***, followed by the subject prefix with **high** tone. The first syllable of the stem has its basic tone, low for low verbs and high for high verbs. The next two stem syllables are high for high and low verbs alike. The final vowel of the stem is ***-i*** in some dialects, ***-e*** in others." There is no *-no-*.

| Person | Negative | Group 4: "… don't speak Ndebele" |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | *handí-* | *Handítaúrí chīNdevére.* |
| you (sg.) | *haú-* | *Haútaúrí chīNdevére heré?* |
| he, she | *haá-* | *Haátaúrí chīNdevére.* |
| we | *hatí-* | *Hatítaúrí chīNdevére.* |
| you (pl.) | *hamú-* | *Hamútaúrí chīNdevére heré?* |
| they | *havá-* | *Havátaúrí chīNdevére.* |

"Note however that the stems of the pro-verbs do not adopt the special tonal pattern described above, and that their final vowels do not change."

**The final -i.** FSI marks it with the sign under the vowel, *handítaúrį*: *-i* or *-e* by dialect. Ask your partner which they say.

**With your speaking partner, this week:**

1. Buy something from them, haggling: *Ánoita marínyi? — Murí kūnyanya kani.*
2. Point at things around you with *this* and *that* in their classes.
3. Tell them what you did today, and what you used to do as a child.

5. Say what you don't do, can't do and don't want to do.

**Central forms.** *Mwazvíṇzwá* and *Mwatíṇyi* carry FSI's dotted *w*; the standard drops it — *Mazvinzwa here?*, as in Stage 1. The dot under the *n* of *-ṇzwá* marks the speakers who say *-zwa*.

**Practice.** Use these with your partner from today on, in Shona only: when you don't understand, say so; when you want it again, ask; when it's too fast, ask for it slowly.

Tone marks as before: *á* high, unmarked low; FSI's *ǎ* is low in the central (standard) reading, *â* high, *ā* a raised low, a grave a lowered syllable; a dot under a letter means some speakers leave it out, a mark under a vowel that two vowels are used. New in this stage: FSI's **ˣ** (written here after the syllable, *Pindáiˣ*) marks a tone that varies between speakers but not by east and west — FSI's Unit 1 says to follow your own tutor, so ask your partner.
Didn't: the past negative:
FSI Unit 13, Note 1:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Handíná kuzvíṇzwá.* | I didn't understand it. |

"The root of this verb is *-nzwá*, the syllable *-zví-* is an object prefix of Class 8, used without a specific noun antecedent" — "it" as "things", in general. Object prefixes are the second half of this stage.

**The formula.** "The formula for past negatives is: ***ha-*** + subject prefix with high tone + ***ná*** + infinitive. These phrases may be used as negative counterparts both for the *-ka-* tense (past before today) and the hodiernal tense (past today)." So one negative covers both pasts.

| Affirmative | Negative (Group 11, "I didn't go with them") |
| --- | --- |
| *Vákaenda kwáMutáre.* | *Handíná kūenda navó.* |
| *Vákaita basa.* | *Handíná kūita basa navó.* |
| *Vákárima munda.* | *Handíná kūrima munda navó.* |
| *Vákaúya pánó.* | *Handíná kuúyá navó.* |
| *Vákadzídzíra chiShóna.* | *Handíná kudzídzírá navó.* |

**With every class** — Group 10, "Is this … good?" "It is not good.":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Iri bhúku rákánaka heré?* | *Harína kūnaka.* |
| *Iyi imbá yákánaka heré?* | *Haína kūnaka.* |
| *Aya mazwí ákánaka heré?* | *Haána kūnaka.* |
| *Uyu mugwagwa wákánaka heré?* | *Haúná kūnaka.* |
| *Ava vaná vákánaka heré?* | *Havána kūnaka.* |
| *Ichi chitóro chákánaka heré?* | *Hachína kūnaka.* |
| *Izvi zvitóro zvákánaka heré?* | *Hazvína kūnaka.* |

**Two other pasts negatives** FSI names, used "in various parts of Mashonaland": with ***-zi*** for *-na* (*handízí kuzvíṇzwá*), and with ***-sa-*** (*handísazvíṇzwá* for today, *handísákazvíṇzwá* for before today) — in this set "the final vowel of the stem remains *-a*". Learn the *-na* one; recognise the others when your partner uses them.
Commands:
FSI Unit 13, Note 2: the **imperative**.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Nyóráí…* | Write …! |
| *Taúráí.* | Speak! |
| *Garáí pasí.* | Sit down! |

"In form, these words consist of the stem of the verb, plus ***-i*** (in some dialects ***-nyi***). The first syllable of a low verb is low; otherwise, stem tones are high. The tone of *-í* is high in some dialects, low in others."

**Singular and plural.** "In the imperative, as in the other forms of the verb, the plural form may be used in speaking to one person, as a mark of respect. The singular form of the imperative is like the plural except that it lacks the suffix." — Group 6:

| To one (familiar) | To several, or to one with respect |
| --- | --- |
| *Téngésá mití yákó.* | *Téngésaiˣ mití yényú.* sell your trees |
| *Pédzá bāsa rákó.* | *Pédzaiˣ basa rényú.* finish your work |
| *Rerá mwaná wákó.* | *Reraiˣ mwaná wényú.* look after your child |
| *Verénga bhúku rákó.* | *Veréngai bhúku rényú.* read your book |

The possessive follows the number: *-ákó* with the singular, *-ényú* with the plural. With anyone you would greet with the plural of respect, use the plural.

**Did you? Then do!** — Groups 2–3, the past of today against the command:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mwapédzá heré bāsa rényú?* | *Pédzaiˣ basa rényú.* |
| *Mwatémá heré mití?* | *Témaiˣ mití.* |
| *Mwadírǐra heré māruva?* | *Diríraiˣ maruva.* |
| *Mwavérěnga heré bhúku?* | *Veréngaiˣ bhúku.* |

**After someone** — Group 8, with a class 18 possessive (*mw-*, agreeing with *mu-* "in"): *Taúráiˣ mūmasúre mwáké* "speak after him", *… mwávó*, *… mwángu*, *… mwédú*.

**Practice.** FSI's free conversation: "Practice giving and receiving directions, using affirmative plural imperative forms." Direct your partner round the room, then let them direct you.
Again: -zve:
FSI Unit 13, Note 3. Compare:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Taúráí.* | Speak! |
| *Taúráizvé.* | Speak again! |
| *Pindá.* | Enter! |
| *Pindázve.* | Enter again! |
| *Wátáura.* | He spoke. |
| *Wátáurazvé.* | He spoke again. |

***-zve*** "again" is an enclitic — fixed to the end of the word, like *-nyi* and *-pí*.

**Its tone.** "The tone of *-zve* is always opposite to the tone of the preceding syllable. The preceding syllable has the same tone that it would have in the corresponding form without *-zve*, unless that form ends with two or more consecutive high tones. When the form without *-zve* ends with two or more high tones, the syllable before *-zve* has low tone": *Taúráí* but *Taúráizvé*.

**From the drills** (Groups 4–5):

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Veréngáiˣ!* | *Veréngáizvé.* Read again. |
| *Endáiˣ!* | *Endáizvé.* Go again. |
| *Úyáiˣ!* | *Úyáizvé.* Come again. |
| *Téngáiˣ.* | *Téngáizvé.* Buy again. |

And *Chíṇyizvé chīmwe?* "What else?" in Unit 15 is *-zve* on *chíṇyi* "what is it?".

**Practice.** Ask your partner to say, read and do things again — *Taúráizvé*, *Itáizvé* — each time they do them.
What do you have? At the vegetable stall:
FSI Unit 14:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndirí kuténgésá masímó.* | I am selling vegetables. |
| *Munéṇyi?* | What do you have? |
| *Ndiné mbatáta, nzungú nékábichi.* | I have potatoes, groundnuts and cabbage. |
| *Ndingádą kábichi.* | I'd like some cabbage. |
| *Ánoita shereni rímwé.* | It's one shilling. |
| *Mungándǐpą mātatú heré?* | Can you give me three? |
| *Zvákánaka, ánoita mashereni matatú.* | All right, that's three shillings. |
| *Mwazvítá, támbíráṇyí.* | Thank you. Here you are. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *símó* | 5, 6 | vegetable |
| *mbatáta* | 9, 10 | potato |
| *nzungú* | 10 | groundnuts |
| *kábichi* | 5, 6 | cabbage |
| *-tambira* | | to receive |

**Three things to notice,** each a lesson of its own below: *-né* in *Munéṇyi?* and *Ndiné* is "have"; *né-* in *nékábichi* is "and"; *-ndi-* in *Mungándǐpą* is "me", an object prefix (*-pa* "give"). ***Támbíráṇyí*** "here you are" is literally "receive!", the plural command of *-tambira*.

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *gwávha* (5, 6) guava | *mángo* (9, 10) mango | *pópo* (5, 6) papaya |
| *ráranji* (5, 6) orange | *ndímu* (5, 6) lemon | *chinánazí* (7, 8) pineapple |
| *nhanga* (5, 6), *díkítí* (5, 6) pumpkin | *ndodzí* (10) peas | *shushururu* (10) beans |
| *gwére* (5, 6), *chibarwé* (7) ear of maize | *tsúnga* (5) a green vegetable | *tsénzá* (9, 10) an edible root |

**Practice.** FSI's free conversation: "What vegetables or fruits have you recently bought or do you presently need? Name two commodities at a time, in this way using the connective *na*."
And, with: na:
FSI Unit 14, Note 1:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Munéṇyi?* | What do you have? |
| *Ndiné mbatáta, nzungú nékábichi.* | I have potatoes, groundnuts, and cabbage. |
| *Váną makoré mána.* | The children are four years old. ('… have four years') |

"It will be useful to consider that the basic stem represented in these forms is ***na***. It consists of a linking morpheme *~a* preceded by the nonconcordial morpheme *n-*. The basic meaning of *na* is approximately that of English 'and' and 'with'."

**Its vowel changes.** "The vowel of the linking morpheme may be *a*, *e*, or *o*, depending on dialect and on the class of the following word. In most dialects, the vowel is ***o*** before nouns of Classes 1, 3, 11, 13, 14, 15 (i.e. those whose class prefix contains *u* or *w*); it is ***a*** before nouns of Classes 2, 6, 12 (i.e. those whose prefix contains *a*); and otherwise ***e***, except with nouns of Class 1a." (In Manyika it is *e* everywhere but 1a.)

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | *nomwana* | 8 | *nezvitoro* |
| 1a | *nababa* | 9 | *nesimbi* |
| 2 | *navana* | 10 | *nenzungu* |
| 3 | *nomuti* | 11 | *norwizi* |
| 4 | *nemiti* | 12 | *nakamwana* (a small child) |
| 5 | *nehobo* | 13 | *notuvana* (small children) |
| 6 | *namahobo* | 14 | *nohuswa* |
| 7 | *nechitoro* | 15 | *nokuenda* |

"Class 1a is a special subdivision of Class 1, such that the members of 1a do not have the *mu-* prefix" — *babá*, *mái*, names.

**Its tone** "presents a fair degree of complexity", by dialect and by the noun after it. In the westerly system, *na* is high and keeps a low-high noun's pattern (*nésípo*, *néchikóro*), takes the tone of a noun's first syllable otherwise, and raises a low-low noun (*nenzíra*); two or more highs after it go low (*néhùnì*). FSI's Groups 5–8 drill each type — *Ndaténgá ndodzí népópo* "I bought peas and papaya", *Ndaténgá mbatáta nedíma* "… potatoes and sweet potato". Learn them by ear from the recording.

**Practice.** FSI's free conversation, again: tell your partner what you bought this week, two things at a time, choosing the vowel.
Having: -ne:
FSI Unit 14: "The connective with *n-* may be used with or without a subject prefix. With a subject prefix, it acts very much like a verb in that it has affirmative and negative, indicative and relative … When it is used in this way in this book, it will be written as the last syllable of a word":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Tiné nzungu.* | We have groundnuts. |

So **"have" is "be with"**: subject prefix + *na* (with the same vowel rule) — *ndiné* I have, *uné* you have, *áne* / *áną* he has, *tiné* we have, *muné* you have, *váne* / *váną* they have, and every class: *íne* (9), *ríne* (5), *chíne* (7).

**Choosing the vowel** — Groups 1–3, "We have good …":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Tiné nzungú dzakánáka.* | (10: *e*) |
| *Tiné chikóro chakánáka.* | (7: *e*) |
| *Tinó/Tiné mwaná wakánáka.* | (1: *o* in some dialects) |
| *Tinó/Tiné munda wakánáka.* | (3) |
| *Tiná/Tiné vaná vakánáka.* | (2: *a* in some) |
| *Tiná/Tiné mabhúku akánáka.* | (6) |

The adjective in each is a relative verb (Stage 3) agreeing with the noun.

**Who has it?** — Group 4, "Does Father have my books?" "Father has your books.":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Babá váną mabhúku ángu heré?* | *Babá váną mabhúku ényú.* |
| *Mujahá áną mabhúku ángu heré?* | *Mujahá áną mabhúku ényú.* |
| *Mhandara íną mabhúku ángu heré?* | *Mhandara íną mabhúku ényú.* |

| *Iwé uną mabhúku ángu heré?* | *Ndiną mabhúku ákó.* |

**From Unit 16**, a house: *Íne mipanda minganí?* "How many rooms does it have?"

**Practice.** Tell your partner what you have at home — in the kitchen, the garden, the bookcase — and ask what they have.
Friends are coming:
FSI Unit 15:

| B | *Dzínósvika ríni?* | When will they get here? |
| A | *Ndinófǔnga mangwáná.* | I think tomorrow. |
| B | *Wagádzǐrirenyí?* | What have you prepared (for the occasion)? |
| A | *Ndagádzira zvinhu zvizhínjí.* | I've prepared many things. |

| A | *Ah! Tichádya mpungá, madima némíchero mizhínjí.* | Oh, we'll have rice, sweet potatoes and a lot of fruit. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *shámwarí* | 9, 10 | friend |
| *-gadzirira* | | to prepare for [something or someone] |

| *chinhu* | 7, 8 | thing |
| *~zhínjí* | | many |

*Shámwarí dzángu* "my friend(s)" is class 10 with a plural verb — FSI translates "my friend" but the concord is plural. *-gadzirira* is *-gadzira* with an extension that adds "for", one of the verb's extensions that come later.

**FSI's supplementary words:** *hámá* (9, 10) kin — *Hámá dzángu dzíchásvika.* "My kinfolk are going to be here."; *nhási* today — *Dzíchásvika nhási.*; *mhando* (9, 10) kind, sort; *sadza* (5, 6) food, thick porridge — *Muchávagádzirira mhandonyí yesádza?* "What kind of food will you fix for them?" — *Tichágádzira mbatáta.* "We'll fix potatoes."

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 15. Then invite your partner to a meal you are planning: who is coming, when, what you have prepared, what you will eat and drink.
Me, you, him, them: object prefixes:
FSI Unit 15. "Notice the non-initial prefixes":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Muchá**va**gádzirirenyí?* | What will you fix for **them** (class 2)? |
| *Ndinó**ku**pá māshereni mana.* | I'll give **you** (sg.) four shillings. |
| *Mungá**dzi**ténga pánó.* | You can buy **them** (class 10) here. |
| cf. *Mungáténgą mbatáta pánó.* | You can buy potatoes here. |

"The underlined syllables are called **OBJECT PREFIXES**. There is an object prefix for each of the person-number combinations and for each of the classes. Choice of prefix is determined by the noun that might have been used in place of it. In general, the object prefix is in the same class as the noun … but where the object is a person or persons, the object prefix is likely to be in the personal class (1 or 2), even if the noun is one which, like *hámá* … is in some other class."

**The personal object prefixes:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | *-ndí-* me | *-tí-* us |
| 2 | *-kú-* you | *-mú-* you |
| 3 | *-mú-* him, her | *-vá-* them |

"Except for the second and third person singular (i.e. *-kú-* and *-mú-*), the vowels and consonants of the object prefixes are identical with those of the subject prefixes used with the *-no-* and *-cha-* tenses." So for things: *-chí-* (7), *-zví-* (8), *-rí-* (5), *-í-* (9), *-dzí-* (10), *-ú-* (3), *-á-* (6) and so on.

**Where it goes:** straight before the verb stem, after any tense prefix — *ndi-no-**ku**-pá*, *mu-cha-**va**-gadzirira*.

**Practice.** FSI's Group 1 — "Did you see my …?" "I saw it in the house." The object prefix agrees with the thing:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Waóná chinánazí chángu heré?* | *Ndachíǒnǎ mumbá.* |
| *Waóná zvinhu zvángu heré?* | *Ndazvíona mumbá.* |
| *Waóná mukórore wángu heré?* | *Ndamúona mumbá.* |
| *Waóná babá vángu heré?* | *Ndaváona mumbá.* |
| *Waóná marí yángu heré?* | *Ndaíona mumbá.* |
| *Waóná bhúku rángu heré?* | *Ndaríona mumbá.* |
| *Waóná mabhúku ángu heré?* | *Ndaáona mumbá.* |
| *Waóná mupungá wángu heré?* | *Ndaúona mumbá.* |

Notice *shámwarí* in FSI's same drill: *Ndaíona* for one friend, *Ndadzíona* for several — class 9 and 10, not the personal class. Both are heard; ask your partner which they use.
Object prefixes and tone:
FSI Unit 15 shows that object prefixes keep the consonants of the subject prefixes, but "their tonal characteristics are different". FSI's table — *-pá* give (one-syllable high stem), *-téngésá* sell (longer high stem), *-gadzira* prepare (low stem) — each with an object prefix:

| | One-syllable high stem | Longer high stem | Low stem |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| today's past, 3rd person | *vákǔpá* | *várǐténgésá* | *várǐgádzira* |
| today's past, 1st and 2nd | *ndakúpǎ* | *ndachíténgěsǎ* | *ndachígǎdzira* |
| *-no-* | *ndinókǔpá* | *ndinóchǐténgésá* | *ndinóchígádzǐra* |
| *-cha-* | *ndichákǔpá* | *ndicháchǐténgésá* | *ndicháchígádzǐra* |
| *-ka-* | *ndakákǔpá* | *ndakáchǐténgésá* | *ndakáchígádzǐra* |
| infinitive | *ndirí kuchídyá* | *ndirí kuchíténgěsǎ* | *ndirí kuchígádzǐra* |
| negative of *-no-* | *handírǐdí* | *handírǐténgěsǐ* | *handírígàdzírǐ* |

Read *ǐ* and *ǎ* central, as low. Two patterns to hear: with a **low stem**, the object prefix is high and lifts the stem's first syllable (*ndinóchígádzǐra* against plain *ndinógadzira*); with a **high stem**, the object prefix is low in the central reading (*ndinóchǐténgésá*, *ndinókǔpá*). The rest is learnt by ear from the recording and your partner.

**FSI's Group 4 — "I cooked it." "They cooked it.":**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndaríbika.* (*sadza*, 5) | *Várǐbíkà.* |
| *Ndarítěngǎ.* | *Várǐténgá.* |
| *Ndadzitenga.* (*mbatáta*, 10) | *Vadzitenga.* |
| *Ndaagadzira.* (*masímó*, 6) | *Vaagadzira.* |
| *Ndaitengesa.* (*michero*, 4) | *Vaitengesa.* |

**Practice.** FSI's Group 3: your partner says "Mother has a lot of pineapples" — *Mái váne zvinánazí zvizhínjí* — and you ask "Has she prepared them?", *Vázvǐgádzira heré?*; then rice (*Vaúgadzira heré?*), bread (*Vaágadzira heré?*), beans (*Vadzígadzira heré?*).
Do you know me?:
FSI Unit 15's Groups 5–6: the *-no-* tense with personal object prefixes, and the verb *-zívá* "know".

**First and second person subjects:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Munóndǐzívá heré?* | Do you know me? |
| — *Ndinómǔzívá.* | — I know you (pl.). |
| *Unóndǐzívá heré?* | Do you (sg.) know me? |
| — *Ndinókǔzívá.* | — I know you. |
| *Munómǔzívá heré?* | Do you know him? |
| — *Ndinómǔzívá.* | — I know him. |
| *Munóvǎzívá heré?* | Do you know them? |
| — *Ndinóvǎzívá.* | — I know them. |

Notice *ndinómǔzívá* is both "I know you (pl.)" and "I know him": *-mú-* is both. Context decides.

**Third person subjects:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ánondízívá heré?* | Does he know me? |
| — *Ánokúzíva kwázvo.* | — He knows you very well. |
| *Anomuziva heré?* | — *Anomuziva kwázvo.* |
| *Anokuziva heré?* | — *Anondiziva kwázvo.* |

**With "I like it"** — Group 7, "Do you like this …?": *Unóda iri bhúku heré?* — *Ndinórǐdá.*; *aya mabhúku* — *Ndinóǎdá.*; *ichi chikóro* — *Ndinochida.*; *iyi marí* — *Ndinoida.*; *uyu mupwéré* — *Ndinomuda.*; *ava vapwéré* — *Ndinovada.*; *idzi nzungú* — *Ndinodzida.*

**Practice.** Ask your partner whether they know people you both know, and whether they like things in the room; they answer with object prefixes, never the noun.
Not, with an object:
FSI Unit 15, Group 8: "The user of this book should make up further exercises in which object prefixes are used with the other tenses, and with the negative of the *-no-* tense. Some samples might be":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Waóná Babá Marata heré?* | Did you see Mr. Marata [today]? |
| *Handíná kuváǒnǎ.* | I didn't see him. (respect: *-vá-*) |
| *Vaná vanozívá āya mazwí heré?* | Do the children know these words? |
| *Haváǎzívǐ.* | They don't know them. (class 6: *-á-*) |
| *Munóvěrenga iri bhúku heré?* | Will/Do you read this book? |
| *Handíríverengi.* | I don't/won't read it. |
| *Mukómaná várera mwaná heré?* | Has the boy taken care of the child? |
| *Haáná kumúrera.* | He didn't. |
| *Mái vánógadzira zvinhu zvédú heré?* | Does/Will Mother prepare our things? |
| *Havázvígadzírį.* | She doesn't/won't. |

The object prefix goes in the same place as always — right before the stem — whether the negative is the *ha-… -i* of the present or the *ha-… ná ku-* of the past: *handí-**rí**-verengi*, *handíná ku-**vá**-ona*.

**From the Unit 16 conversation:** *Murí kuténgésá heré maráranji ényú?* — *Handíná ěkǔténgésá.* "I'm not selling them" — the object prefix *-é-* with *maráranji*, FSI's Manyika *e*.

**Practice.** Make up FSI's "further exercises" with your partner: for each tense you know, one sentence with an object prefix, affirmative and negative.
My house is small:
FSI Unit 16:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | *Imbá yángu ídįkį.* | My house is small. |
| B | *Íne mipanda minganí?* | How many rooms does it have? |
| A | *Mitatú chéte.* | Only three. |
| B | *Ínokúpá bāsa shoma.* | It gives you less work. |
| A | *Unófǔnga kudáro heré?* | Do you think so? |
| B | *Unógěza mafáfitera mashoma.* | You wash few windows. |
| A | *Ndinófǔnga kudáro.* | I think so. |
| B | *Waísa mushongá heré pasí?* | Have you polished the floor? |
| A | *Ndódǎ kuvamba.* | I'm about to begin. |

| *chéte* | | only |

| *mushongá* | 3, 4 | medicine, polish |
| *-vamba* | | to begin |

***Ínokúpá bāsa shoma*** uses the object prefix *-kú-* "you": the house gives you little work. ***kudáro*** is the infinitive of the pro-verb *-dáro* of Stage 1 — "to [be] like that" — and ***Ndinófǔnga kudáro*** is the everyday "I think so".

**Things one washes** (FSI), each in *Árí kūgeza …* "He is washing …":

| --- | --- | --- |
| *maókó* | *ruókó* (11, 6), *muókó* (3, 6) | hand, arm |
| *kusú* · *kumesó* | *usú* (14), *mesó* (9) | face |
| *muviri* | *muviri* (3, 4) | body |
| *nhumbí* · *mbatyá* | (9, 10) | clothes |

| *ndíró* | (9, 6 or 10) | utensil, dish |

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 16. Then FSI's free conversation: "Discuss the size and other qualities of specific fruits, vegetables, houses, etc." — starting with your own house: how many rooms, which are large, what you wash.
It is small: the independent form:
FSI Unit 16, Note 1:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mukúnda wángu **mú**penyú.* | My daughter is fine ('alive'). |
| cf. *mukúnda mupenyú* | a living daughter |
| *Mhuri yávó **í**hǔrǔ.* | Their family is large. |
| cf. *mhuri yávó húrú* | their large family |
| *Imbá yángu **í**díki.* | My house is small. |
| cf. *imbá yángu díki* | my small house |

"When *mupenyú* has low tone on its prefix, it may serve as (a part of) a noun phrase, which in turn fits into a sentence that contains a verb. When it has **high tone on its prefix**, it may itself be the principal word in a complete sentence, without a verb of any kind. A substantive of this latter kind is said to be in its **INDEPENDENT** form. Any noun or adjective has an 'independent' form."

So Shona needs no "is" here: *Imbá yángu ídíki* — "my house [is] small" — the high prefix does it. *Múpenyú zváké* "he's all right" from Stage 1 was one.

**Classes 5, 9, 10.** "The dependent forms of nouns and adjectives of Classes 5, 9, 10 have no prefix syllables: *hobó* (5), *nzungú* (10), *shúka* (9), *gúrú* (5), *húrú* (9, 10). In the independent form, these words have a special '**dummy prefix**' ***i*** which of course has high tone: *íhobó*, *ínzungú*, *íshúka*, *ígǔrǔ*, *íhǔrǔ*." (Consecutive highs after it go low in non-eastern speech.)

**FSI's drills:**

| *Uyu mugwagwa múrefú.* | *Múrefú kwázvo.* This road is long. |

About to: the -o- form, and beginning:
FSI Unit 16, Note 2:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndódǎ kuvamba.* | I'm about to begin. |

"Tonally, it is like the hodiernal tense except that the first syllable has high tone regardless of the person of the subject prefix. This form is **not** completely interchangeable with the *-no-* tense." Further uses come in later units; for now, ***ndódá*** + infinitive is "I'm about to".

**-vamba "begin" + infinitive** — Group 9:

| --- | --- |

| *Wátóvamba kudzídzírá chiShóna.* | He has just begun to study Shona. |

"Began to" doubles as "for the first time".

**~shoma with a class** — Group 1, "Did you wash many …?" "I washed few.": *Wagéza mafáfitera mazhínjí heré?* — *Ndagéza mashoma.*; *nhumbí zhínjí* — *Ndagéza shoma.*; *mipanda mizhínjí* — *Ndagéza mishoma.* *~shoma* and *~zhínjí* take the noun's prefix, like the strong adjectives.

**Then.** Stage 5 follows FSI from Unit 17: *ku-* and *kwa-*, ordinals, left and right, the enclitic *-wo*, and more.
Going to the hospital:
FSI Unit 17:

| --- | --- | --- |

| B | *Ndirí kūenda kwáMutáre.* | I'm going to Mutare (FSI: Umtali). |

| B | *Hapánába.* | No one [special]. ('there is not') |
| B | *Chéte kumáírá vaténda.* | Just to visit the patients. |

| A | *Bandéra rọkutángá mẉótsáúká kūrudyí.* | [At] the first sign, turn to the right. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *muténda* | 1, 2 | patient |
| *-máírá* | | to visit, e.g. a sick person |
| *--ba* | | a negative enclitic |
| *bandéra* | 5, 6 | signboard |
| *-tángá* | | to do first |
| *-tsáúká* | | to turn off |
| *rudyí* | | right (hand) |

**FSI's supplementary words** — for giving directions:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *mberí* (9) | front, ahead |
| *Endá mberí.* | Go straight ahead. |
| *-téndérúka* | to turn about |
| *runzeré* (11) / *munzeré* (3) | left (hand) |
| *Téndérúkà kurunzeré.* / *Téndérúkà kumunzeré.* | Turn to the left. |

**What is in it.** *Murí kūendepí?* is Stage 3's *-ri* + infinitive, "you are going", with Stage 2's *-pí* "where?" on the end of the infinitive, its *-a* turned to *-e*. ***Pahósipitari*** "at the hospital", ***arípó*** "who is there" and ***Hapánába*** "there is not" all carry the place prefix *pa-*, which is the first grammar of this stage. *Hapánába* is *hapána* "there is not" with ***-ba***, a negative enclitic FSI meets again in Unit 18 (*Hatíná kūisa(bá)*, "we didn't put it"). ***kumboóná*** has the new *-mbo-* "just", and ***rọkutángá*** "first" is the ordinal of this stage — both have lessons of their own. FSI leaves *mẉótsáúká* "you turn" unexplained here; learn it whole.

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 17. Then give your speaking partner directions from your door to a shop you both know — straight ahead, the first turning, right, left — and have them direct you back.

Tone marks as before: *á* high, unmarked low; FSI's *ǎ* is low in the central (standard) reading, *â* high, *ā* a raised low, a grave a lowered syllable, **ˣ** a tone that varies between speakers; a dot under a letter means some speakers leave it out, a mark under a vowel (*ọ*, *ą*) that two vowels are used by dialect. FSI's dotted *ẉ* in *mẉa-* "you (pl.)" is eastern, as in Stage 1; the standard says *ma-*.
Pa-, ku-, mu-: the place classes:
FSI Unit 17, Note 1. Stage 2 met *mu-*, *ku-* and *pa-* as "in, at, to" on place names. They are more than that: three noun classes of their own. "Notice the prefixes that have been underlined":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndinósándá **mu**Post Office.* | I work in the Post Office. |
| *Ndinógǎra **mu**guta.* | I live in a town. |
| *Ndicháénda **ku**chitóro.* | I'll go to the store. |
| ***Ku**Nyakatsápá.* | At/to Nyakatsapa. |
| ***Pa**hósipitari.* | At the hospital. |
| *Vánózogara **kw**êgǒrê.* | They'll stay for a year. |
| *Taúráí **mū**masúre mwángu.* | Repeat after me. |

"The basic forms of these prefixes are ***pa*** (Class 16), ***ku*** (Class 17) and ***mu*** (Class 18). Because words which contain them so often have to do with location, these three classes may be called the '**locative**' classes."

**What each one means:**

| Class | Prefix | FSI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 18 | *mu-* | "usually has to do with location inside something" |
| 16 | *pa-* | "has to do with comparatively definite physical location" |
| 17 | *ku-* | "is used for less definite physical location or for talking generally about the existence of something" |

So:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Hapáná nzīra.* | There is no path [here], i.e. 'No thoroughfare.' |
| *Hakúná nzīra.* | There is no path/way. |

**A warning from FSI.** "The locative prefixes do not pair off neatly with English prepositions, and particularly … the difference between *pa* and *ku* is not to be equated with the difference between location at and motion toward a place." And, as *kwêgǒrê* "for a year" and *mūmasúre mwángu* "after me" show, "some uses of the 'locatives' do not refer to location at all."

**They turn up in other places** — words you already know were these classes all along:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *kúnó* (17) | around here |
| *pánó* (16) | here |
| *múnó* (18) | in here |
| *pasí* (16) | earth, floor, down |
| *patyo* (16) | near |
| *Ndíaní arípó?* | Who is there? — the *-pó* is class 16 |

**Practice.** Say where things are in the room with your speaking partner, choosing *pa-*, *ku-* or *mu-* each time — on the table, in the box, around here — and let them correct the choice; FSI says the fit with English is loose, so their ear decides.
There are many: a place as the subject:
FSI Unit 17, Note 1: "the locative prefixes on a noun may determine the class of prefixes used with other words in the sentence":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *masúre* (Cl. 6) | back, behind |
| *mumasúre* (Cl. 18 plus Cl. 6) | behind, after |
| *mumasúre mwángu* | after me — "possessive has concord of Class 18" |

So a place can be the subject of a sentence, and the verb agrees with the place:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Vanhu vazhínjí vánógara muguta.* | Many people live in the town. |
| *Muguta múnógara vanhu vazhínjí.* | Many people live in the town. ('In-town lives many people.') |

| *Pahósipitari páná vānhu vazhínjí heré?* | (people) |

| *Pahósipitari páná vakúrú vazhínjí heré?* | (elders) |

| *Mumbá múną vapwéré vānganí?* | *Múną vāpfumbamwe.* (children, 2) |

Just, for a while, ever: -mbo-:
FSI Unit 17, Note 2. "A new aspect prefix is contained in the sentences":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndinódâ ku**mbo**óná vaténda.* | I just want to see the patients. |
| *Mẉaká**mbó**svika here kwáMútámbara?* | Have you ever been ('arrived') to Mutambara? |
| *Ndichá**mbó**enda.* | I'll go [now but I'll probably be back]. |

***-mbo-*** sits after the tense and before the stem. "The English translation equivalents of *-mbo-* vary greatly according to context, but all have to do with **temporariness, or lack of emphasis or insistence**." So it softens: *kumboóná* "just to see", *ndichámbóenda* "I'll go for a bit". And in a *-ka-* question it is the everyday "**have you ever**": *Mẉakámbósvika …?*

**Group 10** — "Have you ever …?":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mẉakámbósvikapo heré?* | Have you ever been ('arrived') there? |
| *Mẉakámbováká imbá heré?* | … built a house? |
| *Mẉakámbóbika sadza heré?* | … cooked sadza? |
| *Mẉakámbodyá sādza heré?* | … eaten sadza? |
| *Mẉakámbóverenga iri bhúku heré?* | … read this book? |
| *Mẉakámbomwá mahéu heré?* | … drunk *mahéu*? |

The *-po* of *Mẉakámbósvikapo* is the "there" of *arípó*. FSI marks the *-mbo-* variously — *mbó* in its note and on some lines here, *mbo* on others, and *mbǒ* (low in the central reading) throughout Group 6; let the recording and your partner decide.

**With object prefixes** — Group 9, "He is looking for his …" "Have you seen it/them?" The object prefix comes after *-mbo-*. FSI tones the first line only:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Árí kūtsvaka chigěrǒ cháké.* | *Mẉambóchǐóná heré?* (scissors, 7) |
| *Árí kūtsvaka mwana wake.* | *Mẉambomuona heré?* (child, 1) |
| *Árí kūtsvaka baba wake.* | *Mẉambovaona heré?* (father, 2 of respect) |
| *Árí kūtsvaka bhuku rake.* | *Mẉamboriona heré?* (book, 5) |

**Central forms.** All of these carry FSI's eastern *mẉa-*; the standard says *makambo-*: *Makambosvika kuHarare here?*

The first sign, the second town: ordinal:
FSI Unit 17, Group 8 — "At the first sign post you turn right.":

| Cue | |
| --- | --- |
| *rudyí* | *Bandéra rệkǔtángá mẉótsǎǔkǎ kurudyí.* |
| *pirí* | *Bandéra rechípirí mẉótsǎǔkǎ kurudyí.* |
| *runzeré* | *Bandéra rechípirí mẉótsǎǔkǎ kurunzeré.* |
| *tatú* | *Bandéra rechítatú mẉótsǎǔkǎ kurunzeré.* |
| *ina* | *Bandéra rechína mẉótsǎǔkǎ kurudyí.* |
| *shánǔ* | *Bandéra rêchǐshánǔ mẉótsǎǔkǎ kurunzeré.* |

"Ordinal numerals are formed by adding the prefix ***-chi-*** to the stem of the numeral. This form is in turn preceded by a **linking prefix**." So *-pirí* "two" → *chípirí*, and before it *re-*, which agrees with *bandéra* (class 5): *rechípirí* "second". *-tatú* → *rechítatú* "third", *-na* → *rechína* "fourth", *-shánǔ* → *rêchǐshánǔ* "fifth". The linking prefix is the concord of the noun plus a vowel; its rules are a lesson in Unit 19, below.

**"First"** is not *-chi-* + "one" but the linking prefix on the infinitive *kutángá* "to do first" (*-tángá*, from the Unit 17 dialogue): *rọkutángá* in the dialogue, *rệkǔtángá* in Group 8 — FSI's marks under the vowel say it is *o* for some speakers and *e* for others.

Too, also: -wo:
FSI Unit 18, Note 1. "This enclitic has appeared in the following basic sentences":

| | |
| --- | --- |

| *Není**wo** ndingáǐdá.* | And I also would like some. |
| *… kana wáswerá**wo**.* | … if you spent the day also. |
| *… kana wárára**wó**.* | … if you slept also. |
| *Ungázoúyą**wó** heré.* | Could you come too? |

The last three are old friends: the polite return of the Stage 1 greetings, and the invitation of Stage 4.

**Its tone** follows the rule of Stage 4's *-zve*: "The tone of *-wo* is always **opposite** to the tone of the preceding syllable. That syllable in turn has the same tone it has in the corresponding form without *-wo* except when the form without *-wo* ends with two or more consecutive high tones":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ungázoúyą́.* | |
| *Ungázoúyąwó.* | "In cases of this kind, the syllable before *-wo* has low tone, and *-wo* itself has high tone." |

"Note that there is **no vowel change** before *-wo* as there is before *-nyi* and *-pí*" — *Ndaténgawó*, not *-téngewó*.

**Its two uses.** "Besides its basic translation 'also, too', *-wo* sometimes serves as one more way of **softening a question or request**, thus making it more polite." *Ndígashídzewó* "hand it to me" is probably one of these, FSI says.

Put it on the table, take it out of the:
FSI Unit 18, Group 4 — "Choice of locative prefix. Contrasting translations of the same locative prefix." The place prefix says *where*; the **verb** says which way:

| Cue | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *táfura* | *Únzá mūpungá patáfura.* | Bring the rice to the table. |
| *kuisa* | *Isá mūpungá patáfura.* | Put the rice on the table. |
| *ndíró* | *Isá mūpungá mundíró.* | Put the rice in the dish. |
| *kubvisa* | *Bvisá mūpungá mundíró.* | Remove the rice from (in) the dish. |
| *hárí* | *Bvisá mūpungá muhárí.* | Remove the rice from (in) the pot. |
| *kuisa* | *Isá mūpungá muhárí.* | Put the rice into the pot. |
| *chotó* | *Isá mūpungá pāchotó.* | Put the rice on the fire. |

"consist of the **concordial prefix for Class 5** plus the **same linking prefix** that was found with the nonconcordial *n-* in *na-* (Unit 14, Note 1). These combinations of concordial plus linking prefix obey the same tonal rules, and the same rules for vowel change, as were described in Unit 14."

So "of" is built like *na*: the concord of the first noun (*r-* for *sadza*, class 5), then the vowel *na* would take before the second — *o* before classes with *u* or *w*, *a* before classes with *a*, otherwise *e* (Stage 4). *sadza rezviyo* (8: *e*), *bandéra rokutanga* (15: *o*). The ordinals' *rechípirí* is the same thing.

Sentences without a verb:
Shona can leave out "is" more often than English expects. Stage 4's independent form was one way. FSI's Units 19 and 20 give two more.

**A price.** FSI Unit 19, Note 2: "Neither of the two sentences

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Nzungú póndo ina rímwé.* | The nuts [are] four pounds sterling per bag. |
| *Mhunga póndo nêmbǒfána.* | The millet [is] thirty shillings. |

contains a verb. Nor does either sentence contain the independent form of a substantive (Unit 16, Note 1)." The thing, then its price: nothing else is needed. "The word *rímwé* 'one' in the first of these examples has the concordial prefix of Class 5, in agreement with *sakí*" — "four pounds [the] one [sack]".

**An infinitive.** FSI Unit 20, Note 2: "In the sentence

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Muto wêdǒvî kunaka!* | Peanut butter soup [is] good. |

there is no verb that has a subject prefix. There is only the infinitive form of the verb that means 'to become good'." The noun, then *kunaka* — "soup-of-peanut-butter, to-be-good!"

**And the independent form, with a negative beside it** — FSI Unit 19, Group 4, "That fireplace is large but it is not good." Each line has three agreeing words: the demonstrative, the independent form of *-kúrú*, and the past negative of Stage 4:

What is it like? -dini again:
FSI Unit 20, Note 1. The pro-verb ***-díni*** "was first met and discussed briefly in Unit 4" — Stage 1's *Makadini?* "How are you?". "Three points should be noted."

**(1) Indicative and relative tones differ:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Chákàdínì?* | What is it like? |
| *… chàkádìní?* | like what? |

"The tones of these forms alternate between high and low, beginning in the relative with low, and with high in (third person) indicative." So *Chitóro chényú chákadíni?* asks "what is it like?", and *imbá yakádiní?* after a noun is "what sort of house?".

**(2)** "The English translations of this verb vary widely according to context."

**(3)** "With the concord of Class 8 (*zvakadini*), this verb may be used without an antecedent, being comparable in this respect to *zvakanaka*, *zvizhinji*, etc." — "how?" in general.

**Group 4** — "Two-line conversations using *-díni*. Note that some of the forms of *-díni* are indicative and some are relative":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Munógǎra zvakádiní?* | *Tinógǎra zvakánáka kwázvo.* |

| *Muné imbá yakádiní?* — What sort of house do you have? | *Tiné húrú kwázvo.* — We have a very large [one]. |

| *Chikóro chényú chákadíni?* — How is your school? | *Chákánaka.* — It's good. |

The answers use Stage 4's independent form (*chíkǔrǔ*, *Míkǔrǔ*) or a bare adjective after *-ne* (*Tiné díki*, *Tiné húrú*).

**With your speaking partner, this week:**

Six shillings of sugar:
FSI Unit 21. A customer at a store, greeting the storekeeper by his work:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | *Mangwánaní murimisi!* | Good morning! (addressing the other person by his occupation) |
| B | *Mangwánaní babá.* | Good morning. |
| A | *Ndingámǔbátsírą ngéṇyi?* | How (by what) can I help you? |
| B | *Ndingáǒnąwó heré shúka?* | May I have some sugar? |
| A | *Munódâ yêmǎrîṇyǐko?* | How much do you want? |
| B | *Ndaíngadą́ zvángu yąmáshereni matánhatú.* | I'd like six shillings' worth. |
| A | *Zvákánaka zvázvo.* | Fine. |
| A | *Ndingámǔgádzirirą zvángu.* | I'll get it ready for you. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *ngéṇyi* | | with what? by what? |
| *-bátsírá* | | to help |
| *shúka* | 9 | sugar |
| *--ko* | | an optional question enclitic |

**What is in it.** *Murimisi* is a title — FSI's "addressing the other person by his occupation" — as Stage 1's forms of address were. *Ndingámǔbátsírą* is Stage 2's *-nga-* "can" with the object prefix *-mu-* "you (respect)"; *Ndingáǒnąwó* is *-nga-* with Stage 5's softening *-wo*: "might I see some too", a polite way to ask. *Yêmǎrîṇyǐko?* is "of how much money?" — Stage 5's linking prefix on *marí*, *-nyi* "what?", and the new enclitic ***--ko***, which FSI calls optional. ***ngéṇyi*** "with what?" and ***Ndingámǔgádzirirą*** "I'll get it ready for you" carry the two new pieces of grammar in this unit: the prefix *nge-*, and the verb's applicative *-ir-*, each with a lesson of its own.

FSI prints the sum in shillings, the money of 1965; learn the shape (*yąmáshereni matánhatú*, "of six shillings") and put your own money in it.

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 21. Then be the customer at your speaking partner's store: greet them by their work, ask for three things in different amounts — *Ndingáǒnąwó heré …?*, *Ndaíngadą́ zvángu …* — and have them answer *Ndingámǔgádzirirą zvángu.*

Tone marks as before: *á* high, unmarked low; FSI's *ǎ* is low in the central (standard) reading, *â* high, *ā* a raised low, a grave a lowered syllable, **ˣ** a tone that varies between speakers; a dot under a consonant (*ṇ*, *ẉ*, *ỵ*, *ḍ*) means some speakers leave it out or change it, and a mark under a vowel (*ą*, *ọ*, *ę*) that the vowel differs by dialect. FSI also hooks the *g* of *nge-*, which varies by dialect; that mark is not copied here. FSI's *mẉa-* "you (pl.)" and *ẉa-* "he, she" are eastern, as in Stage 1; the standard says *ma-* and *a-*.
For you, for us: the applicative -ir-, -:
FSI Unit 21, Note 1. "Compare the verbs in these sentences":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndagádzira shúka.* | I got the sugar ready. |
| *Ndakúgádzirira shúka.* | I got the sugar ready for you. |
| *Tinódà húní.* | We need firewood. |
| *Áchavádzà húní.* | He will split firewood. |
| *Áchatívádzírà húní.* | He will split firewood for us. |
| *Áchaúnzà húní.* | He will bring firewood. |
| *Áchatíúnzírà húní.* | He will bring firewood for us. |
| *Áchatémà húní mūgomo.* | He will cut firewood on the mountain. |
| *Áchatítémérà húní mūgomo.* | He will cut firewood for us on the mountain. |
| *Áchàtórà húní mūgomo.* | He will get firewood on the mountain. |
| *Áchatítórérà húní mūgomo.* | He will get firewood for us on the mountain. |

"Certain of the verb stems in these sentences contain a suffix — or 'stem extension' — which is either ***-er-*** or ***-ir-***. If the vowel of the preceding syllable is *a, i, u*, the extension is *-ir-*. Otherwise (i.e. if the vowel of the preceding syllable is *e, o*), it has the form *-er-*."

| After *a*, *i*, *u*: *-ir-* | After *e*, *o*: *-er-* |
| --- | --- |
| *-gadzira* → *-gadzirira* | *-tema* → *-temera* |
| *-vadza* → *-vadzira* | *-tora* → *-torera* |
| *-unza* → *-unzira* | *-gocha* → *-gochera* |

"This suffix will be called the '**applicative** extension.' It is used in a number of different ways. The most common … is associated with the idea of doing something **for someone, or with reference to someone**. When it is used in this way, the verb usually has **two objects**, one of which may be an object prefix" — *Áchatí-vádzírà húní*: *-ti-* "us" in the verb, *húní* after it.

**Not only "for".** "The foregoing does not account for all uses of the applicative extension." *kufúndá* or *kudzídzá chiShóna* is "to learn Shona"; *kufúndírá* or *kudzídzírá chiShóna* is "to **study** Shona". And Stage 3 met one "with no object of any kind": *Hapáná inógúrírá heré?* "Isn't there a shorter one?", from *-gura*, for which Hannan's dictionary gives "to cut off or across (e.g. path, country, path of sun)".

**And one that only looks like it.** "Some verbs contain a syllable that looks like the applicative extension, and which was probably just that at an earlier stage in the history of Shona. Such a verb is *-fanira*" — "must" — which is hard to relate to *-fáná* today.

**Group 1** — "Simple vs. applicative stems of some verbs":

| He wants … | I'll do it | I'll do it for him |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Ánodá nyama.* | *Ndichágócha nyama.* I'll roast meat. | *Ndichámúgóchera nyama.* I'll roast him some meat. |
| *Ánodá doví.* | *Ndichágádzira doví.* I'll make peanut butter. | *Ndichámúgádzirira doví.* I'll make it for him. |
| *Vánodá pārafíni.* They want paraffin. | *Tichátěngǎ parafíni.* We'll buy some. | *Tichávǎténgérá parafíni.* We'll buy some for them. |
| *Havágoní kusándá.* They can't work. | *Tichásǎndǎ.* | *Tichávǎsándírá.* We'll work for them. |
| *Haúgoní kūenda kuguta.* You can't go to town. | *Ácháenda kuguta.* He'll go. | *Áchakúéndera kuguta.* He'll go to town for you. |
| *Munódâ imbá.* You want a house. | *Váchavaká imbá.* They'll build one. | *Váchamúvákírá imbá.* They'll build you a house. |

Notice *-enda* → *-endera* (*e*), *-vaka* → *-vakira* (*a*), *-sanda* → *-sandira* (*a*).

**Practice.** Do Group 1 with your speaking partner: they say what someone wants or can't do, you answer first "I'll do it", then "I'll do it for him/them/you". Then make the applicative of five verbs you know — *-bika*, *-nyora*, *-tenga*, *-verenga*, *-gadzira* — choosing *-ir-* or *-er-* by the vowel before it, and use each "for" someone.
Where did you get the firewood?:
FSI Unit 21, Group 2 — "Object prefixes. Places from which various things are usually taken." Stage 4 taught the object prefixes; here they come back in the answer, standing for the thing asked about.

"Where did you get the …?" — "I got it at/on/in …":

| Cue | Question | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *húní* (10) | *Watórepí húní?* | *Ndadzítórá mūgomo.* I got it on the mountain. |
| *murívó* (3) | *Watórepí murívó?* | *Ndaútórá kugádheni.* I got it in the garden. |
| *magwére* (6) | *Watórepí magwére?* | *Ndaátórá kūmunda.* I got them in the field. |
| *mbatyá* (10) | *Watórepí mbatyá?* | *Ndabvá nádzo kuchitóro.* I've come with them from the store. |
| *sadza* (5) | *Watórepí sādza?* | *Ndarítórá muhárí.* I got it from the pot. |

Then go on, FSI says, with *chigěrǒ*, *zingwa*, *pópo*, *ufu*, *mushongá*, supplying the sentences yourself. "The symbol … means that the horizontal row of words … are to be used as cues parallel to the words in the vertical column."

**What to watch.**

| Noun | Class | Object prefix in the answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *húní* | 10 | *-dzi-* |
| *murívó* | 3 | *-u-* |
| *magwére* | 6 | *-a-* |
| *sadza* | 5 | *-ri-* |
| *mbatyá* | 10 | none: *nádzo* "with them" instead |

*Watórepí?* is Stage 3's past of today with Stage 2's *-pí* "where?" on the end, the *-a* turned to *-e*. The answer *Ndabvá nádzo* swaps the object prefix for Stage 5's *na* with the class pronoun — "I've come from the store with them" — which is how you say where something came from when you didn't "take" it.

**Practice.** Your speaking partner names five things from the kitchen and the market; for each, ask *Watórepí …?* and have them answer with the right object prefix and a place — then swap. Get from them the class of any noun you don't know before you answer.
Stop, must, do well, refuse:
FSI Unit 21, supplementary vocabulary: "Four verbs that are commonly followed by infinitives."

| Verb | | Example | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *-regera* | to cease | *Règérá kudyá.* | Stop eating. |
| | | *Ndambórěgera basa.* | I've (temporarily) stopped work. |
| *-fánírá* | to be proper, suitable (in the *-ka-* tense: "must") | *Ndakáfǎnǐrǎ kuenda.* | I must go. |
| *-natsa* | to do well | *Árí kūnatsa kutaura!* | She is speaking very well! |
| *-ramba* | (with infinitive) to refuse | *Árí kūramba kudyá sādza.* | She refuses to eat food. |

**How they work.** Each is an ordinary verb in its own tense, and the action itself follows as an infinitive with *ku-*: *-regera* + *kudyá*, *-ramba* + *kudyá*. Stage 3 built "I can't" and "I don't want to" the same way with *-gona* and *-dá*.

***-fanira* is the odd one.** It means "be proper", and in the *-ka-* tense — Stage 2's past before today — it means "must": *Ndakáfǎnǐrǎ kuenda*, "I must go," not "I had to". The previous lesson's note said it only looks applicative.

*Ndambórěgera* has Stage 5's *-mbo-* "for a while": "I've stopped for now".

**From the practice conversations:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Unoziva kuchaira here?* — Do you know how to drive? | *Handinatsi kuziva(ba).* — I don't know [it] well. |
| *Ndakafanira kuenda mugomo.* — I have to go up on the mountain. | *Kundoiteṇyi?* — To do what? |

FSI leaves these lines for you to tone. *-natsa* in the negative is "not do well": *Handinatsi kuziva*, "I don't know it well". The *(ba)* is Stage 5's negative enclitic.

***-ramba* returns in Unit 25** with a second meaning, "go on", when the verb after it is not an infinitive. Hold this one as "refuse to".

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, tell each other four things: something you must do today (*Ndakáfǎnǐrǎ ku…*), something you've stopped for a while (*Ndambórěgera …*), something someone you know does very well (*Árí kūnatsa ku…*), and something a child refuses to eat (*Árí kūramba kudyá …*). Then give them three commands with *Règérá …!*
With what? The prefix nge-:
FSI Unit 21, Note 2. "The word *ngéṇyi* contains the prefix ***nge-***. In westerly dialects, the prefix has the form ***nde-***, and its vowel is governed by the same principles as the vowel of *na-* (Unit 14, Note 1)" — Stage 4's *na* "and, with". "The tones of forms that contain this prefix are also like those of the corresponding forms with *na-*."

"The translation of *nge-* is variously '**about**' (i.e. concerning), '**by (means of)**', or '**with**'."

So *nge-* is a second "with" beside *na*: the thing you do it *with*, the thing you're glad *about*:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndingámǔbátsírą ngéṇyi?* | How (by what) can I help you? |
| *Tinóbǐka n(g)émugóti.* | We cook with a stick. |
| *Tinósǒna n(g)etsóno.* | We sew with a needle. |

By FSI's rule its vowel follows *na*'s — Stage 4's *no-*, *na-*, *ne-* by class — but in this unit's drills FSI writes it *nge-* almost everywhere; take the vowel your speaking partner uses.

**Group 3** — "The prefix *nde* with demonstratives. Agreement of demonstratives with nouns." "We're glad on account of this …":

| Cue | |
| --- | --- |
| *nyama* (9) | *Tafárá ngeíyi nyama.* |
| *murívó* (3) | *Tafárá ngeúyu murívó.* |
| *pópo* (5) | *Tafárá ngeíri pópo.* |
| *mushá* (3) | *Tafárá ngeúyu mushá.* |
| *mazwí* (6) | *Tafárá ngeaya mazwí.* |
| *mvúrá* (9) | *Tafárá ngeíyi mvúrá.* |
| *sadza* (5) | *Tafárá ngeíri sadza.* |
| *tsíme* (5) | *Tafárá ngeíri tsíme.* |

Before a demonstrative it stays *nge-*, and the demonstrative is Stage 3's "this" of the noun's class: *iyi* (9), *uyu* (3), *iri* (5), *aya* (6). *Tafárá* is the past of today: "we're glad".

(Unit 23 brings *na* back as "by" after a passive verb, and Unit 24 turns *ngéṇyi* at the start of a sentence into "why?".)

**Practice.** Do Group 3 with your speaking partner giving the noun, you the whole sentence. Then answer their *Munó… ngéṇyi?* — "what do you cut/sweep/write/eat with?" — with *nge-* and the tool. Ask them whether they say *nge-* or *nde-*.
An axe for cutting trees:
FSI Unit 21, Group 4 — "Nouns and infinitives connected by *-ọ-*." Stage 5's linking prefix "of" can stand before an infinitive: *démó rọkutémá mití*, "an axe of cutting trees", that is, an axe for cutting them. The concord agrees with the thing; the linking vowel before the *ku-* is *-o-* (FSI's *ọ*: it varies by dialect).

"What do you cut trees with?" — "We cut [them] with an axe." — "I want an axe for cutting trees." — "We want axes for cutting trees.":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Munótémà ngéṇyi mití?* | What do you cut trees with? |
| *Tinótémà ngéděmǒ.* | We cut them with an axe. |
| *Ndinódà démó rọkutémá mití.* | I want an axe for cutting trees. |
| *Tinódâ matémó ọkutémá mití.* | We want axes for cutting trees. |
| *Munótsváírà ngéṇyi pasí?* | What do you sweep the floor with? |
| *Tinótsváírà ngêmǔtsváíro.* | We sweep with a broom. |
| *Ndinódâ mutsváíro wộkǔtsváírá pasí.* | I want a broom for sweeping the floor. |
| *Tinódâ mitsváíro yộkǔtsváírá pasí.* | We want brooms for sweeping the floor. |
| *Munósǒna ngéṇyi mbatyá?* | What do you sew clothes with? |
| *Tinósǒna ngetsóno.* | We sew with a needle. |
| *Ndinódâ tsono yọkúsona mbatyá.* | I want a needle for sewing clothes. |
| *Tinódâ tsono dzọkúsona mbatyá.* | We want needles for sewing clothes. |

"Treat the following sentences in the same way": *Munóchéra ngéṇyi mvúrá?* · *Munógěza ngéṇyi mbatyá?* · *Munóchěka ngéṇyi murívó?*

**The concords:**

| Thing | Class | "for …ing" |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *démó* | 5 | *rọ-ku…* |
| *matémó* | 6 | *ọ-ku…* (*a* + *o*) |
| *mutsváíro* | 3 | *wộ-ku…* |
| *mitsváíro* | 4 | *yộ-ku…* |
| *tsono* | 9 | *yọ-ku…* |
| *tsono* | 10 | *dzọ-ku…* |

The same pattern was in Stage 5's *bandéra rọkutángá* "the first sign" — "the sign of being first". And Unit 26 builds *zvọkudyá* "food", "things of eating", on it.

**FSI's practice conversation** (tones left to you):

| You | Your partner |
| --- | --- |
| *Kwenyu munoisa dovi pamwe nemuto here?* (do they mix peanut butter with gravy?) | *Hatinyanyi kudaro.* |
| *Munodisa muto wàkadini?* (what gravy they like best) | *Tinonyanya kudya muto wenyama ne(we)masimo.* |
| *Ndakafanira kuenda mugomo.* | *Kundoiteṇyi?* |
| *Kundotema huni. Huni dzatiperera.* (you're out of it) | *Ndingandokubatsiraiwo.* |

The last two lines put the unit together: *dzatiperera* "it has run out on us" is the applicative of *-pera*, and *Ndingandokubatsiraiwo* "I could go and help you" has *-ndo-*, an object prefix and *-wo*.

**Practice.** Do Group 4 with your speaking partner for every tool in the unit — stick, axe, broom, needle, soap, pot, knife — asking "what do you … with?", answering with *nge-*, then asking for one and for several "for …ing". Then play the conversation above.
I come from another state:
FSI Unit 22. A Zimbabwean asks an American visitor about home:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | *Munógǎra muNéw York heré?* | Do you live in New York? |
| B | *Kwéte, ndinóbvâ murimwe dúnhú.* | No, I come from another state. |
| A | *Munódyawó sādza rédú heré?* | Do you eat our [kind of] food too? |
| B | *Kwéte zvákábvira kusíyáná.* | No, it is quite different. |
| A | *Ndíaní unómǔbátsírá bāsa rényú?* | Who helps you [to do] your work? |
| B | *Ah! Tinózvǐbâtíra tọ́gá.* | Oh, we do it for ourselves. |
| A | *Ko, munórǐmawó heré sesú?* | Tell me, do you farm the way we do? |
| B | *Zvákáti· síyané, tinónyǎnya michéní.* | It's a little different, we [use] more machines. |
| A | *Kúną vānhu vatemáwo heré?* | Are there also black people? |
| B | *Várì kúnó chaízvo.* | There are a lot. ('They are there very much.') |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *dúnhú*, *matúnhú* | 5, 6 | district |
| *-síyáná* | | to part from one another, to differ |
| *-bvira* | | FSI's gloss here is "[?]"; Unit 25 explains it |
| *~ọ́gá* (*~ega*) | | alone |
| *ko* | | an interrogative word |
| *sesú* | | like us |
| *muchéni* | 3, 4 | machine |
| *~temá* | | black |
| *chaízvo* | | an intensifier |

**What is in it.** *Kwéte zvákábvira kusíyáná* — "it really differs" — uses *-bvira* before an infinitive; FSI leaves it unglossed until Unit 25, which calls it an auxiliary that intensifies. *Ndíaní unómǔbátsírá?* is Stage 3's relative verb after *ndíaní*. ***Tinózvǐbâtíra*** "we do it for ourselves" is the reflexive *-zvi-* on an applicative verb; ***tọ́gá*** "we alone"; ***sesú*** "like us" is the prefix *sa-* on *isú*. All three have lessons below. ***Ko*** opens a question, "tell me, …". *Zvákáti· síyané* is printed with a raised dot after *-ti*, which FSI does not explain; say it after your partner.

FSI writes *-zvǐbâtíra* — *ǐ* low and *â* high in the central reading — and *munórǐmawó* with *ǐ* low; the tones of the reflexive are this unit's hardest point.

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 22. Then let your speaking partner ask you this dialogue's questions about where you come from — where you live, whether you eat sadza, who helps with your work, how farming is done — and answer about your own home. Swap and ask about theirs.
Zezuru, Manyika, Ndau: peoples and custo:
FSI Unit 22, supplementary vocabulary. "People: white, black, coloured, etc."

**Some ethnic groupings** — the people, class 1, the people as a whole with the plural prefix:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *muZezúru* | 1, 2 | a Zezuru |
| *muKárángá* | 1, 2 | a Karanga |
| *muManyíka* | 1, 2 | a Manyika |
| *muKorekore* | 1, 6 | a Korekore |
| *muNdaú* | 1, 2 | a Ndau |
| *muBochá* | 1, 2 | a Bocha |
| *muGárwé* | 1, 2 | a Garwe |
| *muRozví* | 1, 2 | a Rozvi |
| *muChángana* | 1, 6 | a Shangaan |

These are the dialect groups the plan names: Zezuru (the standard's base), Karanga, Korekore, Manyika (FSI's own voice) and Ndau.

**Racial terms**, as FSI lists them in 1965:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *murungu* | 1, 2 | European |
| *bhunú* | 5, 6 | Boer |
| *bwacha* | 5, 6 | Indian |
| *~chená* | | white |
| *~temá* | | black |

**General:**

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *rudzí* | 11, pl. *ndudzí* (10) | tribe, kind |
| *muitiro* | 3, 4 | custom |
| *kusíyáná* | | to leave one another, differ |
| *kufáńáná* | | to be like one another |

The language of each people is the class 7 *chi-* of its name: *chiZezuru*, *chiManyika*, *chiShona*, *chiNdevere*. To ask someone's people: *Urí rudzíṇyí?* "What tribe are you?"

**FSI's oral reading** (tones largely omitted; read aloud and mark them):

> *Muguta reHarare munọ ndudzi dzàkasiyana. Múną vaZezuru vànobva kwaSeké, Chíotá, neMréwa. VaKaranga vanobva Fort Victoria. VaNdevére vánobva Gwerú kusvika Bhurúwayo. VaNdevere havatauri chiShona. Vanotaura chiNdevere. VaManyika vanobva Rusápi kusvikira Nyánga. Vamwe vanobva kwáMaránge kusvika kwaMutambara.*

Vakaranga vanobva kupi? VaNdevere vanobva kupi? VaNdevere vanotaura chiShona here? VaManyika vọse vanobva kwáMutáre here?*

**Practice.** Read the passage aloud to your speaking partner and answer FSI's questions on it. Then ask them their people, where their family comes from, and what dialect they speak — and whether it differs from the standard, and in what words.
Alike and different: -fanana and -siyana:
FSI Unit 22, Group 2. Two verbs of comparison, both with the ending *-ana* "one another": ***-fáńáná*** "to be like one another" and ***-síyáná*** "to differ". In the *-ka-* tense they describe a state — *yákasíyáná* "is different", *wákafánáná* "is alike" — and what it is compared with follows with *na* "with".

"Are the customs of the Zezuru different from [those of] the Manyika?":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Miitiro yaváZezúru yákasíyáná heré néyąváManyíka?* | *Yákadá kufáńáná.* |
| Are the customs of the Zezuru different from those of the Manyika? | |
| *Sadza remáBwacha rákafánáná heré nérẹvárungu?* | *Haríná kufánáná. Rákasíyána kwázvo.* |
| Is the food of the Indians like that of the Europeans? | |
| *Mutauro wą̂mǎChángana wákafánáná heré nêchǐShóna?* | *Wákafánáná zvīshoma.* |
| Is the language of the Shangaans like Shona? | |
| *Chirungu nechíBhunú zvákafánáná heré?* | *Zvákadá kufánáná.* |
| Are English and Afrikaans similar to one another? | |
| *Guta rêHǎráre rákafánáná heré negúta reBhúrúwayo?* | *Harína kufánáná.* |
| Is Salisbury like Bulawayo? | |
| *Matúnhú ényú ákafánáná heré néedú?* | *Haáná kufánáná.* |
| Are your states/districts similar to ours? | |

Then FSI's cues: *makomo, mití, ndwizí, zvikóro, dzimbá, mbatyá* — compare the mountains, trees, rivers, schools, houses and clothes of two places.

**What to notice.**

- ***néyąváManyíka*** "with those of the Manyika", ***nérẹvárungu*** "with that of the Europeans", ***néedú*** "with ours": *na* before a possessive or "of" phrase with no noun — the noun is understood.
- FSI translates only the questions. The answers you can read with what you know — *Haríná kufánáná. Rákasíyána kwázvo* "it isn't alike; it's very different", *Wákafánáná zvīshoma* "it's a little alike" — except ***Yákadá kufáńáná***, *-da* "want" before the infinitive, which FSI leaves unexplained: ask your speaking partner exactly how alike it says they are.
- The negatives are Stage 4's *ha- … na* + infinitive: *Haríná kufánáná*, *Haáná kufánáná*.

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, compare two places you both know — towns, countries, families, kitchens — with *… yákafánáná heré na …?* and *… yákasíyáná heré na …?*, using FSI's six cues and your own. Answer *Wákafánáná zvīshoma* or *Haríná kufánáná. Rákasíyána kwázvo.*
For ourselves: the reflexive -zvi-:
FSI Unit 22, Note 1. The dialogue's *Tinózvǐbâtíra tọ́gá* — FSI gives the line two ways:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Tinózvǐîtǐra basa.* | We do the work for ourselves. |
| *Tinózvǐbâtírâ basa.* | We do the work for ourselves. |

***-zvi-*** is the **reflexive prefix**. It stands "in the same position as object prefixes" — between the tense and the stem — and is "never used with another object prefix". It shows that the object is the same as the subject: I hurt *myself*. With an applicative verb, as here, it is "for oneself".

It is spelled like the class 8 object prefix *-zvi-*; "some dialects" say ***-dzi-***, like the class 10 one. "The only difference" from an object prefix "is in the tonal pattern", and its tones vary a great deal between dialects, so FSI asks you to "make [your] own observations": get one example from your speaking partner for each of high and low verbs of one, two, three and four syllables — *-dá* (one syllable, high only), *-óná*, *-bátsírá*, *-gadzirira*.

**Group 3** — "I bought (my) soap." / "I bought myself some soap.":

| Cue | Plain | Reflexive |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *iní* | *Ndaténgà sípo yángu.* | *Ndazvítèngéra sípo.* |
| *íye* | *Ẉátěngà sípo yáké.* | *Ẉázvítèngéra sípo.* |
| *isú* | *Taténgà sípo yédú.* | *Tazvítèngéra sípo.* |
| *ívo* | *Vátěngà sípo yávó.* | *Vázvítengéra sípo.* |
| *iwé* | *Waténgà sípo yákó heré?* | *Wazvítengéra sípo heré?* |
| *imẉí* | *Mẉaténgà sípo yényú heré?* | *Mẉazvítengéra sípo heré?* |
| *iní* | *Ndabíka sadza rángu.* | *Ndazvíbikíra sadza.* |
| *íye* | *Ẉábíka sadza ráké.* | *Ẉázvíbikíra sadza.* |

Continue with *isú, ívo, imẉí, iwé, babá, majahá, vasíkaná*. (*ẉá-*, *mẉa-*: eastern; the standard says *á-*, *ma-*.)

**Group 4** — "There is no one who can cook for me." / "I must cook for myself.":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Hapáná angándǐbíkirą sadza.* | *Ndakáfǎnǐrǎ kuzvíbikíra.* |
| *Hapáná angándǐtémérą húní.* | *Ndakáfǎnǐrǎ kuzvítemérá.* |
| *Hapáná angákǔgézérą ndíró.* | *Wakáfǎnǐrǎ kuzvígezéra.* |
| *Hapáná angákǔónérą bāsa.* | *Wakáfǎnǐrǎ kuzvíonéra.* |
| *Hapáná angákutáúrirą.* | *Wakáfǎnǐrǎ kuzvítaúríra.* |

FSI's cue *kurima* gets the *-temera* line again — a slip; the answer *Ndakáfǎnǐrǎ kuzvírimíra* "I must farm for myself" is right. Left: an object prefix (*-ndi-* me, *-ku-* you); right: *-zvi-*, never both.

**Alone: *~ọ́gá*.** Group 5 — "Are you going alone?" "We're going alone.":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Munóěnda mwọ́gá heré?* | *Tinóěnda tọ́gá.* |
| *Vánoenda vọ́gá heré?* | *Vánoenda vọ́gá.* |
| *Unóěnda wọ́gá heré?* | *Ndinóěnda ndọ́gá.* |
| *Ánoenda ọ́gá heré?* | *Ánoenda ọ́gá.* |

FSI writes the stem *~ọ́gá (~ega)*: the vowel differs by dialect. It takes the person's prefix: *ndọ́gá* I alone, *wọ́gá* you, *ọ́gá* he/she, *tọ́gá* we, *mwọ́gá* you (pl.), *vọ́gá* they.

**Practice.** Do Groups 3 and 4 with your speaking partner, and collect from them the reflexive of the four verbs FSI names, high and low, so you have their tones. Then tell them three things you do for yourself, alone (*ndọ́gá*), and three things someone does for you.
Like a child: sa-:
FSI Unit 22, Note 2. "The nonconcordial prefix ***s-***" — "like, as". From the dialogue and the note:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Munórǐmawó heré sesú?* | Do you also plow as we do? |
| *Ánófunga sômwǎnâ.* | He thinks like a child. |
| *Ánófunga saMáí.* | She thinks like Mother. |

"Nonconcordial" because it is the same whatever the class. It is "always joined to the linking prefix" — the vowel that Stage 5's "of" uses before each class — so *s-* + linking vowel gives *sa-*, *se-*, *so-*: ***sesú*** (*isú*), ***sômwǎnâ*** (*mwaná*). Its tones are "exactly like" those of the nonconcordial *n-* of *na*; "with Class 1a nouns *sa-* is low regardless".

| --- | --- |
| *mwaná* | *Ánófunga sộmwǎnâ.* |
| *mukúru* | *Ánófunga sộmǔkúrú.* |
| *babá* | *Ánófunga sababá.* |
| *máí* | *Ánófunga samáí.* |

*Ánófunga sọmúnhu* — "he thinks like a person" — FSI glosses "talk sense". Notice the pattern: class 1 nouns in *mu-* take *so-* (FSI's *sọ*, *sộ*: the vowel varies by dialect), and the class 1a *babá*, *máí* take a low *sa-*, as *na* does with them.

**Practice.** Do Group 1 with your speaking partner. Then describe people you both know with *sa-*: someone who talks like a teacher, eats like a child, works like a European, farms like us (*sesú*). Have your partner check the *so-*/*sa-* and the tone each time.

Brothers, sisters, grandfathers:
FSI Unit 23, supplementary vocabulary: "Some kinship terms." Each is given after ***zítá ra-*** "the name of", *zítá* (5, 6) "name", "in order to show the difference between Class 1 and Class 1a":

| | Class | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *(zítá rá)mukóma* | 1, 2 | older sibling of the same sex |
| *(zítá rộ)mǔníng'ína* (or *munúng'úna*) | 1, 2 | younger sibling of the same sex |
| *(zítá rá)sekúru* | 1a; pl. *madzisekúru* (6) | grandfather |
| *(zítá rá)teté* | 1a; pl. *madziteté* (6) | father's sister |
| *(zítá rộ)mǔkádzí* | 1, 2 | woman, wife |
| *(zítá rọ)múbereki* | 1, 2 | parent |
| *hánzvádzi* | 9, 10 | sibling of the opposite sex (from the dialogue) |

**The difference the *ra-* shows.** Before a true class 1 noun in *mu-*, the linking vowel is *o*: *rộmǔníng'ína*, *rộmǔkádzí*, *rọmúbereki*. Before class 1a, which has no prefix, it is *a*: *rásekúru*, *ráteté* — and *rámukóma*, which FSI writes with *ra-* although it is listed 1, 2. Class 1a nouns take the class 1 concords but behave in this like *babá* and *máí*. The plural of 1a is *madzi-* (6): *madzisekúru*.

Shona counts siblings by whether they are your sex: a man's brothers and a woman's sisters are *mukóma* (older) or *muníng'ína* (younger); a man's sister and a woman's brother are *hánzvádzi*. So C's *Hánzvádzi yángu* is "my sister" or "my brother" by who is speaking — FSI's English says both, "sibling of the opposite sex", "he", and "my brother".

| *Unógǎrepí?* | *Ndinógǎrǎ kwáChíotá.* |
| *Murí vánganí mumbá mẉényú?* | *Tirí vashánǔ.* |
| *Ndíaní mukúrú?* | *Hánzvádzi yángu ndíyo húrú.* |
| *Vàkómaná vánganí?* | *Vakómaná tirí vairí.* |

*Zítá rákó ndíaní?* is "your name is who?" — names are asked with *ndíaní*. *Tirí vashánǔ* "we are five"; *ndíyo húrú* "she is the big one", Stage 3's *ndi-* with the class 9 concord.
