Was eaten: the passive -w-:
FSI Unit 23, Note 1. "Compare the sentences":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Tinósévénzésa doví.* | We use peanut butter. |
| *Doví rínosévénzéswa séṇyi?* | How is peanut butter used? |
| *Vaná vádyâ sadza.* | The children ate the sadza. |
| *Sadza rádyǐwǎ nḍą̂vǎnâ.* | The sadza was eaten by the children. |
| *Sadza rádyǐwǎ naBabá.* (or *… ndíBabá.*) | The sadza was eaten by Father. |

"Two sets of facts must be noted concerning the passive construction in Shona. The first set has to do with the suffix, or 'extension', which is added to the stem of the verb. The second … with the non-concordial prefix which is added to the noun that stands for the person or thing by which the action of the verb was accomplished." The second is the next lesson.

**The extension.** "The most frequent form of the passive extension is ***-w-***. It follows all other extensions, and stands immediately before the final vowel of the verb":

| *-sevenz-* | *-es-* | *-w-* | *-a* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 'work' | [causative] | [passive] | [final vowel] |

"For verbs that have monosyllabic stems (e.g. *-dyá*, *-dá*), the passive extension usually has the form ***-iw-***: *-dyíwá*, *-díwá*, *-mwíwá*. Some speakers have *-píwá* as the passive of *-pá* 'give', but others have *-púwá*."

| Active | Passive |
| --- | --- |
| *-cheka* cut | *-chekwa* be cut |
| *-sona* sew | *-sonwa* be sewn |
| *-nyora* write | *-nyorwa* be written |
| *-dyá* eat | *-dyíwá* be eaten |
| *-pá* give | *-píwá* / *-púwá* be given |

The subject of a passive verb is the thing done to, and the verb agrees with it: *Sadza **rá**dyǐwǎ* (class 5), *Muríwó **wá**kachékwá* (class 3).

**Group 1** — "I cut up the muriwo." "The muriwo was cut up by you.":

| Cue | Active | Passive |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *iní* | *Ndakáchěkǎ muríwó.* | *Muríwó wákachékwá nemẉí.* (or *… ndímẉí*) |
| *mukúnda* | *Mukúnda wákachéká muríwó.* | *Muríwó wákachékwá nộmǔkúnda.* |
| *mhandara* | *Mhandara yákachéká muríwó.* | *Muríwó wákachékwá nemhándara.* |
| *muníng'ína* | *Muníng'ína wákachéká muríwó.* | *Muríwó wákachékwá nộmǔníng'ína.* |
| *vasíkaná* | *Vasíkaná vákachéká muríwó.* | *Muríwó wákachékwá ną̂vǎsíkaná.* |

FSI's line pairs *iní* "I" with "by you" (*nemẉí*); take it as a drill of the form.

**Group 3** — "Active with object prefix vs. passive." "My older brother gave me some money." "I was given money by my older brother.":

| Active | Passive |
| --- | --- |
| *Mukóma vándǐpa marí.* | *Ndapíwá marí namukóma.* (*Ndapúwá …*) |
| *Mukóma vádyǎ sadza.* | *Sadza rádyǐwǎ namukóma.* |
| *Mukóma vámwǎ mahéu.* | *Mahéu ámwǐwǎ namukóma.* |
| *Mukóma ánodá vaníng'ina.* | *Vaníng'ína vánodíwá namukóma.* |

The first line shows what English does too: the person given to becomes the subject — *Nda-píwá marí*, "I was given money".

**Practice.** Do Groups 1 and 3 with your speaking partner: they give the active sentence, you turn it passive. Then take five things done in your house this week and say each both ways — who cooked the sadza, and by whom the sadza was cooked.
By whom? The doer after a passive:
FSI Unit 23, Note 1, the second set of facts. "The noun or pronoun that stands for the person or thing by which the action of the verb was accomplished is preceded by a non-concordial prefix, which is either ***n-*** or ***nd-*** or ***ng-*** according to dialect. The non-concordial prefix is, as always, combined with the appropriate form of the linking prefix."

So "by" is Stage 4's *na* — *no-*, *na-*, *ne-* by class — or, in some dialects, *ndi-*: *naBabá* or *ndíBabá* "by Father", *namáí* or *ndímáí* "by Mother".

If you wish: the -chi- form:
FSI Unit 23, Note 2 — "The '-chi- participial' form of verbs." "The basic dialogue contains the expression":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Kuti ùchídá …* | If you wish … |

"This form of the verb *-dá* 'to want, love, like' contains, in addition to the subject prefix *ù-*, the non-initial prefix ***-chí-***. A form of this kind, here called the '**chi-participial**', **never serves as the main verb** in a sentence. It does however have a number of other important uses … The construction which consists of the word ***kuti*** (or ***kana***) plus this form is usually translated into English with an **if-clause**. Other uses of the chi-participial will be met in later units" — Unit 24's "why?" and Unit 25's "go on".

**Its tones.** "In chi-participial forms, the subject prefix is **always low** in tone, whether for first, second, or third person, and the Class 1 prefix is ***à-*** even in those dialects for which the Class 1 subject prefix in indicative forms is *u-*":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *únodá …* (some dialects) | he wants |
| *ánodá …* (standard dialects) | he wants |
| *kuti àchídá* (all of the above dialects) | if he likes |

"The tone of *-chí-* is **always high**. The first tone of a polysyllabic low verb stem that follows *-chí-* is also **raised**. (In some dialects, one or more additional stem syllables may be raised in this way.)":

| High verbs | Low verbs |
| --- | --- |
| *kuti uchídá* | *kuti uchíti* |
| *kuti uchísándá* | *kuti uchísóna* |
| *kuti uchísévénzá* | *kuti uchítáura* |
| *kuti uchísévénzésa* | *kuti uchígádzirira* |

With object prefixes — FSI writes the object prefix *ǐ*, low in the central reading, and the stem after it as before:

| High verbs | Low verbs |
| --- | --- |
| *kuti uchírǐdá* | |
| *kuti uchírǐténgá* | *kuti uchírǐsóna* |
| *kuti uchírǐténgésá* | *kuti uchírǐgádzira* |
| *kuti uchírǐsévénzésa* | *kuti uchírǐgádzirira* |

And *-dáro*: *kuti uchídaró* "if you do so".

| *nhangá* | 9, 10 | yard |
| *-nángísíka* | | to look, appear |

**What is in it.** A unit of verb extensions. ***-kúrá*** grow, and ***-kúdzá*** make grow, grow (flowers); ***-sándísá*** "make work", use, beside Unit 23's *-sévénzésa* — the causative, which FSI names but does not yet teach. ***-díkáná*** "be wanted" (from *-dá*) and ***-nángísíka*** "look, appear" (from *-nángísá* "look at") carry the new neuter extension. ***Ngéṇyi vachíǎdá?*** "Why do they like them?" is the *-chi-* form after "why". *vánoádísá* "they like them very much" is *-dísá*, "like very much", with *-a-* "them" (class 6, *maruva*). *Ndirí kudirira* — Stage 3's *-ri* + infinitive, "I am watering".

| *Ngéṇyi* + *-chi-* form | why? |
| ordinary verb + *ngéṇyi* | with what? by what? (Unit 21) |

Visible, edible, drinkable: -ik-, -ek-:
FSI Unit 24, Note 2 — "The neuter extension *-ik-*." "A new verbal extension is illustrated in the sentences":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Maruva mazhínzhí ánodíkáná.* | Many flowers are needed. |
| *Nhangá dzínonángísíka zvakánáka.* | The yards look nice. |

"The verb stem *-nángísíka* 'to appear, look, seem' is to be compared with the stem *-nángísá* 'to look at', and *-díkáná* with *-dá* 'to want, like, love, need'. Compare also the stems":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *-óná* to see | *-ónéká* be seen, be visible |
| *-ita* to do | *-itika* to be done |
| *-témá* to cut | *-téméká* to be cuttable |

"The extension illustrated by these pairs of stems has two forms: ***-ek-*** when the vowel of the preceding syllable is *o* or *e*, and ***-ik-*** after *i, a, u*. Its tone is high with high stems, and low with low stems." (The same vowel rule as Unit 21's *-er-*/*-ir-*.) FSI's name for it, "neuter", is Fortune's (*An Analytical Grammar of Shona*, §405 ff.).

"The two most common meanings associated with the neuter extension are":

1. "to be ___able": *-ónéká* "to be visible";
2. "to get done, **with no reference to the person or thing that performed the action**": *hazvíìtíkǐ* "it isn't done (in the sense of 'people just don't do it')".

"Compare a similar phrase, in which specification of the actor or doer makes necessary the passive extension, rather than the neuter": *Zvákáitwa ndíaní?* "By whom was it done?" — the next lesson.

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *-búdá* | | to come/go out from |
| *-bvira* | | here, used as an auxiliary verb to intensify the meaning of the verb whose infinitive follows it |
| *mbéú* | 9, 10 | seeds |
| *-ramba* | | to continue [with the chi-participial] |

FSI Unit 25, Note 1 — "Uses of the hodiernal tense of the verb *-vá*." "The sentences":

| infinitive | refuse | *Ánoramba kukúrá.* They refuse to grow. |

**What is in it.** ***nḍévenyú*** "yours" and ***nḍévangú*** "mine" are the independent possessives. ***váỵámẉó*** "they are now in it" is Unit 25's *-aya* with ***-mẉo*** "in there" (class 18) on the end, and ***tinácho*** "we have it" is *-na* with *-cho*, the class 7 concord plus *-o*: both are this unit's *~o* forms. *Váỵá muchikóro* is *-aya* with no infinitive at all: "they now are in school". *Kwákátaurwa nḍộrǔzóróro* is Unit 23's passive with a place-class subject — "it was spoken about the holiday" — and Unit 21's *nge-* (as *nḍọ-*) "about". *Zvộkǔfámbísá* "transport" is Unit 21's linking prefix before an infinitive, with no noun: "things for making go". *dzą(né)zúro* "of yesterday": FSI brackets the *ne*.

*Ehúnde*, like Unit 25's *Hunde*, is "yes" beside *hóngu*; FSI does not say whose it is. *Mẉakáṇzwawó*: *mẉa-* eastern (standard *ma-*), *-ṇzwa* "hear" with the dotted *ṇ* some speakers drop.

FSI Unit 26, Note 1 — "Concords plus *~o* after *-na-*." "The dialogue contains the sentences":

*Vari kuiteṇyiyo?* "what are they doing there?" ends in Unit 26's *-yo*; *nechikochikari* "by oxcart" and *nemudhudhudhu* "by motorcycle" are Unit 23's transport with *na*. FSI glosses nothing in these lines; two words are new — *-kwira* (of the bus) and *mufambiri wezvikoro* (*-famba* "go", *zvikoro* "schools") — so get them from your speaking partner.

**Reading.** Unit 24's oral reading, untoned: read it aloud, mark the tones, translate:

> *Baba, muri kudíkánwá. Kupi? Kuchikoro. Naani? Nọmudzidzisi mukuru. Anodeṇyi? Kwasvika spíkita ['inspector']. Zvakanaka. Ndichambopedza kudyá.*

*kudíkánwá* "being wanted" is the passive of the neuter *-dikana*; *Naani?* "by whom?".

And Unit 21's:

> *Ndiani ẉaenda kundotambira mufundisi? Baba Marata ẉaenda. Ndakatenga mbatya itsva. Wakatenga kupi? Ndakatenga kuMarondera. Unoda dovi pachingwa here? Vana vanodisa dovi here? Mwakamboedza muto wedovi here? Mbuya venyu vanobika zvakanaka here? Mugwagwa mupamhi unoenda kupi? Unoenda kuNyanga. Munotsauka papi kuenda Bòndà? Pabandéra rechípirí. Baba vaenda kuhosipitari. Vaneṇyi? Vanọ ruvoko.*

> *Uchaenda ngépi kwáMutáre? NgekuPéniranga. Ah! Hamúzívi heré mugwagwa mutsva? Mutsvá múpfúpi kupinda wekáre. Ndaiziva zvangu, asi ndaida kuona shamwari ìri Péniranga.*

*Uchaenda ngépi?* is *nge-* on *-pi*, "by where?" — which way; *NgekuPéniranga*, "by way of Peniranga".

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, this week:

1. Offer to do five things *for* them, and ask five things of them, with the applicative: *Ndingakubikira …*, *Ungandigadzirira …?*
2. Tell them what you do for yourself and alone, and what is done for you, and by whom (*-zvi-*, *~oga*, the passive with *na*).
3. Ask and answer "why?" with *Ngenyi … -chi-?* and *Nokuti …*; and make "if" offers with *Kuti uchida …*.
4. Go round a house or farm: what is edible, drinkable, cuttable, visible (*-ik-/-ek-*); what is now growing, now finished (*-aya*); what will go on growing (*-ramba*).
5. Point at things and ask whose they are, whether they have one, and where they keep it — *ndeyangu*, *ndinayo*, *-po* — and let them correct every concord.

**Then.** Stage 7 follows FSI from Unit 27.
Planting flowers:
FSI Unit 27. Someone has planted flowers in stony ground:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | *Ndadyárá maruva ángu.* | I've planted my flowers. |
| B | *Ánoita here paną́ matombó?* | Will they do [all right] where there are rocks? |
| A | *Ndicháédza kunóngá` ọsé.* | I'll try to pick them all [out]. |
| A | *Ndãpédza ndóísa mupfúdze.* | When I've finished, I'll put [on] fertilizer. |
| B | *Zvínóita heré?* | Does that work? |
| A | *Zvínóbvira kuita kwázvo.* | It really does. |
| B | *Ndicházoúyá kundoáóná.* | I'll come later to see them. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *-nóngá* | | to pick up |
| *mupfúdze* | | fertilizer, manure (Note 1 writes *mapfudze*) |
| *matombó* | | rocks, stones |

**What is in it.** *Ndadyárá* is the past of today, and *Ndicháédza* the *-cha-* future. ***paną́ matombó*** "where there are rocks" is class 16 *pa-* with *-na* "have" (Stage 5's *pane*, "there is"); the mark under the vowel says the vowel differs by dialect (*pana/pane*). *ọsé* "all" agrees with *matombó* (class 6: *ose*). *kundoáóná* "to go and see them" has Stage 2's *-ndo-* and the class 6 object *-a-*, for the flowers.

The new thing is ***Ndãpédza*** "when I've finished", with FSI's new mark. It is the subject of the next three lessons. *Ndóísa* "I'll put" is Stage 4's *-o-* form, here "then I put".

**The new mark, *ã*.** FSI, Unit 27: "The symbol /~/ above a vowel letter stands for one or more tonal patterns, according to dialect." It sits on the first syllable of a tonal participial. In both systems FSI sets out, that syllable is **high** — say it high, and take the rest of the word from your partner.

Tone marks as in earlier stages: *á* high, unmarked low, *ǎ* low and *â* high in the central (standard) reading, *ā* a raised low, **ˣ** a tone that varies between speakers. A dot under a letter means some speakers leave it out; FSI's dotted *ẉ* is eastern, and the standard drops it.

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 27 and shadow the dialogue. Then tell your speaking partner what you planted, or would plant, and where; have them ask *Ánoita here …?* and answer with what you'll do first.

When I've finished: tonal participials:
FSI Unit 27, Note 1. "The basic dialogue and the sentences of the supplementary vocabulary section contain the sentences":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ***Ndãpédza** ndóísa mapfudze.* | When I've finished I add manure. |
| ***Tãgúta** tinóbvísa ndíró.* | When we've had enough, we remove the dishes. |
| *Hárí **yãvìra**, ndinóǐsa murívó muhárí.* | When the pot has boiled, I put the murivo into the pot. |
| *Kuti murívó **wãíbva** ndinóbúrá.* | When the murivo is done, I dish it out. |

**The new mark, *ã*.** FSI, Unit 27: "The symbol /~/ above a vowel letter stands for one or more tonal patterns, according to dialect." It sits on the first syllable of a tonal participial. In both systems FSI sets out, that syllable is **high** — say it high, and take the rest of the word from your partner.

**Two systems.** "Its simplest representation is found in some varieties of Manyika. In these dialects, the first syllable of each of these words has high tone regardless of person; the next has low, the next high, and so on, with alternant high and low syllables. A more widespread system has high tone on the first syllable, as in the above. The second syllable has **basic tone** on the first syllable of the root: low for low verbs, high for high verbs":

| | Indicative | Some Manyika | More widespread |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| High verbs | *ndàpédzá* | *ndápèdzá* | *ndápédzà* |
| | *tàgútá* | *tágùtá* | *tágútà* |
| | *váǐbvǎ* | *váìbvá* | *váíbvà* |
| Low verbs | *yávírà* | *yávìrá* | *yávìrá* |

(Here FSI writes every tone out, low with a grave.) So the participial differs from the indicative *ndàpédzá* "I've finished" by tone alone — standard spelling writes both *ndapedza*.

**FSI's caution.** "The details of tonal patterns as used with object prefixes, and with other tenses vary greatly by dialect and will not be discussed here … The student should make certain (1) whether his teacher uses the same tonal pattern for both high and low verbs in these forms, and (2) exactly what the tonal patterns are." Your speaking partner decides.

**What they are for.** "These forms are '**tonal participials**'. As the name implies, they are partially similar in their use to the so-called '*chi*-participial' forms" — Stage 6's *-chi-*. "One important use … is illustrated in this Unit; in this use, the English translation of the tonal participial of the 'hodiernal' tense" — the past of today — "commonly begins with '**when** (subject) **has** (verb).' They may or may not be preceded by ***kuti*** or ***kana***."

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Ndàpédzá.* | indicative | I've finished. |
| *Ndãpédza, …* | tonal participial | When I've finished, … |
| *Kuti ndãpédza, …* / *Kana ndãpédza, …* | the same, with "if, when" | When I've finished, … |

**Practice.** Say the four sentences above to your speaking partner, then make a chain of your own day: *Ndãpédza basa, ndinóenda kumushá* — "when I've finished work …" — each step starting from the last. Ask them which of FSI's two systems they use, and copy it.
I saw him at home: -ri as a participial:
FSI Unit 27, Group 1: "Tonal participial forms of *-ri*, with and without locative concords plus *~o*." Stage 3's *-ri* "be" has a participial too: "I saw him [he being] at home". The right-hand column puts Stage 5's place enclitic on it instead of the place: "I saw him **there**."

| Cue | I saw him (being) at … | I saw him there. |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *pamushá* | *Ndamúǒnǎ` ãri pamushá.* | *Ndamúǒnǎ` ãripó.* |
| *ívo* | *Ndaváǒnǎ` vãri pamushá.* | *Ndaváǒnǎ` ãripó.* (FSI; *vãripó* is meant) |
| *mumbá* | *Ndaváǒnǎ` vãri mumbá.* | *Ndaváǒnǎ` vãrimẉó.* |
| *imẉí* | *Ndakúǒnaṇyí mũri mumbá.* | *Ndaváǒnǎ` mũrimẉo.* (FSI; *Ndakúǒnaṇyí mũrimẉo* is meant) |
| *kudhíbhi* | *Ndakúǒnaṇyí mũri kudhíbhi.* | *Ndakúǒnaṇyí mũriyó.* |
| *iwé* | *Ndakúǒnǎ` ũri kudhíbhi.* | *Ndakúǒnǎ` ũriyó.* |
| *pamunda* | *Ndakúǒnǎ` ũri pamunda.* | *Ndakúǒnǎ` ũripó.* |
| *íye* | *Ndamúǒnǎ` ãri pamunda.* | *Ndamúǒnǎ` ãripó.* |

**How it is built.** The verb before it has the object (*-mú-* him, *-vá-* them, *-kú-* you): *Ndamúǒnǎ* "I saw him". Then the person seen gets *-ri* with **their own** subject prefix in the participial tone: ***ãri*** (he/she), ***vãri*** (they), ***ũri*** (you, sg.), ***mũri*** (you, pl.). For "you (pl.)", cue *imẉí*, FSI writes *Ndakúǒnaṇyí*, with *-nyi* added for the plural.

**The place enclitics** are Stage 5's: *-pó* for a *pa-* place, *-yó* (FSI) for a *ku-* place, *-mẉó* for a *mu-* place. So *ãripó* "he being there (at it)", *vãrimẉó* "they being in there".

**The new mark, *ã*.** FSI, Unit 27: "The symbol /~/ above a vowel letter stands for one or more tonal patterns, according to dialect." It sits on the first syllable of a tonal participial. In both systems FSI sets out, that syllable is **high** — say it high, and take the rest of the word from your partner. So *ãri*, *vãri*, *ũri*, *mũri* all begin high, whatever the person.

FSI's two right-hand slips (*ãripó* for *vãripó*, *Ndaváǒnǎ` mũrimẉo* for *Ndakúǒnaṇyí mũrimẉo*) are corrected in brackets above; say the corrected form.

Tone marks as in earlier stages: *á* high, unmarked low, *ǎ* low and *â* high in the central (standard) reading, *ā* a raised low, **ˣ** a tone that varies between speakers. A dot under a letter means some speakers leave it out; FSI's dotted *ẉ* is eastern, and the standard drops it.

**Practice.** Your speaking partner gives the cue word, you give both columns. Then tell them where you saw three people today — *Ndamúǒnǎ` ãri kuchitóro* — and have them ask *Ndíaní?* and *Kúpǐ?*

FSI Unit 28. A traveller asks the way:

| A | *Ndirí kuenda kwáMurádzikwá.* | I'm going to Muradzikwa. |
| B | *Pachikóro chaípo heré?* | Right to the school? |

| B | *Unópfúúrá nepó ũsiṇg̨amírǐ heré?* | Will you pass there without stopping? |
| A | *Hóngu.* | Yes. |
| B | *Mungátǒrą̌` zvényú uyu mugwagwa.* | You can take this road. |
| B | *Munórǎmba mũiné (mũne) wọkúrunzeré.* | You bear left. ('You continue (you) with the left [hand].') |

| --- | --- | --- |
| *-pfúúrá* | | to pass |
| *-mírá* | | to stand, stop |

Three new forms, each with a lesson of its own:

- ***chaípo*** "itself, right (to)" — Note 2.
- ***ũsiṇg̨amírǐ*** "without stopping, you not stopping" — Note 3, the negative participial.
- ***mũiné*** "(you) having", in *-ramba mũiné …* "keep to …" — Note 1.

*wọkúrunzeré* "of the left" is the linking prefix of Stage 5 on Stage 5's *kurunzeré* "to the left", agreeing with *mugwagwa* (class 3, *w-*).

Bear left: participials with -na:
FSI Unit 28, Note 1. "In the sentence":

> *Munórǎmba **mũiné** wọkúrunzeré.* — You bear left.

"the verb *-ramba* is followed by the participial form ***mũiné*** or (depending on dialect) ***mũne***." Stage 4's *-ne* "have" is the stem *-na*, and it has participials like any verb.

"The latter is perfectly regular from the point of view of the forms discussed in Unit 27, Note 1. The former has the alternating high and low tones that are characteristic of tonal participials, but has the **extra syllable *-i-*** which is not present in the corresponding indicative *mùné*."

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *mùné* | indicative | you (pl.) have |
| *mũne* | participial | you having |
| *mũiné* | participial, with *-i-* | you having |

So *-ramba* + participial is "keep on, continue": *Munórǎmba mũiné wọkúrunzeré*, "you continue having the left" — keep to the left.

Without stopping: the negative participi:
FSI Unit 28, Note 3. "In Sentence 6":

> *Unópfúúrá nepó **ũsǐṇg̨amírǐ** heré?* — 'Will you pass there **you-not-stopping**?'

"the word *ũsǐṇg̨amírǐ* is the negative counterpart of the affirmative *chi*-participial *ùchímírá* (or of the tonal participial *únòmírà*). Its formation is somewhat different however, in two principal ways":

1. "Like the negative indicative *hàúmírí*, the negative participial **ends with the vowel *-i***."
2. "The negative participial is like the affirmative tonal participials in that it **begins with a high tone regardless of the person** of the subject; but the tonal pattern of the remaining syllables is not that of the affirmative tonal participials."

So: subject prefix + ***-singa-*** + stem ending in ***-i***.

| *hàúmírí* | you don't stop (indicative) |
| *ùchímírá* | you stopping (Stage 6) |
| *ũsǐṇg̨amírǐ* | you not stopping, without stopping |

"The negative participial forms that correspond to indicative affirmative forms (e.g. *hamúná*) and participial affirmative (e.g. *múiné*) that contain a subject prefix plus *-na* consist of **the subject prefix plus the negative prefix *-si-* plus *-na***. Its buildings: possessives with two conc:
FSI Unit 29, Note 1. "The dialogue for this unit contains the sentence":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Guta **ráchò** rákakúrá` séṇyi?* | How big is (its) city? |
| *Zvivákó **zvárò** zvákáreba séṇyi?* | How tall are its buildings? |

"The underlined forms are possessives, and the possessor involved is **non-personal**. These forms contain not one but **two concords**":

- "The **first** concord in each of these words agrees with **the thing possessed**, just as with the personal possessives *~ángu, ~ákó* etc. Thus the *r-* in *ráchò* is Class 5 to agree with *guta*, and the *zv-* of *zvárò* agrees with *zvivákó*."
- "The **second** concord in each of these words indicates **the class of the possessor**, if the possessor is specified: the *-r-* in *zvaro* agrees with *guta*. Where the possessor is not specified, the concord ***-ch-*** of Class 7 may be used, as in the first of the above examples."

So: possessed-concord + *-a-* + possessor-concord + *-o*.

"Note that the tonal pattern is **high–low** except when the second concord is a locative: ***dzèmẉó*** 'of in it'." (FSI writes the locative forms *dzemẉó, yemẉó, emẉó* with *e*.)

It is a road: independent nouns:
FSI Unit 29, Note 2: "Independent nouns. [This was covered in less detail in 16.1.]" — Stage 4's independent form, now in full.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Guta ráchò rákakúrá` séṇyi?* | How big is its city? |
| *Íguta gúrú.* | It is a large city. |
| *mùgwagwa* | road |
| *Mùgwagwa wákáreba.* | The road is long. |
| *mùgwagwa wàkáréba* | a long road ('a road which is long') |
| *Múgwágwa wàkáréba.* | It is a long road. ('It is a road which is long.') |

"Except for its first and second person forms, an **indicative** verb (e.g. *wákáreba*) has **high** tone on its first prefix, and it serves as the nucleus of its sentence. A **relative** verb (e.g. *wàkáréba*) does not serve as the nucleus of its sentence, and it has **low** tone on its first prefix."

"Nouns do not usually serve as nucleus of a sentence, and the tone of noun prefixes is ordinarily low: *mùgwagwa*. But a noun may also be used as a nucleus of a sentence, or even as a sentence by itself":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Múgwágwa.* | It is a road. |
| *Múgwágwa murefú.* | It is a long road. |

**The rule.** "When a noun is used in this way, the tone of its **prefix is high** … The **first of two or more consecutive low tones** following the prefix becomes high also." So *mù-gwa-gwa* → *mú-gwá-gwa*.

"What has just been said applies quite clearly to nouns in classes that have overt syllabic prefixes. These are all of the classes except **5, 9, and 10**. Nouns of these last three classes follow the rule … except that the '**dummy prefix**' ***i-*** carries the high tone: *gùtà* 'city' but *íguta* 'it is a city.'"

**In the west, highs drop.** "In westerly dialects, one or more high stem tones that follow the high-toned prefix may be lowered":

| Simple form | | Independent form | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *húkú* | chicken | *íhǔkǔ* | it is a chicken |
| *shúka* | sugar | *íshǔka* | it is sugar |
| *mukómaná* | boy | *múkǒˣmaná* | it is a boy |
| *chivákó* | building | *chívǎkǒ* | it is a building |

Read centrally, *ǔ* and *ǒ* are low: *íhùkù*, *chívàkò*. "This seems to be the case in most or all dialects, if the prefix is followed by only one syllable: *mùtí* tree — *mútì* (and not *\*mútí*)."

Seeing one another: -ana:
FSI Unit 29, Note 3. "The extension ***-an-*** is added to verb stems to carry the idea of **reciprocity**":

| | |

| *Vánozvíòná.* | They see themselves. |
| *Vánoónaná.* | They see one another. |

The four lines set it beside Stage 4's object prefix (*-va-* them) and Stage 6's reflexive (*-zvi-* themselves). *-ona* + *-an-* + *-a* = *-onana*. | A | *Ndiri kutsvaka nzira ìnóěnda Nyánga.* | I'm looking for the road that goes to Nyanga. |
| B | *Tórá ìnósvǐka paWatsómbá.* | Take the one that gets to Watsomba. |
| A | *Handípǎzíví paWatsómbá.* | I don't know Watsomba. |
| B | *Tóráyí iyi nzira. Ínósvika paWatsómbá.* | Take this road. It gets to Watsomba. |

| B | *Unótórá nzira irí kurudyí.* | You take the road on the right. |
| A | *Hapáná ìnótsáúká heré?* | Isn't there one that turns off? |
| B | *Dzọ́sé dzínóenda kurunzeré.* | They all go to the left. |

| *-rásá* | | to throw away, to lose |
| *-vá* | | to become, be |
| *pfungwá* | 9, 10 | thought |

**What is in it.** *Ríniko?* is *ríni?* "when?" with the *-ko* of Unit 28's *kúpiko*. *Musí wọMúgobéra* is Stage 2's "on Saturday" (FSI's mark: *wo-* or *we-* by dialect). *Wakámbótsvaka* has *-mbo-*, which in a question like this is "at all" (Stage 5). *Zvínó zvákáita séṇyi?* "so what happened?" begins with *zvino* "now, so". *Tingámbóedzązvé* is *-nga-* "can" + *-mbo-* "a bit" + *-zve* "again". *Íngavą́ pfungwá yakánáka* is *-nga-* with *-vá* "be": "it would be a good thought".

Three new forms, with lessons of their own:

- ***Ngátíénde*** "let's go" — the **hortative**.
- ***tíbvezvé*** "(and) we leave again" — the **subjunctive** of *-bva*.
- ***zvąndĩnógoná*** "such as I am able" and ***apo tãvàmba*** "where we began" — tonal participials after the linking prefix and after a demonstrative.

**The new mark, *ã*.** FSI, Unit 27: "The symbol /~/ above a vowel letter stands for one or more tonal patterns, according to dialect." It sits on the first syllable of a tonal participial. In both systems FSI sets out, that syllable is **high** — say it high, and take the rest of the word from your partner.

Tone marks as in earlier stages: *á* high, unmarked low, *ǎ* low and *â* high in the central (standard) reading, *ā* a raised low, **ˣ** a tone that varies between speakers. A dot under a letter means some speakers leave it out; FSI's dotted *ẉ* is eastern, and the standard drops it.

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 30. Then lose something in the room with your speaking partner — keys, a pen — and play the dialogue for it: when, where you looked, what happened, and *Ngátíénde …* to look again.

That we may go: the subjunctive:
FSI Unit 30, Note 1. "In the sentence":

> *Ngátíénde **tíbvezvé** apo tãvàmba.* — Let's go and [start] again from where we began.

"the word ***tíbvè*** is a new form of *-bvá* 'to go from'. This form is called **SUBJUNCTIVE**. Subjunctives differ from other forms in two ways":

1. "the subject prefix (*ti-* in this example) may stand **immediately before the root** (*-bv-* in this example). There is **no prefix syllable** associated with the subjunctive."
2. "The **final vowel** in all dialects is ***-è***."

"Another characteristic of subjunctives is that **the subject prefix has high tone regardless of person**. The first stem syllable is also high (e.g. *tíéndè* 'that we may go') unless it is also the last syllable of the word (as in *tíbvè*). At least some dialects have a tonal difference in the subjunctive between high and low verbs with three or more stem syllables":

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low | *títáùrè* | that we may speak |
| High | *tísévénzè* | that we may work |

"Subjunctives may have **aspect prefixes** (*-mbo-, -zo-* etc.) and/or **object prefixes** but **no tense prefixes** (*-no-, -ka-, -cha-* etc.)."

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *ti-* + *-end-* + *-e* | *tíéndè* that we may go |
| *ti-* + *-bv-* + *-e* | *tíbvè* that we may leave |
| *ti-* + *-taur-* + *-e* | *títáùrè* that we may speak |

**Group 5 — infinitive vs. subjunctive:** "They're in the house sewing." / "Let's go into the house and sew." The subjunctive is the second verb, "and (so that we may) …":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Várí mumbá kusona.* | *Ngátípíndewó mumbá tísóne.* |
| *Várí mumbá kubika.* | *Ngátípíndewó mumbá tíbíke.* |
| *Várí mumbá kutaurirana.* | *Ngátípíndewó mumbá títáurirane.* |
| *Várí mumbá kuchéká murívó.* | *Ngátípíndewó mumbá tíchéke murívó.* |
| *Várí mumbá kugadzira tíi.* | *Ngátípíndewó mumbá tígádzire tíi.* |
| *Várí mumbá kumwá tíi.* | *Ngátípíndewó mumbá tímwe tíi.* |
| *Várí mumbá kugezà ndíro.* | *Ngátípíndewó mumbá tígéze ndíró.* |
| *Várí mumbá kuverenga.* | *Ngátípíndewó mumbá tívérenge.* |

(FSI's seventh line has a typing slip, *mukbá* for *mumbá*.) *-sona* is "to sew", from the gloss. The *-wó* on *Ngátípíndewó* softens the suggestion (Stage 5).

Let's go: the hortative:
FSI Unit 30, Note 2. "In the same sentence … was found the word ***ngátíénde*** 'let's go'. This is a **HORTATIVE** form of *-enda*. In its form, the hortative consists simply of an initial prefix ***ngá-*** plus the subjunctive as described above. Hortative forms that have a first person plural subject (as in the example) are ordinarily translated into English with '**let's** ___'. With other subject prefixes, modern English may use a variety of translations":

> *Matombó **ngáá**bvíswè.* — Let the stones be removed. / Have the stones removed. / The stones should be removed.

The field that they ploughed:
FSI Unit 30, Note 3: "Tonal participials used after the linking prefix (or, according to dialect, after a distal demonstrative)." "Group 6 contains the sentences":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Takáǒnǎ munda **wąvãkarima**.* | We saw the field that they ploughed. |
| *Takádyâ sadza **rąvãkabika**.* | We ate the food that they cooked. |

"In these sentences, *wąvãkarima* modifies *munda*, and *rąvãkabika* modifies *sadza*. The two verb forms are thus comparable to English relative clauses."

**Two kinds of "that".** Stage 3's relative verbs were used in sentences like *(Nzira) ìnósvǐka…* "(the path) which gets to …" and *(Munhu) ànózívá…* "(the person) who knows …". "In constructions of this kind, the subject prefix of the relative verb **agrees with** … some noun in the preceding part of the sentence: *ì-* agrees with *nzira*, and *à-* agrees with *munhu*." The path does the getting; the person does the knowing.

"In the two sentences cited at the beginning of this note, the subject prefix of the last verb (*va-*) does **not** agree with anything that precedes it … Furthermore, the tonal pattern of the verb is **participial** (Unit 27, Note 1) and not relative (Unit 11, Note 1). Most striking of all, the verb *vãkarìma* follows a prefix which consists of **a concordial element plus the linking prefix**, (i.e. *wą-* and *rą-*). It is these concordial elements *w-* and *r-* which agree with something else in the sentence (respectively *munda* and *sadza*)."

So when the noun is the **object** — "the field that *they* ploughed" — the verb keeps its own subject (*va-* they), and the noun's concord comes in front, on the linking prefix:

| | noun | concord + link | participial |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the field that they ploughed | *munda* (3) | *wą-* | *vãkarima* |
| the sadza that they cooked | *sadza* (5) | *rą-* | *vãkabika* |
| the letter that I received | *tsamba* (9) | *yą-* | *ndãgashira* |
| the work that you do | *basa* (5) | *rą-* | *ũnoita* |

The mark under the *a* is FSI's: the vowel of the link differs by dialect.

**The Manyika way.** "In some forms of Manyika, and perhaps elsewhere, the combination of concord plus linking prefix is not used. Instead, the distal demonstrative is used, followed by a tonal participial":

| demonstrative | linking prefix | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *apo tãvamba* | *pą̀tãvamba* | where we began |
| *izvo ndĩnogona* | *zvąndĩnogona* | such as I am able |

Both are in Unit 30's dialogue: *apo tãvàmba*, *zvąndĩnógoná*.

Other examples given in the dictionary are *sáimbá* 'householder', *sázǐˣtǎˣ* 'namesake'."

**Group 1** — "I see something." / "What do you see?" ('What-thing of you-seeing?'). FSI heads it "Tonal participles that contain the prefix *-no-*", but the lines run through four tenses:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndinóóná chinhu.* | *Chínhuṇyí chąũnoona?* |
| *Ndaténgá chinhu.* | *Chínhuṇyí chąwãtenga?* |
| *Ndichágádzira chinhu.* | *Chínhuṇyí chąũchagadzira?* |
| *Ndadónhesa chinhu.* | *Chínhuṇyí chąwãdonhesa?* |
| *Ndarásá chinhu.* | *Chínhuṇyí chąwãrasa?* |
| *Ndinóda chinhu.* | *Chínhuṇyí chąũnoda?* |
| *Ndaténgésá chinhu.* | *Chínhuṇyí chąwãtengesa?* |

**Group 2 — "Contrast in tone between indicative and participial tone patterns":**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Vaná vari kuiteṇyi?* | What are the children doing? |
| *Mẉasíyá vaná vãri kuiteṇyi?* | What were the children doing when you left them? |

| *Vaná várí kupangana kundotámbá` zvávó.* | (FSI gives no English) |
| *Tasíyá vaná vãri kupangana kundotámbá` zvávó.* | |
| *Vaná vákarárá.* | |
| *Tasíyá vaná vãkarara.* | |

*várí* "they are" (indicative) beside *vãri* "them being" (participial) — the same letters. The last pair is "the children slept" / "we left the children asleep".

**Group 3 — "Negative tonal participial verbs":**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Áná marí heré?* | Does he have money? |
| *Haáná marí.* | He has no money. |
| *Takámǔsíyá ãsiná marí.* | We left him he-being without money. |
| *Ánozívá heré?* | Does he know? |
| *Haázíví.* | He doesn't know. |
| *Takámǔsíyá ãsíngazíví.* | We left him without his knowing. |
| *Mẉakáda kumúsíyá heré?* | Did you want to leave him? |
| *Hatíná kudá kumúsíyá.* | We didn't want to leave him. |
| *Takámǔsíyá tisíngadí.* | We left him unwillingly. |
| *Mẉakátaura here?* | Did you speak? |
| *Hatíná kutaura.* | We didn't speak. |
| *Takámǔsíyá tisiná kutaura.* | We left him without speaking. |
| *Mẉakámúóná here?* | Did you see him? |
| *Hatíná kumúóná.* | We didn't see him. |
| *Takámǔsíyá tisiná kumúóná.* | We left him without seeing him. |
| *Mẉakámǔbátsírá heré?* | Did you help him? |
| *Hatíná kumúbátsírá.* | We didn't help him. |
| *Takámǔsíyá tisiná kumúbátsírá.* | We left him without helping him. |

Each set of three goes question — negative indicative — negative participial: *haáná* → *ãsiná*, *haázíví* → *ãsíngazíví*, *hatíná kutaura* → *tisiná kutaura*. The participial's subject is whoever is "without": *ãsiná* he, *tisiná* we.

A letter I can't read:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndaóná munhu.* | I saw someone. |
| *Handímǔzívǐ.* | I don't know him. |

| *Handígoní kuiverenga.* | I can't read it. |

| *Wàtáura mazwí.* | You said something ('some words'). |
| *Handíǎṇzwí.* | I don't understand it ('them'). |
| *Wàtáura mazwí ạndisíngaṇzwí.* | You said something that I don't understand. |
| *Ánótaura mutauro.* | He speaks a language. |
| *Handíútaúri.* | I don't speak it. |
| *Ánótaura mutauro wąndisíngátaúri.* | He speaks a language that I don't speak. |
| *Ánóita iro basa.* | He does that work. |
| *Handíríítí.* | I don't do it. |
| *Ánóita basa rąndisíngáití.* | He does work that I don't do. |
| *Ẉákadyá chinhu.* | He ate something. |
| *Handíchǐdyí.* | I don't eat it. |
| *Ẉákadyá chinhu chąndisíngadyí.* | He ate something that I don't eat. |
| *Ánodá bhúku.* | He wants a book. |
| *Handínaró.* | I don't have it. |
| *Ánodá bhúku rąndisiná.* | He wants a book that I don't have. |
| *Ánoóná mhuká.* | He sees some wild animals. |
| *Handídzǐónǐ.* | I don't see it. |
| *Ánoóná mhuká dząndísíngaónǐ.* | He sees wild animals that I don't see. |

**How it is built.** noun's concord + *a* + *ndi-* (I) + *-singa-* + stem + *-i*:

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *tsamba* (9) | *y-a-* | *ndi-singa-goni* | that I can't |
| *mazwi* (6) | *a-* | *ndi-singa-nzwi* | that I don't understand |
| *mutauro* (3) | *w-a-* | *ndi-singa-taur-i* | that I don't speak |
| *chinhu* (7) | *ch-a-* | *ndi-singa-dy-i* | that I don't eat |
| *bhuku* (5) | *r-a-* | *ndi-sina* | that I don't have |

The last line, *dząndísíngaónǐ*, prints clearly and shows the syllable high.

Go and water the seeds:
FSI Unit 31, Group 5: "Indicative vs. imperative or subjunctive; subjunctive as the second verb, following an imperative or a hortative verb." Each set: a question, a command or hortative, a second question and command, and then the two commands joined, the second as a subjunctive.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ẉáénda kugádheni heré?* | Did he go to the garden? |
| *Ngááénde kugádheni.* | Have him go to the garden. |
| *Ẉádírira mbéú heré?* | Did he water the seeds? |
| *Ngáádírire mbéú.* | Have him water the seeds. |
| *Ngááénde kugadheni ádírire mbéú.* | Have him go to the garden and water the seeds. |

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Árí kuramba achíkúrúngá heré?* | Is she continuing to stir? |
| *Ngáárámbe achíkúrúngá.* | She should keep stirring. |
| *Mapúndú ápěrǎ heré?* | Are all the lumps gone? |
| *Mapúndú ngáápére.* | All the lumps should disappear. |
| *Ngáárámbe achíkúrúngá mapúndú ápére.* | Have her keep on stirring so the lumps disappear. |

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mẉatópútsá mavhingẉa heré?* | Have you already broken up the clods? |
| *Pútsáṇyí mavhingẉa.* | Break up the clods. |
| *Ivú rírí nyoré heré?* | Is the earth soft? |
| *Ivú ngáríve nyoré.* | Let the earth be soft. |
| *Pútsáṇyí mavhingẉa ivú ríve nyoré.* | Break up the clods so that the earth will be soft. |

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Wapfútsa mẉotó heré?* | Have you lit the fire? |
| *Pfutsá mẉotó.* | Light the fire. |
| *Tinóda kugocha nyama.* | We want to cook some meat. |
| *Ngátígóche nyama.* | Let's cook some meat. |
| *Pfutsá mẉotó tígóche nyama.* | Light the fire so we [can] cook some meat. |

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Tichákánya zvidhína.* | We'll make some bricks. |
| *Ngátíkanye zvidhína.* | Let's make some bricks. |
| *Tichápǐsǎ zvidhína.* | We'll burn the bricks. |
| *Ngátípíse zvidhína.* | Let's burn the bricks. |
| *Ngátíkánye zvidhína típíse.* | Let's make some bricks and burn [them]. |

**What it shows.** After a hortative (*Ngááénde …*) or a plain command (*Pútsáṇyí …*, *Pfutsá …*), the next verb is a **subjunctive** without *ngá-*: *ádírire*, *ríve*, *tígóche*, *típíse*. It means "and …" or "so that …", and its subject need not be the same — *Pútsáṇyí mavhingẉa ivú ríve nyoré*, "you break the clods so that the soil (5) may be soft". *ríve* is the subjunctive of Unit 30's *-vá* "become, be"; *nyoré* is "soft" here. *Mapúndú ápére* "so that the lumps finish" is Unit 27's sadza again.

Tone marks as in earlier stages: *á* high, unmarked low, *ǎ* low and *â* high in the central (standard) reading, *ā* a raised low, **ˣ** a tone that varies between speakers. A dot under a letter means some speakers leave it out; FSI's dotted *ẉ* is eastern, and the standard drops it.

**Practice.** Do the five sets with your speaking partner: they ask, you give the command, then join the two. Then give them a real job with two steps — "go to the shop and buy bread", "light the fire so we can cook" — and have them give you one.
Stage 7 in conversation:
The end of Stage 7: tonal participials ("when …", "being …"), *-na* and its participials, *chaipo* and *chaizvo*, the negative participial *-singa-* and *-sina*, negative relatives, possessives of things, independent nouns, the reciprocal *-ana*, the subjunctive and the hortative, and "the … that someone did" with the linking prefix.

| *Hongu, takatogara pasi nẹkupangana.* | Yes, we've already sat down and made plans. |

| *Muvaki mẉaẏa naye here?* | What about a builder? Do you have one? |
| *Hongu vaẏa pano.* | Yes, he ('they') is here now. |
| *Munofunga kuvamba rini?* | When do you expect to begin? |
| *Mwedzi ùnouya.* | Next month. |

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Munovakira papi?* | Where are you going to build? |
| *Apo tãkapiwa naSipikita.* | The place assigned to us by the Inspector. |
| *Munofunga kupedza rini?* | When do you expect to finish? |
| *Tinoda kuti ifundirwe gore rìnouya.* | We want it to be used for study next year. |
| *Ndaṇzwá sábhǔˣku achitaura ng̣echibharo.* | I heard the headman talking about the tax. |
| *Ẉati kudini?* | What did he say? |
| *Ẉati vanhu vọse ngavaunze chibharo uko ãri.* | He said everyone should bring the tax to him ('to where he is'). |
| *Anoenda rini nacho kuNyanga?* | When is he taking it to Nyanga? |

| *Kwete, handisati ndãchiona.* | No, I haven't got it yet. |
| *Changu, tichaenda nacho manheru ano.* | **I**'m going to take **mine** this evening. |

Find the stage in it: *Apo tãkapiwa* "where we were given" (Unit 30's demonstrative + participial); *Mwedzi ùnouya*, *gore rìnouya* "the coming month, year" (relatives); *ngavaunze* a hortative and *kuti ifundirwe* a subjunctive after *kuti* "that"; *uko ãri* "where he is" (Unit 27's *-ri* participial); *Changu* "mine", an independent possessive (Stage 6). FSI writes *tonkanyisa* in one line for *tokanyisa*; and *handisati* "not yet" is new — learn it whole.

**Reading.** FSI's Unit 27 and 30 kitchens, untoned as printed — read aloud, mark the tones, translate:

> *Pfutsa mẉoto Sarah. Munoda weṇyi? Ndaẏá kuda kubika. Ndapfutsa mẉoto. Isa mvura muhari. Ndaisa pachoto. Sevha uṗfu mwanangu. Zvakanaka mai. Unza uṗfu. Hari yavira here? Hunde, ibva pamẉoto. Raẏa kukwata.*

> *Ndichambopfutsa mẉoto. Munouda weṇyi? Ndinoda kubika sadza. Ndiani ànobika sadza nhasi? Ndini ndicharibika. Munobikira mupi? Ndichabikira muhari diki. Tinoriguta here? Ndinofunga kudaro.*

FSI's English cues for the second: "What do you want it for?", "What will you cook in?", "Will we get enough to eat?".

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, this week:

1. Tell each other how to cook something, every step a "when I've …" (*ndã-*) or a "then I …" (*ndó-*).
2. Give directions with *-ramba mũiné*, *-singa-* "without stopping" and *chaipo* "right to".
3. Describe your town: its roads, its buildings, its trees (*-aro*, *-acho*, *-emwo*), and say what it is with independent nouns.
4. Plan a job together with hortatives and subjunctives: *Ngátí… tí…*, *Ngáá… á…*.
5. Talk about things you've lost, things you don't know, people you saw — "the … that I …", with and without *-singa-*.

**Then.** Stage 8 follows FSI from Unit 32: agentive nouns, negative commands, the tones of participials in the *-a-* tense, *-dai*, the verb prefix *-na-*, and the diminutive classes 12 and 13.

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *hókwa* | 9, 10 | invitation |
| *-koka* | | to invite a number of people |
| *muchato* | 3, 4 | wedding |
| *-chata* | | to marry |
| *-sanganisa* | | to cause to join one another |
| *musándíri* | 1, 2 | minister of the gospel |

**What is in it.** *Vákakókwa* "were invited" is *-koka* with the passive *-w-* of Stage 6. *Ndíaní ànózovásánganisa?* is a relative "who (is the one that) will join them", with *-zo-* (Stage 2) and the object *-vá-*. *Rwộkǔtángá* "first" is Stage 5's ordinal, *rw-* agreeing with *rugashiro* (11). *Mẉaẏá nêzvǐpô?* is literally "have you already (got) with gifts?"; *Handísatí ndãẏa nácho* "I haven't yet got one" has the *-sati* "not yet" that is this unit's lesson on the *-a-* tense. Line 10 gives two forms of one command — the negative command, a lesson of its own: FSI prints both endings because "the final vowel in negative commands may be /-a/ … or /-e/ …, depending on the dialect."

*muímbí* "singer" is made from *-ímbá* "sing" — the agentive nouns are the unit's first drill.

**FSI's supplementary words: housekeeping chores.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndinótsváírá mumbá.* | I sweep the house. |
| *Ndinógeza mumbá nọkúisa mushongá.* | I wash the house and put down disinfectant (*mushonga*). |
| *Ndinópukuta zvigaro nétáfura nêmǐbhédha.* | I dust the chairs, the table and the beds. |
| *Ndinógeza mafáfitera.* | I wash the windows. |
| *Ndinómísá midzíyó yọ́sé munzvimbo dzáyo.* | I put all the furniture in its places. |
| *Ndinógadzira imbá yọmwéni yộkǔrárá.* | I prepare the guest's room for sleeping. |
| *Ndinóisa zvọkúgezesa nệmǎfútá mumupanda mwáké.* | I put washing things and lotion in his room. |
| *Ndinózádzá mwenje ngẹpárafíni.* | I fill the lamp with paraffin. |
| *Ndinówaridza machírá nêmǐtsámíro zvakáchéna.* | I spread clean sheets and pillows. |

FSI gives these with their words only — *-pukuta* dust, *chigaro* (7, 8) chair, *táfura* (5, 6) table, *mubhédha* (3, 4) bed, *-mísá* put in place, *midzíyó* (4) furniture, utensils, *nzvimbo* (9, 10) place, *mwenje* (3, 4) lamp, candle, *-zárá* become full, *-waridza* spread out, *jírá* (5) / *machírá* (6) cloth, sheet, *mutsámíro* (3, 4) pillow, *-chena* become clean — so the English above is built from them; check it with your partner.

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 32. Then invite your speaking partner to something of your own — who is coming, who will speak, where it will be — and let them ask whether you have a gift yet. Finish with the chores: tell them what you do in the house before a guest comes.

Tone marks as before: *á* high, unmarked low; FSI's *ǎ* is low in the central (standard) reading, *â* high; a grave or \` a lowered syllable; **ˣ** a tone that varies between speakers; *ã* (the tilde) a syllable whose tone goes by dialect (Stage 8's lesson on *-sati* explains it); a dot under a letter means some speakers leave it out, a mark under a vowel (*ọ*, *ą*, *ẹ*) that two vowels are used by dialect. FSI's *mẉa-* "you (pl.)" is eastern; the standard says *ma-*.
Singer and singing: nouns made from verb:
FSI Unit 32, Exercises 1 and 2, and Unit 37, Exercise 3.

**Exercise 1** — "Verbs with agentive nouns." "Who sing?" "They are singers.":

| --- | --- | --- |

FSI leaves the rule for you: "The student should examine for himself the pairs of sentences in 1 and 2, and make a statement which summarizes the relationship between a verb stem and the noun which stands for the person who performs the action." What the pairs show:

| Verb | Person who does it (1 / 2) |
| --- | --- |
| *-ímbá* sing | *mu-ímb-í* / *va-ímb-í* |

| *-nyora* write | *mu-nyor-í* |
| *-fambisa* run (a school) | *mu-fambis-í* |

**Class 1/2 prefix + the verb stem, with its final *-a* changed to *-i*.** The extensions stay: *-fúndísa* teach gives *mufúndísi* teacher, *-téngésá* sell gives *mutengesi*. The tones in the drills are as printed; let your partner settle each one. (FSI's *vanórana? Várápi* has the verb misprinted: the noun is from *-rapa* "to do medical work, to cure", so *murapi* is a healer.)

*Murezi*, from *-reza*, is FSI's eastern form beside Stage 4's *-rera* "look after (a child)".

**The work itself: class 14.** Unit 37, Exercise 3 — "Relationship between verb and abstract noun of Class 14." "The wives are learning to cook." "Oh, so they're studying cookery are they?":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Vadzimáí vánofúndá kubika.* | *Vánofúndá ubikisú?!* |
| *Mąjahá ánòfúndá kuchaira.* | *Vánofúndá uchairisú?!* |
| *Vakómaná vánofúndá kuweza.* | *Vanófundá uwezisú?!* |
| *Varimi vánofúndá kurima.* | *Vánofúndá urimisú?!* |
| *Vasíkaná vánofúndá kurera vaná.* | *Vanofunda ureri kwậvǎnâsú?!* |

The same change makes the art: **class 14 *u-* + stem + *-i***. *ubiki* cookery, *uchairi* driving, *uwezi* woodwork, *urimi* farming, *ureri kwavana* bringing up children. Unit 37's *huroya* (14) "the work of being a lawyer" is another. The *-sú* on the end is the enclitic of surprise, the lesson after next but two.

**Practice.** Ask your speaking partner FSI's two questions in turn — *Ndívanáaní vànó…?* and *Mu… ánóiteṇyí?* — over every verb you know (*-rima*, *-bika*, *-nyora*, *-tengesa*, *-chaira*, *-veza*, *-fundisa*), and answer theirs; then make the class 14 noun for each and say who is studying it.
Don't: usa- and the negative command:
FSI Unit 32, Exercises 3 and 4. Unit 32's dialogue ended *Usanonoka / Usanonoke* "Don't delay!", and FSI's note on it: "the final vowel in negative commands may be /-a/ (as in /usaputsa/) or /-e/ (/usaputse/), depending on the dialect." FSI writes that vowel *ą*: say *a* or *e* as your partner does.

**Exercise 3** — "/-o-/ form vs. negative commands (sg)." "Shall I go into the house now?" "Don't go into the house.":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndópínda mumbá heré?* | *Usápíndą mumbá.* |
| *Ndópǔtsǎ mavhingwa heré?* | *Usáputsą mavhingwa.* |
| *Ndógádzira midárárá heré?* | *Uságádzirą midárárá.* |
| *Ndóchéra makombá heré?* | *Usáchérą makombá.* |
| *Ndódónhesa mbéú heré?* | *Usádónhesą mbéú.* |
| *Ndófúsira mbéú heré?* | *Usáfúsirą mbéú.* |
| *Ndóhǎrǎ mbéú heré?* | *Usáhárą(ba).* |

The *(ba)* is Stage 5's negative enclitic.

**Exercise 4** — the plural, to several or with respect:

| | |

| *Tóísa hárí pachotó heré?* | *Musáísą hárí pachotó.* |

| *Tókwǐdǐbǐdza hárí heré?* | *Musákwídíbídzą hárí.* |

**The form:**

| | Negative command |
| --- | --- |
| to one | ***U-sá-***píndą. don't go in |
| to several, or with respect | ***Mu-sá-***pfútsą. don't light it |

The subject prefix (*u-* you, *mu-* you pl.) + ***-sa-*** + the stem, ending *-a* or *-e* by dialect. In the drills *-sá-* is high and the stem keeps its own first tone: high *Usápíndą*, *Usáchérą*, but low *Usáputsą* (from *Ndópǔtsǎ*). Unlike Stage 4's plural command, the plural negative takes no *-i* on the end: *Musápfútsą*.

**Practice.** Your speaking partner asks Exercises 3 and 4 as they stand — *Ndó…? Tó…?* — and you forbid each one, singular then plural. Then ask them, about the room you are in, "shall I …?" and let them forbid you.
They told us not to: tisa-, with and wit:
FSI Unit 32, Exercise 5 — "Negative subjunctives with and without object prefix." The command of the last lesson has a subjunctive beside it (Stage 7): ***ti-sa-*** + stem + ***-e***, "that we not …", after *kuti* "that":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndayá kuenda kundodirira mbéú.* | I'm just now going to (go and) water the seeds. |
| *Vátítáurira kuti tisádírírę mbéú.* | They told us not to water the seeds. |
| *Vátítáurira kuti tisádzǐdírirę.* | They told us not to water them. |
| *Tóbvísa ndíró heré?* | Shall we remove the dishes now? |
| *Vátítáurira kuti tisábvísę ndíró.* | They told us not to remove the dishes. |
| *Vátítáurira kuti tisádzǐbvísę.* | They told us not to remove them. |
| *Munóda kukanya zvidhína heré?* | Do you want to make some bricks? |
| *Vátítáurira kuti tisákánye zvidhína.* | They told us not to make bricks. |
| *Vátítáurira kuti tisázvǐkánye.* | They told us not to make them. |
| *Endáṇyí múúngánídze marí.* | Go and collect money. |
| *Vátítáurira kuti tisáúngánídzę marí.* | They told us not to collect money. |
| *Vátítáurira kuti tisáǐúngánídzę.* | They told us not to collect it. |

*-kanya* "to mold" — bricks; *-unganidza* collect; *Vátítáurira* "they told us" is *-taurira* "speak to", with *-tí-* "us".

**The object goes after *-sa-*:** *tisá-**dzi**-dírire* (*dzi-*, the seeds, 10), *tisá-**zvi**-kánye* (*zvi-*, the bricks, 8), *tisá-**i**-úngánídze* (*i-*, the money, 9). FSI marks the object prefix *ǐ* — low in the central reading — and the stem after it lower than without one.

FSI will not give the rule from its own marks: "The student should enter here a summary statement concerning the tones of negative subjunctive verbs with and without object prefixes. The statement should of course be based on his own tutor's pronunciation of the verbs in Exercise 5, and not on the tone markings that appear in this book." So the pattern is your partner's to give you.

**Practice.** Have your speaking partner say each of the six things they are about to do; answer twice, *Vátítáurira kuti tisá… [noun]* and then with the object prefix instead of the noun. Ask them to say the pairs slowly first, and copy their tones, not the book's.
Who finished it? The causative answer:
FSI Unit 32, Exercise 6 — "Simple stems vs. causative." "The sugar is all gone." "Who used it up/finished it?" Each line says what happened; the answer asks who *made* it happen, with the causative stem:

| What happened | Who did it? | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Shuka yapera.* the sugar is finished | *Ndiani ẉàipedza?* who finished it? | *-pera* → *-pedza* |
| *Mwana ẉakarara.* the child has gone to sleep | *Ndiani ẉàmuradzika?* who put him to bed? | *-rara* → *-radzika* |
| *Mvura yavira.* the water has boiled | *Ndiani ẉàivirisa / waividza?* who boiled it? | *-vira* → *-virisa*, *-vidza* |
| *Mwaná wágára pasí.* the child has sat down | *Ndiani ẉàmugadzika?* who sat him down? | *-gara* → *-gadzika* |
| *Ndafárá!* I'm happy! | *Wafádzwâ\` ngéṇyi?* what has made you happy? | *-fara* → *-fadza* (+ passive *-w-*) |
| *Tinókúdzá chibarwé.* we grow maize | *Chákǔrǎ zvakádiní?* how big has it grown? | *-kudza* ← *-kura* |
| *Chirongó chádónha pachikúvá.* the pot has fallen from the pot-shelf | *Ndíànì ẉachídónhesa?* who dropped it? | *-donha* → *-donhesa* |
| *Chikóro chírí kufámbá.* the school is going | *Ndíaní àrí kuchífámbísa?* who is running it? | *-famba* → *-fambisa* |
| *Mombe dzámwa.* the cattle have drunk | *Ndíaní ẉàdzímwísá?* who watered them? | *-mwa* → *-mwisa* |

FSI prints the first four untoned. *chikuva* (7, 8) is, in FSI's glossary, a "platform for holding pots".

**What the pairs show.** The commonest causative is ***-isa / -esa*** (*-virisa*, *-donhesa*, *-fambisa*, *-mwisa*), but several verbs make it by changing the last consonant instead: ***-ra* → *-dza*** (*-pera* / *-pedza*, *-fara* / *-fadza*, *-kura* / *-kudza*, *-vira* / *-vidza*) and ***-ra* → *-dzika*** (*-rara* / *-radzika*, *-gara* / *-gadzika*). Learn the pair, not the rule: *-gadzika* "set down" and *-gadzira* "prepare" are different words. The "who?" is Stage 3's relative, *ẉà-* (eastern *w-*; standard *a-*), with the object prefix for the thing: *-i-* sugar (9), *-mu-* the child, *-chi-* the pot (7), *-dzi-* the cattle (10).

**Practice.** Your speaking partner says what happened; you ask who made it happen. Then swap, and add your own pairs from *-pera*, *-rara*, *-gara*, *-fara*, *-kura*, *-famba*.
Not yet: -sati and the -a- tense:
FSI Unit 32, Exercise 7 — "Indicative vs. participial tone patterns in the /-a-/ tense." "We've cultivated our field." "Have you cultivated yours also?" "I haven't cultivated [it] yet.":

| We have | Have you too? | Not yet |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Tarima munda wédú.* | *Mẉarímawó wényú heré?* | *Handísatí ndã̌rimá(ba).* |
| *Tadáídza shámwarí dzédú.* | *Mẉadáídzawó dzényú heré?* | *Handísatí ndã̌dáidzá.* |
| *Tagéza mbatyá dzédú.* | *Mẉagézawó dzényú heré?* | *Handísatí ndã̌dzígezá.* |
| *Tatsváírá mumbá mẉédú.* | *Mẉatsváírawó mẉényú heré?* | *Handísatí ndã̌tsváirá(ba).* |
| *Sadza rédú rákwǎtǎ.* | *Rényú rákwǎtawó heré?* | *Harísatí rã̌kwáta.* |
| *Tadyá sadza rédú.* | *Mẉadyáwo rényú heré?* | *Handísatí ndã̌dya(ba).* |
| *Tapédzísá basa rédú.* | *Mẉapédzísawó rényú heré?* | *Hatísatí tã̌pédzisá.* |
| *Támwa tíi yédú.* | *Mẉamwáwo yényú heré?* | *Handísatí ndã̌mwa.* |
| *Vaeni védú vásvíka.* | *Vényú vásvíkawó heré?* | *Havásatí vã̌sviká.* |
| *Tafúsira mbéú dzédú.* | *Mẉafúsirawo dzényú heré?* | *Handísatí ndã̌fusíra.* |
| *Babá védú vádzóka kudare.* | *Vényú vádzókawó heré?* | *Havásatí vã̌dzoká(ba).* |
| *Vaná védú vaénda kuchikóro.* | *Vényú vaéndawó heré?* | *Havásatí vã̌endá(ba).* |
| *Mwaná wédú wágǔtǎ.* | *Wényú wágútawó heré?* | *Haásatí ã̌gúta.* |
| *Mafútá édú ápěrǎ.* | *Ényú ápěrawó heré?* | *Haásatí ã̌péra.* |

FSI translates only the first set; the rest go the same way — we have called our friends, washed our clothes, swept our house, eaten our sadza, finished our work, drunk our tea; our visitors have arrived, our father has come back from the court (*dare*), our children have gone to school, our child has had enough, our oil is finished. *Sadza rákwǎtǎ* is "our sadza has bubbled" (*-kwata* "to bubble", FSI's glossary).

**The construction.** "Not yet" is **the negative of *-sati*** — *handí-satí*, *harí-satí*, *hatí-satí*, *havá-satí*, *haá-satí* — followed by **the same subject again, in the *-a-* tense** (Stage 3's past of today): *handisati **nda**rima*, "I-not-yet I-have-cultivated". Its object prefix goes in the second verb: *ndadzigeza* "I have washed them". Unit 32's dialogue had it already: *Handísatí ndãẏa nácho* "I don't have one yet."

**Its tones.** The second verb is a **participial** form (Stages 6–7), and its tones are not the indicative's: *Tarima* but *ndã̌rimá*. FSI marks its first syllable with the tilde, explained in Unit 27: "The symbol /~/ above a vowel letter stands for one or more tonal patterns, according to dialect. Its simplest representation is found in some varieties of Manyika. In these dialects, the first syllable of each of these words has high tone regardless of person; the next has low, the next high, and so on, with alternant high and low syllables. A more widespread system has high tone on the first syllable, as in the above. The second syllable has basic tone on the first syllable of the root: low for low verbs, high for high verbs." In this exercise FSI prints the tilde over a caron; the caron gives the central/eastern split as usual, and the tilde says the dialects differ again. FSI's own conclusion is a question: "The participial tone patterns of verbs in the /-a-/ tense are particularly subject to variation among the different dialects of Shona. Using the data in Exercise 7, prepare a summary statement on this matter." Make that statement from your partner's speech.

**Practice.** Go down the table with your speaking partner, three voices: they say "we have", you ask "have you too?", they answer "not yet". Then tell them what you have and haven't done today, *Handísatí nda…*, and let them correct the first syllable.
Bathing the baby:
FSI Unit 33 — the first half of a conversation that runs on into Unit 34:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | *Ndinógeza séṇyi mwaná máí?* | How do I bathe the child, Mother? |
| B | *Unóisa mvúrá mudhíshi.* | You put water in a basin. |
| B | *Wópfǐgǎ misíwo yọ́sé.* | Then close all the doors. |
| B | *Úngánídza zvọ́sé zvọ̃únodá.* | Collect everything that you need. |
| A | *Zvàkádaí ngẹ́ṇyi?* | Like what? |
| B | *Zvàkádaí ngẹ́sípo, mafútá nêmbǎtyâ.* | Like soap, oil, and clothing. |
| B | *Unamúpúkuta ngẹ́jǐrǎ ràkáchéna.* | You should wipe him with a clean cloth. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *dhíshi* | 5, 6 | basin |
| *-pfígá* | | to close |
| *musúwo* / *musíwo* | 3, 4 | doorway |
| *-dáì* | | the demonstrative pro-verb |
| *-pukuta* | | to wipe, rub, dust, polish |
| *jírá* / *machírá* | 5 / 6 | cloth |

**What is in it.** *Ndinógeza séṇyi?* "how do I bathe?" is Stage 1's *sei* "how", in FSI's eastern *-ṇyi* spelling. *Wópfǐgǎ* "then close" is Stage 4's *-o-* form, here "and then (you) …": instructions in order. *Zvọ̃únodá* "that you want" is a relative with the linking *-o-* of "all those that …"; FSI prints a tilde over the *o*, so its tone goes by dialect. ***Zvàkádaí ngẹ́ṇyi?*** "like what?" is the pro-verb *-dai*, the next lesson. ***Unamúpúkuta*** "you should wipe him" has the prefix ***-na-*** "must", the lesson after that. *ngẹ́jǐrǎ* "with a cloth" uses *nge-* for the thing a job is done with, as in Stage 5's *ngẹpárafíni* "with paraffin" — the *nge-* is the same one met in *ngẹ́ṇyi* "with what?".

**Practice.** Play FSI Unit 33. Then have your speaking partner ask you how to do something you know well — make tea, clean a room — and tell them in order with *Unó…* then *Wó…*, the way B does; when they ask *Zvàkádaí ngẹ́ṇyi?*, list the things.
Like what? Like soap: -dai:
FSI Unit 33, Exercise 1 — "'Like, for example …': an important use of the pro-verb /dáì/." "At the market there are many vegetables." "Like what?" "Like cabbages and beans.":

| There are many | Like what? | Like … |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Kumusika kúną masímó mazhínjí.* | *Àkádaí ngẹ́ṇyi?* | *Àkádaí ngệmâkábichi, neshúshururu.* |
| *Mumbá múne midzíyó mizhínjí.* | *Yàkádaí ngẹ́ṇyi?* | *Yàkádaí ngẹzvígaro néhǎrǐ.* |
| *Mudhoróḅa múną vanhu vendudzi zhínjí.* | *Vàkádaí ngẹ́ṇyi?* | *Vàkádaí ngẹMándevére, neMachángana.* |
| *Kwédú kúne michero mizhínjí.* | *Yàkádaí ngẹ́ṇyi?* | *Yakádaí ndậmǎgwávha, mángo ną máhobó.* |

So: in the market, vegetables — cabbages and beans; in the house, furniture — chairs and pots; in town, people of many *ndudzi* (10, the plural of *rudzi*; FSI does not gloss it here — peoples, kinds) — Ndebele and Shangaan; at our place, fruit — guavas, mangoes and bananas (*mahobó*, Stage 3).

**How it is built.** *-dai* is the pro-verb "be like this", Stage 1's family of *kudai*, *kudaro*. Here it is a **relative in the *-ka-* tense**, *-àkádaí* "which are like", and takes **the concord of the thing being listed**:

| Noun | Class | "Like what?" |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *masímó* | 6 | ***À**kádaí ngẹ́ṇyi?* |
| *midzíyó*, *michero* | 4 | ***Yà**kádaí ngẹ́ṇyi?* |
| *vanhu* | 2 | ***Và**kádaí ngẹ́ṇyi?* |
| (things in general, the dialogue) | 8 | ***Zvà**kádaí ngẹ́ṇyi?* |

The examples follow with ***nge-*** before the first noun and ***na-*** "and" before the rest: *ngẹ́sípo, mafútá nêmbǎtyâ* "soap, oil and clothes". In the last line FSI writes ***ndậ**mǎgwávha* — the *nde-* that some dialects say for *nge-*, a lesson in Unit 37.

Stage 5 had the other *-dini*, "what is it like?"; *-dai* answers it.

**Practice.** Your speaking partner says there are many of something — in the market, the house, the town, the garden — and you ask *…kádaí ngẹ́ṇyi?* with the right concord; they list examples. Then swap, and choose nouns from four different classes.
You must: the prefix -na-:
FSI Unit 33, Exercises 2 and 3 — "The verb prefix /-nà-/, expressing obligation." The dialogue had it: *Unamúpúkuta ngẹ́jǐrǎ ràkáchéna* "you should wipe him with a clean cloth". The ***-na-*** goes where a tense prefix goes: subject prefix + ***-na-*** + (object) + stem. FSI prints these drills untoned.

**Exercise 2** — "We must fill the lamps this evening." "We don't fill the lamps every evening." "We don't fill them every evening.":

| Must | Not usually | Not usually, with an object |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Tinazadza mwenje manheru ano.* | *Hatizadzi mwenje manheru ọse.* | *Hatiizadzi manheru ọse.* |
| *Vànàwaridza machira akachena nhasi.* | *Havawaridzi machira akachena mazuva ọse.* | *Havaawaridzi mazuva ọse.* |
| *Tinageza mafafitera mangwanani ano.* | *Hatigezi mafafitera mangwanani ọse.* | *Hatiagezi mangwanani ọse.* |
| *Tinaverenga iri bhuku nhasi.* | *Hativerengi iri bhuku mazuva ọse.* | *Hatiriverengi mazuva ọse.* |
| *Mubiki anatenga upfu nhasi.* | *Haatengi upfu mazuva ọse.* | *Haahutengi mazuva ọse.* |

(FSI prints *mwenji* in the first line and *Havaavaridzi* in the second; they are *mwenje* and *Havaawaridzi*.) So *tinazadza* "we must fill", *vanawaridza* "they must spread out (clean sheets)", *tinageza* "we must wash (the windows)", *tinaverenga* "we must read (this book)", *anatenga* "(the cook) must buy (meal)". The negatives are Stage 3's *-no-* negative, with the object prefix in the third column: *-i-* lamps (4), *-a-* sheets, windows (6), *-ri-* book (5), *-hu-* meal (14).

**Its tone.** FSI marks *-nà-* low, and in *Vànàwaridza* the subject prefix low as well. Its instruction: "Summarize the tonal patterns of verbs that contain the prefix /-nà-/. Pay especial attention to the tone of the subject prefixes for first, second, and third persons." Ask your partner to say *tinazadza*, *unazadza*, *anazadza*, *vanazadza* and write down what you hear.

**Exercise 3** — "Examples of /-na-/ verbs with object prefixes. Active vs. passive stems." "The house must be swept." "It hasn't been swept yet." "We must sweep it.":

| Must be done | Not yet done | We / you must do it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Imba yakafanira kutsvairwa.* | *Haisati yatsvairwa.* | *Tinaitsvaira.* |
| *Mushonga wakafanira kuiswa pasi.* | *Hausati waiswa pasi.* | *Unauisa pasi.* |
| *Zvigaro zvakafanira kupukutwa.* | *Hazvisati zvapukutwa.* | *Unazvipukuta.* |
| *Mafáfitera akafanira kugezwa.* | *Haasati agezwa.* | *Unaageza.* |
| *Midziyo yose yakafanira kumiswa munzvimbo dzáyo.* | *Haisati yamiswa.* | *Unaimisa.* |
| *Mwenje yose yakafanira kuzadzwa.* | *Haisati yazadzwa.* | *Unaizadza.* |
| *Mibhédha yákafánírá kuwaridzwa.* | *Haisati yawaridzwa.* | *Unaiwaridza.* |

Three constructions side by side: ***-kafanira*** + infinitive "has to" (with a passive infinitive, "has to be swept"); Unit 32's ***-sati*** "not yet", here with passive *-a-* forms; and ***-na-*** with the object prefix after it, *tina-**i**-tsvaira* "we must sweep it". FSI again leaves the tones of *-na-* + object to you: "Enter below a statement summarizing the tones of verbs that contain /-nà-/ plus an object prefix."

**Practice.** Your speaking partner names a job that must be done in the house; you say it hasn't been done yet, then that you (or we) must do it, with the object prefix. Then go back through Exercise 2 with their tones, not the book's blank ones.

**Practice conversations** — with a fellow passenger:

| | |
| --- | --- |

| *Ndiri kudzikira zvangu Marondera.* | At Marondera. |

| *Imẉi mẉakwirirepi bhazi?* | Where did you get on the bus? |

and a second, between two women (*Muri kusvika kupi? … Ndini Mai Marata. … Ndini Mai Gomo.*), on where each is going and where she comes from: *Munobva muri papi?* "where do you come from?", *Ndinotẹngesa masimo zvipiri zvọse* "I sell vegetables twice a week", *Tichaonanazve pakudzoka* "we'll see each other again on the way back". **Practice.** Sit side by side with your speaking partner as two passengers. | --- | --- | --- |

"Three words having to do with political matters": *huruménde* (9, 10) government; *mumíríri* (1, 2) representative; *sangano* (5, 6) meeting.

| | Without an object | With an object |
| --- | --- | --- |

Not on the bed, where it is dry:
FSI Unit 34, Exercises 2 and 4: commands with an object, negative and affirmative, and a place said with a relative.

**Exercise 2** — "Negative vs. affirmative commands." "Am I to put the book on the bed now?" "Don't put it on the bed." "Put it on the table.":

| Shall I? | Don't | Do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Ndóísa bhúku pamubhédha heré?* | *Usárǐísą pamubhédha.* | *Ríisé patáfura.* |
| *Ndóísa hárí pachikúvá heré?* | *Usáǐísą pachikúvá.* | *Íisé patáfura.* |
| *Ndóísa bángá pachigaro heré?* | *Usárǐísą pachigaro.* | *Ríisé patáfura.* |
| *Ndóísa mwenje pasí heré?* | *Usáǔísą pasí.* | *Úisé patáfura.* |
| *Ndóísa munyú muhárí heré?* | *Usáǔísą muhárí.* | *Úisé patáfura.* |
| *Ndóísa murívó muhárí heré?* | *Usáǔísa muhárí.* | *Úgezé kutángá.* wash it first |
| *Ndóísa shushururu muhárí heré?* | *Usádzǐísa muhárí.* | *Dzígezé kutángá.* |
| *Ndóísa tsúnga muhárí heré?* | *Usárǐísa muhárí.* | *Rígezé kutángá.* |

Both commands put the object prefix before the stem: ***u-sá-ri-ísą*** "don't put it" (*ri-*, the book, 5), ***rí-isé*** "put it". In the negative FSI marks the object prefix *ǐ* (low, central reading); in the affirmative it is high and the command ends in ***-e***, as with *Ípe* in the last lesson: an imperative with an object prefix ends in *-e*. *bángá* (5) is a knife, *munyú* (3) salt; *kutángá* "first" is the infinitive of Stage 5's *-tanga*.

**Exercise 4** — "Imperatives with and without object prefixes. Relative forms of verbs with subject prefixes from Class 16, used as place expressions.":

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Rádzíká mwaná.* Put the child down to rest. | *Apa pákaómá here?* Is it dry here? ('Is here dried?') | *Múràdzǐkê pàkáǒmǎ.* Put him down where it is dry. |
| *Rádzíká vaná.* Put the children down to rest. | *Apa pákáchena heré?* Is it clean here? | *Váràdzǐkê pàkáchéna.* Put them down in a clean place. |
| *Isá mabhúku pasí.* Put the books down. | *Apa pákáchena heré?* Is it clean here? | *Áisé pasí pàkáchéna.* Put them down where it is clean. |
| *Isá bhúku pasí.* Put the book down. | *Apa pákaómá heré?* Is it dry here? | *Ríisé pasí pàkáǒmǎ.* Put it down in a dry place. |

**The place relative.** *Apa pákaómá?* is a plain sentence with *apa* "here" (16) as subject: "here is dry?". Turn *pá-* into the relative *pà-* — Stage 3's relative by tone — and the verb itself becomes the place: ***pàkáǒmǎ*** "where it is dry", ***pàkáchéna*** "where it is clean". No word for "place" is needed; class 16 *is* the place (Stage 5). *-oma* is "become dry", *-chena* "become clean".

**Practice.** Your speaking partner asks *Ndóísa … …. heré?* about things in the room; forbid it with the object prefix, then say where to put it — first *patáfura*, then with a place relative: *pàkáǒmǎ*, *pàkáchéna*. Ask them to say the *pá-* / *pà-* pair until you hear the difference.
Give us axes so we can split wood:
FSI Unit 34, Exercise 3 — "Subjunctives with subject prefix vs. subjunctives with object prefix." Someone has to do something; they need a thing to do it with; give it to them, so that they can:

| Has to | Needs | Give, so that … |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Ẉákafánírá kuenda kuchikóro.* He has to go to school. | *Ánodá bhúku ráké.* He wants his book. | *Múpe bhúku ráké áénde kuchikóro.* Give him his book, [so] that he may go to school. |
| *Takáfǎnǐrǎ kuvádzâ\` húní.* We must split some firewood. | *Tinódâˣ matémó.* We need axes. | *Típe matémó tívádzẹ húní.* Give us axes so we [can] split firewood. |
| *Vákafánírá kundochérâ\` mvúrá.* They've got to go draw water. | *Vánodá zvirongó.* They need pots. | *Vápe zvirongó vándochére mvúrá.* Give them pots [so] that they may go draw water. |
| *Ẉákafánírá kurárá.* He must sleep. | *Ánodá kudyá.* He needs to eat. | *Múpe zvọkudya árare.* Give him something to eat so he [can] go to sleep. |
| *Ndakáfǎnǐrǎ kupfekedza mwaná.* I must dress the child. | *Ndinóda hémbě.* I need a shirt. | *Ndípe hémbě ndípfékedze mwaná.* Give me a shirt so that I can dress the child. |
| *Takáfǎnǐrǎ kuzádzá mwenje.* We've got to fill the lamp. | *Tinóda parafíni.* We need kerosene. | *Típe parafíni\` tízádze mwenje.* Give us kerosene so [we] may fill the lamp. |

**Two prefixes, one shape.** The same person shows up twice in the third column: as the **object** of the command (*Mú-pe* give him, *Tí-pe* give us, *Vá-pe* give them, *Ndí-pe* give me — Exercise 1's *-pe* form) and as the **subject** of the subjunctive that follows (*á-énde* that he go, *tí-vádze* that we split, *vá-ndochere* that they go and draw, *ndí-pfékedze* that I dress). "So that" needs no word: the subjunctive after a command is its purpose. The dialogue's *Múpe kudyá áráre zvákó* "feed him so he will go to sleep" is the same.

***-kafanira*** + infinitive is "have to, must": *Ẉákafánírá kuenda* "he has to go". *húní* is firewood, *démó* / *matémó* an axe, axes (FSI's *d* ~ *t*: *démó* 5, *matémó* 6), *-chera mvura* "draw water" (*-chera* is also Unit 32's "dig").

**Practice.** Your speaking partner says what someone has to do and what they need; you give the command with its purpose, both prefixes in place. Then make your own: *Ndípe … ndí…*, for things you really need this week.

| --- | --- | --- |
| *-tízá* | | to run |

**What is in it.** Every instruction is a command followed by a subjunctive — Unit 32's negative ***vasá-*** "that they not": *vasátízétíze* "that they don't run about" (the stem doubled, *-tiza-tiza*, for running here and there), *vasáíse* "that they don't put", *vasátámbą* "that they don't play". *Unaóná* "you must see" is Unit 33's *-na-*; *Itá vasá…* "make (it that) they don't" is "keep them from". *Vánopíswâ\` ngẹ́zǔvǎ* is the passive of *-pisa* "burn" with *nge-* for the agent: "burned by the sun". *Zvishomashómá* is *-shoma* "few" doubled.

***Kamwaná*** "baby, little child" is *mwana* in class 12, and its verbs agree: ***ká**ti **ká**rára*, ***Ká**ndorárá*, ***ká**néta*. That class is the next lesson. *Káti kárára here?* "has he yet slept?" is the *-ti* + participial of "already, yet"; *Kándorárá* has *-ndo-*, which FSI says in Unit 36 can mean "still".

**FSI's question:** "What happens to the usual prefix of a noun when one of the diminutive prefixes /-ka-/ (sg.) or /-tu-/ (pl.) is added to it?" From the table:

| Noun | Class 12, one | Class 13, several |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *mwaná* (1) | *ka-mwaná* | *tu-vaná* |
| *munda* (3) | *ka-munda* | *tu-minda* |
| *musụwo* (3) | *ka-musụwo* | *tu-misụwo* |
| *mwenje* (3) | *ka-mwenje* | *tu-mwenje* |
| *rwizí* (11) | *ka-rwizí* | *tu-ndwizí* |
| *imbá* (9) | *ka-imbá* or *kambá* | *tu-dzimbá*, *tu-imbá* or *tumbá* |
| *imbwá* (9) | *ka-imbwá* or *kambwá* | *tu-imbwá* or *tumbwá* |
| *húkú* (9) | *ka-húkú* or *kakúkú* | *tu-húkú* or *tukúkú* |
| *démó* (5) | *ka-témó* or *kadémó* | *tu-matémó* or *tutémó* |
| *bángá* (5) | *ka-pángá* or *kabángá* | *tu-mapángá*, *tupángá* or *tubángá* |
| *fáfitera* (5) | *ka-fífitera* | *tu-mafáfitera* |

So **ka- and tu- usually go in front of the noun's own prefix**, which stays — singular after *ka-*, plural after *tu-* (*kamunda* but *tuminda*; *kamwana* but *tuvana*). With classes 5 and 9, many speakers instead drop the old prefix (*kambá*, *tutémó*), and class 5 nouns may take the consonant of their class 6 plural (*démó* / *matémó* → *katémó*; *bángá* / *mapángá* → *kapángá*). FSI gives the choices in brackets; your partner will use one.

**Their concords** are *ka-* and *tu-* all through: *kamwaná **ka**díkị*, *tuvaná **tu**nganí*, and in the dialogue *kamwaná **ká**ti **ká**rára*. Stage 5 met them with *na*: *nakamwana*, *notuvana*.

**Practice.** Your speaking partner tells you what small things they have, bought or brought; you answer in class 12 with surprise, then ask how many in class 13. Do it once with FSI's nouns, once with things on the table.
So you have one, have you? -su:
FSI Unit 35, Exercise 1, again, and Unit 37, Exercise 3. FSI: "The enclitic /--su/ expresses **mild surprise, and sometimes also dissatisfaction**."

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Tinọ mwaná mudíkị.* We have a small child. | *Muną kamwaná kadíkị**su**?!* So you have a small child, have you? |
| *Tiné imbwá díkị.* We have a small dog. | *Muné kaimbwá kadíkị**su**?!* |
| *Vadzimáí vánofúndá kubika.* The wives are learning to cook. | *Vánofúndá ubiki**sú**?!* Oh, so they're studying cookery are they? |
| *Varimi vánofúndá kurima.* | *Vánofúndá urimi**sú**?!* |
| *Vasíkaná vánofúndá kurera vaná.* | *Vanofunda ureri kwậvǎnâ**sú**?!* |

and in Unit 33's bus conversation, *Ndiko mũnogara **su**?* "so that's where you live?". FSI punctuates the *-su* sentences *?!*: a question that is half an exclamation.

**It goes on the last word of the phrase** — the adjective, the noun, *kwavana* "of children" — not on the verb.

**Its tone** FSI asks rather than tells: "What are its tonal characteristics?" Its own marks: after a low syllable FSI writes it high (*ubikisú*, *urimisú*); after *kadíkị* it writes it low (*kadíkịsu*); after *vǎnâ* high (*kwậvǎnâsú*). Have your partner say the five sentences above and decide.

**Practice.** Your speaking partner tells you surprising things, small and large — *Tine …*, *Vari kufunda …* — and you answer each with the thing said back and *-su?!*, mildly surprised; then once more, dissatisfied. Let them tell you which one you sounded.
Chi- before a command:
FSI Unit 35, Exercise 2 — "Use of /chi-/ as an initial prefix with imperative forms. [The student should write the translations in the blanks, and then use them as cues for producing the Shona sentences.]" FSI leaves every translation blank. The English below is built from FSI's word lists and the earlier units; check each with your partner.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndapédzá kugeza mwana mai.* | I've finished bathing the child, mother. |
| *Chímupúkuta áóme.* | Now wipe him so he gets dry. |
| *Ndapédzá kumúpúkuta.* | I've finished wiping him. |
| *Chímuzórá mafútá.* | Now rub lotion on him. |
| *Ndapédzá kubika sadza.* | I've finished cooking the sadza. |
| *Chíbura tídye.* | Now dish it out so we can eat. |
| *Ndípewózve bhúku rákó.* | Give me your book again, please. |
| *Chímbomíra ndímbopédza (ndimboti ndápédza).* | Wait a moment while I finish (until I've finished). |
| *Ndítemerewo mugóti.* | Cut me a cooking stick, please. |
| *Chímbomíra ndítóre démó rángu.* | Wait a moment while I get my axe. |
| *Ndítaúríre nyayá yánezúro.* | Tell me yesterday's story. |
