The words: *-pukuta* wipe, *-oma* become dry, *-zora* smear, *-bura* dish out, *-pa* give, *-zve* again, *-wo* softening the request (Stage 5), *-mira* stand, stop, *-mbo-* just, for a while (Stage 5), *-tema* cut, *mugoti* the cooking stick (FSI: *Tinobika nemugoti* "we cook with a stick"), *-tora* take, *nyaya* (9, 10) history, story, *yanezuro* "of yesterday".

**What chi- does.** ***Chi-*** stands in front of the whole command — *chí-mupukuta*, *chí-mbomira* — and every *chi-* command answers what was just said: the bathing is done, *chí-* wipe him; you want the book, *chí-mbomira* wait. Unit 34's dialogue line *Uchímuzora mafútá* "**then** rub lotion on him" is the same *-chi-* with a subject prefix. FSI gives the form, not its meaning, so read it as "now, then, first" and let your partner tell you how it sounds to them. Each *chi-* command is followed by a subjunctive of purpose (Unit 34): *áóme* "so he dries", *tídye* "so we eat", *ndímbopédza* "so I finish".

**Practice.** Do FSI's exercise as it asks: your speaking partner gives the first line of each pair, you answer with the *chi-* command, first reading, then from the English alone. Then use *Chímbomíra …* for real whenever they ask you for something this week.
Do it well: -natsa:
FSI Unit 35, Exercise 3 — "Use of /-natsa/ 'to do well, thoroughly.'" "The child is tending the cattle." "He'd better do a good job of it!":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mwaná árí kuchengeta mombe.* | *Ngáánátse kuchengetesa! (Ngáánátsochengetesa!)* |
| *Vasíkaná várí kudirira muríwó.* | *Ngávánátse kudiririsa! (Ngávánátsodiririsa!)* |
| *Máí várí kugadzira mumbá.* | *Ngávánátse kugadzirisa!* |
| *Vakómaná várí kufúndírá.* | *Ngávánátse kufúndírísa!* |
| *Vaímbí várí kuímbá.* | *Ngávánátse kuímbá!* |
| *Varimi várí kufusira chibarwé.* | *Ngávánátse kufusirisa!* |

The girls are watering the vegetables, mother is tidying the house, the boys are studying, the singers singing, the farmers covering the maize: let them do it well!

**The form.** ***-natsa*** "to do something well" is a verb, followed by the infinitive of what is to be done well. Here it is in the *nga-* form "let him, let them" (Stage 7's hortative) with its subjunctive *-e*: *nga-á-nátse*, *nga-vá-nátse*. In four of the six the verb after it also takes the *-isa/-esa* extension: *kuchengetesa* (Unit 35's "look after assiduously"), *kudiririsa*, *kugadzirisa*, *kufusirisa* — doing it properly, thoroughly.

**The contracted form.** FSI: "Notice the pairs of synonymous forms, one of which is a contraction of the other":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ngaanatse kuimba.* | *Ngaanatsoimba.* |
| *Anonatsa kuchengetesa.* | *Anonatsochengetesa.* |

"Write here a statement summarizing the differences in form between the contracted and uncontracted variants." The pairs show it: **the last vowel of *-natsa* and the *ku-* of the infinitive merge into *-o-***, written as one word: *natsa/natse* + *ku-imba* → *natso-imba*. *Anonatsa* "he does it well" is the plain *-no-* tense.

**Practice.** Your speaking partner tells you who is doing what around the house and the village; answer *Ngá…nátse ku…!* and then the contracted form. Then tell them what you yourself do well: *Ndinonatsa ku…*, *Ndinonatso…*.
A girl to help in the house:

| --- | --- | --- |

Still at it: -chi(ri) and -ndo-:
FSI Unit 36. The wedding conversation ended *Vazhínjí váchí kundosvika. / Váchǐˣrí kundosvika* "many are still arriving". FSI's note: "Note still another prefix of the form /-chi-/, this one used to indicate that **an action is still going on**. It may be used with the stem /-ri/, as in /vachiri kundosvika/, or without /-ri/, but still with the infinitive prefix /ku-/ as in /vachi kundosvika/, which means the same thing."

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Vá-**chí**-rí kundosvika.* | They are still arriving. |
| *Vá-**chí** kundosvika.* | (the same) |

So: subject prefix + ***-chi-*** + ***-ri*** + infinitive — Stage 3's *-ri* + infinitive "is doing", with *-chi-* for "still" — or the same without *-ri*.

**And *-ndo-* "still".** FSI goes on: "Note also the use of the aspectual prefix /-ndo-/, which has been met previously with the meaning 'go and' (Unit 6 Note 2). Here, and in many other cases, /-ndo-/ is better translated 'still'. It thus partially overlaps in meaning the use of /-chi-/ that was discussed on the previous page." In *kundosvika* both are at work: "still (*-chi-*) coming in (*-ndo-*)". Unit 35's *Kándorárá zvishomashómá* "he's been sleeping just a short time" is the same *-ndo-*.

**Exercise 4** — "The 'persistive' use of /-chi-/." FSI gives the first translation and leaves the rest for you; the rest are built from the earlier units:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Vaná vábǔdǎ heré muchikóro?* | Have the children come out of the school? |
| *Kwéte. Váchímwó. Váchǐˣri kufúndá.* | No, they're still in there. They're still studying. |
| *Muchato wáti wãvamba heré?* | Has the wedding begun yet? |
| *Kwéte. Váchǐˣri kumírírá musándíri.* | No. They're still waiting for the minister. |
| *Manéta ẉápědzǐsǎ basa ráké heré?* | Has Maneta finished her work? |
| *Kwéte. Áchǐˣrí kutsváírá mumbá.* | No. She's still sweeping the house. |
| *Babá váti vãdzoka heré?* | Has Father come back yet? |
| *Kwéte. Váchiri kumunda.* | No. He's still at the field. |

Two more shapes: ***Váchímwó*** "they are still in there" is *-chi-* with Stage 5's place enclitic *-mwo* (class 18, "in there"), no *-ri*; and ***Váchiri kumunda*** "he's still at the field" is *-chi-ri* with a place, no infinitive. The questions use *-ti* + participial (*wáti wãvamba*, *váti vãdzoka*) for "already, yet". *-mírírá* is "wait for".

**Practice.** Your speaking partner asks whether things are finished — the children, the work, the cooking, the wedding; answer *Kwéte*, they are still at it, with *-chiri ku-*, and the other way, *-chi ku-*. Then tell them three things you are still doing this year.
Had arrived, will have arrived: -nga:
FSI Unit 36: "An exceedingly important construction is illustrated in:"

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ẉákángẹ ãri kutsvaka basa.* | She was looking for work. |
| cf. *Árí kutsvaka basa.* | She is looking for work. |
| and: *Ẉákátsvaka basa.* | She looked for work. |
| *Ndakángẹ ndĩsati ndãziva …* | I didn't know … ('I hadn't known …') |
| cf. *Handísatí ndãziva …* | I don't yet know … ('I haven't yet known …') |
| and: *Ndákazívá …* | I knew … |
| *Ndangá ndichífúnga kudárò.* | I thought so (today). |
| cf. *Ndinófunga kudárò.* | I think so. |

FSI's rule, in full: "The special stem /-nga/ (or /-nge/) takes any of the prefixes that are found with ordinary verb stems, except for object prefixes. The **tense** of the /-nga/ form fixes the general time of the whole verb phrase. The verb that follows /-nga/ is always in one of the **participial** forms, either the type that is characterized by /-chi-/ (as in the last of the above examples) or the type that is characterized by a special tonal pattern (as in the other examples given at the beginning of this note). The tense of the verb that follows /-nga/ sets the action of the verb **with relation to** the general time that was established by the tense of the /-nga/ form. Thus, if on Tuesday we said:"

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tuesday | *Vásvíka.* | They have arrived. |
| Wednesday, of the same arrival | *Vákángẹ vãsvika.* | They had arrived. |
| Monday | *Vánózongą vãsvika.* | They will have arrived. |

So *-nga* is an auxiliary: **SP + tense + *-nga*** sets the time — *vá-ka-nga* (past), *vá-no-zo-nga* (future), *nda-nga* (earlier today) — and **SP + participial** says what was going on then: *ãri kutsvaka* "being looking", *vãsvika* "having arrived", *ndichífúnga* "thinking". It is not Stage 2's *-nga-* "can, may", which is a tense prefix; this is a stem.

**Exercise 1** — "Single verb vs. verb constructions with /-nga/." "Have they begun to eat?" "When we arrived, they had already begun to eat.":

| | Have they? | When we arrived, they had already … |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *kuvamba kudyá* | *Vávámba kudyá heré?* | *Izvo tãsvika, vángą vãtóvambá kudyá.* |
| *kupédzá kudyá* | *Vápědzǎ kudyá heré?* | *Izvo tãsvika, vángą vãtopedza kudyá.* |
| *kuenda kumuchato* | *Vaénda kumuchato heré?* | *Izvo tãsvika, vǎngą vãtoenda kumuchato.* |
| *kuwaridza mibhedha* | *Váwáridza mibhédha heré?* | *Izvo tãsvika, vángą vãtowaridza mibhédha.* |
| *kubura sadza* | *Ṿábúra sadza heré?* | *Izvo tãsvika, vángą vãtobura sadza.* |
| *kugara pasí* | *Vágára pasí heré?* | *Izvo tãsviką, vángą vãtogara pasí.* |
| *kubúdá mumbá* | *Vábǔdǎ mumbá heré?* | *Izvo tãsvika, vángą vãtobúda mumbá.* |
| *kuténgésâ\` húkú* | *Vátěngěsǎ\` húkú heré?* | *Izvo tãsvika, vángą vãtoténgésâ\` húkú.* |

*Izvo tãsvika* "when we arrived" is *izvo* + a participial; *vángą vãto-* "they had already" is *-nga* (here without *-ka-*, the time of today) + participial with ***-to-*** "already".

**Exercise 3** — "Verb phrases in which the /-ngą/ form has the prefix /-no-/ [or, depending on dialect, /-ne-/]." "The children's clothes aren't dirty yet." "But they will be ('will have gotten') dirty [by] this evening.":

| Not yet | But by this evening |
| --- | --- |
| *Mbatyá dzệvǎnâ hadzísatí dzãsvipa.* | *Así dzínọ́ngą dzãsvipa manherú.* |
| *Handísatí ndãnetá.* I'm not tired yet. | *Así unọ́ngą wãneta manherú.* But you'll be tired by evening. |
| *Idzi mbatyá hadzíná kuómá.* These clothes haven't dried. | *Así dzínọ́ngą dzãoma manherú.* But they'll be dry by evening. |
| *Haúsatí wãpedza heré?* Haven't you finished yet? | *Ndinọ́ngą ndãpédza manherú.* I'll have finished by evening. |
| *Parafíni haísatí yãpera.* The paraffin isn't finished yet. | *Así ínọ́ngą yãpera manherú.* But it will be by evening. |

The left column is Unit 32's *-sati* "not yet"; the right turns it into "will have": ***SP + no + nga*** + the same participial.

**Practice.** Tell your speaking partner what had already happened when you arrived somewhere today — *Izvo ndãsvika, vángą vãto…* — and what will have happened by this evening, *…nọ́ngą …*; let them ask *Vá… heré?* first, as in Exercise 1.
Who had been ploughing? -nga in question:
FSI Unit 36, Exercises 2, 5 and 6: the *-nga* phrase as a relative, after "who?" and "why?", and with negatives.

**Exercise 2** — "Verb phrases with /-ngą/, with the /-ngą/ form in the relative mood." "I saw the person who had been ploughing." "Who had been ploughing?":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndakáǒnǎ munhu ẉàkángẹ ãri kurima.* | *Ndíaní ẉàkángẹ ãri kurima?* |
| *Ndadáṇzwǎ munhu ẉàkángẹ ãri kutaura.* | *Ndíaní ẉàkángẹ ãri kutaura?* |
| *Ndaṇzwá munhu àrí kutaura.* | *Ndíaní ẉàngą́ ãri kutaura?* |
| *Ndabátsírá munhu àrí kurima.* | *Ndíaní ẉàngą́ ãri kurima?* |
| *Íye ánǒzǒngą ãneta.* | *Ndíaní ànózóngą ãneta?* |
| *Íye ánọngą ãkafanira kutíbátsírá.* | *Ndíaní anọ́ngą ãkafanira kutíbátsírá?* |

I heard the person who had been speaking; I helped the person who was ploughing; he will be tired — who will be tired?; he ought to help us — who ought to help us? Only the *-nga* form becomes relative (*ẉà-kángẹ*, *à-nózóngą*: Stage 3's relative tone); the participial after it does not change.

**Exercise 5** — "/-ngą/ forms in indicative, relative, and participial moods.":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ẉákángẹ ásíngagoní kutíbátsírá.* | He wasn't able to help us. |
| *Ndíaní ẉàkángẹ ásíngágoní kutíbátsírá?* | Who wasn't able to help us? |
| *Ngẹ́ṇyi ãkangẹ ásíngagoní kutíbátsírá?* | Why wasn't he able to help us? |
| *Ẉákángẹ ásíngazívi kuchaira.* | He couldn't drive ('didn't know how'). |
| *Ndíaní ẉàkángẹ ásíngazívi kuchaira?* | Who couldn't drive? |
| *Ngẹ́ṇyi ãkangẹ ásíngazívi kuchaira?* | Why couldn't he drive? |
| *Ẉánga ásíngadí kuenda.* | He didn't want to go (today). |
| *Ndíaní ẉàngą́ ásíngadí kuenda?* | Who didn't want to go? |
| *Ngẹ́ṇyi ãngą ásíngadí kuenda?* | Why didn't he want to go? |

FSI translates the first set only. Three moods of *-nga*: **indicative** *ẉákángẹ* (a statement), **relative** *ẉàkángẹ* (after *Ndíaní*), **participial** *ãkangẹ* (after *Ngẹ́ṇyi* "why?": *ngé-* + *-nyi*, "for what?"). And the verb after *-nga* is now a **negative participial**, ***á-sínga-***: *ásíngagoní* "not being able", *ásíngazívi*, *ásíngadí* — the negative relatives of Stage 7.

**Exercise 6** — "[The student should examine the following sentences carefully, describe the grammatical points which they illustrate, and practice the sentences, using cue words or phrases in English or in Shona.]":

| Is he? | No | But last week he was |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Árí kutsvaka basa heré?* | *Haárí kutsvaka basa.* | *Ẉákángẹ ãri kutsvaka basa sẏóndo yàkápěrǎ.* |
| *Murí kutsvaka basa heré?* | *Handírí kutsvaka basa.* | *Ndakángẹ ndĩri kutsvaka basa sẏóndo yàkápěrǎ.* |
| *Varimi várí kurima heré?* | *Havárí kurima.* | *Vákángẹ vãri kurima sẏóndo yàkápěrǎ.* |
| *Murí kukanya zvidhína heré?* | *Hatírí kukanya zvidhína.* | *Takángẹ tĩri kukanga zvidhína sẏóndo yàkápěrǎ.* |

The point it illustrates: the present *-ri* + infinitive (Stage 3) and its negative (Stage 5, *haárí*, *handírí*) set beside the same thing in the past, *-kanga* + participial *-ri*, "was …ing" — with Stage 2's *sẏóndo yàkápěrǎ* "last week" (*svondo*, week; *yakapera* "which has ended"). FSI's last line has *kukanga* where the question had *kukanya*; read *kukanya*.

**Practice.** Do Exercise 6 as FSI asks, your speaking partner giving the question and a cue — *nhási*, *sẏóndo yàkápěrǎ* — and you answering in the right tense. Then ask them *Ndíaní ẉàkángẹ …?* and *Ngẹ́ṇyi …?* about something that went wrong this week.
A bright boy and no money:
FSI Unit 37: "BASIC DIALOGUE. [The student should develop the following raw materials into a form which he can learn as the basic dialogue for this unit. The conversation is between a foreigner and the father of a bright boy who is just finishing secondary school.]" FSI gives it untoned and untranslated. The English below is built from its word list and the earlier units; check it, and the tones, with your partner.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndimẉi Baba vaJohn here?* | Are you John's father? |
| *Munofungeṇyi ngẹmwana wenyu?* | What do you think about your son? |
| *Ndiri kunetseka chaizvo.* | I'm really worried. |
| *Mwana wenyu múzivi chaiye.* | Your son is really clever ('a knower'). |
| *Ndezvo chokwadi, asi ndashaya chekuita.* | That's true, but I don't know what to do ('I lack something to do'). |
| *Hamungaedzi here kuti apamhidzire?* | Couldn't you try to let him go on? |
| *Mẉoyo unoda asi mari handinaba.* | My heart is willing, but money I have none. |
| *Mẉakamboedza kumutsvagira nzvimbo here?* | Have you ever tried to look for a place for him? |
| *Ndaedza kazhinzhi, zvino ndaneta.* | I've tried many times, and now I'm tired. |
| *Mungadą here kuedza mhiri kwegungwa?* | Would you like to try overseas? |
| *Dai zvichibvira ndaingazvidą kunyanya.* | If it were possible I'd like it very much. |
| *Mwaida kuti azofunde basaṇyi?* | What work would you like him to study for? |
| *Ndaidisa basa rọhuroya.* | I'd like it to be the law. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *-netseka* | | to be worried, bothered, tired (cf. *-netsa* to worry, bother, tire; *-neta* to become tired) |
| *chókwadí* | 7 | truth |
| *-pàmhìdzà* | | to continue, repeat |
| *mw-òyò* | 3, 4 | heart |
| *-tsvaga* | | (= *-tsvaka*) |
| *mhìrì* | 9 | side (of a river, street, etc.) |
| *gùngwà* | 5, 6 | sea |
| *huroya* | 14 | the work of being a lawyer |
| *-bvira* | | to be possible |
| *mhiri kwegúngwa* | | overseas |

*múzivi* is the agentive noun of *-ziva* "know" (Unit 32); *chekuita* "something to do" is the *ch-* + linking prefix + infinitive of this unit's Exercise 5; *kazhinzhi* "many times" is the *ka-* of frequency, its last lesson; *handinaba* is *handina* with Stage 5's negative *-ba*; *-tsvagira* "look for (on someone's behalf)" is the applicative of *-tsvaga*.

**Kunyanya after the verb.** FSI: "Note the position of the infinitive /kunyanya/. This same verb was met in Unit 9, followed by the infinitive of another verb. Here, with what is apparently the same meaning, it is the infinitive of /-nyanya/ that stands last, and an inflected form of another verb that precedes it."

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndinónyánya kudá …* (Stage 3) | I like … best — *-nyanya* inflected, the other verb in the infinitive |
| *ndaingazvidą kunyanya* | I would like it very much — the other verb inflected, *kunyanya* last |

Both mean "very much, most": put *-nyanya* first and inflect it, or inflect the main verb and add *kunyanya*.

**Practice.** Build the dialogue with your speaking partner as FSI asks: they are the father, you the foreigner; get every line's tones from them, then learn it and play it both ways. Then say what you like very much, both ways — *Ndinonyanya kuda …* and *Ndinoda … kunyanya*.
If it were possible: dai:
FSI Unit 37. "Note also the construction with /dáì/:"

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Dàí zvichíbvíra ndàíngazvídą.* | If it were possible, I'd like it. |
| *Dái uchídâˣ kufúndá waífúndírą mabhúku.* | If you want/wanted to study, you'd study books. |
| *Dái wáingadą kufúndá wáingafúndírą mabhúku.* | (the same) |

**The pattern.** ***Dai*** "if" + a participial for the condition — *zvichíbvíra* "it being possible", *uchídâ* "you wanting" (with *-chi-*) — or the *-ai-* / *-aiṇga-* forms (*wáingadą* "you would want"); then the result in ***-ai-*** "would" (Stage 3's *-i-* tense, "used to, would like"), often with *-nga-*: *ndàíngazvídą* "I would like it", *waífúndírą* "you would study for".

**Exercise 2** — "The conditional construction with /dáì/. [As in Exercise 1, above, the student should practice these sets of sentences, using cues of his own devising.]" FSI gives no English and tones only the last three; the English is built from the earlier units:

| Asked | Answer | If … |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Nditsvakirewo basa.* Find me some work, please. | *Handirioniba.* I don't see any. | *Dai uchịriona ndaizofarą.* If you saw some I'd be happy. |
| *Ndienderewo kudhibi nhasi.* Go to the dip tank for me today, please. | *Handina nguva.* I haven't time. | *Dai uchida ndaizoenda sẏondo ìnouya.* If you like, I'd go next week. |
| *Ndipewo mbeu yenzungu.* Give me some groundnut seed, please. | *Handichina; yakapera.* I haven't any more; it's finished. | *Dai ndichinayo ndaikupa.* If I still had some I'd give you some. |
| *Titengeserewo nyama nhasi.* Sell us some meat today, please. | *Yapera mangwanani ano.* It was finished this morning. | *Dai ichimẉo ndaifara kumutengesera.* If there were still some in there I'd be glad to sell you some. |
| *Ndítèngèréṇyiwó sípo kuchitóro.* Buy me some soap at the store, please. | *Handíendí kuchitóro nhasi.* I'm not going to the store today. | *Dái ndáìngáénda kuchitóro, ndaíngakútèngérá.* If I were going to the store, I'd buy it for you. |
| *Ndítaúríre zítá ráké.* Tell me his name. | *Handírizívi.* I don't know it. | *Dái ndáirízíva, ndaíkútáurira.* If I knew it, I'd tell you. |
| *Ndípewó marí.* Give me some money, please. | *Handíná marí.* I have no money. | *Dái ndíináyo ndaíkǔpá.* If I had it I'd give it to you. |

Every condition is something not so: the answer says it isn't, and *dai* says what would follow if it were. Note *-chi-* "still" from Unit 36 in *ndichinayo* "if I still had it", *ichimẉo* "it still being in there", and *Handichina* "I no longer have". *dhibhi* (5, 6) is a cattle dip tank.

**Practice.** Do Exercise 2 as FSI says: your speaking partner asks a favour of their own devising, you refuse with a reason, then give the *Dai …* sentence. Then tell them three things you would do if they were possible: *Dai zvichibvira, ndaiṇga…*.
Whose is it? Nde- before \"of\", and som:
FSI Unit 37, Exercises 4 and 5: two uses of Stage 5's linking prefix "of".

**Exercise 4** — "The prefix /nge-/ (or, depending on dialect, /nde-/) before a syllable that contains the linking prefix.":

| They have | Whose is it? | It's … |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Vaimbi vane bhúku.* The singers have a book. | *Bhuku ndẹ́raaní?* Whose book is it? | *Ndẹrąváímbí.* It's the singers'. |
| *Hánzvádzi yángu íne húkú.* My sister has a chicken. | *Huku ndẹdzaani?* Whose are the chickens? | *Ndẹ́dzehánzvádzi yángu.* They're my sister's. |
| *Babá váne démó.* Father has an axe. | *Démó ndẹ́raaní?* Whose is the axe? | *Ndẹ́rababá.* It's Father's. |
| *Máí váne tutsono.* Mother has some little needles. | *Tutsono ndẹ́twaaní?* Whose are the little needles? | *Ndẹ́twamáí.* They're Mother's. |

FSI translates none of these; the English follows the words. **"It is X's"** is ***nge-/nde-*** + the owner's linking prefix + the owner: *nde-**r**a-vaimbi* (the book, 5: *ra-*), *nde-**dz**e-hanzvadzi* (chickens, 10: *dza-* + *e-*), *nde-**tw**a-mai* (13: *twa-*, with Unit 35's *tutsono*, *tsono* "needle"). "Whose?" is the same with *-aani* "of whom": *ndẹ́raaní?*. FSI writes the *d* with its dialect hook — some say *nge-*, some *nde-*, as FSI's heading says; Unit 33's *ndậmǎgwávha* is the same prefix before a noun. *hanzvadzi* (9, 10) is, in FSI's glossary, a "sibling of opposite sex".

**Exercise 5** — "The prefix /ch-/ (Cl. 7) plus linking prefix, plus the infinitive of a verb." "What shall I do now?" "I lack something to do.":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndóítẹṇyí?* What shall I do now? | *Ndasháya chọkúita.* I have nothing to do ('I lack something to do'). |
| *Ndógéza ngẹ́ṇyi?* What shall I wash with? | *Ndasháya chọkúgezesa nácho (ndícho).* I have nothing to wash with. |
| *Ndóénda n(a)aní?* Who shall I go with? | *Ndasháya wọkúénda náye.* I have no one to go with. |
| *Ndóyǒra ngẹ́ṇyi?* What shall I write with? | *Ndasháya chộkǔnyóresa nácho (ndícho).* I have nothing to write with. |
| *Ndíaní àchándǐbátsírá?* Who will help me? | *Ndasháya ànóndǐbátsírá.* I have no one to help me. |

"Something to …" is ***ch-*** (class 7, "thing") + the linking ***-o-*** + the infinitive: ***chọ-kú-ita***, the dialogue's *chekuita*. For a person, class 1: ***wọ-kú-enda naye*** "one to go with". The tool goes after with *nacho* (*na* + *icho*, Stage 5; FSI's dialect alternative *ndícho*). The last line uses a relative instead: *ànóndǐbátsírá* "who helps me". *-shaya* is "lack, fail to get". (*Ndóyǒra* is as FSI prints it; the answer has *-nyoresa*, from *-nyora* write.)

**Practice.** Ask your speaking partner whose things in the room are — *… ndẹ́raaní?* — with nouns from as many classes as you can, and answer theirs with *Ndẹ́…*. Then complain to each other: nothing to do, nothing to cook with, no one to go with — *Ndashaya cho…*, *Ndashaya wo…*.
Three times a week: ka- for how often:
FSI Unit 37, Exercise 6 — "The prefix /kà-/ in expressions of frequency." "How many times a week do you go to the store?" "We go three times.":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Pavhíki munóenda kanganí kuchitóro?* | *Tinóenda katatú.* |
| *Pavhíki munóenda kanganí kuchéchi?* | *Tinóenda kaẏirí.* |
| *Pavhíki munóenda kanganí kudhíbhi?* | *Tinóenda kámwé.* |
| *Pamwedzí munóenda kanganí kudhoróḅa?* | *Tinóenda kagúmí.* |

To the store three times; to church (*chechi*) twice; to the dip tank once; to town ten times a month.

**The form.** ***ka-*** + a number stem is "so many times": *ka-tatu* three times, *ka-ẏiri* twice, *ka-mwe* once, *ka-gumi* ten times, and the question ***ka-ngani?*** "how many times?". *Pa-vhiki* "per week", *pa-mwedzi* "per month" are Stage 5's class 16 *pa-* "at". The *ka-* is the class 12 prefix of Unit 35; Unit 37's dialogue had *kazhinzhi* "many times".

The end of Stage 8: nouns for doers and doing, the negative command, "not yet", the causative pairs, *-dai* "like", *-na-* "must", commands with objects and purposes, *ka-* and *tu-*, *-su*, *chi-* and *-natsa*, "still", the *-nga* phrase, *dai* "if", *nde-* "it is X's", "something to do", and *ka-* "times".

| | |

| *Imbwá dzángu mbirí dzírí\`kúpi?* | Where are my two dogs? |
| *Imbwá dzángu nhemá dzírí\`kúpi?* | Where are my black dogs? |
| *Bhurúkwa rángu demá rírí\`kúpi?* | Where are my black trousers? |
| *Bhurúkwa rángu itsvá rírí\`kúpi?* | Where are my new trousers? |
| *Bhurúkwa rángu bamhí / deté / refú / pfúpi rirí\`kúpi?* | … my wide / narrow / long / short trousers? |
| *Mugóti wángu mupfúpi / murefú / mutsvá / muchená / mutetè / mupamhí úrí\`kúpi?* | Where is my short / long / new / white / thin / wide cooking stick? |
| *Zvigaro zvédú zvipamhí / zvina / zvitemá zvírí\`kúpi?* | Where are our wide / four / black chairs? |

FSI's second half gives nouns of every class with *kupi* and with *kuti* — *Mbúdzí dzedu nhema dziri kupi?*, *Chirongó chedu chikuru chiri kupi?*, *Tsono yedu huru iri kupi?*, *Mwenje yedu midịkị iri kuti?*, *Démó redu idzva riri kuti?*, *Mbatyá dzédu itsva dziri kuti?* — untoned. It does not say what *kuti* means here; ask your partner. Note the adjective's class prefix: *mbiri* and *nhema* (10) with no prefix of their own, *dema*, *itsva*, *bamhi* (5), *mu-* (3), *zvi-* (8). FSI's *idzva* / *itsva* is a dialect pair.

**Readings.** Untoned unless FSI marks them — read aloud, have your partner mark the tones, translate:

> *Ndine hókwa yangu musi wemugobera. Ndinoda kukóká vanhu vazhinji. Vanababa navana mai vẹmuguta munokokwa. Panozova nezvọkudya zvizhinji. Ndinokokazve vanakomana nẹvasikana. Iyi hókwa inozovamba masikati. Tinozovamba nemitambo yạvana. Kuti yãpéra tómwǎ zvộkǔmwâ. Vabereki votambavwo yavo. Kudyá kwose kwoburwa kupa vanhu.* (Unit 32: a gathering on Saturday, with FSI's English: "I'm having a gathering on Saturday … When those are over, we'll have some drinks. The parents will have some fun, too. Then all the food is poured out to give to people.")

> *Mweni ari kuuya; todiniko? Unogeza mumba nemafafitera. Ndinoisa mushonga here pasi nezvigariro? … Misa midziyo yẹse munzvimbo dzayo. Ndinogadzira mupandaṇyi wọmweni? Unogadzira mupanda mudịkị. Mune machira àkachena here? Hunde, unotora machira, mitsamiro nezvigezeso zvàkachena. Mwenje une parafini here? Kwete, únoda kuzadzwa.* (Unit 32: a guest is coming — what do we do?)

> *Muri kuona mhando here ngesadza? Kwete handinyanyi kuona mhando. … Ini ndinoda kwazvo sadza asi handizivi kubika kwacho. Mungadą here kudzidza kubika? Oh! ndingadą kwazvo asi handina ànondidzidzisa. Ndingamukoką kwazvo kuti muzouye kumusangano wemadzimai. … Dai mungauyą tingamudzidzisą kubika sadza redu, imẉi muchitidzidzisewo kubika renyu.* (Unit 34: learning to cook sadza, and a women's meeting.)

Hatisati tãnatsa kuziva asi zvimwe Hurumende ichatiti makore matatu. … Murume wangu anochaira mabhazi ànoenda kwaMtoko. Ane nguva yakadini achichaira? Oh! agara kwazvo. … Tafara kuonana nọkuzivana. Ivaṇyi nọkugara kwàkanaka.* (Unit 34: two wives meet in Harare.)

Ndinozongą ndichikupa ____. … Haúóní heré kuti símbi írí kunyanya kupísá? Handifungi kudaro.* (Unit 36: hiring Maneta to wash and iron. FSI: "translate the following material, converting it into the same format as that of the practice conversations.")

Every grammar point of the stage is in these: *Hatisati tãnatsa kuziva* (not yet, and *-natsa*), *Ndinozongą ndichikupa* (the *-nga* phrase), *Dai mungauyą* (*dai*), *ànondidzidzisa* "someone to teach me", *írí kunyanya kupísá* "is too hot" (*-nyanya* before the infinitive).

**With your speaking partner, this week:**

1. Run a household: give orders and forbid things, with objects — *Ípe …*, *Usárǐísą …*, *Ríisé pàkáǒmǎ* — and with purposes, *Ndípe … ndí…*.
2. Say what must be done (*-na-*), what hasn't been done yet (*-sati*), and what will have been done by evening (*-nọ́nga*).
3. Ask after people: who is still doing what (*-chiri ku-*), who had been doing what when you came (*-kanga*), and why someone couldn't (*Ngẹ́ṇyi ãkangẹ ásínga…?*).
4. Talk about small things in class 12 and 13, and be mildly surprised at them with *-su*.
5. Plan a week: how often you do each thing (*ka-*), what you would do if you could (*dai*), and what you lack (*Ndashaya cho…*).
6. Hire someone: what they can do, what they do well (*-natsa*), when they start.

**Then.** Stage 9 follows FSI from Unit 38, whose "dialogue material" FSI leaves "the student … to use his own initiative in deciding how to study".
Writing home: stamps and the post office:
FSI Unit 38 opens with short dialogues and no drills to go with them: "The student should use his own initiative in deciding how to study the short dialogues given below. **The goal is to incorporate into his own repertoire the words and the grammatical constructions which they contain.**" This lesson and the next two give all eight; the grammar they carry has lessons of its own after them.

**Dialogues 1 and 2** — a letter to post, and the way to the post office:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndanyórá tsamba dzọkúmushá.* | I've written a letter (of to) home. |
| *Zvitámbi ndingázvǐóną̀ pápǐ?* | Where can I get stamps? |
| *Izvo mẉãti murí kuenda kudhoróbha.* | As you said, you are going to town. |
| *Post Office írí murùtìvì mẉeMain Street.* | The post office is on Main Street. |
| *Ndíaní àrí kuenda kuRailway Station?* | Who is going to the Railway Station? |
| *Tom ẉákámbóti manheru ndirí kuenda.* | Tom mentioned last night that he was going. |
| *Ángandíbvúnzírąwó heré midzíyó yángu?* | Can you ask [for] my things for me? |
| *Zvíyá nzira yácho írí pápǐ?* | By the way, which (where) is the way to (of) it? |
| *Írí panhasí pámuDzvítí.* | It is below the Native Commissioner['s]. |
| *Írí panhasí zvishoma péBank.* | It's a little below the bank. |
| *Munazobvunza mukangẹ mwãsvika.* | You'll have to ask when you (have) arrive(d). |
| *Ndípo pànótúmírwá tsamba heré?* | Is that where letters are sent? |
| *Hóngu. Chímbídzáí, váẏá kupfígá.* | Yes. Hurry, they're closing. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *chitámbi* | 7, 8 | stamp |
| *rùtìvì* | 11, 6 | side |
| *-bvunza* | | to ask |
| *mudzíyó* | 3, 4 | furniture, household goods, utensils |
| *zvíyą ~ zvíyą̀* | | by the way |
| *panhasí* | 16 | below |
| *-chímbídzá* | | to hurry |

**What is in it.** *tsamba dzọkúmushá* "a letter of to-home" is Stage 5's linking prefix in front of a place word; FSI's *ọ* means *dzo-* in some places, *dze-* in others. *Zvitámbi ndingázvǐóną̀ pápǐ?* puts the thing first and echoes it on the verb with the object prefix *-zvi-* (Stage 4), in Stage 2's *-nga-* tense. *Ángandíbvúnzírąwó* is the same tense with Stage 6's applicative (*-bvunz-ir-* "ask for") and Stage 5's softening *-wo*. *pànótúmírwá* "where they are sent" is a relative (the grave on *pà-*) of the passive *-túmírwa*. *Izvo mẉãti* "as you said", *mukangẹ mwãsvika* "when you have arrived" and *váẏá kupfígá* "they are now closing" each carry a tense or form taught later in this stage — *zvíyá* and *mukangẹ* have lessons of their own; *váẏá* + infinitive is in *Still hot, cool now*. *Dzvítí* is FSI's word for the Native Commissioner of 1965; learn the sentence for *panhasí*, not for the office.

Tone marks as before: *á* high, unmarked low; FSI's *ǎ* is low in the central (standard) reading, *â* high; *ā* a raised low; a grave after a syllable (*ą̀*) a lowered one; **ˣ** a tone that varies between speakers. A dot under a letter means some speakers leave it out (FSI's *mẉa-* "you (pl.)" is eastern; the standard says *ma-*); a mark under a vowel (*ọ*, *ą*, *ẹ*) that two vowels are used by dialect. A **tilde** over a vowel (*mwã-*, *ndã-*) is FSI's mark for **participial tones** — Stage 7's tonal participials — "one or more tonal patterns, according to dialect" (Unit 27); the verb after it is said with those tones.

**Practice.** Play the start of FSI Unit 38. Then ask your speaking partner where three places in your own town are — the post office, a bank, a shop — and have them answer with *írí panhasí*, *írí murùtìvì mwe…*, *zvishoma*; then swap. Ask for stamps with *ndingázvǐóną̀ pápǐ?* and for anything else with the same frame.
Paying the car tax, and a meeting in tow:
FSI Unit 38, Dialogues 3 and 4.

**Dialogue 3** — the car tax:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndinódaˣ kundotèrera mótokari yangu.* | I want to go pay the tax [on] my car. |
| *Zvíyá ndípo tĩnopinda muMain Street?* | Oh, is that where we enter Main Street? |
| *Ah! Mẉatáura.* | Right! (You have spoken.) |
| *Zvákanángísána neCecil Hotel.* | It faces the Cecil Hotel. |
| *Kuti ndikasaenda sóndo ríno haíngafámbǐ.* | If I don't go this week, [the car] can't go [on the roads]. |

**Dialogue 4** — the meeting:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndafúnga kumboenda kuHaráre.* | I thought I'd go over to Salisbury (Harare). |
| *Kúneṇyíko nḥási?* | What is [going on] today? |
| *Musangano úyazvé wàkátáurwa.* | That meeting that was spoken about. |
| *Hóngu! Ndangá ndãkanganwa.* | Oh yes! I'd forgotten. |
| *Únóitirwepí zvíya?* | Where will it be held, by the way? |
| *Únózóngą ũri paChristian Centre.* | It will be at the Christian Centre. |
| *Kubva tózoṇzwá mẉãuya.* | Then we'll hear [about it] when you come [back]. |
| *Así handípǎzívǐ.* | But I don't know the place. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *-tèrera* | | to pay tax; to obey, submit |
| *-kánganwá* | | to forget |

**What is in it.** *Mẉatáura* "you have spoken" is how one agrees: "right!". *Kúneṇyíko?* is Stage 5's *kune* "there is" with *-nyi* "what?" and *-ko*: "what is there [going on]?". *Musangano úyazvé* — "that meeting", the one you both know about — is the *-ya* of this stage, with *-zve*. *Ndangá ndãkanganwa* "I had forgotten" is *-nga* (was) and a participial (*ndã-*), the same pattern as *Únózóngą ũri* "it will be (being) at …". *ndikasaenda* "if I don't go" and *mẉãuya* "when you come" are dependent and participial forms of this stage. *Únóitirwepí* is *-ita* with the applicative and the passive, "where will it be done-at?". Salisbury is Harare now; FSI writes *kuHaráre*.

FSI marks *Ndinódaˣ* with its sign for a tone that varies between speakers; take your partner's.

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, plan a trip to town: say why you are going (*Ndinódaˣ kundo…*), ask what is on (*Kúneṇyíko nḥási?*), ask where it is held, and say "I'd forgotten" when they remind you. Then swap.
Potatoes for Penhalonga, and a burned dr:
FSI Unit 38, Dialogues 5 and 6.

**Dialogue 5** — going to sell potatoes:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndicháénda Péniranga.* | I'm going to go to Penhalonga. |
| *Kúneṇyíko zvíya?* | What's going on? |
| *Ndinódâ kùmbòndòténgésá.* | I want to go and do a little selling. |
| *Hóngu, mbatáta dzíya heré?* | Oh, yes, [to sell] those potatoes? |
| *Ndakádzǐchéra nezúro.* | I dug them yesterday. |
| *Ndinódáírá dzínọ muténgó wàkánáka.* | I hope they bring (have) a good price. |
| *Zvíyá vánoténgá heré muzvitóro?* | By the way, do they sell [lit. buy] them in the stores? |
| *Zvishoma, así pamusika.* | Not much, but [they do] at the market. |

**Dialogue 6** — at home:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mái vápǐsǎ̀ hémbé yávó.* | Mother burned her dress. |
| *Ípi yácho?* | Which one? |
| *Yavo nhemá íya.* | That black one. |
| *Simbí haíri kusándá zvàkánáka.* | The iron isn't working right. |
| *Dáídzáí mugadzirisi.* | Call the repairman. |

**What is in it.** *kùmbòndòténgésá* stacks three prefixes on one infinitive: *-mbo-* "a little" (Stage 5), *-ndo-* "go and" (Stage 2), on *-téngésá* "sell": "to go and do a little selling". *Ndakádzǐchéra* is the *-ka-* past with the object prefix *-dzi-* for the potatoes (class 10). *Ndinódáírá* is FSI's "I hope"; *dzínọ* is *dzine* "they have", with the vowel that varies by dialect. *mbatáta dzíya*, *nhemá íya* — "those potatoes, that black one, the ones we both know of" — are this stage's *-ya*. *vápǐsǎ̀* "she burned" is the past of today of *-pisa*, which in Stage 5 was "be hot": here "burn". *Simbí haíri kusándá* is Stage 5's *ha-* + *-ri* + infinitive, "is not working", with *zvàkánáka* "well" — the *zv-* of this stage.

Tone marks as before: *á* high, unmarked low; FSI's *ǎ* is low in the central (standard) reading, *â* high; *ā* a raised low; a grave after a syllable (*ą̀*) a lowered one; **ˣ** a tone that varies between speakers. A dot under a letter means some speakers leave it out (FSI's *mẉa-* "you (pl.)" is eastern; the standard says *ma-*); a mark under a vowel (*ọ*, *ą*, *ẹ*) that two vowels are used by dialect. A **tilde** over a vowel (*mwã-*, *ndã-*) is FSI's mark for **participial tones** — Stage 7's tonal participials — "one or more tonal patterns, according to dialect" (Unit 27); the verb after it is said with those tones.

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, sell them something you grew or made: say where you are going and why with *kùmbòndò-*, say when you made it with *-ka-* and an object prefix, and hope for a good price. Then tell them something at home has broken (*… haíri kusándá zvàkánáka*) and have them tell you whom to call.
Gogogo: coming in, and visiting the sick:
FSI Unit 38, Dialogues 7 and 8.

**Dialogue 7** — a visit:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Gógógoyí MáíJongwé.* | May I come in, Mrs. Jongwe? |
| *Pindáí̀ zvényú.* | Come in! |
| *Kwáíwáízve shéwe!* | Hello! |
| *Ndaúwe!* | (Courteous expression used by women.) |
| *Nyamazvé shéwe shúmba!* | (Courteous greeting reflecting the fact that the greeter is a woman and that the totemic affiliation of the person greeted is the lion.) |
| *Nyama shéwe humbá!* | (Same, except that the totemic animal of the person greeted is the pig.) |
| *Muchídiní kurwárá?* | How are you feeling now? (How are you now doing to be ill?) |
| *Áiwá, zvírínáne chaízvo.* | Oh, it's much better. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *gògògò* | | (said in lieu of knocking, to seek admittance to a house or room) |
| *kwaiwai / kwaziwai* | | (a greeting) |
| *shúmba* | 9, 10 | lion |
| *humbá* | 9, 10 | bush pig |
| *-rwárá* | | to be ill |

**Dialogue 8** — asking after a sick woman:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Várǎrǎ séṇyi MáíMutí?* | How is Mrs. Muti? (How did Mrs. Muti sleep?) |
| *Áiwáwo nḥási vámbóti ráreṇyí.* | Oh, last night she slept a little better. |
| *Así havásatí vãsimbá.* | But she's not strong yet. |
| *Ndicháũyǎ kuzováóná.* | I'll come to see her. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *-sìmbà* | | to become strong |

**Totems.** *Shúmba* and *humbá* are animals, and here they are also the *mutupo*, the clan totem, of the person greeted: a woman greets someone of the lion totem with *Nyamazvé shéwe shúmba!*, someone of the pig totem with *Nyama shéwe humbá!*. The totem is a form of address, as *shéwe* and *chirombówe* were in Stage 1. Ask your partner what their totem is and how they are greeted by it — FSI gives only these two.

**What is in it.** *Gógógoyí* is *gògògò* "knock knock" made a request; *Pindáí̀ zvényú* "come in" has the *zv-* of this stage after a command, as in Stage 1's *fambai zvenyu*. *Muchídiní kurwárá?* is Stage 7's *-chi-* participial of *-díni*: "how are you now doing [at] being ill?" *Várǎrǎ séṇyi?* is the Stage 1 greeting, asked about a third person. *vámbóti ráreṇyí* "she slept a little better" is the **ideophonic form**, the subject of its own lesson below. *havásatí vãsimbá* "she is not yet strong" is *-sati* "not yet" with a participial.

Tone marks as before: *á* high, unmarked low; FSI's *ǎ* is low in the central (standard) reading, *â* high; *ā* a raised low; a grave after a syllable (*ą̀*) a lowered one; **ˣ** a tone that varies between speakers. A dot under a letter means some speakers leave it out (FSI's *mẉa-* "you (pl.)" is eastern; the standard says *ma-*); a mark under a vowel (*ọ*, *ą*, *ẹ*) that two vowels are used by dialect. A **tilde** over a vowel (*mwã-*, *ndã-*) is FSI's mark for **participial tones** — Stage 7's tonal participials — "one or more tonal patterns, according to dialect" (Unit 27); the verb after it is said with those tones.

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, visit: say *Gógógoyí*, be told to come in, greet (by totem if your partner gives you theirs), and ask how the sick person is today and how they slept; your partner answers "a little better, but not strong yet". Then swap.
Zv- with no noun: a little, well, come i:
FSI Unit 38, Note 1: "The dialogues for this unit illustrate several grammatical situations in which the element ***zv-*** is used **without reference to any antecedent noun in Class 8**. These uses of *zv-* may be loosely described as 'adverbial'."

*Zv-* is the concord of class 8 (*zvi-*, *zva-*: Stage 3). Without a class 8 noun in sight it means "in a way, -ly". FSI's four:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (a) | *panhasí* · *panhasí zvishoma* | below · a little below |
| (b) | *kusándá zvàkanaka* | to work well |
| (c) | *zvíyá ~ zvíyà* | by the way (cf. *zvitámbi zvíyà* "those stamps [that we both know about]"; *chitámbi chíya* "that stamp") |
| (d) | *Pìndáí̀ zvényú.* | Come in. |

So *zvishoma* "a little" is Stage 3's *-shoma* "few" with no noun to agree with; *zvàkanaka* "well" is the relative adjective (Stage 3) of class 8; *zvényú* "yours" after a command is the gentle *zvangu*, *zvavo* of Stage 1. *Zvíyá* is the demonstrative *-ya* (next lesson) with *zv-*, and FSI gives it its own note there.

You have used these since Stage 1 — *zvakanaka* "fine", *fambai zvenyu*, *ndaswera zvangu*, *zvakadini* "how?" (Stage 5) — and Unit 39 adds one more: *zvimwe* "perhaps", "cf. Unit 38, Note 1".

**In this unit's sentences:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Írí panhasí zvishoma péBank.* | It's a little below the bank. |
| *Simbí haíri kusándá zvàkánáka.* | The iron isn't working right. |
| *Zvishoma, así pamusika.* | Not much, but [they do] at the market. |
| *Pindáí̀ zvényú.* | Come in! |
| *Áiwá, zvírínáne chaízvo.* | Oh, it's much better. |

**Practice.** Tell your speaking partner how you do five things — work, cook, sleep, read, drive — with *zvàkanaka*, *zvishoma*, *zvakányánya*, and have them ask *zvakadini?* back. Then give each other three commands softened with *zvényú* or *zvako*.
That one we both know: -ya:
FSI Unit 38, Note 2: "The demonstrative stem ***~ya*** is illustrated several times in the dialogues for this unit":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *musangano úya* | that meeting (that we were talking about, or that we both know about) |
| *mbatáta dzíya* | those potatoes (that we both know about) |
| *nhemá íya* | that black one (that you've seen) |

"Although this is called a 'demonstrative' stem, **it has nothing to do with distance or direction**, but implies that the identity of the person or thing referred to is common knowledge of both speaker and hearer." Stage 3's *uyu* and *uyo* are "this" and "that" by place; *úya* is "that one — you know the one".

"Some further examples":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mukómaná úya wọmẉákaóna ẉákaúyá.* | That boy that you saw came. |
| *Bhúku ríya rẹwãkaténga rákarásíka.* | That book that you bought got lost. |
| *Chitámbi chíya chạnézúro ndakáchǐóná.* | That stamp (of) [that we were looking for] yesterday, I've found it. |

**The concords** — FSI's Drill 1, "Have you seen that boy (that we were talking about)?". Each class puts its own concord before *-ya*:

| Noun | Class | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *mukómaná* | 1 | *Waóná mukómaná úya heré?* |
| *vaímbí* | 2 | *Waóná vaimbi váya heré?* |
| *mushongá* | 3 | *Waóná mushonga úya heré?* |
| *mití* | 4 | *Waóná miti iya heré?* |
| *jírá* | 5 | *Waóná jira riya heré?* |
| *maţaka* | 6 | *Waóná maţaka áya heré?* |
| *chitámbi* | 7 | *Waóná chitambi chiya heré?* |
| *zvipó* | 8 | *Waóná zvipo zviya heré?* |
| *hémbé* | 9 | *Waóná hembe iya heré?* |
| *tsápáto* | 10 | *Waóná tsapato dziya heré?* |
| *rwizí* | 11 | *Waóná rwizi rúya heré?* |
| *kabhudhura* | 12 | *Waóná kabhudhura káya heré?* |
| *tukúkú* | 13 | *Waóná tukuku túya heré?* |
| *uswá* | 14 | *Waóná uswa húya heré?* |
| *chirembá* | 1a | *Waóná chiremba úya heré?* |

FSI marks some of the drill's *-ya* forms high (*úya*, *váya*, *áya*, *rúya*) and leaves others unmarked (*iya*, *riya*, *chiya*); learn the tones from your partner, since FSI's recordings stop at Unit 35. The class 6 noun is printed *maţaka* with a mark under the *t* that does not print clearly; say it as your partner does.

**By the way: *zvíyá*.** "This stem together with the prefix *zvi-* produces a word which occurs several times in these dialogues. It has the expected tonal pattern ***zvíyà*** except when it precedes the main part of the sentence, in which instances it is ***zvíyá***":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Zvíyá nzira yácho írí pápǐ?* | By the way, which is the way to it? |
| *Zvíyá vánoténgá heré muzvitóro?* | By the way, do they sell them in the stores? |
| *Únóitirwepí zvíya?* | Where will it be held, by the way? |
| *Kúneṇyíko zvíya?* | What's going on [, then]? |

**Practice.** Do Drill 1 with your speaking partner giving the noun and you the sentence, every class. Then talk about things you both know of — a film you both saw, a shop you both go to, a person you both met — with *-ya*, and slip one *zvíyá* into each question.
She slept a little better: the ideophoni:
FSI Unit 38, Note 3. "One of the dialogues for this unit contains a new kind of verb form":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *vátì rárèṇyí* | she slept |

"The word ***ráre*** is called the '**ideophonic**' form of the verb whose stem is *-rárá*. In the example cited above, the courteous element *-ṇyi* has been added to it."

**How it is made.** "The ideophonic form of a verb seems always to occur **after either the infinitive or some other form of the special verb *-ti***. It is formed with ***-e*** as the final vowel. The tonal pattern has basic tone on the first syllable (i.e. high for high verbs, low for low verbs), and (at least in some varieties of Shona) with alternating high and low tones on the remaining syllables":

| | Infinitive | Ideophonic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High verbs | *kùrárá* | *rárè* |
| | *kùchísísá* | *chísìsé* |
| Low verbs | *kùswèrà* | *swèré* |
| | *kùpùkùtà* | *pùkútè* |

So *vámbóti ráreṇyí* is "she just-did slept-a-bit": *-ti* "say, do" (Stage 1's pro-verb) with *-mbo-*, then the verb as a sound-picture. The sense, in FSI's drill, is "a little (more) than before".

**FSI's Drill 2** — "Sentences that contain the ideophonic forms of some verbs":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Vámbóti rárẹṇyí.* | She's a little better [than yesterday]. |
| *Vámbóti sweréṇyi zvávó.* | They're a little better this afternoon [than in the morning]. |
| *Ndambóti garéṇyiwó.* | I've done a little more sitting [than before]. |
| *Vámbóti rimérimé kupinda nezúro.* | They've done a little more plowing than yesterday. |

The first two are the Stage 1 greetings again: one asks *Várǎrǎ séṇyi?* "how did they sleep?" and is told *vámbóti ráreṇyí*. *rimérimé* doubles the form for "plowing and plowing".

Then a girl who did not do her work properly — FSI gives no English for these; the glosses are ours, from FSI's words. "Let her do it a little":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Musíkaná haáná kupukuta zvakánáka.* | The girl didn't wipe well. |
| *Ngááti pukúte zvishoma.* | Let her wipe a little. |
| *Musíkaná haáná kuchísá zvakánáka.* | The girl didn't iron well. |
| *Ngááti chísisé zvishoma.* | Let her iron a little. |
| *Vasíkaná haváná kuchenesa mbatyá.* | The girls didn't clean the clothes. |
| *Ngáváti chenésése zvishoma.* | Let them clean a little. |
| *Vakómaná haváná kuchengeta ṃombe.* | The boys didn't look after the cattle. |
| *Ngáváti chengétése zvishoma.* | Let them look after [them] a little. |
| *Vasíkaná haváná kutsváírá zvakánáka.* | The girls didn't sweep well. |
| *Ngáváti tsváírisé zvishoma.* | Let them sweep a little. |
| *Babá haváná kugadzira dangá zvakánáka.* | Father didn't make the kraal well. |
| *Ngáváti gadzírise zvakánáka.* | Let him make it well. |

*Ngááti*, *Ngáváti* are Stage 7's subjunctive of *-ti* with *nga-* "let"; the verb itself is the ideophone.

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, do Drill 2: they say what someone didn't do well, you answer *Ngááti …e zvishoma* with the ideophone. Then ask after their night, their afternoon and their work, and answer with *ndambóti …eṇyi*.
If he goes: the dependent -ka- tense:
FSI Unit 38, Note 4. "In Unit 24, the tense with the non-initial prefix *-chi-* was introduced. This tense is said to be '**dependent**' because a verb in this tense cannot be the only verb in a sentence." (That is Stage 7's participial.)

"There is **another dependent tense** in Shona, illustrated in":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *… mùkàngẹ̀ mwãsvika.* | … when/if you (have) arrive(d). |
| *Ndìkàsàèndà …* | If I don't go … |

"The characteristic prefix for this tense is ***-ka-***, which of course has the same consonant and the same vowel as the prefix for the hesternal tense (Unit 6, Note 1). The two tenses differ, however, in that":

| | Dependent *-ka-* "if, when" | Past *-ka-* (Stage 2) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (1) "the subject prefix syllable does not contain the vowel *-a-*" | *ndikaenda* if I go | *ndakáénda* I went (before today) |
| (2) "the tones of *-ka-*, and of the subject prefix are low, regardless of the person of the subject" | *vàkàenda* if they go | *vákáenda* they went (before today) |

"The tone of an object prefix in this tense is high, and the verb stem itself has its basic tone." The negative puts ***-sa-*** after *-ka-*: *ndìkàsàèndà* "if I don't go".

**FSI's Drill 3** — "Maybe he will go." "If he goes, I can go also." "If he doesn't go, I can't go either.":

| Maybe … | If he … | If he doesn't … |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Zvimwe ácháenda.* | *Akaenda ndingáéndąwó.* | *Akasaenda handíngáendíwo.* |
| *Zvimwe áchafárá.* | *Akafárá ndingáfárąwó.* | *Akasafárá handingafáriwó.* |
| *Zvimwe áchadáídzwá.* | *Akadáídzwá ndingádaidzwąwó.* | *Akasadáídzwá handíngadáidzwíwo.* |
| *Zvimwe áchadáro.* | *Akadáro ndingádarówo.* | *Akasadáro handíngadárowó.* |

The answers pair the dependent *-ka-* with Stage 2's *-nga-* "can" and its negative (*handinga-* … *-i*), and Stage 5's *-wo* "too, either". *Zvimwe* "perhaps" is Unit 39's.

**Drill 4** — "Further examples":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ukamúóná unamúdáídzá.* | If you see him, (you must) call him. |
| *Chikóro chikangẹ chãpera ndicháũyǎ.* | When school is out, I will come. |
| *Mukamútáurira ánoṇzwá.* | If you talk to him, he listens/understands. |
| *Ndikangẹ ndãgona ndinózǒenda.* | If I can, I'll go. |
| *Akabvuma ndinómǔtúmá.* | If he agrees, I will send him. |
| *Ẕvikadá, ndicháénda kwáMréwa.* | If (it is) possible, I will go to Mrewa. |

In *Ukamúóná*, *Mukamútáurira*, the object prefix *-mú-* is high, as the note says. *Zvikadá* "if it wants" is "if possible" — class 8 with no noun again. FSI marks its *Z* with a sign under it that does not print clearly; say *Zvikada* as your partner does.

**Practice.** Do Drill 3 with your speaking partner: they give "maybe he will …" with any verb, you give both "if" answers. Then make your plans for the weekend with *Ndikaenda …*, *Zvikadá …*, *Ndikasa…*, and have them answer with what they will do too.
When it is over: -kange, and -ka- beside:
FSI Unit 38, Drills 5 and 6 — more of the dependent *-ka-*.

**Drill 5** — "The dependent tense with *-kà-* vs. the *-cha-* tense of the same verb." "She'll agree to cook sadza." "If she refuses, I'll report her to Mother." (FSI gives English only for the first pair; the rest are ours, from FSI's words.)

| *-cha-* | dependent *-ka-* |
| --- | --- |
| *Achábvúma kubika sadza.* She'll agree to cook sadza. | *Akaramba ndichámǔtáurira kunáMáí.* If she refuses, I'll report her to Mother. |
| *Áchavaká imbá yédú.* He'll build our house. | *Akavaká, tichámǔpá marí.* If he builds [it], we'll give him money. |
| *Áchápukuta ndíró.* He'll wipe the dishes. | *Akapédzá áchatámbá.* If he finishes, he'll play. |
| *Áchaúngánídza ṃombe.* He'll gather the cattle. | *Akangẹ ãpédza áchadzíúnzá kudangá.* When he has finished, he'll bring them to the kraal. |

**Drill 6** — "The dependent *-kà-* tense in verb phrases with ***-ngą***." "School isn't over yet." "When it is over, I'll come.":

| Not yet | When it has … |
| --- | --- |
| *Chikóro hachísatí chãpera.* | *Chikangẹ chãpera ndicháũyǎ.* |
| *Babá havásatí vãdzoka kudare.* | *Vakangẹ vãdzoka ndichákǔtáurira.* |
| *Hárí haísatí yãzara.* | *Ikangẹ yãzara ndichárega.* |
| *Kunzé hakúsatí kwáchena.* The rain hasn't cleared up. | *Kukangẹ kwãchena, Baba váchaénda kujana.* |
| *Ngúvá haísatí yãkwana.* | *Ikangẹ yãkwana, tichápfǐgǎ.* |

Our glosses for the rest of Drill 6: "Father hasn't come back from the court yet. — When he has come back, I'll tell you." "The pot isn't full yet. — When it is full, I'll stop." "When it has cleared up, Father will go herding [the cattle]." "The time hasn't come yet. — When it has come, we'll close."

**How *-kange* works.** *-nga* "be" (Stage 4's *-ange*, *ndangá* "I was") takes the dependent *-ka-*: *chi-ka-ngẹ* "if/when it is", and the verb after it is participial, with FSI's tilde: *chãpera* "having ended". Together: "when it has ended". The negative of the same idea is *-sati* + participial, "not yet": *hachísatí chãpera*. FSI's *ẹ* in *-kangẹ* is a vowel that varies by dialect.

**Practice.** With your speaking partner: they say something isn't done yet (*… hachísatí chã…*), you say what you'll do when it is (*… -kangẹ …ã…*). Then do Drill 5 the other way round: they say what someone will do with *-cha-*, you say what happens if they do.
The rains, the heat, the harvest: the se:
FSI Unit 39 begins the change FSI announced: "The basic material for this unit consists of **an assortment of short texts**, some in dialogue form, some in the form of monologues, and some in the form of miscellaneous useful sentences. As in Unit 38, the student should use his own initiative in deciding how to study them. As always, the goal is to make the words and the grammatical constructions his own, so that he can draw on them when he listens to Shona, speaks it, or reads it."

The first text is the farming year of Mashonaland. FSI's warning: "seasons in Mashonaland are not directly comparable to seasons in the northern hemisphere."

**Zienzá** — the rains:

| *Ndwizí dzínozárá̀ kwázvo.* | The rivers are very full. |
| *Makombá ánoˣvamba.* | Gullies get started. |
| *Varimi vánodyárá̀ mbésa.* | The farmers plant crops. |

| *Zvipfúyó zvinokora.* | Livestock gets fat. |
| *Mití yọsé inoita mazánhí matsvá.* | All the trees put out new leaves. |
| *Zvikóro zvọsé zvínopfígwá.* | All the schools are closed. |

| *Hángá nedzímwe shiri dzínokanda.* | Guinea fowl and other birds lay eggs. |
| *Ndíyo ngúvá yẹmárindá.* | This is the time for protecting [the fields from baboons]. |

| *Tinópfěkǎ zvìnódzǐyǎ.* | We put on warm [clothing]. |
| *Vanhu vánoténgésá zvirimwá.* | People sell what they have grown ([things] cultivated). |
| *Mumatsútsó tinódyaˣ zvitsvá.* | In matsutso we eat fresh [things]. |
| *Mbésa dzọsé dzínóibva.* | All crops ripen. |

FSI labels *zienzá* class 21, a class this course has not met; in its sentence it agrees like class 5 (*rínónaya*). Ask your partner which form they use, *zienzá* or *maenzá*. The marks: *ˣ* on *ánoˣvamba* and *tinódyaˣ* is FSI's variable tone; a grave after an acute (*dzínozárá̀*) a lowered syllable after it. *pánọngą pãẏa kupísá* and *rínọngą rísíṇgachapísi* are *-nga* "be" with a participial: "it is now hot", "it is no longer hot" (the *-cha-* "still" of the next lessons).

The time for fertilizing: a farmer's dia:
FSI Unit 39 — a short dialogue about farming, in two halves (FSI's English throughout).

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Yásvíka ngúvá yệmǔpfúdze.* | The time for fertilizing has arrived. |
| *Murí varimisu pánó?* | So you're farmers here?! |
| *Tirí kundoedzawó zvédú.* | We do our best. |
| *Chíṇyi chìnónyanya kudíkánwá?* | What is most necessary? |
| *Kuti uchídá kurima, óná kuti uné zvộkǔsándísá heré.* | If you want to farm, be sure whether you have tools ('[things] to use'). |
| *Ndinódawó pẹkúrìma muriwo.* | I'd like a place to raise muriwo. |
| *Mbeú mẉaẏá nadzó heré?* | Do you have any seeds? |
| *Ndiné shoma; ndingázótutsirą.* | I have a few. I may add [some] later. |
| *Icho ndĩsina íbadzá.* | What I lack is a hoe. |
| *Ivú répánó rínodísá mupfúdze.* | The soil around here really needs fertilizer. |
| *Zvé, rínodá mvúrá zhínjí.* | Also, it needs a lot of water. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *-tutsira* | | to add |
| *badzá* / *mapadzá* | 5 / 6 | hoe |
| *zvé* | | in addition, besides |

**What is in it.** *Murí varimisu* "so you are farmers!" has *--su*, which FSI's Glossary calls an "expression of surprised interrogation". *kundoedzawó zvédú* "we just try" — *zv-* again, softening. *Chíṇyi chìnónyanya kudíkánwá?* "what is most needed?" is a relative (*chì-*) of *-nyanya* "do exceedingly" with an infinitive. *zvộkǔsándísá* "things to use" and *pẹkúrìma* "a place to farm" are the linking prefix before an infinitive — "of using", "of farming" — the subject of a lesson below. *Kuti uchídá* "if you want" is Stage 7's *-chi-* participial after *kuti*. *mẉaẏá nadzó* "you now have them" is *-ya-* "now" with *na* + the class pronoun (Stage 5). *ndĩsina* "[that which] I don't have" is a participial negative (FSI's tilde). *Ivú répánó* "the soil of here". *mupfúdze* is "fertilizer, manure"; FSI also prints it *mupfundze* once, and Unit 40 *mupfudza*.

Tone marks as before: *á* high, unmarked low; FSI's *ǎ* is low in the central (standard) reading, *â* high; *ā* a raised low; a grave after a syllable (*ą̀*) a lowered one; **ˣ** a tone that varies between speakers. A dot under a letter means some speakers leave it out (FSI's *mẉa-* "you (pl.)" is eastern; the standard says *ma-*); a mark under a vowel (*ọ*, *ą*, *ẹ*) that two vowels are used by dialect. A **tilde** over a vowel (*mwã-*, *ndã-*) is FSI's mark for **participial tones** — Stage 7's tonal participials — "one or more tonal patterns, according to dialect" (Unit 27); the verb after it is said with those tones.

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, plan a garden: ask what is most needed, say what you have and what you lack (*Icho ndĩsina í…*), what the soil needs, and when you'll add more. Then swap and let them plan theirs.

**What is in it.** *Ngátíchímbóise* "let's just put" and *Ngátívérengezvé* "let's read again" are Stage 7's subjunctive with *nga-* "let us", with *-chi-* "now" and *-mbo-* "for a bit", and Stage 4's *-zve* "again". *Ndíaní àchí nemúbvunzo?* "who still has a question?" is *-chi* "still" (lesson below) as a relative. *Tazónàtsa kuṇzwá* — *-natsa* "to do something well" with an infinitive. *Dzéhǒpezvé?* "of sleep, again?" asks after a traveller's night; *tapúmúzá* "we have rested [from the road]". *muviri wényú úya* "that body of yours" uses *-ya*. A dot under a letter means some speakers leave it out (FSI's *mẉa-* "you (pl.)" is eastern; the standard says *ma-*); a mark under a vowel (*ọ*, *ą*, *ẹ*) that two vowels are used by dialect. **Practice.** Run a lesson with your speaking partner as teacher: say you've read enough, ask to put the books down, tell them they're going too fast, ask to read again together, and ask who still has a question.
