We move constantly: moving house, and se:
FSI Unit 39 ends its texts with a conversation between a Shona speaker and an American (FSI's English).

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Munótámátáma heré?* | Do you change residence often? |
| *Ah! Tinótámátáma kàsíṇgapéri.* | We move constantly. (We move times without end.) |
| *Takátǎmǎ kashánǔ pamakoré maséré àkápěrǎ.* | We've moved five times in the last eight years. |
| *Ah! Zvínhu zvìnónetsa izvi!* | Oh, that's a nuisance! |
| *Hapáná zvọkúita.* | There's nothing to do [about it]. |
| *Munómbofunga ngẹ́hǎmǎ dzényú heré kumushá?* | Do you ever think about your relatives at home? |
| *Hóngu. Tinódzióná kana tichínga tãenda kuU.S.A.* | Oh yes. And we go to see them whenever we are in the U.S. |
| *Vákámbouyá kumúóná heré murí kúnó?* | Have they ever come to see you (while you are) here? |
| *Hazvímbóitíki! Kufámbá kúnodá marí.* | It's impossible! Travel is very expensive. |
| *Mungátiudzẹ nọkúsanduka kwéngǔvǎ pagoré heré?* | Tell me about the change of seasons [in America]? |
| *Tinọ kusanduka kuna, kwàkádaí nge spring, summer, fall, winter.* | We have four changes, namely spring, summer, fall and winter. |
| *'Summer' yákadái ngẹzíenza heré?* | Is summer like zienza? |
| *Hazvíná kunyatsoenzana(ba).* | They're not very similar. |
| *Mu'summer' hamúnyanyónayi.* | In summer it doesn't rain very much. |
| *Zvé, múnóti píse kunyanya.* | Besides, it's very hot. |

**What is in it.** *-támátáma* doubles *-tama* for "move again and again". *kàsíṇgapéri* "times that do not end" and *kashánǔ* "five times" are class 12 *ka-* as "times", the counting of Stage 2 with a new prefix (Stage 8's class 12). *Hazvímbóitíki* "it never happens" is *-mbo-* "ever" in a negative (Stage 5), on *-ita* "do": "it is never done". *Munómbofunga ngẹ́hǎmǎ?* "do you ever think of relatives?" — *-funga* takes *nge-* "about". *tichínga tãenda* "whenever we are having gone" is *-chi-* on *-nga* with a participial. *kwàkádaí nge…* "which are like …" and *yákadái ngẹzíenza* "is like zienza" use Stage 1's *-dai*. *kunyatsoenzana(ba)* has Stage 5's negative enclitic *-ba* in brackets — some speakers add it. *múnóti píse kunyanya* "it is very hot" is an ideophone of *-pisa* after *-ti*: this unit's form. English words inside Shona take Shona prefixes: *Mu'summer'*.

**Practice.** Tell your speaking partner how often you have moved, with *ka-* and a number; ask whether they ever think of home and whether their family visits. Then describe the seasons of the place you come from to them in Shona, comparing each with zienza, chirimo, matsutso and chando.
Some, other: -mwe:
FSI Unit 39, Note 1: "Note that the stem ***~mwè*** corresponds both to English 'some' and to English 'other'. It differs tonally from ***~mwé*** 'one'. Also, *~mwè* usually **precedes** the noun that it goes with, while *~mwé* usually **follows** the noun."

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *~mwé* | one | after the noun — Stage 2: *rímwé*, *mumwé* |
| *~mwè* | some, other | before the noun: *dzímwe shiri*, *vamwe varume* |

From Unit 39's seasons: *Hángá nedzímwe shiri dzínokanda* "guinea fowl and other birds lay eggs"; *Zvipuká nedzímwe shiri zvínotámá* "animals and some birds migrate". From the stories later in this stage: *Vamwe vakadaidzira* "some shouted", *Rimwe zuva* "one day" (lit. some day), *Umwe naumwe* "each one".

"Note the use of ***zvimwe*** by itself as an 'adverbial' modifier, corresponding to English '**perhaps**'. In this respect, cf. Unit 38, Note 1" — class 8 with no noun, as *zvishoma*. So Unit 38's *Zvimwe ácháenda* "maybe he will go".

**FSI's Drill 1** — "Concords with *~mwè* 'some other'." "Is that shirt warm?" "It isn't very warm." "Buy another that is warm.":

| Noun | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *hémbé* (9) | *Iyo hémbé ínodzíyá heré?* | *Haínatsí kudzíyá.* | *Téngá imwe ìnódzíyá.* |
| *tsápáto* (10) | *Idzo tsápáto dzínodzíyá heré?* | *Hadzínatsí kudzíyá.* | *Téngá dzimwe dzìnódzíyá.* |
| *ngowání* (9) | *Iyo ngowání ínodzíyá heré?* | *Haínatsí kudzíyá.* | *Téngá imwe ìnódzíyá.* |
| *bhurúkwa* (5) | *Iro bhurúkwa rínodzíyá heré?* | *Harínatsí kudzíyá.* | *Téngá rimwe rìnódzíyá.* |
| *mbatyá* (10) | *Idzo mbatyá dzínodzíyá heré?* | *Hadzínatsí kudzíyá.* | *Téngá dzimwe dzìnódzíyá.* |

*Haínatsí kudzíyá* "it doesn't do well at being warm" is the negative of *-natsa* "do well" + infinitive: "not very". *ìnódzíyá* after *imwe* is a relative: "another that is warm". *bhurúkwa* is "pair of trousers" (Glossary); *ngowání* is not in FSI's Glossary — ask your partner.

**And *-cha-* "still".** FSI, same note: "In the sentence *zúvá rínọngą rísíngachapísi*, the prefix ***-cha-*** corresponds to English 'still', and does not have future meaning. Compare Unit 7, Note 1." Stage 2 met this: *-cha-* is "will", and with some stems "still". Here in a negative, "it is no longer hot": *rí-si-nga-cha-pís-i* "it not-still-hot".

**Practice.** Do Drill 1 with your speaking partner, with five more things you wear. Then talk about your family with *vamwe … vamwe …* ("some live in town, others at home") and answer three questions with *Zvimwe*.
Nouns made from verbs:
FSI Unit 39, Note 2. "In Unit 32, Note 1, we met one group of nouns which are derived from verbs. These were the **agentive nouns**, in Classes 1 and 2, with the final vowel ***-i***." (Stage 8; and Unit 38's *mugadzirisi* "repairman" is one, from *-gadzirisa*.) "Several other types of nouns that are related to verbs occur in the basic materials for this unit":

| Noun | | Verb | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *chirimwá* (7, 8) | something cultivated | *kùrìmwà* | to be cultivated |
| | | and: *chìnórimwa* | that which is cultivated |
| *mubvùnzò* (3, 4) | question | *kubvùnzà* | to ask |
| *chirìmò* (7, 8) | a season for agriculture | *kurìmà* | to cultivate, plough |
| *mapitsè* (6) | competition | *kupìtsà* | to reply, boast of |
| *marindá* (6) | season for protecting | *kurindà* | to guard, protect |

**What to see in them.** The noun takes a class prefix and keeps the verb's root: *-rim-* "cultivate" gives *chi-rim-o* "a season for agriculture" and, from the passive *-rim-w-a*, *chi-rim-w-á* "something cultivated". *-bvunz-* gives *mu-bvunz-o* "question". The final vowel changes — *-o* for *mubvùnzò*, *chirìmò*; *-e* for *mapitsè*; *-a* kept in *chirimwá*, *marindá*. FSI shows the relative *chìnórimwa* beside *chirimwá* to make the point: a relative verb says "that which is cultivated" as a whole clause, the derived noun says it in one word.

FSI gives *mapitsé* and *marindá* high at the end in the season texts, and *mapitsè* low at the end in this note; follow your partner.

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, take ten verbs you know — *-dzidza*, *-tamba*, *-famba*, *-imba*, *-bika*, *-rima*, *-vaka* … — and ask them which have a noun made from them and what it means. Write down what they give you; do not guess, since the final vowel and class are not predictable from these five.
Dug a little: crops, participials and id:
FSI Unit 39, Drill 2: "Various crops, with verbs appropriate to them; participial vs. ideophonic forms of the verb." "Have the potatoes been dug?" "Just a little.":

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| *Mbatáta dzáti dzãcherwa heré.* | *Dzámbóti cherwé zvishoma.* |
| *Zviyó zváti zvãchekwa heré?* | *Zvámbóti chékwe zvishoma.* |
| *Shushururu dzáti dzãibva heré?* | *Dzándóti íbve zvishoma.* |
| *Mbésa dzáti dzãpupurwa heré?* | *Dzándóti púpurwé rutivi.* ('in part') |
| *Jangano ráti rãvambwa heré?* | *Rándóti vambwé chinhambwe chàpérá.* |
| *Chibarwé cháti chãbviswa mumunda heré?* | *Chámbóti bviswé zvishoma.* |

Our glosses for the rest, from FSI's words: "Has the millet been cut? — It's been cut a little." "Have the shushururu ripened? — They've ripened a little." "Have the crops been reaped? — They've been reaped in part." "Has the work party been started? — It was started a short while ago." "Has the maize been taken out of the field? — It's been taken out a little." (*Shushururu* is a crop FSI does not gloss.)

**The two forms side by side.** Both halves use *-ti* (Stage 1's pro-verb, "say, do"), and differ in what follows it:

| | *-ti* + … | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Question | participial (FSI's tilde): *dzáti dzãcherwa* | "they are already (in the state of) dug?" — *-ti* + participial: "have they been …?" |
| Answer | ideophone: *dzámbóti cherwé* | "they just-did dug-a-bit" — Unit 38's ideophonic form, here of the passive *-cherwa* |

The passive (Stage 6) makes ideophones too: *-cherwa* → *cherwé*, *-pupurwa* → *púpurwé*, *-bviswa* → *bviswé*. With *-ndo-* "went and" for *-mbo-* (*dzándóti*) the sense is "went as far as …ing".

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *zviyó* | 8 | millet |
| *chibarwé* | 7, 8 | maize |
| *-cheka* | | to cut [with knife] |
| *-ibva* | | to become ripe, done, mature |

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, ask about six jobs around the house or the garden in FSI's frame — *… -áti …ã…wa heré?* — and answer each with *-ámbóti …e zvishoma* or *-ándóti …e rutivi*: the dishes washed, the bed made, the grass cut, the letter written.
The time of sowing: the linking prefix b:
FSI Unit 39, Drill 3: "**Linking prefix followed either by the infinitive or by the participial form of a verb.**" Stage 5 joined nouns with the linking prefix, "of": *sadza rêzvǐyô* "sadza of millet". It can join a noun to a verb as well.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Tinódyárá magwére ngúvâṇyǐ?* | [At] what time do we sow maize? |
| *Muzienzá ndíyo ngúvá yộkǔdyárá.* | In zienza (, that) is the time of sowing. |
| *Tinópúpúra ngúvâṇyǐ?* | When do we reap? |
| *Muchando ndíyo ngúvá yộkǔpúpúrá.* | In chando, (, that) is the time of reaping. |
| *Tinórima ngúvâṇyǐ?* | When do we plough? |
| *Mumavambo ezíenzá ndíyo ngúvá yọkúrima.* | In the beginning of zienza is the time of ploughing. |
| *Tinótímbá ngúvâṇyí?* | When do we plough for the second time? |
| *Tãpedza kupúpúrá ndíyo ngúvá yộkǔtímbá.* | When we have finished harvesting is the time for reploughing. |
| *Tinódirira ngúvâṇyǐ?* | When do we water? |
| *Tãpedza kudyárá ndiyo nguva yetĩnodirira.* | When we've finished sowing is when we water. |
| *Tinópfeka dzinódzíyá ngúvâṇyǐ?* | [During] what period do we put on warm [clothes]? |
| *Pachando ndíyo ngúvá yetĩnopfeka dzìnódzíyá.* | ('In cold [weather] is the time of our putting on those [clothes] that are warm.') |
| *Tinochera mupfundze ngúvâṇyǐ?* | When do we dig [?] manure/fertilizer? |
| *Kuvamba kwechírimo ndíyo ngúvá yetĩnochera mupfúdze.* | The beginning of chirimo is the time when we dig [?] fertilizer/manure. |

The "[?]" is FSI's own: it was not sure of "dig" for *-chera* with manure.

**The two kinds:**

| Linking prefix + … | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| infinitive | *ngúvá yọ-kú-dyárá* | the time of sowing |
| participial | *ngúvá ye-tĩ-nodirira* | the time [when] we water — "the time of our watering" |

With the infinitive, the class 9 linking prefix *yọ-* (*yo-* or *ye-* by dialect) sits on *ku-*. With a participial, *ye-* sits on the whole verb — subject prefix (*tĩ-*, with FSI's tilde for participial tones), tense, stem — and English needs "when we …". *ngúvâṇyǐ?* "what time?" is *nguva* with *-nyi* (Stage 3). *Tãpedza kupúpúrá* "we having finished reaping" is a participial standing for "when we have finished". *Mumavambo ezíenzá* "in the beginnings of zienza".

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *magwére* | 6 | maize (sg. *gwere*) |
| *-dirira* | | to water |
| *mavambo* | 6 | beginning (cf. *-vamba*, to begin; our gloss) |

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, ask "when do we …?" with *ngúvâṇyǐ?* about your own year — school, holidays, the garden, the heating — and answer each with *ndíyo ngúvá yọku…* and once with *ndíyo ngúvá yetĩ…*.
Still hot, cool now: -chi- and -ya-:
FSI Unit 39, Drill 4: "**Two contrasting kinds of verbal phrase.**" FSI gives no note to go with it; the drill shows the contrast:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mumbá múchí kutónhórá heré?* | Is it still [cold] in the house? |
| *Kwéte. Mváẏá kudzíyá.* | No, it's [warm] now. |
| *Mvúrá yáẏá kupísá heré?* | Is the water hot now? |
| *Kwéte. Íchí kutónhórá.* | No, it's still cold. |
| *Zvidhína zvíchí kupísá heré?* | Are the bricks still hot? |
| *Kwéte. Hazvíchí kupísá. Zváẏá kupórá.* | No, they're not still hot. They're cool now. |
| *Hárí yápǒrǎ heré?* | Is the pot cooled off? |
| *Kwéte.. Íchí kupísá.* | No, it's still hot. |
| *Ivú rátǒnhǒrǎ herě?* | Has the earth/soil cooled off? |
| *Kwéte. Ríchí kupísá.* | No it's still hot. |

FSI's English for the first pair reads "Is it still hot in the house? — No, it's cool now", which turns the Shona round: *-tónhórá* is "to be cold" and *-dzíyá* "to be warm" in its own word lists. The table gives the Shona's sense in square brackets.

**The two phrases:**

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| subject prefix + ***-chí*** + infinitive | *íchí kupísá* | it is **still** hot |
| subject prefix + ***-a-ẏa*** + infinitive | *yáẏá kupórá* | it is hot **now** (has become so) |
| negative: *ha-* + SP + *-chí* + infinitive | *hazvíchí kupísá* | it is no longer hot |

*-chí* is the "still" of *Ndíaní àchí nemúbvunzo?* "who still has a question?". *-áẏá*, with the dotted *ẏ* some speakers leave out, FSI does not explain; in its sentences it is "now, has come to be", as in *váẏá kupfígá* "they're closing now" and *zváẏá kubvira kuvá* "much better now". The simple past of today does the same work with a stative verb: *Hárí yápǒrǎ?* "has the pot cooled?".

The rest of FSI's drill has no English; the glosses are ours:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *mapfíhwa* | *Mapfíhwa áchí kupísá heré?* — *Kwéte. Átǒnhǒrǎ. / Ápǒrǎ.* | Are the hearth stones still hot? — No. They've gone cold / cooled. |
| *bhíkiri* | *Bhíkiri rápǒrǎ heré?* — *Kwéte. Ríchí kupísá.* | Has the cup cooled? — No, it's still hot. |
| *pachotó* | *Pạchotó pátǒnhǒrǎ heré?* — *Páchí kudzíyá.* | Has the fireplace gone cold? — It's still warm. |
| *kófi* | *Kófi íchí kudzíyá heré?* — *Kwéte. Yáẏá kutónhórá.* | Is the coffee still warm? — No, it's cold now. |
| *símbi* | *Símbi yáẏá kutónhórá heré?* — *Kwéte. Íchí kupísá.* | Is the iron cold now? — No, it's still hot. |
| *mbatáta* | *Mbatáta dzáẏá kudzíyá heré?* — *Kwéte. Dzíchí kupísá.* | Are the potatoes warm now? — No, they're still hot. |
| *nyama* | *Nyama yáẏá kupórá heré?* — *Kwéte. Íchí kupísá.* | Has the meat cooled now? — No, it's still hot. |
| *kunzé* | *Kunzé kúchí kutónhórá heré?* — *Kwéte. Kwáẏá kudzíyá.* | Is it still cold outside? — No, it's warm now. |

*-pórá* "to cool off" is FSI's English only, not in a word list. *zvidhína* "bricks" (Glossary *chi-dhina*), *mapfíhwa* "stones for setting a cooking pot on" and *bhíkiri* "cup" are from earlier units.

**Practice.** Do the whole drill with your speaking partner giving the noun, you the question and they the answer, then swap. Then do it with real things on the table — tea, soup, the oven — *íchí …*, *yáẏá …*.
Congratulations on the new dress:
FSI Unit 40: "Unit 40 consists of two medium-length dialogues, followed by a large number of two-line conversational fragments. The former contain new vocabulary, but the latter are intended as review of vocabulary that has occurred in earlier units. The student should use the blank right-hand column on each page for writing in English translations, or cues of other kinds, so that he may practice producing the Shona sentences."

So FSI gives these dialogues **no English**: the glosses below are ours, built from the words FSI glosses in this unit and earlier ones.

**Dialogue 1** — a new dress:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndakáténgá̀ hémbé itsvá.* | I bought a new dress. |
| *Wàkáténgá yàkaita séṇyi?* | What kind did you buy? (You bought one that is how?) |
| *Ndakáténgá̀ zvángu chená.* | I just bought a white one. |
| *Makórókótó wená wàáne hémbé itsvá!* | Congratulations, you who have a new dress! |
| *Ndiné urombó nokúti handína kuóná iyo ndãida.* | I'm sorry, because I didn't find the one I wanted. |
| *Waída yàkadini?* | What kind did you want? |
| *Ndaída ìne mavárá machená nạmátsvukú.* | I wanted one with white and red colours. |

**Dialogue 2** — a car going fast:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ndaóná mukómaná ãri kumhányísá motokari.* | I saw a young man driving a car fast. |
| *Ẉánga achíéndepí?* | Where was he going? |
| *Handízívi, zvimwe kuTsonzó.* | I don't know, perhaps to Tsonzo. |
| *Ẉánga ãine mótokari yàkaita séṇyi?* | What kind of car did he have? |
| *Ẉánga ãine mótokari tsvukú.* | He had a red car. |

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *makórókótó* | | (an expression of felicitation or congratulation) |
| *tọsé* | | (the usual answer to the above; literally "all of us") |
| *urombó* | 14 | sorrow |
| *wená* | | (a word for "you (sg.)" not found in the Shona dictionary, but present in some other Bantu languages to the south and east of Shona) |
| *mavárá* (6) / *muvárá* (3, 4) | | colour |
| *~tsvukú* | | red, brown, etc. |
| *-mhányá* | | to run, go fast |
| *páchìpámwé* | | (an expression used when meeting a person who has already been greeted on the same day) |

**What is in it.** *yàkaita séṇyi?* "[one] that is how?" and *yàkadini?* "what sort?" are relatives (the grave on *yà-*) — Stage 5's *-dini* and the same question with *-ita séṇyi*. *iyo ndãida* "the one I wanted" has FSI's tilde: participial. *ìne mavárá* "having colours" is a relative of *-ne*. *machená nạmátsvukú* "white ones and red ones" — adjectives agreeing with *mavárá* (6). *ãri kumhányísá* "being making-run", with the causative of *-mhányá*: driving fast. *Ẉánga achíéndepí?* "he was going where?" is *-nga* "was" with Stage 7's *-chi-*. *Makórókótó* is answered *tọsé* "all of us". *wená* is, FSI notes, not even in the dictionary. *Ndiné urombó* is Stage 1's "I'm sorry".

**Practice.** Tell your speaking partner about something new you bought; they congratulate you with *Makórókótó*, you answer *tọsé*, and they ask what kind with *yàkaita séṇyi?*. Then describe a car, a coat and a house by colour. Greet them a second time the same day with *páchìpámwé*.
Two-line conversations: at home and on t:
FSI Unit 40's "two-line fragments of conversations" are "review of vocabulary that has occurred in earlier units", printed untoned and without English. Here are the half that happen at home and in the fields; the next lesson has the rest. The glosses are ours, from FSI's words; where FSI never glosses a word, it is left in Shona and named.

| Line 1 | Line 2 | Our gloss |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Mai wakwidibira sadza.* | *Rega usabate.* | Mother has covered the sadza. — Leave it, don't touch it. |
| *Mẉasvika rini pano?* | *Ndasvika mai vãchi kukubvura sadza.* | When did you arrive here? — I arrived while Mother was still stirring the sadza. |
| *Ndiri kutengesa nhanga.* | *Munoita mariṇyi?* | I'm selling pumpkins. — How much are they? |
| *Vanhu vane basa nguva yẹmarinda.* | *Nguva yạmatsutso vanoiteṇyi?* | People have work at the time of guarding the fields. — At matsutso time, what do they do? |
| *Mazanhi ạmahobo aoma nechando.* | *Baba vasima ṃamwe mahobo nḥasi.* | The banana leaves have dried in the cold. — Father has planted other bananas today. |
| *Ndinoda kugurira miti yangu.* | *Wabvepi nayo?* | I want to cut back my trees. — Where did you get them from? |
| *Ndisekuru vàbatanidza mbatya.* | *Munoda kuisa mumvura ìnodziyasu?* | It's Grandfather who has put the clothes together. — Do you want to put them in warm water, then? |
| *Mwana ẉakanyarara here?* | *Ndamuradzika pamubhedha.* | Has the child gone quiet? — I've put him to bed. |
| *Ndichachisa mbatya nḥasi.* | *Masimbe unao here?* | I'll iron clothes today. — Do you have charcoal? |
| *Munoiteṇyi zienza?* | *Tinorima minda.* | What do you do in zienza? — We plough the fields. |
| *Ngoro yenyu yaendepi nḥasi?* | *Iri kutakura mupfudza.* | Where has your oxcart gone today? — It's carrying manure. |
| *Sadza ranyanya kukora.* | *Ah! waregera richikora zvàkadaro ngeṇyi?* | The sadza is too thick. — Ah! Why did you let it go on getting thick like that? |
| *Tine chimbudzi chakanaka.* | *Ndiani ẉàkachivaka?* | We have a good chimbudzi. — Who built it? |
| *Denga reimba yedu rinonaya.* | *Isu redu ràkagadzirwa nababa.* | The roof of our house leaks. — Ours was made by Father. |
| *Mẉakapupura zvàkadini gore rino?* | *Magwere gumi remasaki, zviyo masaki mana enzungu makumi mairi.* | How did you do at harvest this year? — Maize, ten sacks; millet, four sacks; groundnuts, twenty. |
| *Masanga mbuya.* | *Ndauwe.* | Hello, grandmother. — (a woman's courteous answer) |
| *Munda wenyu une marindasu!* | *Kwete hauna marinda.* | So your field is guarded! — No, it has no guarding. |
| *Munda vạmadhumbe uri pẹtyo here?* | *Kwete, hauri pẹtyo; uri kure.* | Is the coco-yam field near? — No, it isn't near; it's far. |
| *Ndatenga hari ìsina chigadzo.* | *Ukatenga ìne chigadzo, yakapinda kunaka.* | I've bought a pot without a stand. — If you buy one with a stand, it's better. |
| *Baba vaenda kujana nḥasi.* | *Vanoenda kangani pamwedzi?* | Father has gone herding today. — How many times a month does he go? |

**The words, and where FSI glosses them.** *-kwidibira* to cover (Unit 27); *-rega* to desist, leave off; *-bata* to seize, catch; *-kubvura* to stir; *nhanga* pumpkin; *marinda* protection of the fields; *-oma* to become dry; *-sima* to plant (Stage 4's *Simai maruva*); *-gurira* to cut off or across; *-batanidza* to join together; *--su* "an expression of surprised interrogation"; *-radzika* to put to bed; *-chisa* to iron; *masimbe* (6) charcoal; *ngoro* (9, 10) oxcart; *-takura* to lift and carry; *-kora* to become fat, thick; *-regera* to cease; *denga* (5) roof, sky; *madhumbe* (6) coco yams; *chigadzo* (7, 8) the hollow holding a pot upright (Stage 5's kitchen); *jana* (5) herding cattle. **FSI never glosses *chimbudzi***; ask your partner.

**What is in them.** The review is the point: Stage 2's tenses, Stage 3's relatives (*ìnodziya*, *ìsina*, *ìne*), Stage 4's object prefixes (*ndamuradzika*, *ẉàkachivaka*), Stage 5's *-dini* (*zvàkadini*), and this stage's dependent *-ka-* (*Ukatenga*), *ka-* "times" (*kangani* "how many times?") and *--su*. *vãchi kukubvura* "while she was still stirring" is *-chí* "still" in a participial. *Mai wakwidibira* has FSI's eastern *w-* for "she" (Stage 1); the standard is *akwidibira*. *ṃamwe* has a dot: some say *mamwe*, some *amwe*.

**Practice.** FSI's own way: cover our glosses, write your own English in a notebook beside each line, then from your English alone say both lines in Shona to your speaking partner, who answers with line 2. Let them put the tones on every line.

Tsuro and Diro steal sweet potatoes:
FSI Unit 41 begins the last part of the course. "Units 41 – 49 differ from Units 1 – 40 in four ways":

1. "They are not based on dialogues, but on **narrative texts**."
2. "There are **no grammar notes**, and no sets of sentences organized for systematic practice."
3. "The only tone markings are ***~***, which indicates that the verb should have participial tones, and ***\\***, which means that the verb has relative tones."
4. "The texts display occasional **inconsistencies in spelling** and in word division."
5. "Their principal purpose is to give the student an opportunity to develop habits of **self-sufficiency** in adapting, learning and using material from a wide variety of Shona texts; secondary purposes are review of grammar and increase of vocabulary."

**How FSI says to use them** — "in all or most of the following ways":

1. "Working with his tutor, the student should mark all tones in the A version of the story."
2. "Covering the A version, and referring to it as little as possible, the student should read the text aloud at least twice in the hearing of his tutor, reading from the B version. [The B version should never be marked for tones.]"
3. "Read aloud at least twice from the C version, which contains the stems of the words but not the affixes."
4. "Read aloud at least twice from the D version, which contains the affixes but lacks most of the roots."
5. "Answer and ask questions about the text."
6. "Ask the tutor to retell the same material twice in his own words. Ask questions if necessary."
7. "The student should retell the same material in his own words."

Versions A and B are the same text in two columns; C and D are the text with parts blacked out. Here, version A is given with our gloss; for C and D, your partner reads the text to you and you supply the missing half aloud — the roots one time, the affixes the next.

| --- | --- | --- |

| 15 | *Varume vese vakarikomba.* | All the men surrounded it. |

| 17 | *Rakakwira mumuti murefu.* | It climbed into a tall tree. |
| 18 | *Varume vakatora mapfumo avo vakaribaya.* | The men took their spears and stabbed it. |

**FSI's new words** (untoned):

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *-ba* | to steal |
| *mbambaira* (9, 10) | sweet potato |
| *ungwaru* (14) | cleverness |
| *-rinda* | to guard, stand guard |
| *-bvùma* | to agree, consent |
| *-simuka* | to stand up |
| *chinyararire* | silently (cf. *-nyararira*, to be, become silent) |

**Who they are.** FSI never says in English what animals *Tsuro* and *Diro* are; they are the characters' names here. The concords tell you something: *Diro* takes class 5 (*rakabvuma*, *-ri-* "it", *waro* "its"), and *Tsuro* now class 1 (*ẉakati*), now class 12 (*kakatsvaka*, *kakarara* — Stage 8's diminutive class). Ask your partner what each animal is. *Zvanyanya* is a man's name; *Garegare* is Stage 2's *gare gare* "by and by" written as one word — the inconsistent spelling FSI warned of, as *zuwa* for *zuva* in line 1, and *pemwoyo* in A beside *pemworo* in B.

**What is in it.** *kundoba* is *-ndo-* "go and" on the one-syllable *-ba* (Stage 2). *ngatiende* "let us go" is Stage 7's subjunctive with *nga-*. *Vandoti svikeṇyi*, *Rãndoti cherenyi* are this stage's ideophones of *-svika* and *-chera* after *-ti*, with *-ndo-*: "when they had done arriving". *ndichirinda* "while I guard" and *vachiti* "saying" are Stage 7's *-chi-*. *nekusaziva* "with not knowing" puts Unit 38's negative *-sa-* into an infinitive. *ãripo*, *rĩrikuita* and *rãkanzwa* have FSI's tilde: participial — "it being there", "it doing", "it having heard". *hapachina* is *ha-* + *pa-* + *-chi-* "still" + *-na*: "there is no longer". *Rakabva rafa* is *-bva* "come from" with the next verb: "then it died".

FSI prints these texts **without tones**, except two marks it explains at Unit 41: "***~***, which indicates that the verb should have **participial tones**, and ***\\*** [a grave], which means that the verb has **relative tones**." The tones are for you and your partner to put in.

**Practice.** Do FSI's seven steps with your speaking partner, in order: mark the tones of version A together; read it aloud twice from an unmarked copy; read it twice with your partner reading the roots and you the endings, and twice the other way; then retell the story in your own Shona. The questions are the next lesson's.

| yes-no, false | *Vakabayana here?* | Did they stab each other? |
| who? | *Ndiani vakapangana kundoba?* | Who decided together to go and steal? |

Reading on your own: how FSI's last unit:
FSI Units 41–49 are not dialogues but **stories and short essays**. FSI's own note, at the head of Unit 41, governs everything in this stage. "Units 41 – 49 differ from Units 1 – 40 in four ways":

| | |
| --- | --- |
| (1) | "They are not based on dialogues, but on narrative texts." |
| (2) | "There are no grammar notes, and no sets of sentences organized for systematic practice." |
| (3) | "The only tone markings are /~/, which indicates that the verb should have participial tones, and /\`/, which means that the verb has relative tones." |
| (4) | "The texts display occasional inconsistencies in spelling and in word division." |
| (5) | "Their principal purpose is to give the student an opportunity to develop habits of self-sufficiency in adapting, learning and using material from a wide variety of Shona texts; secondary purposes are review of grammar and increase of vocabulary." |

**What each unit holds.** Every text is printed four times, then questioned:

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| Version A | The text, one sentence to a line, headed "[Mark tones in 'A' only.]" — the copy you tone |
| Version B | The same text, "[Do not mark tones in 'B'.]" — the copy you read from |
| Version C | Run on as prose with the **prefixes blacked out**: "the stems of the words but not the affixes" |
| Version D | Run on with the **roots blacked out**: "the affixes but lacks most of the roots" |
| Questions | Four on every sentence, then a handful about your own country |
| New Words | A short list, some glossed with a "(?)", some not glossed at all |

**The seven steps.** "These nine units should therefore be used in all or most of the following ways":

1. "Working with his tutor, the student should mark all tones in the A version of the story."
2. "Covering the A version, and referring to it as little as possible, the student should read the text aloud at least twice in the hearing of his tutor, reading from the B version. [The B version should never be marked for tones.]"

Being, while: the tilde forms:
FSI marks one thing in these texts and one only: "**/~/**, which indicates that the verb should have participial tones." These are the **tonal participials** of FSI Unit 27 (Stage 7): a verb that is not the main verb, made so by tone alone, translated "being …, while …, when … had …".

FSI Unit 27, Note 1: "The symbol /~/ above a vowel letter stands for one or more tonal patterns, according to dialect. Its simplest representation is found in some varieties of Manyika. In these dialects, the first syllable of each of these words has high tone regardless of person; the next has low, the next high, and so on, with alternant high and low syllables. A more widespread system has high tone on the first syllable, as in the above. The second syllable has basic tone on the first syllable of the root: low for low verbs, high for high verbs." And: "the English translation of the tonal participial of the 'hodiernal' tense commonly begins with 'when (subject) has (verb).'"

The Unit 47 forms follow a demonstrative (*iyo*, *idzo*, *apo*) and are best read "where …".

**Its partner mark.** The grave, "the verb has relative tones", appears only twice, and both times — against FSI's own rule — in the Version B copy of Unit 45: *ndine zvìnonaka* "I have **something that is** delicious" and *nevàkasungwa* "by those **who have been tied**".

**Practice.** Read each sentence in the table to your speaking partner and have them say the tilde verb in their own tones; FSI says the pattern differs by dialect, so theirs is the one to learn. Then make "while …" sentences of your own: *Ndãrikufamba, ndakaona …*
Without: -sina, and not: -sika-:
Two negatives turn up again and again in these texts — both participial, both from FSI Unit 28 (Stage 7).

**1. *-sina* "being without".** FSI Unit 28, Note 4: "The negative participial forms that correspond to indicative affirmative forms (e.g. /hamuna/) and participial affirmative (e.g. /muine/) that contain a subject prefix plus /-na/ consist of the subject prefix plus the negative prefix /-si-/ plus /-na/. The first syllable has high tone, and the remaining syllables have alternating low and high tones." FSI's own example: *musinacho* "you [being] without it"; *Ngenyi usina kuenda?* "Why didn't you go?"

So *-sina* is the "not having" of *-ne*, and with an infinitive the "didn't" of a participle:

| In the text | Our gloss |
| --- | --- |
| *Tsoko haina kuda kuenda **ĩsina** nzungu.* (44) | The monkey didn't want to go **without** groundnuts. |
| *… vakange **ãsina** demo.* (44) | … he was **without** an axe. |
| *Ngenyi **asina** kupindura chiro?* (45, Questions) | Why did he **not** answer anything? |
| *Ngenyi **dzisina** kufunga izvozvo?* (46, Questions) | Why did they **not** think of that? |
| *Ngenyi **musina** mhando dzese dzemhuka?* (47, Questions) | Why do you **not have** every kind of animal? |
| *Kune ndudzi here **dzisina** mitupo?* (49, Questions) | Are there clans **without** totems? |

**2. *-singa-*, *-sika-* "not (doing)".** FSI Unit 28, Note 3: the negative participial of the *-no-* tense "ends with the vowel /-i/" like the negative indicative, and "The element /-singa-/ is pronounced /-sika-/ in some dialects." FSI's example: *Unopfuura nepo usingamiri here?* "Will you pass there you-not-stopping?" The questions of these units use the *-sika-* form, after *Ngenyi* "why?":

| In the Questions | Our gloss |
| --- | --- |
| *Ngenyi vanhu **vasikadyi** tsoko?* (44) | Why don't people eat monkeys? |
| *Ngenyi vekumusoro **vasikanyanyi** kukudza zvirimwa?* (47) | Why don't the northerners grow many crops? |
| *Ngenyi **vasikanyanyi** kuvanda?* (49) | Why are they not very many? |

**And the relative.** Note 5: "Negative relatives are spelled exactly like the corresponding negative participials. They differ in pronunciation only in that the tones of the first two syllables are low-high": *Ndiwe usingaendi* "It is you who won't/doesn't go." So *Ndiani **asina** kuda kuzoteera mapenzi?* (46) is "Who is it **that did not** want …?"

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, answer "without": *Wakauya nemari here? — Kwete, ndakauya ndisina mari.* Then ask each other "Why don't you …?" with *-sika-* (or *-singa-*, as your partner says it): *Ngenyi musikadyi nyama?*
Nge-: by, because of, with:
The stories open half their sentences with a word in ***nge-***. FSI Unit 21 (Stage 6), Note 2: "In westerly dialects, the prefix has the form /nde-/, and its vowel is governed by the same principles as the vowel of /na-/ (Unit 14, Note 1). The tones of forms that contain this prefix are also like those of the corresponding forms with /na-/. The translation of /nge-/ is variously 'about' (i.e. concerning), 'by (means of)', or 'with'."

So *nge-* behaves like Stage 4's *na*: *ng(e)* + the noun, its vowel blending with the noun's.

**Because of, out of** — the stories' favourite:

| | Our gloss |
| --- | --- |
| ***Nge**mwoyo wayo, yakapinza ruoko mudende.* (44) | **Out of** its greed (heart), it put its hand in. |
| *Murume **nge**shungu, wakairowa netsvimbo.* (44) | The man, **in** anger, beat it. |
| *Tsuro **nge**unyope hwako kakasvova.* (45) | The Hare, **out of** laziness, sneaked off. |
| *Diro **nge**kupusa kwaro rakati ndisunge.* (45) | Diro, **in** his stupidity, said "Tie me." |
| *Vakarumwa **nge**kuti vakange asina demo.* (44) | He was bitten **because** he had no axe. |

**By (means of), by way of:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Tsuro kakanzwa **nge**mbiri kuti tsime rakapera.* (45) | The Hare heard **by** rumour that the well was finished. |
| *Ava vatungamiri vanotsarwa **nge**kukura kweunhengo.* (49) | These leaders are chosen **by** length (lit. growth) of membership. |
| *… **nge**kubaya majekiseni.* (49) | … **by** giving injections. |

**About, concerning:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Mapepa nhau arikutaura zvizhinji **nge**iyi nyika.* (48) | The newspapers say much **about** this country. |
| *Izvi zvidzidzo zvinotaura **nge**kudya kwakanaka.* (49) | These lessons speak **about** good food. |
| *Mumisangano umu munodzidziswa **nge**kugeza …* (49) | In these meetings there is teaching **about** washing … |

***Ngenyi?* "why?"** is the same prefix on *-nyi* "what?" — "about what?" — and FSI's questions use it on nearly every sentence (*Ngenyi tsoko yakachema?*). Unit 37's other *nge-*, the "it is" before a possessive (*Bhuku ngeraani? — Ngerababa*, Stage 8), is the same word in its other job: *kudai **nge**pa Kwekwe* (47) "such as **(it is) at** Kwekwe".

**Practice.** Tell your speaking partner why you did three things today, each with *nge-*: *Ndakarara ngekuneta*, *Ndakadya ngenzara* — and have them correct the vowel each time, as with *na*.

Was tied, was given: the passive -wa:
These texts are full of passives. FSI Unit 23 (Stage 6), Note 1: "The most frequent form of the passive extension is /-w-/. It follows all other extensions, and stands immediately before the final vowel of the verb." For one-syllable stems "the passive extension usually has the form /-iw-/: /-dyiwa/, /-diwa/, /-mwiwa/. Some speakers have /-piwa/ as the passive of /-pa/ 'give', but others have /-pawa/." And the doer: "The noun or pronoun that stands for the person or thing by which the action of the verb was accomplished is preceded by a non-concordial prefix, which is either /n-/ or /nd-/ or /ng-/ according to dialect … combined with the appropriate form of the linking prefix." FSI's example: *Sadza radyiwa naBaba* "The sadza was eaten by Father."

| *-bvundura* stir | *-bvundurwa* | *mvura yabvundurwa natsuro* (45) | the water **stirred up by** the Hare |
| *-sunungura* untie | *-sunungurwa* | *rakasunungurwa* (45) | he **was untied** |
| *-bata* catch | *-batwa* | *kaa kubatwa* (46) | it was about **to be caught** |
| *-gadzira* make | *-gadzirwa* | *simbi inogadzirwa* (47) | iron **is made** |
| *-kudza* grow | *-kudzwa* | *michero inokudzwa* (47) | fruit **is grown** |
| *-vaka* build | *-vakwa* | *kuvakwa* (47) | **to be built** |
| *-ganura* bound | *-ganurwa* | *yakaganurwa norwizi* (47) | it **is bounded by** the river |
| *-dinda* print | *-dindwa* | *anodindwa pazuva rimwe* (48) | they **are printed** every day |
| *-tsara* choose | *-tsarwa* | *vanotsarwa* (49) | they **are chosen** |
| *-dzidzisa* teach | *-dzidziswa* | *vanodzidziswa zvinhu* (49) | they **are taught** things |
| *-rapa* cure | *-rapwa* | *irapwe*, *vave kurapwa* (49) | (that) it **be cured**; they **are** now **being treated** |
| *-ita* do | *-itwa* | *Kunoitwa musangano* (49) | A meeting **is held** |

**The doer** comes with *na-* + linking vowel, exactly as FSI says: ***na**diro*, ***na**tsuro*, ***ne**vakasungwa*, ***no**rwizi* — Stage 4's *na* again. Some passives have more: *tichauraiswa* (46) "we will be got killed" is *-uraya* "kill" + causative + passive.

**Close cousins.** *-nzwika* (48) "to be heard, be known" and *-rapika* (49, Questions: *Hosha iyi inorapika here?* "Is this disease curable?") are the **neuter** *-ik-* of FSI Unit 24 — "can be …", not "is … by someone".

**Practice.** Turn sentences round with your speaking partner: they say the active (*Imbwa dzakabata tsuro*), you say the passive with the doer (*Tsuro yakabatwa nembwa*). Ten each, then swap.
Ka-: how the hare is spoken of:
Read Units 45 and 46 for their concords and you see the Hare spoken of in two ways at once:

| Class 1 (a person) | Class 12 (*ka-*) |
| --- | --- |
| *Tsuro **wa**kati, urikuendepi shamwari?* (46) | *Tsuro **ka**kasvova.* (45) |
| *Tsuro **wa**kati, tingaenda tese here?* (46) | *Tsuro **ka**kanzwa ngembiri …* (45) |
| *Tsuro anogona kuchera tsime here?* (45, Questions) | *Tsuro **ka**kati, kutiza chete …* (46) |
| | *… **ka**chiti, handiniba ndimagondo.* (46) |
| | *Tsuro kakaona kuti **kaa** kubatwa.* (46) |

**Class 12 is the diminutive.** FSI's class table (Stage 1) pairs 12 *ka-* with 13 *tu-*, and FSI Unit 35 (Stage 8) drills them: *huku* "chicken" → *kahuku kadikisu* "a tiny little chicken", *tuhuku tungani?* "how many little chickens?"; *mwenje* → *kamwenje*. FSI asks there: "What happens to the usual prefix of a noun when one of the diminutive prefixes /-ka-/ (sg.) or /-tu-/ (pl.) is added to it?" Speaking of the Hare in class 12 makes him "the little one". (Why he is little and the Hyena is not, FSI does not say; the tales treat the Hare as the small clever one.)

**Its possessive.** The class 12 "its, his" is ***-ko***, which looks like the *-ko* "your" of Stage 2 but is not:

| | Our gloss |
| --- | --- |
| *Tsuro ngeunyope **hwako** kakasvova.* (45) | The Hare, out of **his** laziness, sneaked off. |
| *Kakauya neuchi **hwako** mudende.* (45) | It came with **its** honey in a gourd. |
| *Kakasamba muviri **wako**.* (45) | It bathed **its** body. |
| *Kakagara nenyota **yako** here?* (45, Questions) | Did it stay with **its** thirst? |

*hw-* agrees with the class 14 nouns *unyope*, *uchi*; *w-* with class 3 *muviri*; *y-* with class 9 *nyota* — and *-ko* with the owner, class 12.

**Ka- for "times" is another *ka-*.** FSI Unit 37 (Stage 8) — "The prefix /ka-/ in expressions of frequency": *Tinoenda katatu* "We go three times", *kayiri* twice, *kamwe* once. Unit 49 has it: *Kunoitwa musangano mukuru **kamwe** pagore* "A big meeting is held **once** a year"; *Vanoita kangani …?* "How many times …?"

**Practice.** Tell your speaking partner a short story about a little animal, all in class 12: *Kambwa kakaona … kakatiza …* Then ask each other "How many times a week …?" and answer with *kamwe*, *kaviri*, *katatu*.
W for v: the Manyika spellings:
FSI's course is Manyika-based (Stage 1), and these texts were written as their writers spoke. The commonest sign is ***w* where the standard has *v***. Read past it; say the standard form.

| In FSI's text | Standard | | Where |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *Wana tsuro* | *vana* | title before a name | 45 |
| *wakawamba* | *vakavamba* | they began | 45; but *dzakavamba* in line 26 |
| *Wakapedza* | *Vakapedza* | they finished (the plural, as the Questions' *Ndiwanaani* "who (pl.)?" shows) | 45 |
| *wairowa* | *wairova* | he beat it — FSI's New Word is *-rova* | 44 |
| *kuwa nhengo* | *kuva nhengo* | to be members | 49 |
| *yawa patyo*, *Yawa nenzvimbo* | *yava* | it has come to be | 47, 48 |
| *iwenyoro* | *ive nyore* | that it be easy | 48 |
| *kuwe nyore* | *kuve nyore* | that it be easy | 47 |
| *huvandu* / Glossary *u-wandu* | (both) | amount, numerousness | 47 |
| *nguwa* (Questions) | *nguva* | time | 47, 48 |
| *-wova* (New Words) / *kuwowa* (text) | — | water at the mouth | 46 |
| *Rhodesia ichava*, *vava nhengo* | (already *v*) | | 47, 49 |

The same writer uses both, sometimes in one sentence, so this is not a rule of the language but a habit of the page.

**Other spellings to read past:**

| In the text | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| *ngeiyi nyika*, *cheiyinyika* | word division wanders: *ngeiyi*, *chei yi nyika* |
| *Mapepa nhau*, *mapepanhau*, *muma pepa nhau* | the same word, "newspapers", written three ways |
| *kwazvo* (A) / *kwazo* (B) | one is a misprint (49, Part II) |
| *iwenyoro* (A) / *iwenyore* (B) | FSI disagrees with itself (48) |
| *vatungamiriri* / *vatungamiri* | both in Unit 49, lines 5 and 6 |
| *zvose* / *zvese*, *tese* | *-ose* "all" (Stage 5) with Manyika *-ese* |
| *Magondo wakati* / *Magondo vakati* | the Hyena in singular and respect plural, Unit 46 |

**The class 1 *w-*.** *Tsuro wakati*, *Kamba wakati*, *Murume wakatiza* — this *w-* is the eastern subject prefix "he, she" that Stage 1's correction labels **eastern**; the standard says *akati*, *akatiza*.

**Practice.** Read Unit 45 aloud to your speaking partner, saying every *w*-for-*v* word in its standard form, and the class 1 *wa-* as *a-*; have them stop you each time you miss one.
The hyena and the hare:
FSI Unit 46, lines 1–15. **Magondo** is the Hyena — FSI's own gloss, in Unit 42 (Stage 9). Glosses ours, from FSI's words.

| | Version A | Our gloss |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | *Magondo wakasangana natsuro panzira.* | The Hyena met the Hare on the path. |
| 2 | *Tsuro wakati, urikuendepi shamwari?* | The Hare said, "Where are you going, friend?" |
| 3 | *Magondo wakati, kundotsvaka zvekudya.* | The Hyena said, "To go and look for food." |
| 4 | *Tsuro wakati, tingaenda tese here?* | The Hare said, "Can we go together?" |
| 5 | *Kutiuchizogona kutiza ngatiende.* | "If you'll be able to run, let's go." |
| 6 | *Tsuro kakati, kutiza chete, ibasaredu.* | The Hare said, "Running? Why, that's our very work." |
| 7 | *Vakabatana vakaenda rwendo rwavo.* | They joined up and went on their journey. |
| 8 | *Vãrikufamba, vakaona mhuru dzãkarara.* | As they were walking, they saw calves lying asleep. |
| 9 | *Magondo wakavamba kuwowa masiriri.* | The Hyena began to water at the mouth. |
| 10 | *Tsuro kakati, shamwari, imhuru dzevaridzi.* | The Hare said, "Friend, they are calves that have owners." |
| 11 | *Magondo vakati ndadini.* | The Hyena said, "What have I done?" |
| 12 | *Kakati, waa kuda kubata mhurudzevanhu.* | It said, "You already want to catch people's calves." |
| 13 | *Vãri kutaudzana imbwa dzakasvika.* | While they were talking, dogs arrived. |
| 14 | *Dzakadzingirira tsuro, panzvimbo yamagondo.* | They chased the Hare, instead of the Hyena. |
| 15 | *Tsuro kakatiza kachiti, handiniba ndimagondo.* | The Hare ran, saying, "It's not me — it's the Hyena!" |

**FSI's New Words** (Glossary tones beside them):

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *mhuru* | 9, 10 | calf, foal — *mhurú* |
| *-wova masiriri* | | to water at the mouth |
| *-taudzana* | | to converse (?) — Glossary "to converse" |

From the Glossary: *-sangana* "to join, meet one another", *-tsvaka* "to look for, seek", *nzvimbo* "place", *shamwari* "friend", *-dzinga* "to drive off" (Unit 42) — *-dzingirira* is it with the applicative doubled, "chase after".

**What is in it.** *kundotsvaka* is Stage 2's *-ndo-* "go and …" in the infinitive. *tingaenda* "could we go" is Stage 2's *-nga-*. *Kutiuchizogona* is *kuti* + the *-chi-* form, FSI's "if" (*Kuti uchida* "If you wish", Unit 23). *ngatiende* is the hortative, "let's go" (a lesson to come). *ibasaredu* is *i-* + *basa redu*, Stage 4's independent form: "it is our work". *Magondo vakati ndadini* — Stage 1's *-dini*, "what have I done?", with the Hyena now in respect plural. *panzvimbo ya-* "in the place of" is "instead of". *handiniba* is *handini* "it is not I" with Stage 5's negative enclitic *-ba*. *ndimagondo* "it is the Hyena" is Stage 3's *ndi-*.

**Practice.** FSI's steps with your speaking partner for lines 1–15. Then act lines 1–12 as a dialogue, you the Hare, they the Hyena, with the tones you marked; swap.
The hyena in the anthill:
FSI Unit 46, lines 16–28 — the dogs, the owners, and the end of the Hyena. Glosses ours, from FSI's words.

| | Version A | Our gloss |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 16 | *Ndanyangadza here kutaurira magondo?* | "Have I done wrong to tell on the Hyena?" (*-nyangadza*: no FSI gloss) |
| 17 | *Imbwa hadzina kufunga izvozvo.* | The dogs didn't think of that. |
| 18 | *Dzaida nyama yatsuro chete.* | They wanted only the Hare's meat. |
| 19 | *Tsuro kakati mutsa unouraisa vakomana.* | The Hare said, "*Mutsa* gets you killed, boys." |
| 20 | *Magondo wakasara ãkahwanda, achifunga kutindapona.* | The Hyena stayed behind, hidden, thinking, "I've escaped." |
| 21 | *Varidzi vemhuru vakateera imbwadzavo.* | The owners of the calves followed their dogs. |
| 22 | *Vakaona magondo ãri muchidzere.* | They saw the Hyena in a small anthill. |
| 23 | *Vakamukomba, akati hu-mwi! nditsuro wanga ãva kubata mhuru.* | They surrounded him; he said, "*Hu-mwi!* It's the Hare who was about to catch the calves." |
| 24 | *Varume vakamugarira vakamuuraya.* | The men set upon him and killed him. |
| 25 | *Tsuro kakaona kuti kaa kubatwa.* | The Hare saw that it was about to be caught. |
| 26 | *Kakapindamuguru kakahwanda.* | It went into a *guru* (a hole) and hid. |
| 27 | *Kakati tichauraiswa magondo wemwoyo.* | It said, "We'll get killed by greedy hyenas." (Version B: *navana magondo wemwoyo*) |
| 28 | *Tsuro kakati handichazoteerizve mapenzi.* | The Hare said, "I'll never again follow fools." |

**FSI's New Words:**

| Word | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *-pona* | | to escape, recover — *-póná* |
| *chidzere* | 7, 8 | small ant hill (Glossary "anthill") |
| *hu* | | (ideoph.) |
| *mwi* | | (ideoph.) |
| *mutsa* | | "(ideoph. from /-mutsa/?)" — FSI is unsure |
| *-hwanda* | | to hide, be hidden — *-hwándá* |
| *benzi* | 5; *mapenzi* 6 | fool |

From the Glossary: *-komba* "to surround" (Unit 40), *-tevera* "to follow" (Unit 42; the text's *-teera* is the same word), *-uraya* "to kill". *muguru* and *-garira* are not glossed; read them from the questions — *Kakahwanda muguru here?* "Did it hide in the *guru*?" — and ask your partner.

**What is in it.** *mutsa* is FSI's puzzle; the Questions treat it as something one has or lacks — *Kaiwa nemutsa here?* "Was it [being] with *mutsa*?", *Ngenyi magondo akange asina mutsa?* "Why had the Hyena no *mutsa*?" — so your partner's meaning is the one to take. *kutindapona* is *kuti* + *ndapona*: "thinking (that) 'I have escaped'" — the direct-only reported speech of Stage 2. *wanga ãva kubata* "who was about to catch" and *kaa kubatwa* "it was about to be caught" have lessons of their own. *-uraisa* "get killed" is *-uraya* + causative, *-uraiswa* its passive. *wemwoyo* "of heart" is "greedy", the *ngemwoyo* of Unit 44.

**Ideophones.** *Hu-mwi!* and Unit 44's *gorokoto* are ideophones: sound-pictures FSI does not translate. FSI Unit 38 (Stage 9) on the "ideophonic form of the verb": it "seems always to occur after either the infinitive or some other form of the special verb /-ti/" — and so here: *akati hu-mwi*, *ikati gorokoto*. *-ti* "say" introduces sounds as well as words.

**Practice.** Have your speaking partner retell all of Unit 46 (FSI's step 6), then retell it yourself (step 7). Ask them for two ideophones they use and the *-ti* sentence each goes in.
Let's go, tie me: the subjunctive in the:
The texts use the **subjunctive** constantly — for "let's", for "that it may", and after verbs of wanting and needing. FSI Unit 30 (Stage 7), Note 1: "Subjunctives differ from other forms in two ways: (1) the subject prefix … may stand immediately before the root … There is no prefix syllable associated with the subjunctive. (2) The final vowel in all dialects is /-e/. Another characteristic of subjunctives is that the subject prefix has high tone regardless of person." "Subjunctives may have aspect prefixes (/-mbo-, -zo-/ etc.) and/or object prefixes but no tense prefixes." Note 2, the hortative: "the hortative consists simply of an initial prefix /nga-/ plus the subjunctive", "ordinarily translated into English with 'let's'".

**Let's** — the hortative:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Kutiuchizogona kutiza **ngatiende**.* (46) | If you can run, **let's go**. |

**A command with an object** — the subjunctive with an object prefix:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Diro … rakati **ndisunge**.* (45) | Diro said, "**Tie me**." |
| *tsuro **ndisunge**!* (45) | "Hare, **tie me**!" |

**After *kuti* "that", with wanting and needing:**

| | Our gloss |
| --- | --- |
| *Hurumende irikukarirwa kuti **ienzane** muzvinhu zvose.* (48) | The government is hoped to **be** fair in all things. |
| *Tiri kukarira vazhinji kuti **vabatsire**.* (48) | We are hoping that many **will help**. |
| *… nzira yekuti fundo **iwe** nyore …* (48) | … a way for education **to be** easy … |
| *Zviri mumaziso ehutongi kuti **huve** maererano nenyika.* (48) | It is for the government to see that it **be** in keeping with the country. |
| *Nyika dzose dzinoda kuti vanhu vadzo **vafunde** mabasa ose.* (48) | All countries want their people **to learn** all kinds of work. |
| *Zvakatora nguva huru kuti iyi hosha **irapwe**.* (49) | It took a long time for this disease **to be cured**. |
| *Zvakafanirazve kuti vanhu **vapfeke** …* (49) | It is right too that people **wear** … |
| *Izvi zvinoreva kuti **muziwane** parudzi.* (49) | This means that you **know one another** by clan. |

***-pfeke*, *-funde*, *-rapwe*** show the *-e*; ***iwe*, *huve*** are the subjunctive of *-va* "be, become" (in FSI's Manyika *w*); *irapwe* is a passive subjunctive.

**The negative subjunctive** has ***-sa-***:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Zvinorewazve kuti rudzi **rusaroorane**.* (49) | It also means that a clan **should not marry** among itself. |

*ru-sa-roor-an-e*: subject prefix, *-sa-* "not", *-roora* "marry", reciprocal *-an-* (FSI Unit 29), final *-e*.

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, say what you want others to do, each with *kuti* + subjunctive: *Ndinoda kuti mudzidze …*, *Zvakafanira kuti tiende …*; then a "let's" for each: *Ngatiende*, *Ngatidye*. Have them mark the subjunctive's high subject prefix as you say it.
Saying, thinking, running: -chi- in a st:
The other participle of these texts is the ***-chi-*** form of FSI Unit 23 (Stage 6), Note 2: "A form of this kind, here called the 'chi-participial', never serves as the main verb in a sentence. … In chi-participial forms, the subject prefix is always low in tone, whether for first, second, or third person, and the Class 1 prefix is /a-/ even in those dialects for which the Class 1 subject prefix in indicative forms is /u-/." With *kuti* or *kana* it is "if"; in a story it is "while, as, …ing".

**In the stories:**

| | Our gloss |
| --- | --- |
| *Tsoko **ichitizawo** kukwira mugomo.* (44) | The monkey, **running too**, climbed into the hills. |
| *Rakadaidzira **richiti**, tsuro ndisunge!* (45) | He shouted, **saying**, "Hare, tie me!" |
| *Tsuro kakatiza **kachiti**, handiniba ndimagondo.* (46) | The Hare ran, **saying**, "It's not me!" |
| *Magondo wakasara akahwanda, **achifunga** kutindapona.* (46) | The Hyena stayed hidden, **thinking** "I've escaped." |
| ***Kutiuchizogona** kutiza ngatiende.* (46) | **If you'll be able** to run, let's go. |

***-chiti* "saying"** is the participle of *-ti*, the story-teller's quotation mark: *richiti*, *kachiti*, *achiti* (Unit 45 Questions: *Ndiani wakadaidzira achiti, 'Tsuro ndisunge'?* "Who called out, saying …?").

**After *Ngenyi* "why?".** FSI Unit 24 (Stage 6) taught "the chi-participial form in 'why' questions", and the Questions of these units ask *ngenyi* with it almost every time:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Ngenyi vanhu **vachirima** nzungu?* (44) | Why do people grow groundnuts? |
| *Ngenyi **dzichitonhora**?* (47) | Why are they cold? |
| *Ngenyi **vachisangana** pamwe?* (49) | Why do they meet together? |
| *Ngenyi **vachipika** neshiri?* (49) | Why do they vow by a bird? |
| *Ngenyi **zvichitumirwa**?* (49) | Why are they sent? |

And with *kuti* "when": *Kuti vanhu **vachikwazisana** vanotaura mutupo* (49) "When people **greet one another** they say the totem."

**Practice.** Tell your speaking partner what you did this morning, every second verb a *-chi-* form: *Ndakamuka ndichifunga …, ndakadya ndichiverenga …* Then ask them five *Ngenyi …?* questions with *-chi-* about their week.
Had been, had already: -kange and -nga:
*Vakange ãsina demo*, *Kakange kãkwana*, *wanga ãva kubata* — a short helper verb, then a participle. FSI Unit 36 (Stage 8), on "Verb phrases in which the first word contains the stem /-nga/": "The special stem /-nga/ (or /-nge/) takes any of the prefixes that are found with ordinary verb stems, except for object prefixes. The tense of the /-nga/ form fixes the general time of the whole verb phrase. The verb that follows /-nga/ is always in one of the participial forms … The tense of the verb that follows /-nga/ sets the action of the verb with relation to the general time that was established by the tense of the /-nga/ form." FSI's example: on Tuesday *Vasvika* "They have arrived"; on Wednesday *Vakange vasvika* "They had arrived"; on Monday *Vanozonge vasvika* "They will have arrived". And: *Izvo tasvika, vanga vatovamba kudya* "When we arrived, they had already begun to eat."

**In these texts:**

| *-nga* form | + participle | Our gloss |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *vakange* | *ãsina demo* (44) | he **had** no axe |
| *Kakange* | *kãkwana nenyota* (45) | it **had had** enough of thirst |
| *wanga* | *ãva kubata mhuru* (46) | who **was** now about to catch the calves |

**In the Questions,** where FSI asks about the past state of things:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| *Tsoko yakange ine mwoyo here?* (44) | Had the monkey [been] greedy? |
| *Yakange iri kudini?* (44) | What had it been doing? |
| *Mudende mwakange munenyi?* (44) | What had there been in the gourd? |
| *Tsime rakange rapera here kucherwa?* (45) | Had the well been finished being dug? |
| *Patsime pakange pachirindwa here?* (45) | Had the well been [being] guarded? |
| *Magondo wakange ahwanda muchidzere here?* (46) | Had the Hyena hidden in the anthill? |
| *Diro wakange aripi?* (45) | Where had Diro been? |

Two halves, every time: *-kange*/*-nga* sets the time — before then — and the second verb says what was so: *-ne*, *-ri*, *-sina*, the past of today (*rapera*, *ahwanda*), or *-chi-* (*pachirindwa*).

**Practice.** Tell your speaking partner what had happened before you arrived somewhere today — *Ndasvika, vakange vapedza kudya* — and what had not: *vakange vasina kuuya*. Then ask them FSI's *-kange* questions on Unit 44.
Already, now: -a-, -aa- and -ava:
A small family of forms in these texts means "now, already, by now", built on *-va* "be, become". FSI Unit 25 (Stage 6) taught the uses of "the hodiernal tense of the verb /-va/"; here are the forms as the texts use them.

**SP + *-va*, *-ava*, *-ave* "has now become, is now":**

| | Our gloss |
| --- | --- |
| *Vadzimai vazhinji kwazvo **vava** nhengo dzemisono.* (49) | Very many women **are now** members of the women's clubs. |
| *Mazuva ano vanhu vazhinji **vave** kurapwa.* (49) | These days many people **are now** being treated. |
| *Nyasaland **yawa** patyo pekuita zvese izvi.* (48) | Nyasaland **has come** near to doing all this. |
| *Southern Rhodesia **yawa ne**manyuko akasimba emagetsi …* (47) | Southern Rhodesia **has come to have** a strong source of electricity … |
| *wanga **ãva** kubata mhuru* (46) | who was **now** about to catch the calves |

*yawa ne-* is "has become with" — "has got, now has".

**SP + *-aa-* / *-aaku-* "already (doing), is now about to":**

| | Our gloss |
| --- | --- |
| *Kakati, **waa** kuda kubata mhuru dzevanhu.* (46) | It said, "You **are already** wanting to catch people's calves." |
| *Tsuro kakaona kuti **kaa** kubatwa.* (46) | The Hare saw that it **was about** to be caught. |
| *Zuva **rãakunyura** …* (45) | When the sun **was setting** … |
| *Ine nzvimbo **dzaakugadzira** masabasita.* (47) | It has places **already producing** asbestos. |

*waa*, *kaa* we read as *wava*, *kava* with the *v* of *-va* dropped, as FSI's Manyika speakers write it (our reading); *raakunyura* and *dzaakugadzira* run *-aa-* together with the infinitive *ku-*. FSI gives no note on these in Units 44–49; take the tones from your partner.

**Practice.** Tell your speaking partner what has now changed in your life — *Ndava kugara …*, *Ndava kudzidza chiShona* — and what is about to happen: *Ndaa kuenda*, *Zuva raakunyura*. Ask them to say each in the standard form.
Then, so, afterwards: how the stories jo:
A story is held together by small words and by one tense. Here are both, as Units 44–46 use them.

**One past after another: *-ka-* … *-ka-*.** Stage 2's *-ka-* past, repeated, makes "and then": *Tsuro kakatora tambo **kaka**risunga* "The Hare took a rope **and** tied him." So *Vakabatana vakaenda*, *Varume vakamugarira vakamuuraya*, *kakachera mvura kakaenda*. In *rakasunungurwa **rika**tizira* (45) the second verb has *ri-ka-*, not *ra-ka-*: FSI Unit 38 (Stage 9) names it "the dependent tense that contains /-ka-/" — the "and then" of a story.

**-bva + participle "then, there and then":** *Nzungu nedende zvakabva zvãsarapo* (44) "The groundnuts and gourd were then left there"; in the Questions, *Wakabva afa here?* (46) "Did he then die?"

**The joining words:**

| Word | Gloss | In the text |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *asi* | but | *Yakada kuburitsa nzungu, asi ruoko rwakarambira.* (44) |
| *ndizvo* | and so, that's how | *Ndizvo rakapiwa uchi.* (45) |
| *mumasure* | afterwards | *Mumasure kakachera mvura kakaenda.* (45) |
| *kuti* | that; if; when | *kakanzwa … kuti tsime rakapera* (45); *Kutiuchizogona …* (46); *Kuti vanhu vachikwazisana …* (49) |
| *ngekuti* | because | *Vakarumwa ngekuti …* (44) |
| *izvo* | when (in the Questions) | *Izvo tsuro kakasvika …* (45, Questions 14) — "When the Hare arrived …" |
| *zve nazve* | again and again | (44) |
| *rimwe gore*, *rimwe zuva* | one year, one day | (45; Questions 12) |
| *zuva raakunyura* | at sunset | (45) |
| *panzvimbo ya-* | instead of | (46) |
| *chete* | only; just | *Dzaida nyama yatsuro chete.* (46) |

***Izvo* "when"** is FSI's usage (Unit 36: *Izvo tasvika, vanga vatovamba kudya* "When we arrived, they had already begun to eat").

**Practice.** Tell your speaking partner a story of your own day in a chain of *-ka-* verbs — *Ndakamuka, ndikageza, ndikadya …* — with *asi*, *ndizvo* and *mumasure* where they fit, and let them correct the *-ka-* forms that follow the first.

From the Glossary: *mucheni* "machine" (the text also spells it *muchina*); *mafuta* "fat, oil"; *sipo* "soap"; *gwere* (*magwere*) "maize"; *muchero* "fruit"; *chipfuyo* "livestock"; *-kudza* "to grow (trans.)"; *-kura* "to grow (intrans.)"; *-sandisa* "to cause to work, use"; *tii* "tea"; *nyore* "easy"; *-tevera* "to follow"; *mberi* "front, ahead".

**What is in it.** ***kudai*** "such as" opens a list: *kudai ndi Wankie*, *kudai ngepa Kwekwe*, *zvakadai ngemafuta*, and in Part II *akadai ndi Mutare* — it is *-dai* "be like this" (FSI Unit 37), with *ndi-* or *nge-* "it is" before the example. ***mu-* + infinitive**, "in doing": *mukugadzira* "in making", *mukukudza* "in growing". ***-kura* / *-kudza***: grow (by itself) and grow (something), the causative pair. *zvinobuda nezvinouya* "things going out and things coming in" is the essay's "exports and imports". *-fambira mberi* "walk forward" is "progress".

**Practice.** Tell your speaking partner what your own country has, grows and makes, sentence by sentence on FSI's model — *Nyika yedu ine …*, *Kune zvirimwa zvizhinji kudai ne …* — and answer FSI's own questions: *Nyika yenyu ineupfuto here? Migodhi yenyi iri muno?*
Bounded by rivers: north, south, east an:

| 8 | *Iri kutsvaka nzira yekuti fundo iwenyoro kumunhu vose.* | It is looking for a way to make learning easy for everyone. |

From the Glossary: *hurumende* (*huruménde*) "government"; *patyo* "near"; *fundo* — not glossed, but *-funda* "read, study" is the verb of line 16 and the Questions; *pepa* "(news)paper"; *nhau* "topic, news"; *-sanduka* "to change"; *-tsva* "new"; *pfungwa* (*pfungwá*) "thought, idea"; *maziso* "eyes".

**What is in it.** ***-ri ku-* everywhere**: *irikukarirwa*, *dziri kutarisira*, *Tirikunangisira*, *arikutaura*, *hurikusanduka* — Stage 3's "is …ing", the newspaper's present. ***Mapepa nhau*** "newspapers" is two words, *pepa* + *nhau*, "papers of news". *utongi* and *hutongi* are one word (class 14, *u-* or *hu-*, as Stage 1's table says). *mazuva ano* "these days".

From the Glossary: *-sangana* "to join, meet one another" — *musangano* (Stage 9) "meeting"; *mhepo* "wind" (here "the air"); *-chisa* "to iron (clothing)"; *-sona* "to sew"; *-chengeta* "to take care (of)"; *-geza* — the Glossary prints "to work", a slip: Stage 5's *Tinógěza nhumbí* is "We wash clothes".

Each and every: rimwe narimwe:
Unit 48 and Unit 49 say "each, every" the same way: ***~mwe* "one" + *na* + *~mwe***, the concord of the noun on both halves — "one and one".

| | Our gloss |
| --- | --- |
| *pazuva **rimwe narimwe*** (48) | on **each and every** day — *zuva*, class 5 |
| *muchikwata **chimwe nachimwe*** (49) | in **each** group — *chikwata*, class 7 |
| *Rudzi **rumwe narumwe** runopika nezita remhuka.* (49) | **Each** clan vows by the name of an animal — *rudzi*, class 11 |

So for any class: *munhu **mumwe nemumwe*** (1), *imba **imwe neimwe*** (9) — make them with your partner, as the vowel of *na* blends.

**The same *~mwe* alone is "some, other, one"** — FSI Unit 39 (Stage 9), "The stem /-mwe/ 'some, other'":

| | Our gloss |
| --- | --- |
| ***Rimwe** gore mvura yakaramba kunaya.* (45) | **One** year the rain refused to fall. |
| ***Dzimwe** dzakaita basa kwemazuva matatu.* (45) | **The others** worked for three days. |
| ***Mamwe** anodindwa … **Mamwe** anonzi 'week end edition.'* (48) | **Some** are printed … **Some** are called … |
| ***Dzimwe** nzvimbo dzayo dzinotonhora **dzimwe** dzinopisa.* (47) | **Some** of its places are cold, **others** hot. |
| *… ichava **imwe** yenyika dzirikufambira mberi.* (47) | … will be **one** of the countries going forward. |
| *… kunoenda mumiriri **umwe** …* (49) | … goes **one** representative … |
| *… nekutumira **zvimwe** zvidzidzo.* (49) | … and sending **some** lessons. |

Before the noun, *~mwe* is "some, one (of many)"; *dzimwe … dzimwe* is "some … others". And **doubling** a verb stem, as in *yakasiyanasiyana* (49) "various, of every kind", is the same idea of "each one different".

**Practice.** Say "every …" to your speaking partner for ten nouns of different classes, building *~mwe na~mwe* yourself, and have them correct the concords. Then describe your town with *dzimwe … dzimwe*: *Dzimwe dzimba hombe, dzimwe diki.*

**What is in it.** *iri hosha inobatira* "is a disease that spreads": *-ri* "be" + noun + relative. *Zvakatora nguva huru* "it took a long time" uses class 8 *zv-* with no noun, "things, it" in general, as Stage 5's *Zvínónaka*. *-pfeka* puts on clothes; *-fuka* covers the body with a blanket or wrap — both together are "dress warmly".

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, give advice for a cold or a cough in this text's pattern — *Zvakafanira kuti …*, *Munofanira kupfeka …*, *Musadya …* — and then answer FSI's questions: *Kune hosha dzinobatira here munyika menyu? Inokasika kurapwa senyi?*
Totems: mitupo:

**What is in it.** Three reciprocals in *-an-* (FSI Unit 29, Stage 7): *muziwane* "that you know one another", *rusaroorane* and *rwaroorana* "marry one another", *vachikwazisana* "greeting one another" (*-kwazisa* "greet"; the Glossary's *kwaziwai* is a greeting). *Rudzi rwaroorana* "a clan that has intermarried" is a relative of the past of today, made by tone; *rwagura mutemo* "has broken the law". *maShona* "the Shona people", class 6 of a people's name. *Kuti … vachikwazisana* "when … greeting" is *kuti* + *-chi-*. *mutupo vababa* — *va-* the possessive of respect for *baba*, "the father's".

**The culture strand.** The plan names totems as part of the culture the language lives in; this short text is FSI's whole account. Ask your partner the rest.

**Practice.** Ask your speaking partner FSI's questions — *Ndivanaani vane mutupo? Marudzi enyu ane mitupo here? Munozivana senyi kuti ihama? Munyika mwenyu vanhu vanokwazisana senyi?* — and, if they have one, their *mutupo* and how it is used when greeting.
Here? Who? Why? FSI's four questions:
FSI's step 5 is "Answer and ask questions about the text", and every sentence of every text has **four** questions, always in the same order. Unit 44, sentence 1 (*Tsoko yakaona dende rinenzungu*):

| | FSI | Our gloss | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | *Tsoko yakaona dende rine nzungu here?* | Did the monkey see a gourd with groundnuts? | *Hongu, yakaona.* |
| 2 | *Yakaona dende rine nyimo here?* | Did it see a gourd with Bambara groundnuts (*nyimo*)? | *Kwete, haina kuona dende rine nyimo.* |
| 3 | *Ndiani wakaona dende rine nzungu?* | Who saw a gourd with groundnuts? | *Tsoko.* |
| 4 | *Tsoko yakaonenyi?* | What did the monkey see? | *Dende rine nzungu.* |

**The pattern:** (1) a *here?* question the text answers **yes**; (2) a *here?* question with one thing changed, answered **no** — with the past negative of Stage 4 or the *-no-* negative of Stage 3; (3) a ***Ndiani*** "who?" question; (4) a "what, where, how, why" question — *-nyi*, *-pi*, *senyi* "how?", *ngenyi* "why?".

**More from the units:**

| Unit | Question | Our gloss |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 44 | *Ngenyi yakapinza ruoko rwayo mudende?* | Why did it put its hand in the gourd? |
| 44 | *Ruoko rwakaita senyi?* | What did the hand do? (lit. how did it do?) |
| 44 | *Murume wakarumwa papi?* | Where was the man bitten? |
| 45 | *Ndiani wakashatirwa?* | Who was angry? |
| 45 | *Kakataurirenyi kudaro?* | Why did it say so? (*-taurira* + *-nyi*) |
| 46 | *Magondo natsuro wakasonganepi?* | Where did the Hyena and the Hare meet? |
| 46 | *Ndiani vakaona mhuru?* | Who saw the calves? |
| 47 | *Rwizinyi rwakaganura kumusoro?* | Which river bounds it to the north? |
| 48 | *Anodindwa kwenguwanyi?* | How often are they printed? |
| 49 | *Musangano mukuru unoitwa kangani pagore?* | How many times a year is the big meeting held? |

***-nyi* on a noun is "which?"**: *Rwizinyi?* "which river?", *Micheninyi?* "which machines?", *Ihoshanyi?* "which disease is it?" — Stage 3's *-nyi*, with Stage 4's independent *i-*. And ***-pi*, *-nyi* on the verb** change its *-a* to *-e*, as Stage 2 taught: *wakasonganepi?*, *Kakataurirenyi?*.

**After the four, the unit's own questions** turn to your country: *Munopfuya tsoko here munyika menyu?* (44) "Do you keep monkeys in your country?"; *Mune mhuka dzakawanda zvakadini?* (45) "How many animals are there?"; *Kunyika kwenyu kunotonhora senyi?* (46) "How cold is it in your country?"

**Practice.** For one text a week, have your speaking partner ask you FSI's four questions on each sentence, answering in full sentences; then you ask them the four on a sentence of your choosing. End with the unit's questions about your own country.

The end of Stage 10, and of FSI's basic course: three tales, three essays, three short notices — and with them the tilde participles, *-sina* and *-sika-*, *nge-*, the passive, class 12's *ka-*, the subjunctive and *nga-*, *-chi-*, *-kange*, *-ava* and *-aa-*, the joining words, *kudai*, *~mwe na~mwe*, and FSI's four questions.

**Practice.** With your speaking partner, this week:
