**Then.** FSI's basic course ends here; its Glossary follows. The curriculum moves on to reading — the Shona Bible and the proverbs, *tsumo* — with the same partner and the same habit FSI set these last units for: tone it together, read it clean, ask about it, tell it back.
Let there be light: the Shona Bible:
Stage 11 leaves the course book. FSI's forty-nine units are done; from here the reading is a real book, and the first real book is one you already know in English.

**The text.** The Shona here is **Biblica® Bhaibheri Dzvene Rakasununguka MuChiShona Chanhasi** — in English, the *Open Shona Contemporary Bible* — copyright © 2005, 2018 Biblica, Inc. It is published under the **Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0** licence (CC BY-SA), which is why a lesson may quote it verse by verse: anything built from it must name Biblica and carry the same licence. The English beside it is the **Berean Standard Bible** (BSB), which is public domain. Both were taken from eBible.org's files, one verse to a line.

The title is a first reading lesson. *Bhaibheri* is "Bible" and *Dzvene* "holy" (the word is in *zita rake dzvene*, "His holy name", Ps 103:1). *Rakasununguka* stands where the English has "Open", and *MuChiShona Chanhasi* where it has "Contemporary" — "in the Shona of today", *chiShona* with the *chi-* of languages, like FSI's *chi-ngezi* "English (language)". Those last two glosses are read off the English title, not from FSI.

**It is untoned.** Like all ordinary Shona print, Biblica marks no tone. Everything the course taught you about high and low has to be brought to the page by you, and checked by your speaking partner. Where a word is in FSI's glossary these lessons give FSI's toned form beside it, read from the glossary's page images; where it is not — and most of the Bible's vocabulary is not, since FSI taught village and market Shona in 1965 — the lesson says so and the tone is your partner's to give.

**It is not FSI's voice.** FSI recorded two Manyika speakers, an eastern voice. Biblica is written standard Shona, the central standard this curriculum teaches. Differences you will meet from the first chapter:

- The past prefixes are the standard ones Stage 1 settled on: *akasika* "he created", *akati* "he said" — the central *a-*, not FSI's eastern *w-*.
- The linking vowel before an infinitive is **o**: *zuva rokutanga* "the first day", where FSI writes *rọkutángá* (Stage 5's ordinals) and marks that vowel as one that differs by dialect. Biblica is consistent about it: *nokuti* "because" is in the text more than three thousand times, *nekuti* never.
- Words FSI glosses one way, Biblica uses another: FSI's *dénga* (5, plural *matenga*) is "roof, sky"; here *matenga* are "the heavens". Each lesson flags these as they come.

**Where the Psalms are concerned,** both texts number them the Hebrew way. An Orthodox Psalter follows the Septuagint, one lower for most of the book: the lessons give both, so Psalm 51 is "Psalm 51 (50)".

**The passage** — the first five verses of Genesis (Biblica: *Genesisi*):

| v. | Biblica (Shona) | BSB (English) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Pakutanga Mwari akasika matenga nenyika. | In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. |
| 2 | Zvino nyika yakanga isina kugadzirwa uye isina chinhu, rima rakanga riri pamusoro pemvura yakadzika, uye Mweya waMwari wakanga uchigara pamusoro pemvura. | Now the earth was formless and void, and darkness was over the surface of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters. |
| 3 | Uye Mwari akati, “Chiedza ngachivepo,” chiedza chikavapo. | And God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. |
| 4 | Mwari akaona kuti chiedza chakanga chakanaka, uye akaparadzanisa chiedza nerima. | And God saw that the light was good, and He separated the light from the darkness. |
| 5 | Mwari akatumidza chiedza kuti “masikati,” uye rima akaritumidza kuti “usiku.” Uye madekwana akavapo, namangwanani akavapo, zuva rokutanga. | God called the light “day,” and the darkness He called “night.” And there was evening, and there was morning—the first day. |

**Words and forms.**

- ***Pakutanga*** "in the beginning": Stage 5's place prefix *pa-* (16) on the infinitive of FSI's ***-tángá*** "to do first" — "at the doing-first". You met the same verb in *rọkutángá* "first" (Stage 5, *The first sign, the second town: ordinals*).
- ***Mwari*** "God" is not in FSI's glossary; the gloss is the BSB's. It takes the plural of respect (Stage 1): *Mwari akaona* … but *Baba vedu* in the next lesson.
- ***akasika*** "created" — the *-ka-* tense (Stage 2, *The -ka- tense: yesterday or before*), the tense of narrative. Genesis is told in it: *akati*, *akaona*, *akaparadzanisa*, *akatumidza*.
- ***matenga nenyika*** "the heavens and the earth": *na* "and" (Stage 4, *And, with: na*) fused with *nyika*, FSI's *nyìka* (9, 10) "land".
- ***Chiedza ngachivepo*** "let there be light": the **hortative**, *nga-* + subject prefix + subjunctive (FSI Unit 30, Stage 7). FSI: "the hortative consists simply of an initial prefix *nga-* plus the subjunctive", the subjunctive ending in *-e* — so FSI's ***-vá*** "to be, become" gives *-ve*, and Stage 5's *-po* "there" closes it: *chi-* (agreeing with *chiedza*, class 7) + *ve* + *po*.
- ***chiedza chikavapo*** "and there was light": the same verb, now with *-ka-* after a subject prefix that has no *-a-* — the shape of FSI's dependent tense with *-ka-* (Unit 38). FSI gives that tense the sense "if, when"; here it carries the story on, "and so it was". That second sense is read from the BSB, not from FSI.
- ***chakanga chakanaka*** "was good": Stage 3's relative verb, *-naka* "become good" (FSI), with *chakanga* "it had been" before it.
- ***masikati*** — Stage 1's midday greeting — is here simply "day", and ***mangwanani*** "morning" is the morning greeting. ***usiku*** "night" is FSI's *usíkú* (14). ***madekwana*** "evening" is not in FSI (its evening is *manheru*); BSB gloss.
- ***rima*** "darkness" (5) is a different word from FSI's *-rima* "to plough". Ask your partner to say both.

Tones in this lesson are FSI's, read from its glossary pages: *á* high, unmarked low, a grave (*ì*) a lowered syllable, a dot under a letter a sound some speakers leave out. The Bible text itself carries no tone; your speaking partner supplies it.

**Practice.** Read the five verses aloud to your speaking partner, slowly, then at speaking pace. Let them correct every tone you miss — the page gives you none, so expect many. Then read verse 3 alone until you can say it without looking, and pray it in the morning as the light comes.
Our Father: Baba vedu:
The Lord's Prayer from Matthew (Biblica: *Mateo*), the prayer said at every service and before every meal. Biblica, like the BSB, ends at "the evil one": the doxology the priest sings — "For thine is the kingdom" — is not in these verses.

| v. | Biblica (Shona) | BSB (English) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 9 | “Zvino aya ndiwo manyengeterero amunofanira kuita: “ ‘Baba vedu vari kudenga, zita renyu ngarikudzwe, | So then, this is how you should pray: ‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. |
| 10 | umambo hwenyu ngahuuye, kuda kwenyu ngakuitwe panyika sezvinoitwa kudenga. | Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. |
| 11 | Tipei nhasi chingwa chedu chamazuva namazuva. | Give us this day our daily bread. |
| 12 | Tiregererei zvatinokutadzirai, sezvatinoregererawo vanotitadzira isu. | And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. |
| 13 | Musatitungamirira mukuedzwa, uye mutinunure kubva kuno wakaipa.’ | And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’ |

**Words and forms.**

- ***Baba vedu vari kudenga*** "our Father in heaven": FSI's *babá* (1a) "father", which FSI notes "is often used with plural concords as mark of respect" — hence *vedu* (*~édú* "our", Stage 2, *My, your, his: possessives*) and *vari*, not *wedu*, *ari*. *vari kudenga* is *-ri* "be" (Stage 3, *-ri: am, is, are*) with *ku-* (17, Stage 5) on *denga*, FSI's *dénga* "roof, sky" — "who are at heaven".
- ***zita renyu ngarikudzwe*** "hallowed be Your name": *zita* is FSI's *zítá* (5, 6) "name", so its concord is *ri-*: *renyu* "your (pl. of respect)", and *ngarikudzwe*, the hortative (FSI Unit 30) of a passive (FSI Unit 23, Stage 6, *-w-*) of FSI's ***-kúdzá*** "to grow (trans.), cause to grow, exalt": "let it be exalted".
- ***umambo hwenyu ngahuuye*** "Your kingdom come": *umambo* is class 14 (*hu-*); *nga-hu-uy-e*, hortative of FSI's *-úyá* "to come".
- ***kuda kwenyu ngakuitwe*** "Your will be done": the infinitive *kuda* (FSI's *-dá* "to want, like, love, need") used as a noun, class 15, so *kwenyu*, *ngakuitwe*. ***sezvinoitwa kudenga*** "as it is done in heaven": *se-* "as" + a relative (Stage 3).
- ***Tipei nhasi chingwa chedu chamazuva namazuva*** "give us this day our daily bread": a plural command with an object prefix (Stage 4, *Commands*; *Me, you, him, them: object prefixes*), *ti-* "us" + FSI's *-pá* "give" + *-i* of the plural; *nhasi* (FSI *nhási*); FSI's *chi-ngwa* (7, 8) "bread"; *chamazuva namazuva* "of days and days", the linking prefix of Stage 5.
- ***Tiregererei zvatinokutadzirai*** "forgive us what we sin against you": *-regerera* "forgive" is not in FSI (BSB gloss). *zvatinokutadzirai* is a relative, "the things we …", with *-ku-* … *-i*, the object "you" in its plural of respect; its *-ir-* is the applicative (FSI Unit 21, Stage 6), "sin *against*".
- ***sezvatinoregererawo vanotitadzira isu*** — Stage 5's *-wo* "too": "as we also forgive those who sin against us".
- ***Musatitungamirira mukuedzwa*** "lead us not into temptation": the negative command, *musa-* + verb (FSI Unit 32: "the final vowel in negative commands may be *-a* … or *-e*, depending on the dialect"; Biblica has *-a*), with FSI's ***-túngámíra*** "to lead". *mukuedzwa* is *mu-* (18) + the passive infinitive of FSI's *-edza* "to try, attempt": "in being tried".
- ***mutinunure kubva kuno wakaipa*** "deliver us from the evil one": a subjunctive (FSI Unit 30) after the command, then Stage 2's *-bva* "from".

Tones in this lesson are FSI's, read from its glossary pages: *á* high, unmarked low, a grave (*ì*) a lowered syllable, a dot under a letter a sound some speakers leave out. The Bible text itself carries no tone; your speaking partner supplies it.

**Practice.** Say it with your speaking partner line by line, they first and you after, until the tones are theirs and not English ones. Then pray it in Shona morning and evening this week, aloud, and once at table before you eat.
God, have mercy on me: the publican:
The parable read on the Sunday that opens the Triodion, and the words of the publican that the Jesus Prayer grows from. Luke is *Ruka* in Biblica.

| v. | Biblica (Shona) | BSB (English) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 9 | Jesu akataura mufananidzo uyu, kuna vamwe vakanga vachivimba nokururama kwavo uye vaizvidza vamwe akati, | To some who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt, He also told this parable: |
| 10 | “Varume vaviri vakakwira kutemberi kundonyengetera, mumwe akanga ari muFarisi uye mumwe ari muteresi. | “Two men went up to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. |
| 11 | MuFarisi akasimuka akazvinyengeterera achiti, ‘Mwari, ndinokuvongai nokuti handina kufanana navamwe vanhu, makororo, vaiti vezvakaipa, mhombwe, kana kunyange muteresi uyu. | The Pharisee stood by himself and prayed, ‘God, I thank You that I am not like the other men—swindlers, evildoers, adulterers—or even like this tax collector. |
| 12 | Ndinozvinyima zvokudya kaviri pavhiki uye ndinopa chegumi chezvose zvandinowana.’ | I fast twice a week and pay tithes of all that I acquire.’ |
| 13 | “Asi muteresi akamira ari nechokure, asingadi kunyange kutarira kudenga, asi akazvirova chipfuva akati, ‘Mwari, ndinzwirei tsitsi, ini mutadzi.’ | But the tax collector stood at a distance, unwilling even to lift up his eyes to heaven. Instead, he beat his breast and said, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner!’ |
| 14 | “Ndinokuudzai kuti munhu uyu, akadzokera kumba kwake aruramiswa pamberi paMwari kupinda muFarisi. Nokuti mumwe nomumwe anozvikudza achaninipiswa, uye uyo anozvininipisa achakudzwa.” | I tell you, this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” |

**Words and forms.**

- ***Mwari, ndinzwirei tsitsi, ini mutadzi.*** "God, have mercy on me, a sinner." Take it apart: *ndi-* "me" (Stage 4 object prefixes) + *-nzwira* + *-ei*, the plural command of respect. *-nzwira* is FSI's ***-nzwá*** "to hear, feel, perceive, understand" with the applicative *-ir-* (FSI Unit 21, Stage 6): "feel *for*". *tsitsi* "mercy" is the BSB's gloss. So: "feel mercy for me". *ini* "I" is Stage 2's pronoun; ***mutadzi*** "sinner" is an agentive noun (FSI Unit 32), *mu-* + a verb *-tadza* + *-i*, "one who sins".
- ***vakakwira kutemberi kundonyengetera*** "went up to the temple to pray": FSI's ***-kwírá*** "to climb", and Stage 2's *-ndo-* "go and do". *-nyengetera* "pray" is the BSB's gloss; you will meet it every day from now on.
- ***MuFarisi akasimuka akazvinyengeterera achiti*** "the Pharisee stood and prayed by himself, saying": FSI's ***-símúká*** "to stand up"; *-zvi-*, the reflexive (FSI Unit 22, Stage 6), "himself"; and ***achiti***, the *-chi-* participial (FSI Unit 23, Stage 6) of *-ti* "say" — "saying". FSI: the participial "never serves as the main verb in a sentence", and its subject prefix is always low.

**Words and forms.**

- ***vafudzi*** "shepherds", an agentive noun (FSI Unit 32), ***vachichengeta makwai avo usiku*** "keeping watch over their flocks by night": the *-chi-* participial of FSI's ***-chengeta*** "to take care (of)", and FSI's *usíkú* "night".
- ***Mutumwa waShe akazviratidza kwavari*** "an angel of the Lord stood before them", word for word "showed himself": the reflexive *-zvi-* (FSI Unit 22, Stage 6). ***kubwinya kwaJehovha*** "the glory of the Lord". FSI's word for glory is *mbiri* "renown, glory"; Biblica's is *kubwinya*.
- ***vakatya kwazvo*** "they were terrified": FSI's *kwázvo* "very much, indeed" (Stage 3).
- ***"Musatya. Ndauya nenhau dzakanaka dzomufaro mukuru uchava wavanhu vose."*** "Do not be afraid! I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people." *Musatya*, the plural negative command; *ndauya*, past of today; *nhau* "news" (10, so *dzakanaka*); *mufaro* "joy", the noun of FSI's *-fárá*.
- ***Nhasi muguta raDhavhidhi mazvarwa Muponesi; ndiye Kristu Ishe.*** "Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you. He is Christ the Lord!" *mazvarwa* is *ma-* "you (pl.)" + the passive of *-zvara* "give birth": "you have had born for you". ***ndiye*** is Stage 3's *ndi-* with the class 1 pronoun (*ndini · ndiwe · ndiye*).
- ***pamwe chete*** "together": FSI's *pámwé* "together" (class 16 with *~mwé* "one") + *chéte* "only".
- ***"Mwari ngaarumbidzwe kumusoro-soro, uye rugare panyika nokuvanhu vaanofarira."*** "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men on whom His favor rests!" *ngaarumbidzwe* is the hortative of a passive, "let God be praised"; *kumusoro-soro*, doubled for "the very highest". The second half has no verb (Stage 5).
- ***vafudzi vakataurirana vachiti, "Handei kuBheterehema tindoona …"*** "the shepherds said to one another, 'Let us go to Bethlehem and see …'": *-taurirana* is FSI's *-taura* "to speak" with the applicative *-ir-* and the reciprocal *-an-* (FSI Unit 29): "speak to one another". *Handei* "let us go" (BSB), then *tindoona*, a subjunctive with *-ndo-*.
- ***Asi Maria akachengeta zvinhu zvose izvi akazvifungisisa mumwoyo make.*** "But Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart." FSI's *-chengeta* "take care of" — she kept them; *-fungisisa* is FSI's *-funga* "to think" made intensive (my analysis): "thought hard about them". *mumwoyo make*: class 18 *mu-*, and *make* "her" in class 18 to match.

- ***Pakutanga pakanga pane Shoko*** "in the beginning was the Word": Lesson 1's *Pakutanga*, then Stage 5's *pane* "there is" — a place as subject (class 16) — in the past, *pakanga pane* "there was". ***Shoko*** "word" (5) is the singular of FSI's *masoko* (6) "news"; FSI's other word, *inzwí* (5, 6) "word, voice", is not used here.
- ***Shoko rakanga riri kuna Mwari … rakanga riri Mwari*** "the Word was with God … the Word was God": *rakanga riri*, *-ri* "be" after *-kanga* "had been" — "was being". *kuna* "with, at" before a person.
- ***Iye aiva kuna Mwari*** "He was with God": *aiva* is Stage 3's *-i-* tense of FSI's *-vá* "to be, become" (*The -i- tense: used to, and would like*), Biblica's ordinary "was".
- ***Zvinhu zvose zvakaitwa kubudikidza naye*** "through Him all things were made": a passive, and *kubudikidza* "through", from FSI's *-budikidza* "to come or go through". ***kunze kwake*** "without Him", from FSI's *kunzé* (17) "outside".
- ***Maari maiva noupenyu*** "in Him was life": *maari*, class 18 "in him"; *maiva* "there was (in it)".
- ***Chiedza chinovhenekera murima, asi rima harina kuchikunda.*** "The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it." Stage 4's past negative (*harina ku-*), with the class 7 object prefix *-chi-* (Stage 4, *Me, you, him, them: object prefixes*) standing for *chiedza*.
- ***Pakanga pano murume akatumwa*** "there came a man who was sent": FSI's *-túmá*, passive. ***zita rake rainzi Johani*** "his name was John": "his name used to be called".
- ***chiedza chiya*** "that Light": the demonstrative stem *-ya* "that (which we spoke of)", FSI Unit 38 (*Waona mukomana uya here?* "have you seen that boy we were talking about?").
- ***nyika haina kumuziva*** "the world did not recognize Him": FSI's *nyìka* "land" is "the world", with *-mu-* "him" and FSI's *-zívá*.
- ***vokwake havana kumugamuchira*** "His own did not receive Him": Biblica's *-gamuchira* "receive" is not FSI's, which has *-gashira* "to receive [from someone's hand]" and *-támbírá* "to receive" (Stage 4). Learn Biblica's; know FSI's.
- ***akavapa simba rokuti vave vana vaMwari*** "He gave the right to become children of God": *vave*, the subjunctive (FSI Unit 30) of *-va*.
- ***vana vasina kuberekwa neropa*** "children born not of blood": *vasina ku-*, the negative participial with *-na* (Lesson 11) before an infinitive — "not having been born".
- ***Shoko rakava nyama uye rakagara pakati pedu.*** "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us." FSI's ***nyama*** (9) is "meat"; here "flesh". FSI's *-gara* "reside"; FSI's ***pakatí*** (16) "between" — *pakati pedu* "among us".
- ***kwaIye Mumwe Oga*** "of the one and only Son": FSI's *~mwé* "one" + *~ọ́gá* "alone" — "the One Alone", the Only-begotten. ***azere nenyasha uye nechokwadi*** "full of grace and truth": FSI's *chókwadí* "truth" (Stage 4).

- ***Ida Ishe Mwari wako nomwoyo wako wose*** "Love the Lord your God with all your heart": a singular command of FSI's *-dá* "love". It is a one-syllable verb (Stage 2, *One-syllable verbs*), so its command takes an *i-*. ***Ida muvakidzani wako sokuda kwaunozviita iwe*** "love your neighbour as you love yourself".
- ***"Wapindura zvakanaka. Ita izvozvo ugorarama."*** "You have answered correctly. Do this and you will live." - ***"Muvakidzani wangu ndianiko?"*** "Who is my neighbor?": *ndiani* "it is who?" — Stage 3's *ndi-* + FSI's *aní* "who?".
- ***Vakamubvisa nguo dzake, vakamurova ndokuenda zvavo, vachimusiya oda kufa.*** "They stripped him, beat him, and went away, leaving him half dead." FSI's *-bvìsa* "remove", *-róvá* "beat", *-síyá* "leave behind"; ***oda kufa*** "about to die" is Stage 4's *-o-* form (*About to: the -o- form, and beginning*).
- ***muSamaria, aiva parwendo*** "a Samaritan on a journey": FSI's *rwendo* (11) "trip, journey".
- ***akaadira mafuta newaini*** "pouring on oil and wine": FSI's ***mafútá*** (6) "fat, oil". ***akamukwidza pambongoro yake*** "put him on his own animal": the causative of *-kwírá*, "made him climb onto"; ***akamuendesa kuimba yavaeni*** "brought him to an inn" — Lesson 12's inn; ***akamuchengeta*** "took care of him", FSI's *-chengeta*.
- ***Akatora mari yesirivha*** "took out two denarii": FSI's *-tórá*, *marí* "money"; Biblica says "silver money" where the BSB names the coin.
- ***"Ndianiko pavanhu vatatu ava …?"*** "Which of these three …?": FSI's *~tatú* "three" with the class 2 prefix.
- ***"Enda unoita saizvozvo."*** "Go and do likewise."

- ***Pakanga pano mumwe murume akanga ane vanakomana vake vaviri.*** "There was a man who had two sons." *pakanga pano* "there was here", a place as subject with FSI's *pánó* "here" (Stage 5); *ane* "who had" (Stage 4 *-ne*); *vaviri* "two", FSI's *~viri* with class 2.

- ***Mazuva mashoma asati apera*** "after a few days", word for word "before a few days had ended": FSI's *~shoma* "few, little" (Stage 4) and *-pérá*; *asati* "not yet, before".
- ***akaunganidza zvose zvaakanga anazvo*** "got everything together": FSI's ***-úngánídza*** "to collect (transitive)"; *zvaakanga anazvo* "what he had", the *-na* + *-zvo* of Stage 5's *na* with the class pronouns.
- ***kunyika iri kure*** "to a distant country": FSI's *kure* "far away" after the relative *iri*.
- ***Shure kwokunge apedza zvose*** "after he had spent all he had": FSI's *-pédzá* "to finish". ***akatanga kushayiwa*** "began to be in need": FSI's *-tángá* "do first" with an infinitive is "begin", and *kushayiwa* is the passive of FSI's *-shaya* "to lack".
- ***akandozvitsvakira basa*** "went and hired himself out", word for word "went and sought work for himself": *-ndo-*, the reflexive, and the applicative on FSI's *-tsvaka* "to seek" — three of the verb's slots at once.
- ***kuminda yake*** "into his fields": FSI's *munda* (3, 4) "field".
- ***Akati apengenuka mupfungwa dzake*** "finally he came to his senses": *mupfungwa* "in his thoughts", FSI's ***pfungwá*** (9, 10) "thought, idea".
- ***Ndichasimuka ndiende kuna baba vangu ndinoti kwavari: Baba, ndakatadzira denga napamberi penyuwo.*** "I will get up and go back to my father and say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.'" The *-cha-* tense, then a subjunctive *ndiende* to follow it, then Lesson 2's *-tadzira* "sin against". *penyuwo* ends in Stage 5's *-wo*.
- ***Handichafaniri kunzi mwanakomana wenyu*** "I am no longer worthy to be called your son": the negative of the *-cha-* tense is "no longer" — Stage 2's "still", negated — on FSI's *-fánírá* "be suitable".
- ***akati achiri kure*** "while he was still in the distance": Lesson 12's *-chiri*. ***vakamhanyira kumwanakomana wavo*** "he ran to his son": FSI's ***-mhányá*** "to run" with *-ir-*, "ran *to*".
- ***Kurumidzai! Uyai nenguo dzakaisvonaka mumupfekedze.*** "Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him." *Uyai na-* "come with" is "bring"; *mumupfekedze* is FSI's ***-pfekedza*** "to cause to put on (clothing)", in a subjunctive with *-mu-* "him".
- ***Muise mhete pamunwe wake*** "put a ring on his finger": FSI's *-isa* and *munwe* (3, 4) "finger".
- ***Muuye nemhuru yakakodzwa muibaye. Ngatidyei tipembere.*** "Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let us feast and celebrate." FSI's *mhuru* "calf", FSI's *-baya* "to kill". ***Ngatidyei tipembere*** is FSI Unit 30's own pattern — "a hortative form … may be followed by one or more subjunctive verbs", and FSI's example is *Ngatidye*, "Let's eat". Biblica adds the plural *-i*.
- ***akanga afa, zvino araramazve; akanga arasika, zvino awanikwa*** "was dead and is alive again! He was lost and is found!": *araramazve* with Stage 4's *-zve*; *arasika*, FSI's *-rásá* "to lose" with the neuter *-ik-* — "become lost"; *awanikwa*, a passive of *-wana* "find".

Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known. |

**"If I": the dependent tense with *-ka-*.** ***Kunyange ndikataura nendimi*** "if I speak in the tongues", ***Kana ndikagovera zvose*** "if I give all I possess": FSI Unit 38 — "*ndikaenda* if I go … but: *ndakaenda* I went". The subject prefix has no *-a-*, and FSI says the tones of *-ka-* and of the subject prefix are low "regardless of the person". *Kunyange* is "even if", *kana* "if" (Stage 2).

**"Not having love."** ***asi ndisina rudo*** "but have not love": the negative participial with *-na* of Lesson 11 (FSI Unit 28), first person. ***handisi chinhu*** "I am nothing" — "I am not a thing". ***hazvindibatsiri chinhu*** "I gain nothing", word for word "it does not help me at all": the negative of the *-no-* tense (Stage 3) of FSI's *-bátsírá* "to help".

**What love is and does.** *Rudo* is class 11, so every verb begins *ru-*:

- ***Rudo runo mwoyo murefu, rudo runo mwoyo munyoro.*** "Love is patient, love is kind": "love has a long heart … a soft heart". *runo* is Biblica's form of "has" beside *rune* in verse 7 — both appear; FSI teaches *-ne*. FSI's *~refú* "long".
- ***Haruna godo, haruna manyawi haruzvikudzi*** "it does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud": *haruna* "it has no"; *haruzvikudzi*, the negative with the reflexive — "it does not exalt itself".
- ***harutsvaki zvarwo*** "it is not self-seeking", "it does not seek its own": FSI's *-tsvaka*.
- ***Runodzivirira nguva dzose, runovimba nguva dzose, rune tariro nguva dzose, runotsungirira nguva dzose.*** "It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things." FSI glosses *-dzivirira* "to prevent"; Biblica uses it for "bear, shelter". *nguva dzose* four times: Stage 5's "all the time".
- ***Rudo harutongoperi.*** "Love never fails": *-tongo-* "never at all" inside the negative of FSI's *-pérá* "come to an end".

**When I was a child: the *-i-* tense.** ***Pandaiva mwana ndaitaura somwana, ndaifunga somwana, ndairangarira somwana.*** "When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child." Stage 3's *-i-* tense, *The -i- tense: used to, and would like*: *ndaitaura* "I used to speak". *Pandaiva* "when I was", *pa-* + a relative.

**Face to face.** ***tichaonana chiso nechiso*** "we shall see face to face": FSI's *-óná* with the reciprocal *-an-* (FSI Unit 29) — "we shall see one another".

**The end.** ***Uye zvinhu zvitatu izvi ndizvo zvinogara, zvinoti kutenda, tariro norudo. Asi chikuru pakati peizvi ndirwo rudo.*** "And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love." *ndizvo*, *ndirwo*: Stage 3's *Concords with ndi-*, class 8 and class 11. *chikuru* "the great thing" is FSI's *~kúrú* with class 7.

The BSB's "exult in the surrender of my body" (v. 3) follows a different Greek reading from Biblica's *kuti upiswe* "to be burned". Read the Shona as it stands.

- ***Varindi*** "the guards", the agentive of FSI's *-rinda* "to protect, stand guard".

**Words and forms.**

- ***mikova yakazarirwa*** "the doors locked": *mikova* (4) "doors", where FSI's door is *musúwo* (3), plural *misíwo*. Biblica has both words: *musiwo* in Mt 6:6.
- ***"Rugare ngaruve kwamuri!"*** "Peace be with you!": the hortative of FSI's *-vá* "be", agreeing with *rugare* (11), and *kwamuri* "to you (pl.)". The words the priest says to the people at every service are this greeting.
- ***akavaratidza maoko ake naparutivi pake*** "He showed them His hands and His side": *maoko*, the plural of FSI's *ruókó* (11, 6) "hand, arm"; FSI's *rutivi* (11) "side".
- ***"Sezvo Baba vakandituma, ndiri kukutumaiwo."*** "As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you." FSI's *-túmá* twice: *vakandituma* "sent me"; *ndiri kukutumai* "I am sending you", *-ri* + infinitive with *-ku-* … *-i*; and *-wo* "also".
- ***"Gamuchirai Mweya Mutsvene."*** "Receive the Holy Spirit." Lesson 14's *-gamuchira*, as a command.
- ***Kana muchiregerera ani zvake zvivi zvake, zvicharegererwa; kana musingavaregereri, havaregererwi.*** "If you forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven; if you withhold forgiveness from anyone, it is withheld." *kana* + the *-chi-* participial (Lesson 5); then its negative, *musinga-* … *-i* (FSI Unit 28, negative participials of the *-no-* tense); and the passive.
- ***mumwe wavane gumi navaviri*** "one of the Twelve": FSI's *gúmí* "ten" and *~viri* "two", "those who are ten and two".
- ***"Taona Ishe!"*** "We have seen the Lord!": the past of today. ***handingatendi*** "I will never believe": the negative of the *-nga-* tense (Stage 2, *The -nga- tense: can, may, would like*), "I could not believe".
- ***"Isa munwe wako pano; ona maoko angu. Tambanudza ruoko rwako uise parutivi rwangu. Rega kukahadzika uye utende."*** "Put your finger here and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting and believe." Singular commands: FSI's *-isa* "put", *-óná* "see"; then a subjunctive *uise*. ***Rega kukahadzika*** "stop doubting" is FSI's *-rega* "to desist, leave off" + infinitive — Lesson 7's other way of saying "don't".
- ***"Ishe wangu naMwari wangu!"*** "My Lord and my God!" — Stage 2's possessives, and *na* "and" before a name.
- ***vakaropafadzwa avo vasina kuona asi vakatenda*** "blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed": the Beatitudes' *vakaropafadzwa*, and *vasina ku-*, "who have not …" (Lesson 14).
- ***kuti mugotenda … uye kuti kana mukatenda muve noupenyu muzita rake*** "so that you may believe … and that by believing you may have life in His name": *mukatenda* is Lesson 19's dependent *-ka-*, "if you believe"; *muve*, a subjunctive.

Tones in this lesson are FSI's, read from its glossary pages: *á* high, unmarked low, a grave (*ì*) a lowered syllable, a dot under a letter a sound some speakers leave out. The Bible text itself carries no tone; your speaking partner supplies it.

**Practice.** Read the passage with your speaking partner, they Jesus and you Thomas and the disciples. On Thomas Sunday, say verse 28 when the Gospel reaches it; and answer the priest's "Peace be unto all" this week, in your head, with *Rugare ngaruve kwamuri*.

**Words and forms.**

- ***varume vaviri vakanga vachienda kumusha wainzi Emausi*** "two of them were going to a village called Emmaus": *vakanga vachienda* "were going", *-kanga* + the participial; FSI's *mushá* (3, 4) "village, home". Biblica measures the way as *makiromita anenge gumi nerimwe* "about eleven kilometres"; the BSB has "about seven miles".
- ***Vakanga vachitaurirana*** "they were talking with each other": Lesson 13's reciprocal. ***zvakanga zvaitika*** "that had happened": *-itika*, the neuter of *-ita*.
- ***Jesu pachake akabva asvika uye akafamba navo*** "Jesus Himself came up and walked along with them": *pachake* "himself"; *akafamba navo* "walked with them" — FSI's *-fámbírá* "to visit" and *-fámbísá* "to cause to go" are built on this *-famba*.
- ***asi meso avo akabatwa zvokuti havana kumuziva*** "but their eyes were kept from recognizing Him": the passive of FSI's *-bátá* "seize" — "their eyes were held" — and the past negative.
- ***"Muri kukurukurirana pamusoro peiko, zvamuri kufamba kudai?"*** "What are you discussing so intently as you walk along?" *muri ku-* "you are …-ing"; *peiko* "about what?" — *pamusoro pe-* "about" + Biblica's *-i* "what" + *-ko*. ***Vakamira vakanyarara*** "they stood still": FSI's *-mírá* "stand" and ***-nyárárá*** "to become or be quiet".
- ***"Ndiwe woga mushanyi muJerusarema asingazivi …?"*** "Are You the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know …?": *ndiwe* "it is you" (Stage 3, *ndini · ndiwe · ndiye*); *woga* "alone", FSI's *~ọ́gá*; *asingazivi*, a negative relative of FSI's *-zívá*. The question ends in FSI's *here* (Stage 2).
- ***"Zveiko?"*** "What things?" — the same *-i* + *-ko*, on *zv-* (8).
- ***Aiva muprofita, aiva nesimba mushoko napamabasa*** "This man was a prophet, powerful in speech and action": *aiva*, the *-i-* tense; *simba* "power", the noun beside FSI's *-simba* "to become strong".
- ***Vaprista vakuru navatongi vedu vakamuendesa kuti andotongerwa rufu*** "Our chief priests and rulers delivered Him up to the sentence of death": *vatongi* (Lesson 11); *andotongerwa* is FSI's *-tóngá* "to judge" with *-ndo-*, the applicative and the passive.
- ***isu takanga tichitarisira kuti ndiye akanga achizodzikinura vaIsraeri*** "we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel": FSI's ***-tàrisira*** "to expect"; *-zo-* in the participial; *-dzikinura* "redeem" from Psalm 103:4.
- ***ratova zuva rechitatu kubvira pazvakaitika*** "it is the third day since these things took place": Stage 5's ordinal *rechitatu*, agreeing with *zuva* (5).
- ***Vaenda kuguva nhasi mambakwedza*** "They were at the tomb early this morning": FSI's *nhási* "today" and *mambákwedzá* "dawn".

**Words and forms.**

- ***"Haiwa imi vokusanzwisisa, uye vane mwoyo inononoka kutenda"*** "O foolish ones, how slow are your hearts to believe": *vokusanzwisisa* "of not understanding" — the linking prefix on an infinitive with *-sa-* "not" and an intensive of FSI's *-nzwá* "hear … understand"; *mwoyo inononoka*, the plural *mwoyo* (4) with FSI's *-nonoka* "to be late" (Lesson 8).
- ***"Ko, Kristu akanga asingafaniri kutambudzika …?"*** "Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer …?": FSI's *-fánírá*, negative; *-tambudzika* (Lesson 10). ***agozopinda mukubwinya kwake here?*** "and then to enter His glory?": *-go-* and *-zo-*, FSI's *-pinda*, and the question *here*.
- ***akavatsanangurira zvakanyorwa pamusoro pake mumagwaro*** "He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself": the passive of FSI's *-nyórá* "to write".
- ***Jesu akaita sokunge oda kupfuurira*** "He seemed to be going farther": Stage 4's *-o-* form again, *oda* "about to", and FSI's ***-pfúúrá*** "to pass".
- ***"Garai nesu, nokuti kwava kudoka; zuva rava kuvira."*** "Stay with us, for it is nearly evening and the day is almost over." FSI's *-gara* "stay" as a plural command; *nesu* "with us" (Stage 5); *kwava* … *rava* "it is now …". *zuva rava kuvira* is "the sun is going down": FSI's *-vira* means "to boil (intransitive)", and FSI's sunset verb is *-nyúrá* — Biblica's *-vira* here is a different verb that sounds the same. Have your partner say both.
- ***Akati agara navo patafura, akatora chingwa, akavonga, akachimedura akatanga kuvapa.*** "While He was reclining at the table with them, He took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to them." The words of every Liturgy: took, gave thanks, broke, gave. FSI's *táfura* "table" (Stage 5); *-tórá* "take"; *-vonga* "give thanks" (Lesson 3's *ndinokuvongai*); *akachimedura*, with *-chi-* standing for *chingwa* (7); *akatanga kuvapa* "began to give them", FSI's *-tángá* + *-pá*. Four *-ka-* verbs, one after another — the way Shona tells a story.
- ***Ipapo meso avo akasvinudzwa vakamuziva, akabva anyangarika pamberi pavo.*** "Then their eyes were opened and they recognized Jesus — and He disappeared from their sight." A passive; and *akabva* + another verb, "then straightaway".
- ***"Ko, mwoyo yedu yanga isingapisi neiko mukati medu …?"*** "Were not our hearts burning within us …?": a negative participial of FSI's *-písá* "to burn, be hot", and *mukati medu* "within us" (class 18).
- ***achitizarurira magwaro*** "and opened the Scriptures to us": Psalm 51:15's *-zarura* "open" with the applicative.
- ***"Ichokwadi! Ishe amuka uye azviratidza kuna Simoni."*** "The Lord has indeed risen and has appeared to Simon!" ***Ichokwadi*** "it is true!" is Stage 4's independent form of FSI's *chókwadí* "truth" — "it is truth". *azviratidza*, the reflexive "has shown himself".
- ***vakaziva sei Jesu paakamedura chingwa*** "how they had recognized Jesus in the breaking of the bread": *sei* "how" once more.

Stage 11 in conversation:
The end of Stage 11: twenty-three passages, from the Lord's Prayer to Emmaus, every one a text you pray or hear in church. The grammar of the whole FSI course came back in them — the tenses of Stage 2, *-ri* and the relatives of Stage 3, commands and object prefixes from Stage 4, the place classes, *-wo* and *~ose* of Stage 5 — and beside them the forms of FSI's later units that the Bible leans on hardest: the hortative *nga-* and the subjunctive, the passive *-w-*, the applicative *-ir-*, the reflexive *-zvi-*, the reciprocal *-an-*, the neuter *-ik-*, the *-chi-* participial, negative relatives with *-si-*, and the dependent *-ka-* of "if I …".

**What to carry away.** Biblica is the standard you are learning, untoned and in its own spelling: *-o-* in *nokuti* and *rokutanga*; *sei* for FSI's *senyi*; *meso*, *chiso*, *mikova*, *-gamuchira*, *-teerera*, *-udza* beside FSI's *mésó*, *usú*, *musúwo*, *-gashira*, *-tèrera*, *-údzírá*. And words FSI glosses one way and the Bible another: *denga* "sky" and "heaven", *nyama* "meat" and "flesh", *mhandara* "girl" and "virgin", *chando* "cold" and "snow". When the two differ, Biblica is the standard and FSI the 1965 eastern voice, and your speaking partner decides.

**Reading.** Two passages you have not read in these lessons. Read them aloud to your speaking partner first, without the English; say what you understand; then check against the BSB.

**With your speaking partner, this week:**

1. Pray the Lord's Prayer together in Shona, morning and evening, until neither of you needs the page.
2. Read one Gospel passage of this stage aloud each day, they listening only for tone; at the end of the week, read the one they corrected most again.
3. Retell a parable — the publican, the Samaritan, the prodigal — in your own Shona, in the *-ka-* tense, and let them ask you questions with *ndiani*, *sei* and *-i-ko*.
4. Greet each other as the Gospels do: *Kwaziwai*; *Rugare ngaruve kwamuri*. Ask your partner how a Shona Orthodox parish says "Christ is risen" and its answer, and learn it from them.
5. Choose one verse of the stage for the week, learn it by heart, and say it at the end of your evening prayers.

**Then.** Keep reading. The Gospel of the day in Shona, beside the English you already know, is the best long reading there is; read it aloud, and keep giving your partner its tones to correct.
What comes after the course:
Stage 12 has no end, as Japanese's last stage has none. FSI ends at Unit 49 and the Bible stage ends at Emmaus; Shona does not end anywhere.

**What there is no finishing line for.** Not "fluent", which is not a state. Not a word count. Not the last unit of a course, because FSI itself says its last units are texts to study "on his own initiative" — the course hands over to the learner before it stops.

**What there is instead: things you can do,** which accumulate:

- Greet and be greeted by anyone, at any hour, in the right form for their age and standing — the plural of respect without thinking about it.
- Follow two speakers talking to each other, not to you.
- Read a page of Shona prose — a newspaper, a chapter, a psalm — without stopping at every word.
- Hear the tone of a word you have only ever read, and know it from how it sounds.
- Tell a story: one of FSI's tales of the Hare, retold so that the listener laughs where they should.
- Pray in Shona, in your own words and not only the Lord's Prayer.

**Tone is the long one.** Biblica's text, the newspapers and almost everything written is untoned. From here the tone comes from listening and from your speaking partner, never from the page. That is the one thing that will keep improving for years, and that is how it should be.

**The deck past this point.** Cards keep coming from what you read and hear; five new a day is plenty when the words are rare. The reviews are the thing to keep.

**Practice.** Tell your speaking partner, in Shona, three things you want to be able to do in Shona in five years. Have them correct it, then write it down and keep it.
A Shona shelf, and Shona on the air:
A long target is more use than a level.

**Read.** The aim is volume: reading Shona every week, not reading hard Shona.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| The Shona Bible | Biblica's text, used in Stage 11, read straight through — one Gospel, then Acts, then the Psalms |
| A newspaper | *Kwayedza*, the weekly newspaper in Shona: short, current, and full of the vocabulary FSI's Unit 48 began on |
| Novels | *Feso* (Solomon Mutswairo, 1956), the first novel published in Shona, and whatever your speaking partner grew up reading |
| Your own notes | the sketchpad beside each card, written in Shona |

**Listen.** Radio Zimbabwe, the national station's Shona and Ndebele service, gives you speech at a natural speed, all day. Listen for the tone of words you already know before trying to follow everything.

**Speak.** Stages 1–11 named "your speaking partner" in every lesson. From here, add more voices: a parish, a family, a market — anyone who will talk to you in Shona and not switch to English.

**Track it.** Keep a list of what you have read and when. The second reading of a book a year later is a measure as well as a pleasure.

**Practice.** Choose the first three things to read and the first station or programme to listen to. Ask your speaking partner what they would put first, and start this week.
Keeping Shona, year on year:
How a language at this level is kept, lost and got back.

**What goes first: speaking.** A few months without conversation and the words are still there but will not come. Tone goes with it, because tone is kept by the ear and the mouth, not the page.

**What goes slowly: reading.** It is the sturdiest skill, and the one that holds a language together through a quiet stretch.

**What stays: the structure.** The noun classes and their concords, the verb and its extensions, the participials — learned once, they do not leave.

**A floor, not a target.** Twenty minutes of reading most days holds what you have. One real conversation a week keeps speaking and tone alive. Make the floor small enough to survive your worst week, because a routine that asks for an hour a day gets abandoned, and then nothing is done at all.

**Getting it back is quick.** A year away costs perhaps a month, mostly in speaking. The fear of losing it is worse than the loss.

**What keeps people going:** a reason that is not the language — a person, a parish, a place; something unfinished, the next book already chosen; and not stopping on a bad week.

**Practice.** Decide your floor — the least you will do in your worst week — and tell your speaking partner what it is, in Shona.
